Indeed, the terms of degrees zero and one in $Y$ are precisely the two terms removed on the left. Put $h=b-a$. The two root equations give

$$0=h\bigl(f'(a)+hH(a,h)\bigr).$$

The second factor reduces modulo $\mathfrak m$ to the nonzero residue of $f'(a)$, so is a unit of the local ring. Hence $h=0$. No monicity of $f$ or henselianity of $R$ is required. ∎

#### Lemma. Making a quasi-finite algebra finite étale locally

Let $S$ be a finite type $R$-algebra and let $\mathfrak p\subset R$. There are an étale map $R\to R'$ and a prime $\mathfrak p'$ above $\mathfrak p$, with canonical residue-field isomorphism $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\simeq\kappa(\mathfrak p')$, such that

$$S\otimes_RR'=A_1\times\cdots\times A_n\times B.$$

Every $A_i$ is finite over $R'$ and has exactly one prime above $\mathfrak p'$. The map $R'\to B$ is not quasi-finite at any prime above $\mathfrak p'$.

**Proof.** The fibre ring $F=S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is a finite type algebra over a field. It has finitely many isolated points: each such point is a zero-dimensional irreducible component, and a Noetherian spectrum has finitely many components. By the [isolated-fibre criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-isolated-point-fibre), these are exactly the quasi-finite points over $\mathfrak p$. Induct on their number.

If there are none, take $R'=R$, $\mathfrak p'=\mathfrak p$, $B=S$ and no $A_i$. Otherwise select one point and apply the [one-prime finite decomposition](#native-algebra-lemma-etale-makes-quasi-finite-finite-one-prime). Its complete geometric construction is *Étale neighbourhoods, henselization and quasi-finite morphisms*, Theorem 4.2. In the affine situation its proof descends an idempotent, and therefore supplies an actual product

$$S\otimes_RR_1=A_1\times B_1,$$

with $R_1/R$ étale, a marked prime $\mathfrak p_1$ of the same residue field, and $A_1$ finite with precisely the selected point in its marked fibre. The proof descends monic equations for finitely many algebra generators, so finite type suffices here even without finite presentation of $S$.

The marked fibre of $B_1$ has one fewer isolated point, since the base residue field has not changed and the selected fibre factor has been removed. Apply the induction hypothesis to $R_1\to B_1$. It produces an étale $R_1\to R_2$, a marked $\mathfrak p_2$ with unchanged residue field, and

$$B_1\otimes_{R_1}R_2=A_2\times\cdots\times A_n\times B.$$

Take $R'=R_2$ and $\mathfrak p'=\mathfrak p_2$. Composition preserves étaleness, and the composite residue map is still the canonical isomorphism from $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. Base change of the first product gives

$$S\otimes_RR_2=(A_1\otimes_{R_1}R_2)\times A_2\times\cdots\times A_n\times B.$$

The first factor remains finite. Its marked fibre is canonically $A_1\otimes_{R_1}\kappa(\mathfrak p_1)$, because $\kappa(\mathfrak p_1)\to\kappa(\mathfrak p_2)$ is an isomorphism. It therefore still has exactly one prime there. All other finite factors and the assertion about $B$ come from induction. Renaming the first factor proves every stated property. ∎

#### Lemma. Grothendieck's fibrewise nonzerodivisor criterion

Let $R\to S$ be a local map of local rings, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ in $R$. Suppose $S$ is flat and essentially of finite presentation over $R$. If multiplication by $f\in S$ is injective on $S/\mathfrak mS$, then multiplication by $f$ is injective on $S$, and $S/fS$ is flat over $R$.

**Proof.** Apply the [general fibrewise injectivity criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-mod-injective-general) to

$$u:S\longrightarrow S,\qquad s\longmapsto fs.$$

Its source and target are free of rank one, hence finitely presented over $S$; its target is $R$-flat by hypothesis; and its closed-fibre map is injective by the assumption on $f$. The essentially finite-presentation hypothesis on $S/R$ is exactly the remaining hypothesis of that criterion. It gives injectivity of $u$ and flatness of its cokernel, which is $S/fS$. ∎

#### Lemma. Finite flat modules over a local ring

Every finite flat module over a local ring is finite free. Here **finite** means finitely generated; finite presentation is not an additional hypothesis. Compare the [distinction between the two finiteness notions](#native-algebra-remark-warning).

**Proof.** Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be local and let $M$ be finite flat. Lift a basis of $M/\mathfrak mM$ to $x_1,\ldots,x_r\in M$. Nakayama makes them generators. If $r=0$, then $M=0$, which is free of rank zero.

The complete equational proof, including a matrix proof of independence, is *Tor and flat modules*, Theorems 5.1–5.2. The following induction proves the stronger independence assertion used here: any finite list in a flat module whose residues are linearly independent is itself linearly independent over $R$.

For one element $x\notin\mathfrak mM$ and a relation $ax=0$, the equational criterion gives a finite expression $x=\sum_j b_jy_j$ with $ab_j=0$ for every $j$. Some $b_j$ is outside $\mathfrak m$, since otherwise $x\in\mathfrak mM$. That coefficient is a unit, so $a=0$.

For the induction step, take a relation $\sum_{i=1}^n a_ix_i=0$ among a residue-independent list. The equational criterion supplies

$$x_i=\sum_j b_{ij}y_j,\qquad
\sum_i a_ib_{ij}=0\quad\text{for every }j.$$

Since $x_n\notin\mathfrak mM$, choose a column $j$ with $b_{nj}$ a unit. Put $c_i=b_{ij}/b_{nj}$ for $i<n$. The corresponding coefficient equation gives $a_n=-\sum_{i<n}c_i a_i$, so the original relation becomes

$$\sum_{i<n}a_i(x_i-c_ix_n)=0.$$

The $n-1$ displayed elements remain residue-independent: any linear relation between their residues would, on expansion, be a relation between the original $n$ independent residues, forcing all its first $n-1$ coefficients to vanish. Induction gives $a_1=\cdots=a_{n-1}=0$, and then the formula for $a_n$ gives $a_n=0$. Apply this to the generating list $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ to obtain a free basis. ∎

#### Lemma. Maps into a henselian local ring

Let $R\to S$ be a map with $S$ henselian local, and put $k_S=S/\mathfrak m_S$ and $\mathfrak p=R\cap\mathfrak m_S$. Suppose $A$ is an étale $R$-algebra, $\mathfrak q\subset A$ lies over $\mathfrak p$, and

$$\tau:\kappa(\mathfrak q)\longrightarrow k_S$$

is a $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-algebra map. There is exactly one $R$-algebra map $f:A\to S$ whose inverse image of $\mathfrak m_S$ is $\mathfrak q$ and whose residue-field map is $\tau$.

**Proof.** The complete general evaluation theorem is *Henselian local rings and henselization*, Theorem 1.2. We spell out the passage from the specified residue map to its section.

Define $\epsilon:A\to k_S$ by composing $A\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ with $\tau$. A field homomorphism is injective, so $\ker\epsilon=\mathfrak q$. Compatibility over $R$ makes the formula

$$\widetilde\epsilon:A\otimes_RS\longrightarrow k_S,
\qquad a\otimes s\longmapsto\epsilon(a)\bar s$$

well-defined. It is surjective, because its restriction to $1\otimes S$ is the residue map. Thus its kernel $\mathfrak q'$ is a prime above $\mathfrak m_S$ whose residue field is canonically $k_S$. The algebra $A\otimes_RS$ is étale over $S$. The section criterion gives a unique $S$-algebra map $\sigma:A\otimes_RS\to S$ through this marked prime. Its reduction is $\widetilde\epsilon$: the quotient by $\mathfrak q'$ is $k_S$, and an $S$-algebra map from that quotient to $k_S$ is its identity under the given identification.

Now set $f(a)=\sigma(a\otimes1)$. Its reduction is $\epsilon$, so its residue kernel is $\mathfrak q$. Localizing at $\mathfrak q$ extends this equality to the specified field map $\tau$, since every element outside $\mathfrak q$ has nonzero residue and hence maps to a unit of $S$.

Conversely, any map with the stated properties reduces to $\epsilon$ and defines the $S$-algebra retraction $a\otimes s\mapsto f(a)s$. Its reduction is $\widetilde\epsilon$, so its marked prime is $\mathfrak q'$. Uniqueness of $\sigma$ forces uniqueness of $f$. ∎

#### Lemma. Descent of Noetherianity

If $R\to S$ is faithfully flat and $S$ is Noetherian, then $R$ is Noetherian.

**Proof.** For an increasing chain $I_0\subseteq I_1\subseteq\cdots$ of ideals of $R$, the extended ideals $I_jS$ eventually agree because $S$ is Noetherian. Faithful flatness gives

$$I_j=\{r\in R:r\text{ maps into }I_jS\}.$$

Indeed, the [universal injection theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-faithfully-flat-universally-injective) applied to $R/I_j$ makes $R/I_j\to S/I_jS$ injective. Contracting the stationary extended chain therefore makes the original chain stationary. This is the ascending chain condition for $R$. ∎

#### Lemma. Flatness in a filtered ring colimit

Let $(R_i)$ be a directed system of rings with colimit $R$.

1. If an $R$-module $M$ is flat over every $R_i$, then it is flat over $R$.
2. More generally, suppose each $M_i$ is flat over $R_i$, and transition maps $M_i\to M_j$ are linear with respect to $R_i\to R_j$ and compose compatibly. Then $M=\operatorname{colim}_iM_i$, with its induced $R$-module structure, is flat over $R$.

**Proof.** Part (1) follows from (2) by taking the constant system of groups $M_i=M$ and identity transitions. For (2), use the [finitely generated ideal test](#native-algebra-lemma-flat). Let $I=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\subset R$. Represent these generators at one stage $R_i$ and, for $j\geq i$, let $I_j\subset R_j$ be the ideal their images generate.

The canonical map $\operatorname{colim}_{j\geq i}I_j\to I$ is an isomorphism. Surjectivity follows by representing the finitely many coefficients in an ideal expression at a common stage. If an element of some $I_j$ maps to zero in $R$, it becomes zero at a later ring stage, and hence in the corresponding later ideal. This proves injectivity without assuming injective transition maps.

There is also a canonical isomorphism

$$I\otimes_R M\simeq
\operatorname{colim}_{j\geq i}(I_j\otimes_{R_j}M_j).$$

For surjectivity, represent the finitely many entries of a tensor at a common stage. For injectivity, an equality of tensors follows from finitely many additivity and scalar-balancing relations. Represent all elements and scalars in those relations at one further stage; any equalities among their representatives hold after increasing the stage again. Thus the equality is already witnessed on the right.

Each multiplication map $I_j\otimes_{R_j}M_j\to M_j$ is injective by flatness. Their colimit remains injective: an element whose image becomes zero does so at a stage where that stage's multiplication map is injective, so its preimage becomes zero there. Under the displayed isomorphism, this is $I\otimes_RM\to M$. The ideal test proves flatness. ∎

#### Lemma. A strict henselization map extending a henselization map

Let $R\to S$ be a ring map, let $\mathfrak q\subset S$ lie over $\mathfrak p\subset R$, and suppose the canonical map of residue fields is an isomorphism. Write their common residue field as $k$ and choose $k^{\mathrm{sep}}$. With this choice on both sides, there is a canonical isomorphism

$$ (S_{\mathfrak q})^{sh}\simeq
(S_{\mathfrak q})^h\otimes_{(R_{\mathfrak p})^h}(R_{\mathfrak p})^{sh}.$$

**Proof.** Put $A=(R_{\mathfrak p})^h$ and $B=(S_{\mathfrak q})^h$. The universal property of ordinary henselization gives a local map $A\to B$ inducing the given identity on $k$. The complete ordinary and strict universal properties are *Henselian local rings and henselization*, Theorems 4.2 and 5.1.

For each finite subextension $k\subset L\subset k^{\mathrm{sep}}$, the [finite étale henselian equivalence](#native-algebra-lemma-henselian-cat-finite-etale) supplies a finite étale local $A$-algebra $A_L$ with specified residue field $L$. The same equivalence supplies the unique transition maps inducing inclusions of these subfields. These transitions are local because their residue maps are field embeddings. Each $A_L$ is henselian, as a finite local algebra over $A$.

The colimit $C=\operatorname{colim}_L A_L$ is local with residue field $k^{\mathrm{sep}}$: an element with nonzero residue is already a unit in its local stage, and the maximal ideals form the residue kernel. It is henselian. To lift a simple residue root of a monic polynomial, represent its finitely many coefficients and the root in one finite extension stage; field embeddings detect both the root equation and nonvanishing of its derivative there. Henselianity at that stage gives the lift.

Moreover, if $A\to T$ is a local map to a henselian local ring with a specified embedding $k^{\mathrm{sep}}\to\kappa(T)$, the [henselian evaluation theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-map-into-henselian) gives unique maps $A_L\to T$ with those residues. Uniqueness makes them compatible. They give the unique local map $C\to T$ inducing the embedding. Thus $C$ has the strict universal property and is canonically $A^{sh}$, which is also $(R_{\mathfrak p})^{sh}$ by the ordinary universal property.

Now $B_L=B\otimes_A A_L$ is finite étale over $B$ and

$$B_L/\mathfrak m_BB_L\simeq L.$$

Every maximal ideal of a finite $B$-algebra lies above $\mathfrak m_B$, so this field quotient shows $B_L$ is local. It is precisely the finite étale local $B$-algebra with marked residue $L$, by the henselian equivalence for $B$. These identifications respect transition maps, again by uniqueness on residues. Repeating the preceding colimit argument over $B$ gives

$$B^{sh}\simeq\operatorname{colim}_L B_L
\simeq B\otimes_A\operatorname{colim}_L A_L
\simeq B\otimes_A A^{sh}.$$

Ordinary henselization does not change the strict henselization with its chosen closure, so this is the asserted isomorphism. It is canonical relative to the residue identification and $k^{\mathrm{sep}}$ fixed in the statement. ∎

#### Lemma. Functoriality of strict henselization

Let $R\to S$ be a local map. Choose separable closures $k_R^{\mathrm{sep}}$ and $k_S^{\mathrm{sep}}$ of their residue fields, and an embedding

$$\phi:k_R^{\mathrm{sep}}\longrightarrow k_S^{\mathrm{sep}}$$

extending the induced residue-field map $k_R\to k_S$. There is a unique local homomorphism $R^{sh}\to S^{sh}$ extending $R\to S\to S^{sh}$ and inducing $\phi$ on residues.

**Proof.** Apply the strict universal property, Theorem 5.1, to the henselian local target $S^{sh}$ and the specified embedding $\phi$.

The filtered-evaluation description makes the maps explicit. For every pointed étale algebra $(E,\epsilon:E\to k_R^{\mathrm{sep}})$ defining $R^{sh}$, compose $\epsilon$ with $\phi$. The henselian evaluation theorem gives one map $E\to S^{sh}$ with that residue. These maps agree along all transitions by uniqueness, so induce $R^{sh}\to S^{sh}$. An element in the maximal ideal has zero residue and maps into the maximal ideal of $S^{sh}$, proving locality. Any competing local map inducing $\phi$ agrees at each stage and hence on the colimit. The residue embedding is part of the required data. ∎

#### Lemma. A finite cover by affine localizations

Let $R$ be a ring, let $M$ be an $R$-module and $S$ an $R$-algebra, and suppose $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ generate the unit ideal. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}R=\bigcup_iD(f_i)$. Then:

1. If $M_{f_i}=0$ for every $i$, then $M=0$.
2. If every $M_{f_i}$ is finite over $R_{f_i}$, then $M$ is finite over $R$.
3. If every $M_{f_i}$ is finitely presented over $R_{f_i}$, then $M$ is finitely presented over $R$.
4. A map $M\to N$ is an isomorphism if its localization at every $f_i$ is an isomorphism.
5. A complex $0\to M''\to M\to M'\to0$ is exact if all its localizations at the $f_i$ are exact.
6. If every $R_{f_i}$ is Noetherian, then $R$ is Noetherian.
7. Finite algebra generation on each member of the cover implies that $S$ is a finite type $R$-algebra.
8. If every $S_{f_i}$ is finitely presented over $R_{f_i}$, then $S$ is finitely presented over $R$.

**Proof.** The local detection and module gluing arguments, including the finite-kernel assertion used below, are proved in *Localization, local properties and support*, §5. We give all eight deductions.

For (1), fix $x\in M$. Since $x$ vanishes in each localization, some power $f_i^{a_i}$ kills $x$ for each $i$. The ideal generated by these powers is the unit ideal: any prime containing it would contain every $f_i$. A linear combination equal to one therefore kills $x$, so $x=0$. Alternatively, every prime lies in some $D(f_i)$; further localization makes every stalk of $M$ zero, and local detection gives the same conclusion.

For (2), choose finite lists of local generators and take their numerators in $M$. Let $M_0$ be the submodule generated by all these finitely many numerators. Inverting $f_i$ makes the discarded denominators units, so $(M/M_0)_{f_i}=0$ for every $i$. Part (1) gives $M=M_0$.

For (3), part (2) supplies a finite free surjection $R^r\to M$. Let $K$ be its kernel. Each $K_{f_i}$ is finite, since $M_{f_i}$ is finitely presented and localization preserves exactness. Here the finite-kernel assertion applies to any finite free surjection: compare it with one from a finite presentation by forming their pullback. The pullback splits over either free source, so the new kernel is a direct summand of a finite module. Part (2), now applied to $K$, makes it finite over $R$, proving finite presentation of $M$.

For (4), localization commutes with kernels and cokernels. The localized kernel and cokernel of the map vanish, and (1) makes both zero. For (5), the same reasoning applies to each homology module of the complex, including those at its endpoints.

For (6), take any ideal $I\subset R$. Its localization is an ideal of the Noetherian ring $R_{f_i}$, and hence is finite. Part (2) makes $I$ finite. Since every ideal is finitely generated, $R$ is Noetherian.

For (7), select numerators of algebra generators on each member of the cover and let $T\subset S$ be the $R$-subalgebra they generate. Their union is finite. Each $T_{f_i}\to S_{f_i}$ is onto. The quotient $S/T$ as an $R$-module therefore vanishes after every localization; by (1) it is zero. Thus $T=S$.

For (8), use (7) to choose a finite polynomial surjection $P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_r]\to S$, with kernel $J$. Each localized ideal $J_{f_i}$ is finitely generated because $S_{f_i}$ is finitely presented over $R_{f_i}$; this is the [finite-presentation permanence rule](#native-algebra-lemma-compose-finite-type) applied to this polynomial surjection. The elements $f_i$ generate the unit ideal also in $P$. Part (2), over the ring $P$, makes $J$ finite as a $P$-module. Its generators give the desired finite presentation. The empty cover can occur only for the zero ring, in which case every assertion is immediate. ∎

#### Lemma. The smooth locus under flat base change

Let $R\to S$ be finitely presented, let $R\to R'$ be flat, and put $S'=S\otimes_RR'$. If $U\subset\operatorname{Spec}S$ and $V\subset\operatorname{Spec}S'$ are the respective smooth loci, then $V$ is the inverse image of $U$.

**Proof.** Smoothness survives base change, so every point above $U$ belongs to $V$. For the converse, let $\mathfrak q'\in V$ contract to $\mathfrak q\subset S$. The local map

$$A=S_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow B=S'_{\mathfrak q'}$$

is flat and local, hence faithfully flat. The [flat base-change comparison for the naive cotangent complex](#native-algebra-lemma-change-base-nl), followed by localization, identifies the complex over $B$ with the base change of the one over $A$. Flatness commutes with its homology. Since the degree-one homology vanishes at the smooth point $\mathfrak q'$, faithful flatness makes it vanish at $\mathfrak q$.

Also $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SB\simeq\Omega_{S'/R'}\otimes_{S'}B$ is finite projective. The module $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_S A$ is finitely presented, since a finite algebra presentation gives a finite presentation of differentials. By [faithfully flat descent of finite projectivity](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-projective-descends), it is projective over $A$. These two conclusions are exactly the [smooth-point criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-smooth-at-point), so $\mathfrak q\in U$. ∎

#### Lemma. Support under base change

For a ring map $R\to R'$ and a finite $R$-module $M$, the support of $M\otimes_RR'$ is the inverse image of the support of $M$ under $\operatorname{Spec}R'\to\operatorname{Spec}R$.

**Proof.** Suppose $\mathfrak p'\subset R'$ lies over $\mathfrak p\subset R$. If $M_{\mathfrak p}=0$, then

$$ (M\otimes_RR')_{\mathfrak p'}
\simeq M_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_{R_{\mathfrak p}}R'_{\mathfrak p'}=0.$$

Conversely, if $M_{\mathfrak p}\ne0$, Nakayama for this finite local module gives $M\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\ne0$. Extending this nonzero vector space along the field embedding $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak p')$ keeps it nonzero. But that extension is

$$ (M\otimes_RR')\otimes_{R'}\kappa(\mathfrak p'),$$

the residue quotient of the localized module at $\mathfrak p'$. That localized module is therefore nonzero. The two implications prove the assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Finite presentation and formal smoothness over a Noetherian ring

Every smooth map $R\to S$ is obtained by base change from a smooth map $R_0\to S_0$, where $R_0\subset R$ is a subring of finite type over $\mathbb Z$:

$$S\simeq R\otimes_{R_0}S_0.$$

**Proof.** Write $P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ and $S=P/I$. The [formal-smoothness criterion](#native-algebra-proposition-characterize-formally-smooth) supplies an $R$-algebra section $\sigma:S\to P/I^2$. Choose polynomials $h_i\in P$ representing $\sigma(\bar X_i)$. The section identity gives polynomials $b_{ij}$ with

$$X_i-h_i=\sum_j b_{ij}f_j.$$

Since the relations of $S$ vanish under $\sigma$, there are polynomials $a_{jkl}$ such that, for each $j$,

$$f_j(h_1,\ldots,h_n)=\sum_{k,l=1}^{m}a_{jkl}f_kf_l.$$

Let $R_0$ be generated over the image of $\mathbb Z$ by all coefficients of the finite lists $f_j,h_i,b_{ij},a_{jkl}$. Put $P_0=R_0[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, $I_0=(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ and $S_0=P_0/I_0$. Both displayed identities hold already in $P_0$, since it is a subring of $P$. The second makes $\bar X_i\mapsto h_i\bmod I_0^2$ a well-defined map $S_0\to P_0/I_0^2$; the first makes it a section of the quotient. Hence $S_0$ is formally smooth over $R_0$. It is finitely presented by construction, so is smooth. Base change of its displayed presentation gives $S$, proving the claim. ∎

#### Lemma. Relative dimension in a Cohen–Macaulay family

Suppose $R\to S$ is flat and finitely presented, and every fibre is Cohen–Macaulay. There is a finite product decomposition

$$S=S_0\times\cdots\times S_n$$

such that every $S_d$ is flat and finitely presented over $R$, has Cohen–Macaulay fibres, and each of its nonempty fibres is equidimensional of dimension $d$.

**Proof.** Let $W_d$ consist of the points where the dimension of the fibre at that point is $d$. The [openness theorem for the Cohen–Macaulay fibre locus of fixed dimension](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-presentation-flat-cm-locus-open) makes each $W_d$ open under the stated hypotheses. These subsets are disjoint and cover $\operatorname{Spec}S$. Quasi-compactness implies that only finitely many are nonempty: a finite subcover of a disjoint cover contains every nonempty member. Each $W_d$ is also closed, since its complement is the union of the other open members.

The clopen-idempotent correspondence gives orthogonal idempotents $e_d$ with $D(e_d)=W_d$ and $\sum_de_d=1$. Set $S_d=e_dS\simeq S_{e_d}$, inserting zero factors for missing indices between zero and the largest occurring dimension. Each factor is a direct summand of the flat $R$-module $S$, hence flat. It is a principal localization of a finitely presented $R$-algebra, hence finitely presented. Its fibres are clopen pieces of the original fibres, so remain Cohen–Macaulay.

At every point of a nonempty fibre of $S_d$, the fibre dimension is $d$. This also gives equidimensionality. In a finite type scheme over a field, the dimension at the generic point of an irreducible component equals that component's dimension: any neighborhood meets the component in a dense open of the same dimension, and finitely many other components can be removed near that generic point. Thus every component of this fibre has dimension $d$. If $S=0$, choose $n=0$ and $S_0=0$. ∎

#### Lemma. Products of smooth algebras

For $R$-algebras $S',S''$, the product $S=S'\times S''$ is smooth over $R$ exactly when both factors are smooth over $R$.

**Proof.** The coordinate idempotents give a disjoint open cover

$$\operatorname{Spec}S=\operatorname{Spec}S'\amalg\operatorname{Spec}S''.$$

Each factor is the corresponding principal localization of $S$. Smoothness of $S/R$ therefore implies smoothness of both factors. Conversely, if both factors are smooth, every point of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ has a principal neighborhood on which the map from $R$ is smooth, namely its whole factor. The [locality criterion for smoothness](#native-algebra-lemma-locally-smooth) then makes $S/R$ smooth. Equivalently the two idempotent localizations form a finite cover, so finite presentation glues and the pointwise smoothness criterion holds everywhere. This also includes a zero factor. ∎

#### Example. Factorization of polynomials

Fix positive integers $n,m$. Put

$$R=\mathbf Z[a_1,\ldots,a_{n+m}],\qquad S=\mathbf Z[b_1,\ldots,b_n,c_1,\ldots,c_m].$$

Define $R\to S$ by requiring that

$$X^{n+m}+a_1X^{n+m-1}+\cdots+a_{n+m}
=(X^n+b_1X^{n-1}+\cdots+b_n)(X^m+c_1X^{m-1}+\cdots+c_m).$$

More explicitly, set $b_0=c_0=1$ and set coefficients outside the indicated ranges to zero. The image of $a_j$ is $\sum_{u+v=j}b_uc_v$. Thus $a_1$ maps to $b_1+c_1$, $a_2$ to $b_2+b_1c_1+c_2$, and $a_{n+m}$ to $b_nc_m$.

This gives a presentation of $S$ over $R$ with $n+m$ variables and $n+m$ coefficient equations. It is a relative global complete intersection: every field fibre is nonempty and has dimension zero. Here are two ways to establish this dimension assertion.

First, for any $R\to k$, let $F\in k[X]$ be the monic polynomial obtained from the displayed left side. After a field extension $k\subset K$, a point of the fibre with values in $K$ is precisely an ordered factorization $F=GH$, with $G,H$ monic of degrees $n,m$. Over an algebraic closure, the multiplicity of each root in $G$ is an integer between zero and its multiplicity in $F$; it also determines its multiplicity in $H$. Only finitely many choices occur. At least one choice has degree $n$, so the fibre over the algebraic closure is nonempty. The Nullstellensatz identifies its closed points with these finitely many coefficient tuples. A finite type algebra over a field is Jacobson; consequently, if it has only finitely many maximal ideals, every prime is maximal. Indeed, a prime is the intersection of the maximal ideals containing it, and a finite intersection can be prime only if it equals one of those ideals. This proves dimension zero. The original $k$-algebra has finitely many maximal ideals as well: each maximal ideal has a finite residue extension and therefore lifts to one of these geometric points. The same Jacobson argument proves dimension zero before extending the field.

Second, the coefficient map is finite. Write $A$ for the image of $R$ inside the domain $S$, and embed $S$ in its fraction field. In an algebraic closure of that field, every root of the displayed product satisfies the monic polynomial with coefficients in $A$, so it is integral over $A$. The coefficients of each monic factor are elementary symmetric expressions in the corresponding roots. Integral elements form a ring; hence every $b_i$ and every $c_j$ is integral over $A$. This is also the [monic-divisor coefficient argument](#native-algebra-lemma-polynomials-divide). Finitely many integral algebra generators make $S$ finite as an $R$-module: reduce powers of each generator using a monic equation to obtain a finite spanning list. Field fibres are therefore finite-dimensional and have dimension zero whenever nonempty. Their nonemptiness follows from factoring $F$ over an algebraic closure as above. Either proof supplies the required fibre dimension for the given complete-intersection presentation.

#### Lemma. Idempotent ideals and connected components

Suppose an ideal $I$ of $R$ is finitely generated and satisfies $I^2=I$. Then there is an element $e$ with $e^2=e$ and $I=eR$. For $e'=1-e$ one has a canonical isomorphism $R/I\simeq R_{e'}$, and $V(I)$ is both open and closed in $\operatorname{Spec}R$.

**Proof.** Apply the determinant form of [Nakayama's lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-nak) to the finite module $I=II$. It supplies $f\in1+I$ such that $fI=0$. Since $f-1\in I$, the equality $f(f-1)=0$ says that $f$ is idempotent. Put $e=1-f$. Then $e\in I$, $e^2=e$, and multiplication by $e$ fixes every element of $I$, because $fI=0$. These observations give $I=eR$.

The element $e'=f$ becomes $1$ modulo $I$, so the quotient map factors through $R_f$. Conversely, $f$ being invertible forces its complementary idempotent $e$ to vanish, so localization factors through $R/I$. The two factorizations are inverse by their universal properties. Explicitly, an idempotent that is invertible equals $1$, and the localization kernel consists of those $r$ with $fr=0$. Such an $r$ satisfies $r=er$, giving exactly the ideal $eR$.

Finally, $ef=0$ and $e+f=1$. A prime contains exactly one of these two elements. It follows that $V(I)=V(e)=D(f)$, which exhibits the same subset as closed and open. These conclusions include $I=0$ and $I=R$. ∎

#### Lemma. Closed subsets of an affine spectrum

For any ideal $I\subset R$, contraction identifies $\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)$ homeomorphically with $V(I)$. Its inverse sends a prime $\mathfrak p\supset I$ to $\mathfrak p/I$.

**Proof.** A prime in the quotient contracts to a prime containing $I$. Conversely, $(R/I)/(\mathfrak p/I)\simeq R/\mathfrak p$ is a domain, so $\mathfrak p/I$ is prime; these operations are inverse. The principal open defined by the class of $r\in R$ corresponds exactly to $D(r)\cap V(I)$. These sets form bases for the two topologies, proving the homeomorphism. ∎

#### Proposition. Openness of flat finitely presented maps

A finitely presented ring map $R\to S$ induces an open map on spectra if it has going down. In particular, every flat finitely presented ring map has this property.

**Proof.** Flat maps have [going down](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-going-down), so it suffices to use that prime-lifting property. We check the image of each principal open $D(g)$ of $\operatorname{Spec}S$. Its ring is $S_g$, which remains finitely presented over $R$: adjoin one variable $Y$ and the relation $gY-1$ to a finite presentation of $S$.

Going down also remains valid for $R\to S_g$. In fact, start with a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$ avoiding $g$ and a smaller prime of $R$ than its contraction. Going down in $S$ produces a prime contained in $\mathfrak q$ over that smaller prime; it still avoids $g$ and thus defines a prime of $S_g$.

The image $E_g$ of $\operatorname{Spec}S_g$ is constructible by *Quasi-finite morphisms and Chevalley's theorem*, Theorem 5.1. Its complete proof in §§3–5 first establishes the Noetherian theorem and then descends the finite presentation and Boolean conditions to a finitely generated $\mathbf Z$-subalgebra. The equality of the image after base change is justified there by the nonzero tensor product of two residue fields. It therefore applies to this arbitrary base ring.

Going down says directly that $E_g$ is stable under generalization: any smaller base prime lifts below a source prime giving a point of $E_g$. The constructible-topology argument of *Flat morphisms*, Lemma 3.1 now makes $E_g$ open. More explicitly, its constructible complement is compact in the constructible topology and stable under specialization; the lemma proves such a subset is Zariski closed. Since every open of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ is a union of principal opens, its image is a union of these open sets $E_g$. ∎

#### Lemma. Detecting a zero module by localization

Let $R$ be any ring. In each of the following six assertions, the stated global condition is equivalent both to its validity after localization at every prime of $R$ and to its validity after localization at every maximal ideal:

1. A specified element $x\in M$ is zero.
2. A specified $R$-module $M$ is zero.
3. A complex $M_1\to M_2\to M_3$ is exact at $M_2$.
4. A homomorphism $u:M\to N$ is injective.
5. A homomorphism $u:M\to N$ is surjective.
6. A homomorphism $u:M\to N$ is bijective.

In (1) this also says that the natural map $M\to\prod_{\mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}M_{\mathfrak m}$ is injective. No finiteness assumption on any module is required.

**Proof.** A global assertion gives all its localized assertions, since localization is exact; the prime assertions include the maximal ones. We prove the reverse implications from maximal ideals.

If $x\ne0$, its annihilator $\operatorname{Ann}_R(x)$ is a proper ideal, so choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ containing it. Vanishing of $x/1$ in $M_{\mathfrak m}$ would give an element outside $\mathfrak m$ annihilating $x$, contradicting the choice of $\mathfrak m$. Thus (1) holds, including the assertion about the product. Applying it to each element of $M$ proves (2).

For (3), put $H=\ker(M_2\to M_3)/\operatorname{im}(M_1\to M_2)$. Exactness of localization identifies $H_{\mathfrak m}$ with the homology of the localized complex. If all those complexes are exact, (2) gives $H=0$, as required. A map is injective when its kernel vanishes and surjective when its cokernel vanishes. These modules commute with localization, so (2) proves (4) and (5). Both conditions together are bijectivity, yielding (6). For the zero ring every unital module is zero, which also covers the case of an empty set of maximal ideals. ∎

#### Lemma. Elements integral over an ideal form a submodule

For a ring map $R\to S$ and an ideal $I\subset R$, the elements of $S$ integral over $I$ form an $R$-submodule. Moreover, multiplying such an element by any element integral over $R$ preserves integrality over $I$.

**Proof.** Use the graded ring $A=\bigoplus_{j\geq0}I^jt^j\subset R[t]$, mapped naturally to $S[t]$. The [criterion for integrality over an ideal](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-integral-ideal) says that $z\in S$ is integral over $I$ exactly when $zt$ is integral over $A$. One direction multiplies an equation with coefficient of index $j$ in $I^j$ by its total power of $t$. For the other, take the homogeneous component of total degree $d$ in a monic equation of degree $d$ for $zt$; its coefficient of index $j$ contributes its degree-$j$ part in $I^jt^j$. This recovers the required equation for $z$.

The [integral elements form a subring](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-closure-is-ring) of $S[t]$. If $z$ and $w$ are integral over $I$, then $zt+wt=(z+w)t$ and $-zt$ are integral over $A$. This proves addition and additive inverses. Every $r\in R$ is already in the degree-zero part of $A$, so multiplying by its image proves closure under $R$-scalars. More generally, an element $s$ integral over $R$ satisfies its same monic equation over $A$ as a degree-zero element of $S[t]$. The product $s(zt)$ is then integral over $A$, and the homogeneous criterion gives integrality of $sz$ over $I$. This proof permits noninjective $R\to S$ and arbitrary ideals. ∎

#### Lemma. Surjectivity on spectra of an integral overring

An inclusion $R\subset S$ with $S$ integral over $R$ induces a surjection $\operatorname{Spec}S\to\operatorname{Spec}R$.

**Proof.** Fix $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$. Localization preserves the inclusion and integrality, so replace the rings by $R_{\mathfrak p}\subset S_{\mathfrak p}$. Write $\mathfrak m$ for the maximal ideal of the new base. We show $\mathfrak mS_{\mathfrak p}$ is proper. Otherwise there is an equality $1=\sum_{i=1}^r a_is_i$ with $a_i\in\mathfrak m$. The finitely many integral elements $s_i$ generate a finite algebra $T=R_{\mathfrak p}[s_1,\ldots,s_r]$ containing $R_{\mathfrak p}$. The equality puts $1$ in $\mathfrak mT$, hence $T=\mathfrak mT$. Nakayama makes $T=0$, contradicting the inclusion of the nonzero local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$.

Choose a prime of $S_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak mS_{\mathfrak p}$, which is possible because this quotient is nonzero. Its inverse image contracts to $\mathfrak m$, and pulling it back before localization gives a prime of $S$ contracting to the original $\mathfrak p$. ∎

#### Lemma. Composition of going-up and going-down maps

If both $R\to S$ and $S\to T$ have going down, so does $R\to T$. The same statement holds for going up.

**Proof.** For going down, take $\mathfrak p_0\subset\mathfrak p_1$ in $R$ and a prime $\mathfrak r_1$ of $T$ contracting to $\mathfrak p_1$. Contract it first to $\mathfrak q_1\subset S$. Going down for $R\to S$ gives $\mathfrak q_0\subset\mathfrak q_1$ over $\mathfrak p_0$. Going down for $S\to T$, applied to $\mathfrak r_1$, then gives $\mathfrak r_0\subset\mathfrak r_1$ over $\mathfrak q_0$. Its contraction to $R$ is $\mathfrak p_0$.

For going up, begin instead with $\mathfrak r_0$ over $\mathfrak p_0$ and contract to $\mathfrak q_0$. Lift $\mathfrak p_1$ to $\mathfrak q_1\supset\mathfrak q_0$ in $S$, and then lift $\mathfrak q_1$ to $\mathfrak r_1\supset\mathfrak r_0$ in $T$. Its contraction is $\mathfrak p_1$, proving the assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Closed images stable under specialization

Let $E$ be the image of $\operatorname{Spec}S\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ for any ring homomorphism. If $E$ is stable under specialization, it is closed.

**Proof by localization.** Take $\mathfrak p$ in the closure of $E$. For every $f\notin\mathfrak p$, the neighbourhood $D(f)$ meets $E$, so $S_f$ is nonzero. Consequently $S_{\mathfrak p}$ is nonzero: if $1/1=0$ there, some single $f\notin\mathfrak p$ would kill $1$ in $S$, making $S_f=0$. Choose a prime of $S_{\mathfrak p}$. Its inverse image in $S$ contracts to a prime $\mathfrak p'\subset\mathfrak p$ belonging to $E$. Specialization stability now puts $\mathfrak p$ in $E$. Thus $E$ contains its closure.

**Proof using minimal primes.** Put $I=\ker(R\to S)$ and replace the base by $R/I$. This identifies its spectrum with the closed subset $V(I)$, so it suffices to prove that the image for this injective map is the entire spectrum. If $\mathfrak p$ is minimal in $R/I$, the localization of $R/I$ at $\mathfrak p$ is nonzero and injects into the corresponding localization of $S$. A prime in the latter ring contracts to the unique prime of the former, because primes in that base localization correspond to primes contained in the minimal prime $\mathfrak p$. Therefore every minimal prime belongs to the image. Every prime contains a minimal prime; specialization stability gives every remaining point. Returning to the original base, the image is exactly $V(I)$, hence closed. ∎

#### Lemma. Cotangent complexes and differentials

Suppose $A\to B\to C$ are ring maps and the composite onto $C$ is surjective. Set $I=\ker(A\to C)$ and $J=\ker(B\to C)$. There is an exact sequence of $C$-modules

$$I/I^2\longrightarrow J/J^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_B C\longrightarrow0.$$

The first arrow comes from $A\to B$; the second sends the class of $j$ to $dj\otimes1$.

**Proof.** The map $B\to C$ is also onto. For a surjective ring map, the naive cotangent complex has first homology equal to its conormal module and zero zeroth homology. Apply the [transitivity sequence](#native-algebra-lemma-exact-sequence-nl) to this tower, using this [surjection calculation](#native-algebra-lemma-nl-surjection) for both maps ending in $C$. The relevant part is

$$H_1(\mathrm{NL}_{C/A})\longrightarrow H_1(\mathrm{NL}_{C/B})
\longrightarrow\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_B C\longrightarrow\Omega_{C/A}\longrightarrow0.$$

Here the first two terms are $I/I^2$ and $J/J^2$, and the last differential module vanishes. The maps in transitivity are exactly the two stated maps, giving the assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Cotangent complexes, differentials and formal smoothness

In the preceding situation, assume in addition that $B$ is formally smooth over $A$. Then the sequence extends to a split short exact sequence

$$0\longrightarrow I/I^2\longrightarrow J/J^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_B C\longrightarrow0.$$

**Proof.** The surjection $A/I^2\to A/I=C$ has square-zero kernel. Formal smoothness lifts $B\to C$ to an $A$-algebra map $\sigma:B\to A/I^2$. Thus $\sigma(J)$ lies in $I/I^2$, and $\sigma(J^2)=0$. It induces a $C$-linear map $J/J^2\to I/I^2$. Because $\sigma$ is an $A$-algebra map, its composite with $I/I^2\to J/J^2$ is the identity. The first arrow is therefore injective and admits a retraction. The preceding exact sequence identifies the complementary summand with $\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_B C$, proving split exactness. ∎

#### Lemma. A cover of the target spectrum

Let $R\to S$ be a ring map, and let $g_1,\ldots,g_n\in S$ generate the unit ideal, so their principal opens cover $\operatorname{Spec}S$.

1. If every $S_{g_i}$ is finite type over $R$, then $S$ is finite type over $R$.
2. If every $S_{g_i}$ is finitely presented over $R$, then $S$ is finitely presented over $R$.

**Proof.** Choose $h_i\in S$ with $\sum_i h_ig_i=1$.

For (1), take finitely many algebra generators for each $S_{g_i}$ and express them as fractions with numerators in $S$ and denominators powers of $g_i$. Let $T$ be the $R$-subalgebra of $S$ generated by all these numerators, the $g_i$ and the $h_i$. This is a finite list. Each map $T_{g_i}\to S_{g_i}$ is injective by exactness of localization and surjective by the choice of generators. Moreover the identity $\sum_i h_ig_i=1$ holds already in $T$. The finite-cover criterion applied to the $T$-module $S/T$ makes it zero. Hence $T=S$, proving finite type.

For (2), apply (1) and choose a surjection $P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_r]\to S$ with kernel $J$. Lift $g_i,h_i$ to $\widetilde g_i,\widetilde h_i\in P$. Adjoining an inverse of $g_i$ gives

$$S_{g_i}\simeq P[Y]/\bigl(JP[Y]+(1-Y\widetilde g_i)\bigr).$$

Since this algebra is finitely presented over $R$, the kernel of this particular finite polynomial presentation is finitely generated. Choose generators and expand each as a finite combination of elements of $J$ and $1-Y\widetilde g_i$. Collecting the finitely many elements of $J$ that occur gives $f_{ij}\in J$ with

$$JP[Y]+(1-Y\widetilde g_i)=(f_{ij}\text{ for all }j,\ 1-Y\widetilde g_i).$$

Now form the finitely presented $R$-algebra

$$T=P/\left(\sum_i\widetilde h_i\widetilde g_i-1,\ f_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j\right).$$

All these relations vanish in $S$, so $T\to S$ is onto. The images of the $\widetilde g_i$ generate the unit ideal in $T$. The displayed localized presentations show that $T_{\widetilde g_i}\to S_{g_i}$ is an isomorphism: the relations $f_{ij}$ for this $i$ already generate the localized kernel, and all additional imposed relations belong to that kernel. The finite-cover criterion annihilates the kernel of $T\to S$. Hence $T\simeq S$ and (2) follows. If the cover is empty, $S=0$, which is the finitely presented algebra $R/(1)$. ∎

#### Lemma. Nakayama's lemma after localization

Let $S\subset R$ be multiplicative, let $I\subset R$ be an ideal, and let $M$ be a finite $R$-module. Suppose $x_1,\ldots,x_r\in M$ generate $S^{-1}(M/IM)$ over $S^{-1}(R/I)$. There is an element $f\in S+I$ for which the same elements generate $M_f$ over $R_f$.[^4]

**Proof.** First take $I=0$ and fix finite generators $y_1,\ldots,y_s$ of $M$. In $S^{-1}M$, write each $y_i$ as a combination of the $x_j$. A common denominator $u\in S$ clears all coefficients. For each of the finitely many resulting equalities, another element of $S$ makes it valid already in $M$, by the vanishing criterion for localization. Multiplying these elements together gives $v\in S$ such that every $y_i$ is in the span of the $x_j$ after inverting $uv$. This proves the claim when $I=0$.

For general $I$, apply that case to $M/IM$. It gives $s\in S$ such that the chosen elements generate $(M/IM)_s$. Nakayama applied over $R_s$ to the finite module $M_s/\sum_j R_sx_j$ supplies $g\in1+I_s$ annihilating that quotient. Write $g=1+i/s^N$ with $i\in I$ and $N\geq0$. Set

$$f=s^{N+1}+si=s(s^N+i).$$

Its first summand belongs to $S$ and its second to $I$, so $f\in S+I$. In $R_f$ both $s$ and $s^N+i$ are units, hence so is $g$. Conversely, inverting $s$ and $g$ inverts $f=s^{N+1}g$. Thus $R_f\simeq(R_s)_g$, and the quotient module vanishes there. This is exactly the required generation assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Localization of a flat module

Let $R$ be a ring and $U\subset R$ a multiplicative set.

1. The algebra $U^{-1}R$ is flat over $R$.
2. A module over $U^{-1}R$ is flat over $R$ exactly when it is flat over $U^{-1}R$.
3. An $R$-module $M$ is flat exactly when $M_{\mathfrak p}$ is flat over $R_{\mathfrak p}$ for every prime $\mathfrak p$.
4. In (3) it is enough to test all maximal ideals.
5. If $R\to A$, $M$ is an $A$-module, and $g_1,\ldots,g_t$ generate the unit ideal of $A$, then $M$ is $R$-flat exactly when every $M_{g_i}$ is $R$-flat.
6. For an $A$-module $M$, flatness over $R$ is equivalent to flatness of $M_{\mathfrak q}$ over $R_{\mathfrak p}$ for every $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}A$, where $\mathfrak p$ is its inverse image in $R$.
7. In (6) it is enough to test maximal ideals $\mathfrak q$ of $A$; their contractions in $R$ need not be maximal.

**Proof.** Tensoring with $U^{-1}R$ is the exact localization functor, proving (1). For (2), a flat $U^{-1}R$-module is $R$-flat by composition with (1). In the other direction, if $N$ is a $U^{-1}R$-module, tensoring it with $M$ over $R$ agrees with tensoring over $U^{-1}R$. Exactness over $R$ therefore tests exactness over the localization too.

We prove (6) and (7) together using the [ideal criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-flat). If $M$ is $R$-flat and $J\subset R$ is an ideal, the injection $J\otimes_R M\to M$ remains injective on localization as a map of $A$-modules. For a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $A$ over $\mathfrak p$, every ideal $L\subset R_{\mathfrak p}$ is $J_{\mathfrak p}$ for its contraction $J\subset R$. The localized map is

$$L\otimes_{R_{\mathfrak p}}M_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow M_{\mathfrak q},$$

so the ideal criterion proves $R_{\mathfrak p}$-flatness of $M_{\mathfrak q}$.

Conversely, suppose these localized modules are flat for all maximal $\mathfrak q$ of $A$. For any ideal $J\subset R$, let $K$ be the kernel of $J\otimes_R M\to M$, viewed as an $A$-module. At a maximal $\mathfrak q$ its localization is the kernel of

$$J_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_{R_{\mathfrak p}}M_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow M_{\mathfrak q},$$

and this is zero by the assumed flatness. Local detection over $A$ gives $K=0$. The ideal criterion then makes $M$ flat over $R$. Testing all primes implies testing all maximal primes, and the forward argument gave all primes, establishing both (6) and (7). Taking $A=R$ proves (3) and (4).

For (5), if $M$ is $R$-flat, localize each injection $J\otimes_R M\to M$ at $g_i$ and apply the ideal criterion to $M_{g_i}$. Conversely, if all those localized modules are flat, the same kernel $K$ has $K_{g_i}=0$ for each $i$. The finite-cover criterion over $A$ gives $K=0$, again proving flatness. This also treats the empty cover, for which $A=0$ and $M=0$. ∎

#### Lemma. Hom from a finitely presented module

Let $M$ be finitely presented over $R$, and let $N$ be any $R$-module. For a multiplicative subset $U$ there are canonical identifications

$$U^{-1}\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{U^{-1}R}(U^{-1}M,U^{-1}N)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_R(U^{-1}M,U^{-1}N).$$

Taking $U=\{1,f,f^2,\ldots\}$ gives, in particular,

$$\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)_f\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{R_f}(M_f,N_f)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_f,N_f).$$

**Proof.** Choose a finite presentation $R^a\to R^b\to M\to0$. Applying Hom into $N$ identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ with the kernel of the induced map $N^b\to N^a$. Localization is exact and commutes with these finite direct sums. Thus its localization is the kernel of $(U^{-1}N)^b\to(U^{-1}N)^a$. Localizing the chosen presentation of $M$ shows that this is precisely $\operatorname{Hom}_{U^{-1}R}(U^{-1}M,U^{-1}N)$, with its natural localization map. Finally, any $R$-linear map between modules on which every $u\in U$ acts invertibly must commute with $u^{-1}$ as well as with $u$. It is automatically $U^{-1}R$-linear, proving the second identification. ∎

#### Lemma. A characteristic polynomial with coefficients in an ideal

Suppose $M$ is a finite $R$-module, $I\subset R$ is an ideal, and an endomorphism $\varphi$ satisfies $\varphi(M)\subset IM$. There is a monic polynomial

$$P(T)=T^n+a_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n,\qquad a_j\in I^j,$$

such that $P(\varphi)=0$ on $M$.

**Proof.** Choose generators $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ of $M$, using one zero generator if necessary when $M=0$. For each $j$ choose $a_{ij}\in I$ with $\varphi(x_j)=\sum_i a_{ij}x_i$. Let $A=(a_{ij})$ act on the free module with basis $e_j$ by $Ae_j=\sum_i a_{ij}e_i$. The surjection $q:R^n\to M$ given by $q(e_j)=x_j$ satisfies $qA=\varphi q$.

Take $P(T)=\det(T1_n-A)$. The coefficient of index $j$ is a signed sum of products of $j$ matrix entries, so it lies in $I^j$. The [Cayley–Hamilton identity](#native-algebra-lemma-charpoly) gives $P(A)=0$. Therefore $P(\varphi)q=qP(A)=0$, and surjectivity of $q$ gives the required annihilation. The matrix need not descend to a chosen free presentation of the relations; the intertwining identity with $q$ is all that is used. ∎

#### Lemma. Finite module presentations in a filtered colimit

Write $R=\operatorname*{colim}_{\lambda\in\Lambda}R_\lambda$ for a directed system of rings. Finitely presented modules and their maps can be recovered at finite stages in the following precise sense.

1. Every finitely presented $R$-module is isomorphic to $M_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R$ for some finitely presented $R_\lambda$-module $M_\lambda$.
2. Given finitely presented $M_\lambda,N_\lambda$ at a common stage, every map between their extensions to $R$ is the extension of a map $M_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu\to N_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu$ for some $\mu\geq\lambda$.
3. If two maps $M_\lambda\to N_\lambda$ become equal over $R$, they become equal over some $R_\mu$ with $\mu\geq\lambda$.

**Proof.** Present the module in (1) as the cokernel of a finite matrix $R^a\to R^b$. Its finitely many entries come from a common stage $R_\lambda$. The cokernel of that matrix at the stage is finitely presented and has the required base change, since tensor product preserves cokernels.

For (2), choose a finite presentation of $M_\lambda$. The images under the proposed map of its finitely many generators are elements of $N_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R$. This module is the directed colimit of $N_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu$, so these images are represented together at one later stage. Each of the finitely many defining relations of $M_\lambda$ maps to zero in the colimit. The vanishing criterion for a directed colimit makes it zero at some later stage. Directedness lets us choose one stage where all the relations vanish. The chosen generator images then define the desired module map there.

For (3), the difference of the maps vanishes on a finite generating list after passage to $R$. Each of these finitely many zero equalities holds at a later stage; one common upper bound makes them all hold. The maps then agree on every element. The argument uses the equality and vanishing rules for directed colimits, and does not require injective or flat transition maps. ∎

#### Lemma. Flat modules in a short exact sequence

For a short exact sequence $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$, flatness of $M'$ and $M''$ implies flatness of $M$. Flatness of $M$ and $M''$ implies flatness of $M'$.

**Proof.** Fix an ideal $I\subset R$ and compare the given exact sequence with the right exact sequence obtained by tensoring with $I$. The vertical maps in this comparison are the multiplication maps $I\otimes_R N\to N$.

For the first assertion, let $z\in I\otimes_R M$ have zero image in $M$. Its image in $I\otimes_R M''$ has zero image in $M''$, so it vanishes because $M''$ is flat. Right exactness gives $z'$ in $I\otimes_R M'$ mapping to $z$. Its image in $M'$ maps to zero in $M$; the original injection makes this image zero. Flatness of $M'$ then gives $z'=0$, hence $z=0$. The ideal criterion proves flatness of $M$.

For the second assertion, flatness of $M''$ makes $I\otimes_R M'\to I\otimes_R M$ injective, by the vanishing of $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(I,M'')$. The composite of this injection with the injective multiplication map $I\otimes_R M\to M$ factors through $M'$. It follows that $I\otimes_R M'\to M'$ is injective. Apply the ideal criterion once more. ∎

#### Lemma. Quasi-regular and regular ideals in a Noetherian ring

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, and let $M\ne0$ be finite over $R$. Every $M$-quasi-regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_c$ contained in $\mathfrak m$ is $M$-regular.

**Proof.** For $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$, quasi-regularity identifies the associated graded module with the polynomial module

$$\operatorname{gr}_J(M)\simeq(M/JM)[T_1,\ldots,T_c],$$

where multiplication by the initial form of $f_i$ corresponds to multiplication by $T_i$. The empty sequence requires nothing. Suppose $c>0$. For a nonzero $x\in M$, [Krull intersection](#native-algebra-lemma-intersect-powers-ideal-module-zero) gives an integer $a\geq0$ such that $x\in J^aM\setminus J^{a+1}M$. Multiplication by $T_1$ is injective on a polynomial module, regardless of zero divisors in its coefficients. Thus the initial form of $f_1x$ in degree $a+1$ is nonzero, proving $f_1x\ne0$.

The remaining sequence is quasi-regular on $M/f_1M$ by the [truncation lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-truncate-quasi-regular). Its graded calculation can be seen directly: for $a\geq1$,

$$J^aM\cap f_1M=f_1J^{a-1}M.$$

Indeed, if $f_1y\in J^aM$ but $y\notin J^{a-1}M$, choose its last nonzero graded position below degree $a-1$. Multiplication by $T_1$ would give a nonzero initial form of $f_1y$ in a degree below $a$, a contradiction. Taking the graded quotient therefore sets $T_1$ equal to zero. Nakayama ensures that the finite module $M/f_1M$ is nonzero, since $f_1\in\mathfrak m$. Induct on $c$ in the Noetherian local ring $R/(f_1)$. This proves successive injectivity and the required nonzero final quotient. ∎

#### Lemma. Height and dimension in a polynomial ring

For primes $\mathfrak p\subset\mathfrak q$ of $P=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, every maximal chain in the interval from $\mathfrak p$ to $\mathfrak q$ has length

$$\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p).$$

**Proof.** Polynomial local rings over a field are regular and hence Cohen–Macaulay. The [maximal-chain theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-maximal-chain-cm) therefore applies in both $P_{\mathfrak p}$ and $P_{\mathfrak q}$. Choose a maximal chain from $(0)$ to $\mathfrak p$; its length is $\dim P_{\mathfrak p}=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$. Adjoin the proposed maximal chain from $\mathfrak p$ to $\mathfrak q$. The concatenation is saturated, begins at the unique minimal prime $(0)$ of the domain $P$, and ends at $\mathfrak q$. In $P_{\mathfrak q}$ it is a maximal chain, so its length is $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)$. Subtracting the first length proves the formula, including the case $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q$.

One may equivalently complete the chains to a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supset\mathfrak q$. Its local polynomial ring has dimension $n$. All maximal chains from $(0)$ to $\mathfrak m$ have length $n$ by the same Cohen–Macaulay theorem. Using a fixed saturated tail from $\mathfrak q$ to $\mathfrak m$ and cancelling its length gives the identical interval formula. ∎

#### Lemma. Noether normalization

Let $S=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/I$ be nonzero, with $k$ any field. There are polynomials $y_1,\ldots,y_r$ whose images in $S$ are algebraically independent over $k$ and make $S$ finite over $k[y_1,\ldots,y_r]$. Their number is $r=\dim S$. The $y_i$ can be chosen in the image of $\mathbf Z[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$ inside $k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$.

**Proof.** Induct on $n$. For $n=0$, the nonzero quotient is $k$ and the empty list works. If $I=0$, take all the original variables. Otherwise choose $0\ne F\in I$; it is nonconstant because $I$ is proper.

We give the monic-coordinate step explicitly. Choose an integer $e\geq2$ larger than every exponent of every monomial occurring in $F$, and set

$$Z_i=X_i-X_n^{e^i}\qquad(1\leq i<n).$$

These are polynomial coordinates together with $X_n$, since $X_i=Z_i+X_n^{e^i}$. Under this substitution, a monomial $X_1^{a_1}\cdots X_n^{a_n}$ contributes a highest power of $X_n$ of degree

$$a_n+a_1e+\cdots+a_{n-1}e^{n-1}.$$

Base-$e$ expansion makes these degrees distinct for the distinct monomials of $F$. Any term involving a $Z_i$ has smaller $X_n$-degree than that monomial's highest term. Hence the unique largest degree in the whole substituted polynomial has a nonzero coefficient belonging to $k$. Dividing by that coefficient gives a monic equation for the image of $X_n$ over the subalgebra $S_0\subset S$ generated by the images of the $Z_i$. This is the [one-relation construction](#native-algebra-lemma-one-relation). Since the other variables are $Z_i+X_n^{e^i}$, the algebra $S$ is generated by this one integral element over $S_0$, and is finite over $S_0$.

The nonzero algebra $S_0$ is a quotient of a polynomial ring in $n-1$ variables. Induction supplies algebraically independent parameters in it, given by integer polynomials in those variables, over which $S_0$ is finite. Composing those integer polynomials with the displayed $Z_i$ gives integer polynomials in the original $X_i$. Their images stay algebraically independent because $S_0\subset S$, and finiteness composes. This proves the existence claim with its coefficient restriction over finite fields as well as infinite fields.

Finally, an integral inclusion has equal dimensions by the complete chain-lifting and incomparability proof in *Integral extensions: lying over, going up and going down*, Theorem 5.1. The polynomial subring in $r$ independent variables has dimension $r$. Applying these two facts to its finite inclusion in $S$ gives $\dim S=r$. ∎

#### Proposition. Dimension and codimension

For a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$ and an integer $d\geq0$, the following are equivalent:

1. The Krull dimension of $R$ is $d$.
2. The Hilbert–Samuel degree $d(R)$ is $d$.
3. An ideal of definition can be generated by $d$ elements, and none can be generated by fewer elements.

Here an ideal of definition has radical $\mathfrak m$, and $d(R)$ is the degree of the eventual polynomial $\ell_R(R/I^N)$ for any such ideal $I$.

**Proof.** We retain the three-inequality argument, with finite dimensionality established before induction on dimension. Its growth and parameter steps are proved in full in *Dimension theory of Noetherian local rings*, §§1–2, especially Theorem 2.1. Let $\delta(R)$ be the minimum number of generators of an ideal of definition. This number is finite since $\mathfrak m$ itself is finitely generated.

First, if $I$ has $t\geq1$ generators, its degree-$j$ monomials give a surjection from $\binom{t+j-1}{j}$ copies of $R/I$ onto $I^j/I^{j+1}$. Summing lengths for $0\leq j<N$ gives

$$\ell_R(R/I^N)\leq\ell_R(R/I)\binom{N+t-1}{t}.$$

The degree of the eventual polynomial is therefore at most $t$. If $t=0$, then $I=0$ is an ideal of definition; $R$ has finite length and its degree is zero. Thus $d(R)\leq\delta(R)$ in all cases.

Next prove $\dim R\leq d(R)$ by induction on the finite nonnegative integer $d(R)$, simultaneously for all Noetherian local rings. If the degree is zero, the lengths $\ell_R(R/\mathfrak m^N)$ eventually stabilize. It follows that $\mathfrak m^N=\mathfrak m^{N+1}$ for large $N$. Nakayama gives $\mathfrak m^N=0$, so the only prime is $\mathfrak m$ and the dimension is zero.

For positive degree, take a strict chain $\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_l$. There is nothing to prove for $l=0$. Otherwise put $B=R/\mathfrak p_0$ and choose $x\in\mathfrak p_1\setminus\mathfrak p_0$. The quotient is a local domain and $x$ is a nonzero nonunit there. The [degree and leading-term formula for a short exact sequence](#native-algebra-lemma-hilbert-ses-chi) gives $d(B)\leq d(R)$. Applied to

$$0\longrightarrow B\xrightarrow{x}B\longrightarrow B/xB\longrightarrow0,$$

it gives the strict inequality $d(B/xB)<d(B)$: equality would make the positive leading coefficient of $B/xB$ equal to the difference of the identical leading coefficients of the two copies of $B$. The degree-zero case cannot occur for this domain with a nonzero nonunit. The quotient $C=B/xB$ is nonzero, and its primes coming from $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_l$ form a chain of length $l-1$. Induction yields

$$l-1\leq\dim C\leq d(C)\leq d(R)-1.$$

Thus every chain has length at most $d(R)$, proving the second inequality and, in particular, finiteness of $\dim R$.

Finally put $D=\dim R$ and induct on $D$ to prove $\delta(R)\leq D$. When $D=0$, the zero ideal has radical $\mathfrak m$ and the empty generating list suffices. For $D>0$, the finitely many minimal primes are all strictly smaller than $\mathfrak m$. Prime avoidance supplies $x\in\mathfrak m$ outside their union. For any chain in $R/xR$, its smallest prime lifts to a prime containing $x$ and hence properly containing a minimal prime of $R$. Prepending that minimal prime extends the chain by one. Consequently $\dim(R/xR)\leq D-1$. By induction choose at most $D-1$ generators of an ideal of definition in the quotient. Their lifts together with $x$ generate an ideal with radical $\mathfrak m$. This proves the final inequality.

The cycle $\dim R\leq d(R)\leq\delta(R)\leq\dim R$ proves equality of all three invariants, which is exactly the three stated conditions. ∎

#### Lemma. Criteria for a separable field extension

Let $K/k$ be any extension of fields of characteristic $p>0$. The following conditions are equivalent:

1. The extension is separable: every intermediate field finitely generated over $k$ is separably generated.
2. For each finite $k$-linearly independent family $a_1,\ldots,a_m$ in $K$, the family $a_1^p,\ldots,a_m^p$ is also $k$-linearly independent.
3. The algebra $K\otimes_k k^{1/p}$ is reduced.
4. The field $K$ is geometrically reduced over $k$, meaning that $K\otimes_k L$ is reduced for every extension field $L/k$.

**Proof.** The [separable scalar-extension lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-separable-extension-preserves-reducedness), applied to the reduced $k$-algebra $L$, proves (1)$\Rightarrow$(4). Taking $L=k^{1/p}$ gives (4)$\Rightarrow$(3).

Assume (3). There is a ring homomorphism

$$F:K\otimes_k k^{1/p}\longrightarrow K,\qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto a^pb^p.$$

It is well defined by the tensor balancing relation and additivity of Frobenius. For every $z$ in its domain, $z^p=F(z)\otimes1$. Reducedness thus makes $F$ injective. Suppose $\sum_i c_ia_i^p=0$ for a linearly independent family and coefficients $c_i\in k$. Choose $b_i\in k^{1/p}$ with $b_i^p=c_i$. Then $F(\sum_i a_i\otimes b_i)=0$, so $\sum_i a_i\otimes b_i=0$. Independence remains true after the field extension $k\subset k^{1/p}$; hence every $b_i$, and therefore every $c_i$, is zero. This proves (2).

Now assume (2). It is inherited by intermediate fields, so it is enough to show that a finitely generated $K/k$ has a separating transcendence basis. Among all transcendence bases $x_1,\ldots,x_d$, choose one minimizing the inseparable degree of the finite extension $K/k(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$. Denote this rational subfield by $F$. If the extension over $F$ is separable, the claim holds. Otherwise choose $a\in K$ inseparable over $F$ and put $E=F(a)$; then $[E:F]_i>1$.

Apply the [elementary separating-basis lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-mini-separability) to the field $E=k(x_1,\ldots,x_d,a)$, which still satisfies (2). It gives an index $1\leq j\leq d+1$ such that the field $L$ generated by all but the $j$-th member of the list $x_1,\ldots,x_d,a$ is rational of transcendence degree $d$ over $k$, and $E/L$ is finite separable. Multiplicativity of inseparable degrees now gives

$$[K:L]_i=[K:E]_i
< [K:E]_i[E:F]_i=[K:F]_i,$$

contrary to minimality. Thus the chosen minimum is one and $K/k$ is separably generated. This also covers $d=0$, when the omitted-list field in the lemma is $k$. Applying the result to every finitely generated intermediate field proves (1) without any finiteness hypothesis on the original extension. ∎

#### Lemma. Formal smoothness over a prime field

Every field extension in characteristic zero is formally smooth. In characteristic $p>0$, a field extension $K/k$ is formally smooth exactly when it is separable.

**Proof.** The [elementary formally smooth extensions lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth-extensions-easy) proves formal smoothness for every separable extension, including arbitrary transcendence degree and infinite algebraic degree. All extensions in characteristic zero are separable. The converse in positive characteristic is the following lemma. Together these assertions prove both claims. ∎

#### Lemma. A formally smooth field extension is separable

If $K$ is formally smooth over a field $k$, then $K/k$ is separable.

**Proof.** In characteristic zero this is automatic. In characteristic $p$, apply the [split differential sequence for a formally smooth last map](#native-algebra-lemma-ses-formally-smooth) to $\mathbf F_p\to k\to K$. It makes

$$K\otimes_k\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}$$

injective. Here the splitting can also be constructed directly. Put $V=K\otimes_k\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}$ and make the square-zero ring $K\oplus V$ a $k$-algebra by $a\mapsto(a,1\otimes da)$. Formal smoothness lifts the identity of $K$ through $K\oplus V\to K$. Its second component is an $\mathbf F_p$-derivation $D:K\to V$ with $D(a)=1\otimes da$ for $a\in k$. The induced map $\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}\to V$ is a left inverse to the displayed map. The differential separability criterion proved next therefore gives the result. ∎

#### Lemma. Differentials of a separable field extension

For fields $k\subset K$ of characteristic $p>0$, the extension $K/k$ is separable if and only if the canonical map

$$\iota:K\otimes_k\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}$$

is injective.

**Proof.** We first justify reduction to finitely generated intermediate fields $E/k$. If $\iota$ is injective, each corresponding map for $E$ is injective: a nonzero vector in its kernel remains nonzero on extending scalars from $E$ to $K$, but would then map to zero under $\iota$. Conversely, assume all the finitely generated instances are injective. A putative kernel vector for $\iota$ uses finitely many coefficients of $K$, so comes from one such field $E$. If its differential vanishes over $K$, the [filtered-colimit rule for differentials](#native-algebra-lemma-colimit-differentials) makes it vanish in a larger finitely generated field. Injectivity there makes the vector zero. Thus injectivity is equivalent to injectivity at every finite-type field stage, just as separability is. No injectivity of the transition maps between the differential modules has been assumed.

Suppose now $K/k$ is finitely generated and separable. Choose a separating transcendence basis $u_1,\ldots,u_r$ and a primitive element $u_{r+1}$ for the finite separable extension over $k(u_1,\ldots,u_r)$. In the trivial finite extension one may use $u_{r+1}=0$. Clearing denominators and removing content from its minimal polynomial gives an irreducible

$$G(U_1,\ldots,U_{r+1})=\sum_I a_IU^I\in k[U_1,\ldots,U_{r+1}]$$

with $K$ the fraction field of $k[U]/(G)$ and $\partial G/\partial U_{r+1}\ne0$. The differential presentation, followed by localization, identifies

$$\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}\simeq
\frac{(K\otimes_k\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p})\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{r+1}K\,dU_j}
{K\left(\sum_I u^I\otimes da_I+\sum_{j=1}^{r+1}\frac{\partial G}{\partial U_j}(u)\,dU_j\right)}.$$

The last derivative has nonzero image in $K$. Indeed, its degree in $U_{r+1}$ is smaller than that of $G$, so a nonzero such polynomial cannot belong to the principal kernel $(G)$. The relation vector in this presentation therefore has a nonzero coordinate in the free summand. Its span intersects the first summand only in zero. This proves injectivity of $\iota$.

Conversely, suppose $K/k$ is finitely generated and $\iota$ is injective. Choose a transcendence basis $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ minimizing $[K:F]_i$, where $F=k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$. If $K/F$ were inseparable, choose $a\in K$ inseparable over $F$. Its irreducible polynomial over $F$ has zero derivative in its variable $T$. By Gauss' lemma, clearing denominators and content yields an irreducible polynomial

$$G(X_1,\ldots,X_r,T)=\sum_{I,j}a_{I,j}X^IT^j\in k[X_1,\ldots,X_r,T^p]$$

whose evaluation at $(x_1,\ldots,x_r,a)$ is zero and generates the kernel of that evaluation on the polynomial ring. Divide by one nonzero scalar coefficient so that $a_{I_0,j_0}=1$.

Assume for a contradiction that all partial derivatives of $G$ with respect to the $X_i$ also vanish. Then every exponent appearing in $G$ is divisible by $p$. Differentiating the relation in $\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}$ leaves only

$$\sum_{(I,j)\ne(I_0,j_0)}x^Ia^j\,da_{I,j}=0.$$

The monomials in this sum with nonzero coefficients are linearly independent over $k$. To see this, a dependence would be a polynomial $H$ in the kernel $(G)$ supported on those monomials. It has total degree at most $\deg G$, so if nonzero it must be a scalar multiple of $G$. Its coefficient at the omitted monomial is zero, whereas that coefficient of $G$ is one, forcing the scalar and $H$ to be zero. Injectivity of $\iota$ and this independence imply $da_{I,j}=0$ in $\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}$ for every coefficient. The normalized coefficient has differential zero as well.

The zero-differential lemma below, applied over the perfect field $\mathbf F_p$, gives $a_{I,j}=b_{I,j}^p$ in $k$. Since all monomial exponents are multiples of $p$, it follows that

$$G=\left(\sum_{I,j}b_{I,j}X^{I/p}T^{j/p}\right)^p,$$

contradicting irreducibility of this nonconstant polynomial. Consequently at least one $X_i$-derivative is nonzero. This also rules out the supposed inseparable extension when $r=0$.

After renumbering, take $\partial G/\partial X_1\ne0$ and let $L=k(x_2,\ldots,x_r,a)$. The displayed generators of $L$ are algebraically independent: a relation among them would lie in $(G)$ while having degree zero in $X_1$, although $G$ has positive $X_1$-degree. Gauss' lemma makes $G$ irreducible over this rational field when regarded as a polynomial in $X_1$, and its nonzero derivative makes $x_1$ separable over $L$. Hence $E=F(a)$ is finite separable over $L$. The tower calculations give

$$[K:L]_i=[K:E]_i<[K:E]_i[E:F]_i=[K:F]_i,$$

because $a$ was inseparable over $F$. This contradicts the chosen minimum. Thus $K/F$ is separable, proving the converse and, by the initial reduction, the full assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Polynomials with zero derivative in characteristic p

Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p>0$ and $K/k$ any field extension. For $a\in K$,

$$da=0\text{ in }\Omega_{K/k}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\in K^p.$$

**Proof.** A $p$-th power has zero differential by the product rule. For the reverse implication, the filtered-colimit formula for differentials puts $a$ and the equality $da=0$ inside a subfield finitely generated over $k$. It suffices to work in this subfield; a root constructed there is also a root in $K$.

Perfectness supplies a separating transcendence basis $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ for this finitely generated extension. Put $F=k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$, so $K/F$ is finite separable. The complete derivation-extension proof in *Kähler differentials*, Lemma 6.1 and Theorem 6.2 gives

$$\Omega_{F/k}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r F\,dx_i,\qquad
\Omega_{K/k}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r K\,dx_i.$$

We spell out the rational-function calculation. Since $k$ is perfect, $k=k^p$. The monomials $x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_r^{e_r}$ with $0\leq e_i<p$ form a basis of $F$ over $F^p=k(x_1^p,\ldots,x_r^p)$. Polynomial monomials separate according to their exponents modulo $p$, giving independence after clearing denominators. They also span rational functions: replace a denominator $h$ by $h^p$ by multiplying the numerator by $h^{p-1}$, then separate the numerator monomials in the same way. Differentiating the unique expansion in this basis shows that all partial derivatives vanish only if every coefficient with a nonzero exponent vector is zero. Indeed, for each fixed $i$, differentiation sends the monomials with $e_i>0$ to distinct monomials with nonzero coefficients $e_i$. Thus the constants of all the partial derivatives on $F$ are exactly $F^p$.

Let $P(T)=T^d+\sum_{j=1}^d c_jT^{d-j}$ be the minimal polynomial of $a$ over $F$. From $da=0$ we get

$$0=dP(a)=\sum_{j=1}^d a^{d-j}\,dc_j.$$

Expand each $dc_j$ in the basis $dx_i$ above. Since $1,a,\ldots,a^{d-1}$ are linearly independent over $F$, each coordinate of every $dc_j$ vanishes. The rational-function calculation therefore writes $c_j=b_j^p$ with $b_j\in F$.

Choose the unique $p$-th root $\beta$ of $a$ in an algebraic closure of $K$, and put $Q(T)=T^d+\sum_j b_jT^{d-j}$. Then $Q(\beta)^p=P(a)=0$, hence $Q(\beta)=0$. It follows that $[F(\beta):F]\leq d$. But $F(a)\subset F(\beta)$ and $[F(a):F]=d$, so the two fields coincide. Thus $\beta\in F(a)\subset K$, proving that $a$ is a $p$-th power in $K$. The argument includes $r=0$, when the differential bases are empty and $F=k=k^p$. ∎

#### Lemma. Noetherianity under finite-type base change

Given ring maps $R\to S$ and $R\to R'$, assume that $S$ is Noetherian and $R'$ is a finite type $R$-algebra. Then $R'\otimes_R S$ is Noetherian.

**Proof.** A finite list of algebra generators for $R'$ over $R$ gives a finite list of generators for $R'\otimes_R S$ over $S$ after tensoring. Thus the new algebra is finite type over the Noetherian ring $S$, and the permanence lemma below applies. ∎

#### Lemma. Permanence of Noetherian rings

Every finite type algebra over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian. Every localization of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian as well.

**Proof.** Quotient ideals correspond to ideals of the original ring containing the quotient kernel, so quotients preserve the ascending chain condition. For a localization $U^{-1}R$, each ideal is the extension of its contraction to $R$: if $a/u$ belongs to it, multiplication by the unit $u/1$ puts $a/1$ in it. Finite generators of the contracted ideal therefore give finite generators after localization.

It remains to treat polynomial rings in one variable; induction and passage to a quotient then handle every finite type algebra. Let $J_1\subset J_2\subset\cdots$ be an ascending chain of ideals of $R[T]$. For $i,d\geq0$ with $i\geq1$, let $C_{i,d}$ be zero together with all leading coefficients of polynomials of degree exactly $d$ in $J_i$. This is an ideal of $R$: addition and scalar multiplication produce the required leading coefficient unless it becomes zero, which is included by definition. Multiplication of a polynomial by $T$ shows that

$$C_{i,d}\subset C_{i',d'}\qquad\text{if }i\leq i'\text{ and }d\leq d'.$$

The directed union $C=\bigcup_{i,d}C_{i,d}$ is an ideal and is finitely generated. Its finite generating list lies in some $C_{i_0,d_0}$, so that ideal equals $C$. Consequently $C_{i,d}=C$ whenever $i\geq i_0$ and $d\geq d_0$. For each of the finitely many degrees $d<d_0$, the ascending sequence $C_{i,d}$ stabilizes by Noetherianity of $R$. Choose $i_1\geq i_0$ after all these stabilizations. Then

$$C_{i,d}=C_{i_1,d}\qquad(i\geq i_1,\ d\geq0).$$

For $f\in J_i$ with $i\geq i_1$, induction on its degree now proves $f\in J_{i_1}$. If $f\ne0$ has degree $d$, the displayed equality supplies $g\in J_{i_1}$ with that degree and the same leading coefficient. The polynomial $f-g$ belongs to $J_i$ and has smaller degree, so the induction applies. Zero needs no reduction. Thus $J_i=J_{i_1}$ for all later $i$, proving that $R[T]$ is Noetherian. ∎

#### Lemma. Obtaining a separable extension

For a finitely generated field extension $K/k$, there are finite purely inseparable extensions $k'/k$ and $K'/K$, compatible with the inclusion $k\subset K$, such that $K'/k'$ is separable. They can be chosen with

$$K'=k'K\simeq(k'\otimes_k K)_{\mathrm{red}},$$

where the first expression is the compositum in a common extension field.

**Proof.** The [finite purely inseparable enlargement lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-make-separably-generated) supplies such a compatible pair with the upper field, say $E$, separably generated over $k'$. A [separably generated extension is separable](#native-algebra-lemma-separably-generated-separable). Replace $E$ by its subfield $K'=k'K$. Separability over $k'$ passes to this subfield because every finitely generated subextension of it is also one of $E/k'$. The extension $K'/K$ remains finite purely inseparable, either as a subextension of $E/K$ or by using the finite purely inseparable generators of $k'/k$.

To identify the reduced tensor product, work in characteristic $p>0$ and choose $e$ with $(k')^{p^e}\subset k$. The multiplication map $\mu:k'\otimes_k K\to k'K$ has the following property: for every tensor $z=\sum_j a_j\otimes b_j$,

$$z^{p^e}=1\otimes\sum_j a_j^{p^e}b_j^{p^e}\in1\otimes K.$$

If $\mu(z)=0$, the field inclusion $K\subset k'K$ makes the right side zero, so $z$ is nilpotent. Conversely, every nilpotent maps to zero in the field $k'K$. Thus the kernel of $\mu$ is precisely the nilradical. Its image is a finite-dimensional $K$-algebra that is a domain, and hence a field. It contains both $K$ and $k'$, so it is exactly their compositum. This proves the displayed identification. In characteristic zero one takes $k'=k$ and $K'=K$, and the same conclusion is immediate. ∎

#### Lemma. Descent of regularity

If $R\to S$ is faithfully flat and $S$ is regular, then $R$ is regular.

**Proof.** The [Noetherian descent lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-descent-noetherian) first makes $R$ Noetherian. For every prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$, faithful flatness supplies a prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ contracting to it. Localization gives a flat local map $R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}$ of Noetherian local rings. The target is regular by the hypothesis on $S$. The [local descent theorem for a flat map into a regular ring](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-under-regular) therefore makes $R_{\mathfrak p}$ regular. This holds at every prime, which is the assertion that the Noetherian ring $R$ is regular. ∎

#### Lemma. Radical ideals under a surjection of spectra

For $\varphi:R\to S$, the following are equivalent:

1. The induced map $\operatorname{Spec}S\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is surjective.
2. For every ideal $I\subset R$, one has $\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{IS})=\sqrt I$.
3. For every radical ideal $I\subset R$, one has $\varphi^{-1}(IS)=I$.
4. For every prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$, one has $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak pS)=\mathfrak p$.

These conditions are preserved by every base change $R\to R'$.

**Proof.** Radicals commute with contraction:

$$\sqrt{\varphi^{-1}(J)}=\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt J)$$

for every ideal $J\subset S$, since either membership condition says that some positive power of an element maps into $J$. If (2) holds and $I$ is radical, then

$$I\subset\varphi^{-1}(IS)\subset\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{IS})=I,$$

giving (3). Conversely, for arbitrary $I$, put $H=\sqrt I$. The equality $\sqrt{HS}=\sqrt{IS}$ follows because each element of $H$ has a power in $I$. Under (3), radical contraction gives

$$\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{IS})=\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{HS})
=\sqrt{\varphi^{-1}(HS)}=H,$$
