which proves (2). Condition (3) immediately implies (4). Under (4), if an element maps into $\sqrt{IS}$, it maps into $\sqrt{\mathfrak pS}$ for every prime $\mathfrak p\supset I$. Radical contraction and (4) put it in every such $\mathfrak p$, hence in their intersection $\sqrt I$. The opposite inclusion always holds. This proves (4)$\Rightarrow$(2).

For the remaining equivalence, fix $\mathfrak p$. Condition (4) at this prime says that $\mathfrak pS$ meets the image of $R\setminus\mathfrak p$ in no element. This is equivalent to the nonzero fibre algebra $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, whose primes correspond to primes of $S$ contracting to $\mathfrak p$. Thus (4) holds at every prime exactly when the spectrum map is onto.

Finally let $\mathfrak p'\in\operatorname{Spec}R'$ contract to $\mathfrak p$. The fibre of the base-changed map is

$$ (R'\otimes_R S)\otimes_{R'}\kappa(\mathfrak p')
\simeq (S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p))\otimes_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak p').$$

The first factor on the right is nonzero by (1), and extension of scalars between fields preserves a nonzero vector space. Hence the new fibre is nonzero. Surjectivity, and consequently all four equivalent conditions, persists after base change. ∎

#### Lemma. A reformulation of the local algebraic condition

Let $I$ be any ideal of $R$ and let $M$ be any $R$-module. Suppose $M/IM$ is flat over $R/I$ and $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R/I,M)=0$. Then:

1. The module $M/I^nM$ is flat over $R/I^n$ for every $n\geq1$.
2. If $I^mN=0$ for some $m\geq0$, then $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)=0$.

In particular, a nilpotent $I$ makes $M$ flat over $R$.

**Proof.** First take a module $N$ killed by $I$, and choose a free presentation over $R/I$ with an arbitrary basis set $E$:

$$0\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow(R/I)^{(E)}\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow0.$$

Tor commutes with direct sums in this argument, as is seen by taking the direct sum of free resolutions. The assumed Tor vanishing therefore gives an injection

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)\longrightarrow Q\otimes_R M$$

whose image is the kernel of $Q\otimes_R M\to(R/I)^{(E)}\otimes_R M$. Both modules before tensoring are annihilated by $I$, so this map is their tensor product over $R/I$ with $M/IM$. Flatness over $R/I$ makes it injective. Hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)=0$.

Induct on $m$ for (2). For $m=0$, the hypothesis says $N=0$, and the case $m=1$ was just proved. For $m>1$, use

$$0\longrightarrow IN\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow N/IN\longrightarrow0.$$

Here $I^{m-1}(IN)=0$, while $N/IN$ is killed by $I$. The two outside terms of

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(IN,M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N,M)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(N/IN,M)$$

vanish by induction, proving (2).

For (1), consider an injection of $R/I^n$-modules. Its cokernel is killed by $I^n$, so (2) shows that tensoring this injection over $R$ with $M$ remains injective. For any such module $N$ there is a canonical equality

$$N\otimes_R M\simeq N\otimes_{R/I^n}(M/I^nM).$$

Thus the latter tensor functor preserves injections and is exact, proving flatness over $R/I^n$. If $I$ is nilpotent, choose $n$ with $I^n=0$ and apply (1). No Noetherian or finite-generation hypotheses enter this proof. ∎

#### Remark. Tor for a quotient by an ideal

For any ideal $I\subset R$ and any module $M$, the canonical identification is

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)\simeq\ker(I\otimes_R M\longrightarrow M).$$

Indeed, tensor the exact sequence $0\to I\to R\to R/I\to0$ with $M$ and use $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R)=0$. The long exact sequence identifies the Tor term with this kernel. The map to $M$ is multiplication through the inclusion $I\subset R$.

#### Lemma. Finite modules over a finite ring extension

Let $S$ be a finite $R$-algebra and $M$ an $S$-module. Then $M$ is finite over $R$ if and only if it is finite over $S$.

**Proof.** Any finite list generating $M$ over $R$ also generates it over $S$, since the $S$-span contains its $R$-span. Conversely, choose $R$-module generators $s_1,\ldots,s_a$ of $S$ and $S$-module generators $m_1,\ldots,m_b$ of $M$. Expanding each $S$-coefficient in the first list shows that the finitely many products $s_im_j$ generate $M$ over $R$. ∎

#### Lemma. Finitely many maximal ideals in an Artinian ring

An Artinian ring has finitely many maximal ideals.

**Proof.** If there were infinitely many, choose distinct maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_1,\mathfrak m_2,\ldots$. The finite intersections $J_n=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\mathfrak m_i$ would form a strictly descending chain. For strictness, the Chinese remainder theorem supplies an element with residue zero at the first $n$ maximal ideals and residue one at $\mathfrak m_{n+1}$, because distinct maximal ideals are pairwise comaximal. This element lies in $J_n$ and not in $J_{n+1}$. The resulting chain contradicts the Artinian condition. The zero ring has no maximal ideals and satisfies the assertion as well. ∎

#### Lemma. Nilpotence of the radical of an Artinian ring

The Jacobson radical of an Artinian ring is nilpotent.

**Proof.** Let $I$ be that radical. The descending chain of its powers stabilizes, so choose $n\geq1$ with $I^n=I^{n+1}$. Put $J=\operatorname{Ann}_R(I^n)$. We prove $J=R$ without assuming that $I^n$ is finitely generated.

If $J\ne R$, the descending chain condition in $R/J$ supplies a minimal nonzero ideal. Its inverse image is an ideal $J'\supsetneq J$ for which $J'/J$ is a simple $R$-module. Every simple module is $R/\mathfrak m$ for a maximal ideal: a nonzero element generates it, and its annihilator is maximal. Thus $\mathfrak mJ'\subset J$. Multiplication by $I^n$ gives

$$\mathfrak m I^nJ'=0.$$

Since $I\subset\mathfrak m$, this implies $I^{n+1}J'=0$. The equality $I^{n+1}=I^n$ now puts every element of $J'$ in $\operatorname{Ann}_R(I^n)=J$, contradicting $J'\supsetneq J$. Hence $J=R$ and $I^n=0$, as required. ∎

#### Lemma. Vector-space dimension and module length

If $\mathfrak m$ is a maximal ideal of $R$ and $\mathfrak mM=0$, then the length of $M$ over $R$ equals its dimension as an $R/\mathfrak m$-vector space, with both taken to be infinite when there is no finite bound. In particular, this length is finite exactly when $M$ is a finite $R$-module.

**Proof.** The action factors through the field $R/\mathfrak m$, and the $R$-submodules are exactly its vector subspaces. For a finite basis, the successive spans give a composition series with one-dimensional factors. Conversely, a simple nonzero vector space has dimension one, so every composition series has exactly the number of factors given by the dimension. An infinite-dimensional vector space contains independent lists of every finite size; their spans produce strict chains of arbitrarily large finite length, giving infinite length. Finally, a list generates over $R$ exactly when it spans over $R/\mathfrak m$, proving the finiteness equivalence, including $M=0$. ∎

#### Lemma. Lifting a map from a finite free module

Suppose $\alpha\colon R^n\to M$ and $\beta\colon N\to M$ are linear maps and $\alpha(R^n)\subset\beta(N)$. There is an $R$-linear map $\gamma\colon R^n\to N$ with $\beta\gamma=\alpha$.

**Proof.** For each standard basis vector $e_i$, select $u_i\in N$ mapping to $\alpha(e_i)$. The formula $\gamma(\sum_i a_ie_i)=\sum_i a_iu_i$ defines the required map: its composite with $\beta$ agrees with $\alpha$ on a basis. When $n=0$, the unique map from the zero module works. ∎

#### Lemma. Generic smoothness for an inclusion of domains

Let $R\subset S$ be domains, with $S$ finitely generated as an $R$-algebra. Write $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and $L=\operatorname{Frac}(S)$. The map $R\to S$ is smooth at the zero prime precisely when $L/K$ is separable.

**Proof.** Suppose first that a nonzero $h\in S$ makes $S_h$ smooth over $R$. For every extension field $K'/K$, [smooth base change](#native-algebra-lemma-base-change-smooth) makes $S_h\otimes_R K'$ smooth over $K'$. The complete parameter and Jacobian proof in AG-CA 18, Sections 1–2, Theorem 2.1 makes this ring regular, hence reduced. Localizing it further gives $L\otimes_K K'$, which is therefore reduced as well. Thus $L$ is geometrically reduced over $K$, using [localization permanence](#native-algebra-lemma-geometrically-reduced-permanence). The [field separability criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-separable-field-extensions) now proves that $L/K$ is separable.

For the reverse implication, [generic finite presentation](#native-algebra-lemma-generic-finite-presentation) supplies nonzero $f\in R$ and $g\in S$ for which $R_f\to S_{fg}$ is finitely presented. Both localizations matter here. Put $T=S_{fg}\otimes_{R_f}K$. This is a finite-type domain over $K$, and its local ring at zero is $L$. That local ring is regular, and its residue extension over $K$ is separable. Consequently AG-CA 18, Theorem 3.2 and its complete split-cotangent proof show that $T$ is smooth over $K$ at zero. Here a finitely generated separable field extension is separably generated, by the earlier [separability tests](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-separable-field-extensions).

Apply [descent of the smooth locus under flat base change](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-base-change-locus-smooth) to $R_f\to S_{fg}$ and $R_f\to K$, at their zero primes. It gives smoothness of $R_f\to S_{fg}$ at zero. After one further principal localization of the target, this map is smooth everywhere. Its composite with the smooth localization $R\to R_f$ is smooth, proving the assertion about $R\to S$. ∎

#### Lemma. The open part of an integral closure for a quasi-finite algebra

Let $S$ be a finite-type, quasi-finite $R$-algebra, and let $C\subset S$ be the subalgebra of elements integral over $R$. Then:

1. The map $\operatorname{Spec}S\to\operatorname{Spec}C$ identifies the source homeomorphically with an open subset $U$.
2. Whenever $g\in C$ satisfies $D_C(g)\subset U$, the natural map $C_g\to S_g$ is an isomorphism.
3. There is an $R$-subalgebra $D\subset C$, finite as an $R$-module, for which both preceding conclusions hold with $D$ in place of $C$.

**Proof.** At each prime of $S$, use the pointwise algebraic Zariski Main Theorem: its complete monogenic, conductor and induction proof is AG-MO 06, Section 2A, Theorem 2A.1, with the two conductor prerequisites identified there. This is also the [affine algebra theorem](#native-algebra-theorem-main-theorem) used below. It supplies an element of $C$ outside the given prime whose localization makes $C$ and $S$ equal. By [quasi-compactness](#native-algebra-lemma-quasi-compact), choose finitely many such elements $g_1,\ldots,g_r$ covering $\operatorname{Spec}S$. Thus

$$C_{g_i}=S_{g_i},\qquad \operatorname{Spec}S=\bigcup_i D_S(g_i).$$

Each displayed chart maps isomorphically to $D_C(g_i)$. The whole image is therefore $U=\bigcup_iD_C(g_i)$, an open subset. To check injectivity globally, suppose two primes of $S$ contract to the same prime of $C$. Choose $g_i$ outside the first prime. Since $g_i\in C$, it is outside the second as well. Both points belong to the same chart, where the map is injective, so they coincide. On these charts the map and its inverse are continuous; the charts cover source and image. This proves (1).

If $D_C(g)\subset U$, the elements $g_i$ generate the unit ideal in $C_g$: their principal opens cover its spectrum. After localizing at any $g_i$, the map $C_g\to S_g$ becomes the known isomorphism $C_{gg_i}\to S_{gg_i}$. The [finite-cover module criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-cover), applied to its kernel and cokernel, proves (2).

For (3), choose for each $i$ a finite algebra generating list for $S_{g_i}$ over $R$. Express its members in $C_{g_i}$ as fractions with numerators $c_{ij}\in C$ and powers of $g_i$ as denominators. Let

$$D=R[g_1,\ldots,g_r,c_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j]\subset C.$$

All the adjoined elements are integral over $R$, so the [finite integral-generation criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-finite-in-terms-of-integral) makes $D$ finite over $R$. The localization $D_{g_i}\to S_{g_i}$ is injective because $D\subset S$, and is surjective by the chosen generating list. The same chart, injectivity and gluing arguments now prove (1) and (2) for $D\to S$. They require the $g_i$ to cover $\operatorname{Spec}S$, not all of $\operatorname{Spec}D$. If $S=0$, take $C=D=0$; all assertions hold on empty spectra. ∎

#### Lemma. A finite closed fibre gives a finite map of completions

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)$ be a local ring homomorphism. Assume that both maximal ideals are finitely generated and that $S/\mathfrak mS$ has finite dimension over $R/\mathfrak m$. Denote the maximal-ideal completions by $\widehat R$ and $\widehat S$. Then $\widehat S$ is canonically the $\mathfrak mS$-adic completion of $S$, and is a finite $\widehat R$-module.

**Proof.** Locality gives $\mathfrak mS\subset\mathfrak n$. The quotient $S/\mathfrak mS$ is a finite-dimensional algebra over a field, so it is Artinian; its unique prime is its maximal ideal. Thus $\sqrt{\mathfrak mS}=\mathfrak n$. Since $\mathfrak n$ has a finite generating list, some positive integer $t$ satisfies $\mathfrak n^t\subset\mathfrak mS$: choose a power of each generator in $\mathfrak mS$, and use a sufficiently large total degree. Consequently

$$\mathfrak n^{tq}\subset\mathfrak m^qS\subset\mathfrak n^q\qquad(q\geq1).$$

These cofinal filtrations give the first identification by [change of completion ideal](#native-algebra-lemma-change-ideal-completion).

The [completion theorem for a finitely generated ideal](#native-algebra-lemma-hathat-finitely-generated), applied to $\mathfrak m$ and the $R$-modules $R,S$, identifies the kernels of the quotient projections with the powers of the extended ideal. In particular, for $I=\mathfrak m\widehat R$, both $\widehat R$ and $\widehat S$ are $I$-adically complete and

$$\widehat R/I=R/\mathfrak m,\qquad \widehat S/I\widehat S=S/\mathfrak mS.$$

The second quotient is finite over the first. Apply the [finite-module theorem over a complete ring](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-over-complete-ring) to the separated $\widehat R$-module $\widehat S$. It is finite, as asserted. No Noetherian hypothesis has been used. ∎

#### Proposition. Ten descriptions of an Artinian ring

For a commutative ring $R$, the following conditions are equivalent:

1. Descending chains of ideals in $R$ stabilize.
2. The ring is Noetherian and has Krull dimension at most zero.
3. The $R$-module $R$ has finite length.
4. The ring is a finite product of Artinian local rings.
5. The ring is Noetherian and its spectrum is finite and discrete.
6. The ring is a finite product of Noetherian local rings of dimension zero.
7. The ring is a finite product of Noetherian local rings $R_i$ with $d(R_i)=0$.
8. The ring is a finite product of Noetherian local rings with nilpotent maximal ideals.
9. The ring is Noetherian, its maximal ideals form a finite set, and its Jacobson radical is nilpotent.
10. The ring is Noetherian and no prime properly contains another prime.

Here $d(R_i)$ is the least number of generators of an ideal of definition in the local ring, as in the [local dimension theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-dimension). The empty product is the zero ring; every local factor in a nonempty product is nonzero.

**Proof.** The complete finite-length and radical arguments in AG-CA 03, Sections 3–4, Theorem 4.2 prove (1), (2) and (3) equivalent. They also identify an Artinian ring with the product of its finitely many maximal localizations. Thus (1) implies (4). Conversely, ideals in a finite product split into their coordinate ideals by multiplication with the coordinate idempotents. A descending chain stabilizes in every Artinian factor, hence in the product. This proves (4) implies (1) and retains the [local-product description](#native-algebra-lemma-product-local).

Apply the same structure theorem to a nonzero local ring. It is Artinian exactly when it is Noetherian of dimension zero. The [dimension and parameter theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-dimension) equates its dimension with $d(R_i)$. In a Noetherian local ring of dimension zero, the maximal ideal is the nilradical and is nilpotent: it has finitely many generators, each nilpotent. Conversely, a nilpotent maximal ideal is contained in every prime, so it is the only prime. These observations prove the equivalence of (4), (6), (7) and (8), factor by factor.

The local-product description makes the spectrum of an Artinian ring a finite discrete set, proving (1) implies (5). If (5) holds, every point of the spectrum is closed. Since the closure of $\{\mathfrak p\}$ consists of the primes containing $\mathfrak p$, this gives (10). Conditions (10) and (2) agree by the definition of dimension.

Finally, the radical proof in the cited structure theorem gives (1) implies (9). Suppose (9), and write $J$ for the Jacobson radical. Chinese remainders identify $R/J$ with the finite product of the residue fields at the maximal ideals. Each $J^a/J^{a+1}$ is finite, since $R$ is Noetherian, and is a module over this product of fields. Its coordinate vector spaces are therefore finite-dimensional, so it has finite length. A power of $J$ is zero; adding the lengths along this finite filtration proves (3). The zero ring satisfies all ten conditions, with the empty-product convention. ∎

#### Lemma. Regularity descends along a flat local map

Suppose $(R,\mathfrak m)\to S$ is a flat local homomorphism between Noetherian local rings. If $S$ is regular, then $R$ is regular.

**Proof.** A flat local map is faithfully flat. Let $d=\dim S$. When $d=0$, regularity makes $S$ a field. The local map sends $\mathfrak m$ to zero, whereas faithful flatness makes $R\to S$ injective. Hence $\mathfrak m=0$, and $R$ is a field as well.

Assume $d\geq1$, and put $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. Noetherianity permits a free resolution of $\kappa$ with finite terms $F_i$. Write $F_{-1}=\kappa$ for the augmented target and set

$$K_d=\ker(F_{d-1}\longrightarrow F_{d-2}).$$

For $d=1$, this means the kernel of $F_0\to\kappa$. Flatness preserves the exact sequence

$$0\longrightarrow K_d\otimes_R S\longrightarrow F_{d-1}\otimes_R S\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_0\otimes_R S\longrightarrow\kappa\otimes_R S\longrightarrow0.$$

The complete homological criterion in AG-CA 14, Section 2, Theorem 2.2 gives $\operatorname{gl.dim}S=d$. Thus this $d$th syzygy is projective, by [independence of projective resolutions](#native-algebra-lemma-independent-resolution). It is finite, since $K_d$ is finite over $R$, and hence is free over the local ring $S$. By [faithfully flat descent of finite projectivity](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-projective-descends), $K_d$ is finite projective over $R$, and therefore free. Truncating the resolution at $K_d$ gives finite projective dimension to $\kappa$. The converse in the same homological criterion now proves that $R$ is regular. ∎

#### Lemma. Normalization after restricting a domain base

Let $R\subset S$ be an inclusion with $R$ a domain and $S$ a finite-type $R$-algebra. There are algebraically independent elements $y_1,\ldots,y_d$ over $R$ and an intermediate ring

$$R\subset R[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\subset D\subset S$$

such that $D$ is finite over $R[y_1,\ldots,y_d]$ and $D_f=S_f$ for some nonzero $f\in R$.

**Proof.** Choose algebra generators $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ for $S/R$ and put $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. The algebra $S_K$ is nonzero because $R\subset S$. The [integer-coordinate form of Noether normalization](#native-algebra-lemma-noether-normalization) supplies elements $y_j$ that are integer polynomials in the $x_i$, with $K[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\subset S_K$ finite. In particular the $y_j$ are elements of $S$. Any polynomial relation over $R$ between them would remain a relation over $K$, so $R[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\to S$ is injective.

Each $x_i$ satisfies a monic polynomial $P_i(T)\in K[y_1,\ldots,y_d][T]$ of positive degree $e_i$. Choose nonzero $f_0\in R$ clearing all its coefficients. The element $f_0P_i(x_i)\in S$ vanishes in $S_K$, hence is annihilated by some nonzero element of $R$. Multiplying $f_0$ by these finitely many annihilators gives nonzero $f\in R$ such that all coefficients of $fP_i$ lie in $R[y_1,\ldots,y_d]$ and all $fP_i(x_i)$ vanish in $S$. This additional annihilation step allows $S$ to have $R$-torsion.

The polynomial

$$Q_i(T)=f^{e_i}P_i(T/f)$$

is monic over $R[y_1,\ldots,y_d]$: the coefficient of $T^j$ for $j<e_i$ is $f^{e_i-j}$ times the corresponding coefficient of $P_i$, and $e_i-j\geq1$. Moreover $Q_i(fx_i)=f^{e_i-1}(fP_i(x_i))=0$. Therefore

$$D=R[y_1,\ldots,y_d,fx_1,\ldots,fx_n]$$

is finite over the polynomial subring, by the [integral-generation criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-finite-in-terms-of-integral). Localization preserves its inclusion in $S$, and every $x_i=(fx_i)/f$ lies in $D_f$. This proves $D_f=S_f$. ∎

#### Lemma. Completion for cofinal ideal powers

Suppose ideals $I,J\subset R$ satisfy $I^c\subset J$ and $J^d\subset I$ for positive integers $c,d$. Every $R$-module has canonically isomorphic $I$-adic and $J$-adic completions. In particular, completeness for either ideal is equivalent to completeness for the other.

**Proof.** For each $n\geq1$,

$$I^{cn}M\subset J^nM,\qquad J^{dn}M\subset I^nM.$$

The resulting quotient maps induce maps in both directions between the inverse limits. Their composites are the transition maps obtained by passing to the cofinal indices $cdn$, hence act as the identity on each inverse limit. These isomorphisms commute with the canonical map from $M$, proving the completeness assertion. Equivalently, one may index the quotient maps by $M/I^nM\to M/J^{\lfloor n/c\rfloor}M$ and $M/J^nM\to M/I^{\lfloor n/d\rfloor}M$, omitting initial zero indices. ∎

#### Lemma. Lifting finite generation over a complete ring

Let $R$ be complete for the powers of an ideal $I$, and let $M$ be an $R$-module with $\bigcap_{n\geq1}I^nM=0$. If $M/IM$ is finite over $R/I$, then $M$ is finite over $R$.

**Proof.** Lift a finite generating list of $M/IM$ to $x_1,\ldots,x_r\in M$, and put $M_0=\sum_iRx_i$. Then $M=M_0+IM$, and multiplication by $I^n$ gives

$$I^nM=I^nM_0+I^{n+1}M.$$

For $x\in M$, choose coefficients $a_i^{(1)}$ making $x-\sum_i a_i^{(1)}x_i\in IM$. Given coefficients with error in $I^nM$, the displayed equality supplies corrections in $I^n$ making the next error lie in $I^{n+1}M$. Thus we may arrange

$$a_i^{(n+1)}-a_i^{(n)}\in I^n,\qquad x-\sum_i a_i^{(n)}x_i\in I^nM.$$

Completeness of $R$ supplies $a_i\in R$ with $a_i-a_i^{(n)}\in I^n$ for every $n$. It follows that $x-\sum_i a_ix_i$ belongs to every $I^nM$, and is zero by separation. Hence the $x_i$ generate $M$. Neither finite generation of $I$ nor completeness of $M$ was assumed.

The original completion argument gives the same result and also identifies the completion of $M$. By [completion generalities](#native-algebra-lemma-completion-generalities), the map $\widehat M_0\to\widehat M$ is surjective, since $M_0/IM_0\to M/IM$ is surjective. The submodule $M_0$ is separated because $I^nM_0\subset I^nM$. It is finite, so the [finite separated module theorem over a complete ring](#native-algebra-lemma-when-finite-module-complete-over-complete-ring) makes $M_0$ complete. Thus $M_0\to\widehat M$ is surjective. The map $M\to\widehat M$ is injective by separation; since $M_0\subset M$, these statements force $M=M_0\cong\widehat M$. ∎

#### Lemma. Integral maps and dimension

An integral homomorphism $R\to S$ satisfies $\dim S\leq\dim R$. Under its spectrum map, the image of a closed point is again closed.

**Proof.** In a strict prime chain of $S$, consecutive primes have different contractions by [incomparability](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-no-inclusion). Contraction therefore gives a strict chain of the same length in $R$, proving the dimension inequality. For a maximal ideal $\mathfrak q$ of $S$, put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. The field $S/\mathfrak q$ is integral over the embedded domain $R/\mathfrak p$. For a nonzero element $a$ of this domain, its inverse in that field satisfies a monic equation. Multiplication of that equation by $a^{n-1}$ expresses $a^{-1}$ as an element of $R/\mathfrak p$. Thus $R/\mathfrak p$ is a field and $\mathfrak p$ is maximal, as in the [maximal-prime criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-going-up-maximal-on-top). ∎

#### Lemma. A reduced ring at a minimal prime

If $\mathfrak p$ is minimal among the primes of $R$, every element of $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$ is nilpotent. When $R$ is reduced, $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a field.

**Proof.** Primes of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ correspond to primes of $R$ contained in $\mathfrak p$, so its maximal ideal is its only prime. It is therefore the nilradical. Equivalently, a nonnilpotent element in that maximal ideal would define a nonempty principal open by the [spectrum criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-zariski-topology), whereas the unique point would not belong to it. If $R$ is reduced, so is its localization: a nilpotent fraction $a/s$ has $ta^n=0$ for some inverted $t$, so $(ta)^n=0$, hence $ta=0$ and $a/s=0$. Its maximal ideal is consequently zero, making this nonzero local ring a field. ∎

#### Lemma. Geometric regularity over a directed union of subfields

Suppose $k$ is the directed union of subfields $k_i$ and $A$ is a $k$-algebra. If $A$ is geometrically regular as a $k_i$-algebra for every $i$, it is geometrically regular over $k$.

**Proof.** The hypothesis already makes $A$ Noetherian and regular. By the [finite purely inseparable test](#native-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular), it remains to check regularity of $A\otimes_k k'$ for a finite purely inseparable extension $k'/k$.

In positive characteristic, express this extension as a finite tower adjoining elements $\alpha_j$ with minimal polynomials $X^{p^{e_j}}-b_j$ over the preceding field. Each $b_j$ is a rational expression in the earlier $\alpha$'s with finitely many coefficients in $k$. Choose one $k_i$ containing all these coefficients, and form the corresponding tower inside $k'$ starting at $k_i$. Each displayed polynomial is still irreducible over this smaller preceding field, because a factorization there would also be a factorization over the larger preceding field. Thus the smaller tower, with final field $k_i'$, has the same successive degrees. Multiplication gives a surjection $k\otimes_{k_i}k_i'\to k'$: the image contains $k$ and all the $\alpha_j$, and is a finite-dimensional domain over $k$, hence a field. The two sides have the same dimension over $k$, so this map is an isomorphism. The extension $k_i'/k_i$ is finite purely inseparable by construction. Therefore

$$A\otimes_k k'\cong A\otimes_{k_i}k_i'$$

is regular by the hypothesis. In characteristic zero the only finite purely inseparable extension is the field itself, so the test is immediate. ∎

#### Lemma. Smooth ascent of geometric regularity

For a smooth homomorphism $A\to B$ of $k$-algebras, geometric regularity of $A$ over the field $k$ implies geometric regularity of $B$ over $k$.

**Proof.** For any finitely generated extension field $k'/k$, [base change](#native-algebra-lemma-base-change-smooth) makes $A\otimes_k k'\to B\otimes_k k'$ smooth. Its source is regular by assumption, and [regularity ascent](#native-algebra-lemma-regular-goes-up) makes its target regular. Noetherianity of the target follows as well from finite type over the Noetherian source. This is the defining field-extension test for geometric regularity of $B$. ∎

#### Definition. Formal smoothness

An $R$-algebra $S$ is **formally smooth over $R$** if the following lifting property holds. For every $R$-algebra $A$, every ideal $I\subset A$ with $I^2=0$, and every $R$-algebra homomorphism $u\colon S\to A/I$, there is an $R$-algebra homomorphism $\widetilde u\colon S\to A$ whose composite with $A\to A/I$ is $u$. Thus the lift must respect the specified map from $R$, as well as the quotient map.

#### Lemma. Completion at a finitely generated ideal is complete

*Historical source credit:* Matlis, Theorem 15, is the citation in the original source. The proof below follows the argument credited there to Bjorn Poonen's email of 5 November 2016.

For a finitely generated ideal $I\subset R$ and an arbitrary $R$-module $M$, put $\widehat M=\varprojlim_r M/I^rM$. Then, for every $n\geq1$, the natural maps identify

$$I^n\widehat M=\ker(\widehat M\longrightarrow M/I^nM)=\widehat{I^nM}.$$

In particular, $\widehat M$ is complete for its $I$-adic filtration. Taking $M=R$ gives $I^n\widehat R=\widehat{I^n}$ and $\widehat R/I^n\widehat R=R/I^n$.

**Proof.** The ideal $I^n$ has a finite generating list $a_1,\ldots,a_s$. Complete the surjection

$$M^s\longrightarrow I^nM,\qquad (m_j)_j\longmapsto\sum_j a_jm_j.$$

The [surjectivity theorem for completions](#native-algebra-lemma-completion-generalities) and commutation of inverse limits with finite products give a surjection $(\widehat M)^s\to\widehat{I^nM}$. The intrinsic filtration on $I^nM$ consists of $I^{n+r}M$, so

$$\widehat{I^nM}=\varprojlim_{r\geq n}I^nM/I^rM.$$

This limit embeds naturally in $\widehat M$ and is exactly the kernel of its projection to $M/I^nM$: an element of that kernel has, at every later level $r$, a component in $I^nM/I^rM$, and conversely such compatible components give an element of the kernel. The composite from $(\widehat M)^s$ to $\widehat M$ is multiplication by the list $(a_j)$, whose image is $I^n\widehat M$. This proves all three identifications. The quotient projection is surjective, since every residue class has a representative in $M$. Hence

$$\widehat M/I^n\widehat M\cong M/I^nM.$$

These isomorphisms respect the transition maps. Taking their inverse limit identifies the canonical map from $\widehat M$ to its own completion with an isomorphism, proving completeness without any Noetherian hypothesis. ∎

#### Lemma. Flat ascent of the condition $(R_k)$

Let $R\to S$ be flat, with both rings Noetherian. Suppose $R$ and every fibre algebra $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ satisfy $(R_k)$, meaning regularity at primes whose local rings have dimension at most $k$. Then $S$ satisfies $(R_k)$.

**Proof.** Choose $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ with $\dim S_{\mathfrak q}\leq k$, and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. The induced local map is flat. The [dimension equality for a flat local map](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-base-fibre-equals-total) reads

$$\dim S_{\mathfrak q}=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim(S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}).$$

Both summands are nonnegative, so each is at most $k$. The assumptions make $R_{\mathfrak p}$ regular and make the displayed local fibre regular. The [regular-base and regular-fibre criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre) therefore makes $S_{\mathfrak q}$ regular. This checks every required prime. ∎

#### Lemma. Every module is a directed colimit of finitely presented modules

An arbitrary $R$-module $M$ is the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented $R$-modules.

**Proof.** For a finite subset $F\subset M$, let $R^F\to M$ send the basis vector $e_x$ to $x$. Choose any finite subset $E$ of its kernel and form

$$M_{F,E}=R^F/\langle E\rangle.$$

It has a presentation with finitely many generators and relations, and its evaluation map to $M$ is well-defined. Order the pairs $(F,E)$ by enlarging $F$ and enlarging $E$ after extending old relation vectors by zero in the new coordinates. The resulting coordinate inclusions induce compatible maps between these modules. Any two pairs have a common upper bound: take the union of their finite generating subsets and the union of their extended relation subsets. Thus the index set is directed.

Every $x\in M$ comes from the stage with $F=\{x\}$ and no relations, proving surjectivity of the colimit map. An element at a stage that maps to zero in $M$ is represented by a vector $v\in R^F$ in the evaluation kernel. Adjoining the single relation $v$ to $E$ kills this element at a later stage. This proves injectivity and establishes the asserted colimit, including the zero module. ∎

#### Lemma. Exactness of a countable Mittag–Leffler inverse limit

Let a countable directed set index short exact sequences of abelian groups

$$0\longrightarrow A_i\longrightarrow B_i\longrightarrow C_i\longrightarrow0,$$

compatible with inverse-system transition maps. If the system $(A_i)$ is Mittag–Leffler, then

$$0\longrightarrow\varprojlim_i A_i\longrightarrow\varprojlim_i B_i\longrightarrow\varprojlim_i C_i\longrightarrow0$$

is exact. The Mittag–Leffler hypothesis says that, for each $i$, the images of $A_j\to A_i$ are constant once $j$ is sufficiently large.

**Proof.** Limits preserve kernels, which gives exactness at the first two terms. Fix a compatible family $c=(c_i)$ in the last limit, and let $E_i\subset B_i$ be the inverse image of $c_i$. These are nonempty sets, preserved by the transition maps. A compatible family in the $E_i$ is exactly a lift of $c$.

View $A_i$ as a subgroup of $B_i$. Fix $i$ and choose $j\geq i$ for which the images of $A_k\to A_i$ have stabilized for all $k\geq j$. To prove the same stabilization for $E_k\to E_i$, choose $e_j\in E_j$ and any $e_k'\in E_k$. If $e_j'$ is the image of $e_k'$ in $B_j$, then $e_j-e_j'\in A_j$. Stabilization supplies $a_k\in A_k$ whose image in $A_i$ equals the image of $e_j-e_j'$. Thus $e_k'+a_k\in E_k$ maps to the same element of $E_i$ as $e_j$. The opposite image inclusion follows from the transition maps. Hence $(E_i)$ is a Mittag–Leffler system of nonempty sets.

Here is the [nonempty-limit argument](#native-algebra-lemma-ml-limit-nonempty) explicitly. Enumerate the countable index set and, by directedness, choose an increasing cofinal sequence dominating successive entries. Restriction to it leaves the inverse limit unchanged. For a sequence of nonempty Mittag–Leffler sets, replace each set by the eventual image of all sufficiently late sets in it. The replacement sets remain nonempty and their transition maps are surjective: for an element of an earlier eventual image, lift it from a stage late enough to realize both relevant eventual images. Starting with any element in the first replacement set, choose a preimage at each successive stage. The resulting compatible sequence gives an element of the original limit. Applying this to $(E_i)$ lifts $c$ and proves surjectivity. ∎

#### Lemma. Maps out of a localized module

Let $\Sigma\subset R$ be multiplicative and suppose multiplication by each $s\in\Sigma$ is an automorphism of the $R$-module $N$. For every $R$-module $M$, restriction along $M\to\Sigma^{-1}M$ gives an isomorphism

$$\operatorname{Hom}_R(\Sigma^{-1}M,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N).$$

**Proof.** Write $s^{-1}$ for the inverse of the multiplication operator on $N$. A map $v\colon\Sigma^{-1}M\to N$ must satisfy $v(m/s)=s^{-1}v(m/1)$, so restriction determines it uniquely.

Conversely, given $u\colon M\to N$, define $v(m/s)=s^{-1}u(m)$. If $m/s=m'/s'$, there is $t\in\Sigma$ with $t(s'm-sm')=0$. Applying $u$ and canceling the invertible operator $t$ gives $s'u(m)=su(m')$. Applying $(ss')^{-1}$ proves that the two proposed values agree. The inverse multiplication operators are $R$-linear and commute. Using a common denominator $ss'$ therefore gives

$$v(rm/s+r'm'/s')=r\,s^{-1}u(m)+r'\,(s')^{-1}u(m')$$

for $r,r'\in R$. Thus $v$ is linear and restricts to $u$. Both constructions are linear and inverse, proving the isomorphism. ∎

#### Lemma. Stable module isomorphism from a two-term homotopy equivalence

Let $A_1\xrightarrow{d_A}A_0$ and $B_1\xrightarrow{d_B}B_0$ be complexes of $R$-modules. If chain maps $\varphi\colon A_\bullet\to B_\bullet$ and $\psi\colon B_\bullet\to A_\bullet$ are inverse up to chain homotopy, then

$$A_1\oplus B_0\cong B_1\oplus A_0.$$

**Proof.** Choose homotopies $h\colon A_0\to A_1$ and $h'\colon B_0\to B_1$ with

$$1-\psi_1\varphi_1=h d_A,\qquad 1-\psi_0\varphi_0=d_Ah,$$
$$1-\varphi_1\psi_1=h'd_B,\qquad 1-\varphi_0\psi_0=d_Bh'.$$

Consider the maps in the indicated direct-sum orders

$$F=\begin{pmatrix}\varphi_1&-h'\\ d_A&\psi_0\end{pmatrix}\colon A_1\oplus B_0\longrightarrow B_1\oplus A_0,$$
$$G=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_1&h\\ -d_B&\varphi_0\end{pmatrix}\colon B_1\oplus A_0\longrightarrow A_1\oplus B_0.$$

The homotopy equations give their diagonal entries, while the chain-map equations $d_B\varphi_1=\varphi_0d_A$ and $d_A\psi_1=\psi_0d_B$ make their lower-left entries zero. Multiplication in both orders yields

$$GF=\begin{pmatrix}1&h\psi_0-\psi_1h'\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad FG=\begin{pmatrix}1&\varphi_1h-h'\varphi_0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Each matrix is invertible, with inverse obtained by negating its upper-right entry. Thus $(GF)^{-1}G$ is a left inverse of $F$, and $G(FG)^{-1}$ is a right inverse. A left and a right inverse of the same map coincide, so $F$ is the required isomorphism. ∎

#### Lemma. Lifting a regular sequence from the closed fibre

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)$ be a flat local map of Noetherian local rings. Suppose the images of $f_1,\ldots,f_c\in S$ form a regular sequence in $S/\mathfrak mS$. Then the sequence is regular in $S$, and each $S/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)$ is flat over $R$.

**Proof.** Regularity of the fibre sequence includes properness of its final ideal. In a local ring this places every image, and hence every $f_i$, in the maximal ideal. Use the complete injection and quotient-flatness proof in AG-CA 08, Section 5, Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.3. It first makes $f_1$ a nonzerodivisor in $S$ and makes $S/f_1S$ flat over $R$. This quotient is again Noetherian local, and its closed fibre is the quotient of the original closed fibre by $\overline f_1$. Apply the same assertion to $f_2$, and repeat. At each step the next fibre element is regular by hypothesis and remains in the maximal ideal, so the quotient stays nonzero. This proves both the full regular sequence and every claimed flatness statement. For $c=0$, the sequence is empty and the assertion is the given flatness. ∎

#### Lemma. A finite-type integer model for a relative global complete intersection

Suppose the presentation $S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ is a relative global complete intersection. There is a finite-type $\mathbf Z$-subalgebra $R_0\subset R$ containing all coefficients of the $f_i$ such that the same presentation

$$S_0=R_0[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$$

is a relative global complete intersection over $R_0$.

**Proof.** Begin with the integer subalgebra generated by the finitely many coefficients, denoted $R_0$ provisionally. Then $S=R\otimes_{R_0}S_0$. If $S=0$, the relation $1\in(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ has finitely many polynomial coefficients in $R$. Adjoin these coefficients to $R_0$. The same relation then gives $S_0=0$, which satisfies the definition because it has no nonempty fibres.

Assume $S\ne0$. A prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$ contracts to primes $\mathfrak p\subset R$, $\mathfrak q_0\subset S_0$ and $\mathfrak p_0\subset R_0$. Its fibre over $\mathfrak p$ has dimension $n-c$. This fibre is obtained from $S_0\otimes_{R_0}\kappa(\mathfrak p_0)$ by extending the field to $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The [field-extension dimension theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-preserved-field-extension) therefore gives dimension $n-c$ to the earlier fibre as well. The [local upper bound on fibre dimension](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-fibres-bounded-open-upstairs) supplies a principal neighborhood $D(g)$ of $\mathfrak q_0$ on which all fibre dimensions are at most $n-c$.

As $\mathfrak q$ varies, these principal opens pull back to a cover of $\operatorname{Spec}S$. Choose finitely many of them, with elements $g_1,\ldots,g_r\in S_0$. Their images generate the unit ideal in $S$, so there are $u_i\in S$ with $\sum_i u_ig_i=1$. Represent the $u_i$ by polynomials over $R$, and represent this equality modulo $(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ by finitely many polynomial relations. Adjoin all their coefficients to $R_0$. For the resulting larger finite-type integer subalgebra, the same equality holds in $S_0$, and the $D(g_i)$ cover its entire spectrum.

The fibre bound on each chart survives this enlargement: each new fibre is an extension of the earlier residue field followed by the same localization, and field extension preserves dimension. Thus every nonempty fibre of the new $S_0/R_0$ has dimension at most $n-c$. For the reverse inequality, choose a maximal ideal in any such fibre. The polynomial local ring at its inverse image has dimension $n$, by the [polynomial dimension theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-prime-polynomial-ring). All $c$ equations lie in its maximal ideal. Applying the [one-equation dimension bound](#native-algebra-lemma-one-equation) successively shows that the fibre's local ring there has dimension at least $n-c$. Thus the whole fibre also has dimension at least $n-c$. The two inequalities give the required equality on every nonempty fibre, proving the statement for this final $R_0$. ∎

#### Lemma. Filtered colimits commute with homology

For a directed system of three-term complexes of $R$-modules

$$L_i\xrightarrow{u_i}M_i\xrightarrow{v_i}N_i,$$

write $H_i=\ker(v_i)/\operatorname{im}(u_i)$. The colimit is a complex, and its middle homology is canonically $\varinjlim_i H_i$. In particular, directed colimits are exact. The same assertions hold for any filtered index category.

**Proof.** The transition maps preserve cycles and boundaries, hence induce maps on the $H_i$ and a canonical map from their colimit to the homology $H$ of the colimit complex. Composition is zero in the colimit because it is zero at every stage.

We use the element description of a directed colimit: each element has a representative at a stage, and two representatives agree exactly when they agree at a common later stage. Thus a cycle in $\varinjlim_iM_i$ has a representative $m_i\in M_i$ whose image under $v_i$ becomes zero later. Move to that later stage; the representative is now a cycle there. This proves surjectivity onto $H$.

For injectivity, suppose a cycle $m_i$ represents a class mapping to zero in $H$. Its colimit image is the image of some element represented by $l_j\in L_j$. At a common later stage, the images of $m_i$ and $u_j(l_j)$ agree. The class of $m_i$ is therefore zero in that stage's homology, so it is zero in $\varinjlim_iH_i$.

For a filtered category, the same element description holds with arrows to a common object in place of passage to a larger index. Indeed, form the equivalence relation on the disjoint union of the underlying sets by declaring two elements equivalent when arrows to a common object give equal images. Filteredness supplies common targets, and its equalization of parallel arrows makes this relation transitive and makes addition and scalar multiplication independent of all choices. It gives the module colimit. Consequently every zero or equality used in the two preceding paragraphs is again witnessed at one object. Those arguments prove the filtered assertion too. Applying homology commutation to exact complexes, including zero end terms, proves exactness of filtered colimits. ∎

#### Lemma. A quasi-finite polynomial model near a point

Let $S$ be a finite-type $R$-algebra, and let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ have fibre dimension $\dim_{\mathfrak q}(S/R)=n$. For some $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$, there is an $R$-algebra homomorphism $R[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to S_g$ that makes $S_g$ quasi-finite over this polynomial algebra.

**Proof.** Put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$ and $\overline S=S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The fibre point has an open neighborhood of dimension $n$, by the definition of dimension at a point. The topology of the fibre is the subspace topology from $\operatorname{Spec}S$, as described in the [fundamental fibre diagram](#native-algebra-remark-fundamental-diagram). Choose a principal neighborhood of $\mathfrak q$ whose intersection with the fibre lies inside that open. After this localization, the fibre has dimension exactly $n$: it is at most $n$ by inclusion in the chosen open, and at least $n$ because it is still a neighborhood of the given fibre point.

Choose a finite algebra generating list for this localized $S/R$. The [integer-coordinate normalization theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-noether-normalization), applied to $\overline S$, produces $n$ elements $y_i$ that are integer polynomials in the images of these generators and make $\overline S$ finite over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)[y_1,\ldots,y_n]$. The same integer polynomials lift the $y_i$ to the localized $S$, so they define a map from $R[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$. Its fibre at the contraction of $\mathfrak q$ is a localization and quotient of this finite algebra, and is finite-dimensional over the corresponding residue field. Hence this map is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$.

The complete proof of openness of the quasi-finite locus is AG-MO 06, Section 2A, Theorem 2A.4, based there on the pointwise algebraic Zariski Main Theorem. It gives a further principal neighborhood of $\mathfrak q$ on which the map is quasi-finite. Combining the two localizations gives $S_g$ for one $g$ in the original ring outside $\mathfrak q$: write the second denominator as a fraction in the first localization and multiply its numerator by the first denominator. This proves the assertion with the original $R$ and $S$. ∎

#### Lemma. Dimension bound for a quasi-finite algebra over affine space

Suppose $k$ is a field and a homomorphism $P=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to S$ makes $S$ a quasi-finite finite-type $P$-algebra. Then $\dim S\leq n$.

**Proof.** The [quasi-finite integral-closure theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-quasi-finite-open-integral-closure) supplies a finite $P$-subalgebra $D\subset S$ for which $\operatorname{Spec}S$ is homeomorphic to an open subset of $\operatorname{Spec}D$. The integral [prime-chain dimension inequality](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-dim-up) gives $\dim D\leq\dim P=n$. Any chain in the open subset is a chain in $\operatorname{Spec}D$, yielding the conclusion.

This also makes the original local-dimension argument explicit. For $\mathfrak q\subset S$, write $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak q\cap D$ and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap P$. A chart of that open embedding identifies $S_{\mathfrak q}$ with $D_{\mathfrak r}$. A chain of primes contained in $\mathfrak r$ contracts under the integral map to a strict chain contained in $\mathfrak p$, by incomparability. Therefore $\dim S_{\mathfrak q}\leq\dim P_{\mathfrak p}\leq n$. Taking the supremum over $\mathfrak q$ recovers the same bound. The empty spectrum causes no exception. ∎

#### Lemma. Dimension of a finite-type algebra after field extension

For a field extension $K/k$ and a finite-type $k$-algebra $S$, the rings $S$ and $K\otimes_kS$ have the same Krull dimension.

**Proof.** If $S=0$, both rings are zero. Otherwise [Noether normalization](#native-algebra-lemma-noether-normalization) gives a polynomial subalgebra $k[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\subset S$ with $S$ finite over it and $d=\dim S$. Flatness of the field extension preserves this inclusion, and base change preserves the finite generating list. Hence

$$K[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\subset K\otimes_kS$$

is a finite injective map. The [dimension equality for an integral inclusion](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-sub-dim-equal), proved by going up and incomparability, makes the right-hand dimension equal to $d$. ∎

#### Lemma. The surjectivity locus of a map with finite target

Let $u\colon M\to N$ be an $R$-linear map, with $N$ finitely generated. The following two subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ coincide and are open:

$$\{\mathfrak p:u_{\mathfrak p}\text{ is surjective}\}=\{\mathfrak p:u\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\text{ is surjective}\}.$$

Call this subset $U$. If $D(f)\subset U$, then $M_f\to N_f$ is surjective. No finite-generation assumption on $M$ is needed.

**Proof.** The cokernel $C$ is finite because it is a quotient of $N$. Right exactness identifies the two surjectivity conditions with $C_{\mathfrak p}=0$ and $C_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pC_{\mathfrak p}=0$, respectively. They are equivalent by [Nakayama's lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-nak). If $C_{\mathfrak p}=0$, choose a finite generating list for $C$ and, for each generator, an annihilating denominator outside $\mathfrak p$. Their product $h\notin\mathfrak p$ makes $C_h=0$, so $D(h)\subset U$. This proves openness. Finally, when $D(f)\subset U$, every prime localization of $C_f$ vanishes. [Local detection of a zero module](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-zero-local) gives $C_f=0$, proving the last assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Five local complete-intersection criteria

Let $S$ be a local $k$-algebra essentially of finite type over a field $k$. The following conditions are equivalent:

1. The local algebra $S$ is a complete intersection over $k$.
2. Every surjection $T\to S$ from a regular local $k$-algebra essentially of finite presentation has kernel generated by a regular sequence.
3. For some such surjection $T\to S$, its kernel has a generating list of length $\dim T-\dim S$.
4. There is a global complete-intersection $k$-algebra $A$ and a prime $\mathfrak a\subset A$ with $S\cong A_{\mathfrak a}$ as $k$-algebras.
5. The same description exists with $A$ a local complete-intersection $k$-algebra.

**Proof.** We first supply the two comparison arguments used in changing presentations.

For surjective local maps $P\to T\to S$ with $P,T$ regular local, the kernel of $P\to S$ is generated by a regular sequence if and only if the kernel of $T\to S$ is. In either ring, this is equivalent to generation by the dimension of that ring minus $\dim S$, by the [Cohen–Macaulay parameter criterion](#native-algebra-proposition-cm-module). Indeed, regular local rings are Cohen–Macaulay, and a regular quotient lowers dimension by the length of the sequence.

To compare the generator counts, put $J=\ker(P\to T)$ and $I=\ker(P\to S)$. The full regular-quotient proof in AG-CA 14, Section 1, Proposition 1.4 makes $J$ generated by part of a regular system of parameters, of length $\dim P-\dim T$. Lifting generators of $I/J$ and adjoining those of $J$ proves the implication from the expected count over $T$ to the expected count over $P$.

For the reverse implication, suppose $I$ has the expected count and $J\ne0$. If $\mathfrak m$ is the maximal ideal of $P$, the composite

$$J/\mathfrak mJ\longrightarrow I/\mathfrak mI\longrightarrow\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$$

is injective, because the parameter generators of $J$ are independent in the last space. Choose $x\in J$ with nonzero class there. It is part of a minimal generating list of $I$ and of a regular system of parameters of $P$. Replace $P$ by $P/xP$. Its dimension and the minimal number of generators of the new kernel $I/(x)$ both decrease by one, while $T$ and $S$ stay fixed. Induction on $\dim P-\dim T$ gives the expected count over $T$. When this difference is zero, the regular-quotient statement gives $J=0$. This proves the comparison in all cases.

The second comparison says that isomorphic local rings of finitely presented algebras over any fixed base ring come from isomorphic principal neighborhoods. Here are the finite-data and splitting steps. First consider a finitely presented map $B\to C$ inducing $B_{\mathfrak p}\cong C_{\mathfrak q}$. Choose a finite presentation for $C/B$. After inverting one element of $B\setminus\mathfrak p$, the images of all its algebra generators in $C_{\mathfrak q}$ have representatives in $B$. Subtract those representatives from the generators. Their new images vanish in $C_{\mathfrak q}$. The constant coefficients of the finitely many defining relations therefore vanish in $B_{\mathfrak p}$; a further base localization makes them zero in $B$. Evaluation of the new generators at zero now gives a retraction $\epsilon\colon C\to B$ whose kernel $H$ is generated by those generators.

Their vanishing in $C_{\mathfrak q}$ supplies one $v\in C\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $vH=0$. The local isomorphism identifies $\mathfrak q$ with $\epsilon^{-1}(\mathfrak p)$, so $a=\epsilon(v)$ lies outside $\mathfrak p$. Invert $a$ in the base, and write $v=a+w$ with $w\in H$. Set $e=-a^{-1}w$. Then $e\in H$, and $vh=0$ gives $eh=h$ for every $h\in H$. Taking $h=e$ shows $e^2=e$, and consequently $H=eC$. The idempotent decomposition gives

$$C\cong B\times eC$$

over the localized base, with the first projection equal to $\epsilon$. The selected prime lies on the $B$ factor. Localizing at its complementary idempotent isolates that factor.

Now let $A_{\mathfrak a}\cong B_{\mathfrak b}$ as $Q$-algebras, where $A,B$ are finitely presented over a ring $Q$. Represent the images of finitely many algebra generators of $A$ by fractions in $B_{\mathfrak b}$ and clear their denominators. Clear, in addition, the finitely many witnesses that its defining relations vanish. This produces a $Q$-algebra map $A\to B_s$, with $s\notin\mathfrak b$, inducing the given local isomorphism. The map is finitely presented: a finite presentation of $B_s/Q$, together with equations specifying the images of finitely many generators of $A/Q$, is a finite presentation over $A$. Apply the preceding splitting argument. It identifies $A_t$ with a localization of $B_s$ at one further base element and the complementary idempotent. Clearing their denominators expresses the latter as $B_{s'}$ for $s'\notin\mathfrak b$. Here $t\notin\mathfrak a$. This proves the neighborhood comparison, including the prescribed local isomorphism, and applies in particular to $Q=k$.

We can now prove the five equivalences. Condition (2) implies (1) by the definition of a complete-intersection local algebra. Condition (1) gives a regular-sequence presentation, whose length is the dimension difference, proving (3). Finite type and finite presentation agree over the field and its finite-type algebras by Noetherianity. Condition (4) implies (5) by the definition of a local complete intersection.

Assume (3). Write $T=(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J)_{\mathfrak q}$ and let $I$ be the kernel of the composite polynomial map to $S$. Then

$$P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow S$$

are surjective local maps with $P,T$ regular. The first comparison gives $\dim P-\dim S$ generators for $I_{\mathfrak q}$. The [five-test criterion for a polynomial presentation](#native-algebra-lemma-lci) supplies a global complete-intersection principal neighborhood of the point in $k[x]/I$. Its local ring is $S$, proving (4).

Finally assume (5), and fix any surjection $T\to S$ as in (2). Choose the same polynomial presentation $P=k[y]_{\mathfrak q}\to T$ and write $S=(k[y]/I)_{\mathfrak q}$. The second comparison identifies a principal neighborhood in $A$ with one in $k[y]/I$. Localizing a local complete intersection preserves that property, by its defining principal cover and [localization of global complete intersections](#native-algebra-lemma-localize-relative-complete-intersection). Hence the polynomial five-test criterion makes $I_{\mathfrak q}$ generated by a regular sequence in $P$. The first comparison for $P\to T\to S$ gives a regular sequence for $\ker(T\to S)$. Since the surjection was arbitrary, (2) follows. ∎

#### Lemma. Dimension at a point over a field

For a finite-type $k$-algebra $S$, a prime $\mathfrak p\subset S$, and the corresponding point $x$ of $X=\operatorname{Spec}S$, one has

$$\dim_xX=\dim S_{\mathfrak p}+\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak p).$$

**Proof.** The complete component and chain arguments are AG-CA 09, Sections 5–6, Theorem 6.1. Let $\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_m$ be the minimal primes contained in $\mathfrak p$, and put $d_j=\dim(S/\mathfrak q_j)$. Every neighborhood of $x$ meets each of these components in a nonempty open subset of dimension $d_j$. Removing the other finitely many components gives a neighborhood of dimension $\max_jd_j$. Thus $\dim_xX=\max_jd_j$.

To retain the prime-chain calculation, put $r=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak p)=\dim(S/\mathfrak p)$. A maximal chain starting at $\mathfrak p$ and ending at a maximal ideal has length $r$. For each $j$, choose a saturated chain from $\mathfrak q_j$ to $\mathfrak p$ of length $s_j$. The catenarity proof in Section 5 shows that every such chain has that length. Concatenation gives a maximal chain in the finite-type domain $S/\mathfrak q_j$, so $d_j=s_j+r$. Localization identifies the minimal primes below $\mathfrak p$ and all their chains, giving $\dim S_{\mathfrak p}=\max_js_j$. Taking maxima in the previous equality proves the formula. ∎

#### Proposition. Regularity and global dimension of a polynomial algebra

*Historical source:* FAC, Chapter III, §4, no. 68, p. 261, uses Hilbert-syzygy vanishing for internal graded Ext over $K[t_0,\ldots,t_r]$ in degrees greater than $r+1$. The proposition here gives the ordinary global-dimension bound; the [graded-to-ordinary Ext comparison](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-graded-ext-properties) is a separate input to that graded statement. FAC, Chapter III, §5, no. 74, pp. 268–269, uses the bound $r$ for finite modules at stalks of projective $r$-space. Its standard affine charts have $r$ polynomial coordinates, so that local bound follows by localization from the result below.

If $P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ for a field $k$, then $P$ is regular and has global dimension $n$. Every maximal localization is regular local of dimension $n$.

**Proof.** Polynomial regularity, including inseparable closed residue fields, is proved in AG-CA 14, Section 3, Proposition 3.3. Its argument adjoins one variable at a time, uses the flat local dimension equality, and lifts generators from the regular base and the zero- or one-dimensional fibre. The polynomial height formula and the Nullstellensatz give dimension $n$ at every maximal ideal. The homological criterion in Section 2 then gives global dimension $n$ to each of these local rings.

To pass to the global ring, take a finite $P$-module $M$. For $n\geq1$, form the first $n$ steps of a resolution by finite free modules and let $K_n$ be its $n$th syzygy. Noetherianity makes $K_n$ finite and finitely presented. At every maximal ideal, the local global-dimension bound makes $(K_n)_{\mathfrak m}$ projective, hence free. The [finite-projectivity criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-projective) therefore makes $K_n$ projective over $P$. Truncation gives $\operatorname{pd}_P M\leq n$. For $n=0$, $P=k$ and every module is a vector space, hence free.

The passage from finite modules to all modules is the full cyclic test in AG-CA 13, Section 1, Theorem 1.5. Its transfinite filtration and horseshoe construction show that a uniform bound for the cyclic quotients $P/I$ bounds the projective dimensions of arbitrary $P$-modules. Thus $\operatorname{gl.dim}P\leq n$. Conversely, localization of a projective resolution gives $\operatorname{gl.dim}P_{\mathfrak m}\leq\operatorname{gl.dim}P$: any $P_{\mathfrak m}$-module can first be regarded as a $P$-module and then localized back to itself. Choosing $\mathfrak m=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ supplies the opposite bound $n$, proving equality. ∎

#### Lemma. A dimension-lowering equation on a Cohen–Macaulay module

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local and let $M$ be a nonzero finite Cohen–Macaulay module. Put $d=\dim\operatorname{Supp}M$. If $g\in\mathfrak m$ satisfies

$$\dim(\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(g))=d-1,$$

then multiplication by $g$ is injective on $M$, and $M/gM$ is Cohen–Macaulay of depth $d-1$.

**Proof.** The complete associated-prime proof is AG-CA 12, Sections 3–4, Theorem 4.2. Each associated prime of a CM module is a component of its support of dimension $d$. If $g$ were a zero divisor, it would lie in one of these primes and leave that whole $d$-dimensional component inside $\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(g)$, a contradiction. The regular-element depth formula lowers depth by one, and the support identity for the quotient gives the stated dimension. This proves both conclusions.

Here is also the original proof through a regular sequence and an auxiliary equation. Fix an $M$-regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_d$. Call an element $a\in\mathfrak m$ good for this list if

$$\dim\bigl(\operatorname{Supp}(M/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)M)\cap V(a)\bigr)=d-i-1\quad(0\leq i<d).$$

A good element is a nonzerodivisor on $M$, and $f_1,\ldots,f_{d-1}$ is a regular sequence of maximal length on $M/aM$. We verify this by induction on $d$. For $d=1$, the kernel $K$ of multiplication by $a$ is supported only at the maximal ideal, so it has finite length. Multiplication by $f_1$ is injective on $K$; finite length makes this endomorphism surjective. Nakayama then forces $K=0$. The quotient $M/aM$ is nonzero by Nakayama and has dimension zero, hence is CM of depth zero.

For use in the induction, recall explicitly the two-element permutation argument. If $u,v\in\mathfrak m$ form a regular sequence on a finite module $L$, and $K=\ker(v:L\to L)$, regularity modulo $u$ gives $K=uK$: writing $z=uz'$ for $z\in K$, injectivity of $u$ gives $vz'=0$. The finite module $K$ vanishes by Nakayama. If $uz=vw$, reduction modulo $u$ then gives $w=uw'$; cancellation of $u$ gives $z=vw'$. Thus $u$ is injective on $L/vL$. The final quotient is unchanged and nonzero, so $v,u$ is a regular sequence too.

Now suppose $d>1$ and $a$ is good. It is good for $M/f_1M$ and the remaining list. The induction hypothesis makes $a$ regular on that quotient and makes $f_2,\ldots,f_{d-1}$ regular on $M/(f_1,a)M$. Permuting $f_1,a$ by the preceding argument shows that $a$ is regular on $M$ and that $f_1,\ldots,f_{d-1}$ is regular on $M/aM$. Its support dimension is $d-1$ by goodness, so this sequence has maximal possible length and the quotient is CM. This proves the claim about good elements.

Return to the given $g$. For $d=1$, the dimension hypothesis says exactly that $g$ is good, so the claim applies. The case $d=0$ cannot satisfy the hypothesis, since $M/gM$ is nonzero and cannot have support dimension $-1$. For $d>1$, use [prime avoidance](#native-algebra-lemma-silly) to choose $h\in\mathfrak m$ outside the finitely many minimal primes of the supports

$$\operatorname{Supp}(M/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)M)\quad(0\leq i<d),\qquad \operatorname{Supp}(M/gM).$$

All these closed supports have positive dimension, so none of their minimal primes is the maximal ideal. The [one-equation dimension bounds](#native-algebra-lemma-one-equation), applied to their support rings, show that intersecting each with $V(h)$ lowers its dimension by one. Thus $h$ is good and

$$\dim(\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(h,g))=d-2.$$

The good-element claim makes $M/hM$ CM. Induction on the present lemma, applied to $g$ on that quotient, makes $g$ regular there and makes $M/(h,g)M$ CM of depth $d-2$. Permute the regular pair $h,g$ once more. This gives injectivity of $g$ on $M$ and injectivity of $h$ on $M/gM$. The regular-element depth formula yields $\operatorname{depth}(M/gM)=d-1$. Its support has dimension $d-1$ by hypothesis, completing this second proof. ∎

#### Lemma. Maximal prime chains in the support of a Cohen–Macaulay module

Suppose a Noetherian local ring $R$ has a finite Cohen–Macaulay module $M$ with $\operatorname{Supp}M=\operatorname{Spec}R$. Every maximal prime chain in $R$ has length $\dim R$. In particular, this holds for a Cohen–Macaulay local ring by taking $M=R$.

**Proof.** Write $d=\dim R$ and induct on $d$. When $d=0$, all maximal chains consist of one prime and have length zero. For $d>0$, take a maximal chain

$$\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_r.$$

It begins at a minimal prime, ends at the maximal ideal, and has no prime between consecutive entries. It has at least one strict step: the associated-component theorem for CM modules gives dimension $d$ to every minimal-prime quotient of $R$, using full support.

Choose $x\in\mathfrak p_1$ outside every minimal prime of $R$. Such a choice follows from [prime avoidance](#native-algebra-lemma-silly), since the nonminimal prime $\mathfrak p_1$ is contained in none of those minimal primes. The [one-equation dimension theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-one-equation) gives $\dim R/xR=d-1$. Full support and the local Nakayama test give

$$\operatorname{Supp}(M/xM)=V(x).$$

The preceding CM equation lemma therefore makes $M/xM$ a CM module of dimension $d-1$. The same statements hold with $x^N$ for every $N\geq1$, because $V(x^N)=V(x)$.

We next choose $N$ so that $\mathfrak p_1$ is associated to $M/x^NM$, retaining the required power in this argument. The prime $\mathfrak p_0$ is associated to $M$, by the associated-component theorem, so choose a submodule $L\subset M$ isomorphic to $R/\mathfrak p_0$. [Artin–Rees](#native-algebra-lemma-artin-rees) supplies $N$ with

$$L\cap x^NM\subset xL.$$

The image $\overline L=L/(L\cap x^NM)$ inside $M/x^NM$ therefore surjects onto $L/xL=R/(\mathfrak p_0+(x))$. Because the pair $\mathfrak p_0\subset\mathfrak p_1$ is saturated and $x\in\mathfrak p_1\setminus\mathfrak p_0$, the prime $\mathfrak p_1$ is minimal over $\mathfrak p_0+(x)$. It belongs to $\operatorname{Supp}\overline L$ by the surjection. The annihilator of $\overline L$ contains $\mathfrak p_0$ and $x^N$, so $\mathfrak p_1$ is minimal in this support. A minimal support prime of a finite module is associated; the inclusion $\overline L\subset M/x^NM$ then makes it associated to $M/x^NM$.

The complete support and associated-prime arguments used here are given in AG-CA 12, Sections 3–5. In particular, the CM module $M/x^NM$ has no embedded associated primes. Thus $\mathfrak p_1/(x^N)$ is minimal in $R/x^NR$. The remaining chain, from $\mathfrak p_1/(x^N)$ to $\mathfrak p_r/(x^N)$, is maximal in that quotient. The module $M/x^NM$ has full support over $R/x^NR$, and its depth and dimension there agree with those computed over $R$, since the action factors through the quotient. Induction gives $r-1=d-1$, hence $r=d$. ∎

#### Lemma. A prime containing a product of ideals

If $I,J\subset R$ are ideals and a prime $\mathfrak p$ contains $IJ$, then $I\subset\mathfrak p$ or $J\subset\mathfrak p$.

**Proof.** If $I$ is not contained in $\mathfrak p$, choose $a\in I\setminus\mathfrak p$. Every $b\in J$ has $ab\in IJ\subset\mathfrak p$. Primality and $a\notin\mathfrak p$ force $b\in\mathfrak p$. Thus $J\subset\mathfrak p$. ∎

#### Lemma. The differential sequence of a quotient

For a surjection of $R$-algebras $S\to S'=S/I$, the natural sequence of $S'$-modules

$$I/I^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SS'\longrightarrow\Omega_{S'/R}\longrightarrow0$$

is exact. Its first map sends the class of $f\in I$ to $df\otimes1$. No injectivity is asserted for that map.

**Proof.** For $f_1,f_2\in I$, the Leibniz identity gives $d(f_1f_2)=f_1df_2+f_2df_1$, which becomes zero after tensoring with $S/I$. The first map is therefore well-defined on $I/I^2$. For $s\in S$ and $f\in I$, the identity $d(sf)=s\,df+f\,ds$ shows its $S/I$-linearity.

Let $Q$ be the quotient of $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SS'$ by the submodule generated by all $df\otimes1$ with $f\in I$. The rule

$$S'\longrightarrow Q,\qquad \overline s\longmapsto[ds\otimes1]$$

does not depend on the lift $s$, because changing the lift adds an element of $I$. It is an $R$-derivation by the Leibniz rule. Every $R$-derivation from $S'$ to an $S'$-module, composed with $S\to S'$, kills $I$. The universal property of $\Omega_{S/R}$ therefore factors it uniquely through this displayed derivation. Thus $Q$ represents the universal $R$-derivation of $S'$, giving the canonical identification $Q\cong\Omega_{S'/R}$. This proves exactness. Surjectivity is also visible directly: the target is generated by the differentials of elements of $S'$, all of which lift from $S$.

In terms of the original relation calculation, the kernel of $\Omega_{S/R}\to\Omega_{S'/R}$ is generated by $I\Omega_{S/R}$ and the differentials of elements of $I$. The identity $i\,ds=d(is)-s\,di$ even puts the first set of generators in the span of the second. If the differential presentation expresses a relation using an element $a\in S$ whose image in $S'$ comes from $r\in R$, then $a-\alpha(r)\in I$ and $da=d(a-\alpha(r))$, because $d\alpha(r)=0$. This recovers exactly the stated first map with the base ring fixed. ∎

#### Theorem. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz

Let $k$ be a field. In the polynomial ring $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, and more generally in every finite-type $k$-algebra $A$:

1. The residue field at a maximal ideal is a finite extension of $k$.
2. A radical ideal is the intersection of the maximal ideals that contain it.

**Proof.** A complete proof of field finiteness that precedes dimension theory is AG-CA 06, Section 1, Theorem 1.3. It proves Artin–Tate, then shows that a rational function field of positive transcendence degree cannot be generated by finitely many algebra elements, because any finite list of denominators misses an irreducible polynomial. Applied to the finite-type field $A/\mathfrak m$, this proves (1). Section 2, Theorems 2.1–2.2 gives both conclusions, including their localization argument.

We retain also the polynomial induction through constructibility. It suffices for (1) to consider polynomial rings, since every finite-type algebra is their quotient. The assertion for zero variables is immediate. For the induction step, put $L=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak m$ and let $\mathfrak p$ be the contraction to $k[x_n]$. If $\mathfrak p\ne0$, it is generated by an irreducible polynomial, and $k'=k[x_n]/\mathfrak p$ is a finite field extension of $k$ embedded in $L$. The remaining images generate $L$ as an algebra over $k'$, so there is a surjection $k'[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}]\to L$. Induction makes $L/k'$ finite, hence makes $L/k$ finite.

If $\mathfrak p=0$, the inclusion $k[x_n]\subset L$ is finite type and, since its base is Noetherian, finitely presented. [Chevalley's theorem](#native-algebra-theorem-chevalley), with its complete affine proof in AG-MO 06, Sections 3–5, makes its spectrum image constructible. That image is the singleton containing the generic point. A constructible subset containing the generic point of this integral spectrum contains a nonempty basic open $D(f)$: in a finite union of locally closed pieces, one piece contains the generic point, and its closed part is then the whole spectrum. Such a $D(f)$ has infinitely many closed points. Indeed, the Euclidean argument gives infinitely many monic irreducibles in $k[x_n]$—a product of any finite proposed list, plus one, has a new irreducible factor—and only finitely many divide $f$. This contradicts the singleton image. The induction is complete. It is an alternative once Chevalley's theorem is available; the field-finiteness proof in AG-CA 06 supplies the result independently of that route.

For (2), let $I\subset A$ be radical and choose $f\notin I$. The ring $B=(A/I)_f$ is nonzero: otherwise some power of $f$ would lie in $I$, contradicting radicality. Choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$ of $B$ and put $L=B/\mathfrak n$. Part (1) makes $L/k$ finite. The contraction $\mathfrak m\subset A$ contains $I$ and avoids $f$, since $f$ is invertible in $B$. The domain $A/\mathfrak m$ is a $k$-subalgebra of the finite-dimensional field $L$, hence is itself finite-dimensional over $k$. Multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective linear endomorphism of this domain and therefore surjective. It has an inverse in the domain, showing that $A/\mathfrak m$ is a field. Thus $\mathfrak m$ is maximal.

Every element outside $I$ is consequently excluded by some maximal ideal containing $I$, proving the required intersection equality. The reverse inclusion is immediate. For $I=A$, the intersection is empty and is interpreted as $A$, so this case is included as well. ∎

#### Lemma. Transporting the local flatness criterion

Consider a commutative square

$$\begin{array}{ccc}
R&\longrightarrow&R'\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
S&\longrightarrow&S'
\end{array}$$

whose rings are Noetherian and local and whose homomorphisms are local. Suppose $S'$ is a localization of $S\otimes_RR'$. Let $I$ be a proper ideal of $R$, let $M$ be a finite $S$-module, and put

$$I'=IR',\qquad M'=M\otimes_SS'.$$

If $M/IM$ is flat over $R/I$ and the natural map

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',R'/I')$$

is zero, then $M'$ is flat over $R'$.

**Proof.** Write $B=R/I$, $B'=R'/I'$, $A=S\otimes_RR'$ and $N=M\otimes_RR'$. The ideal $I'$ is proper because $R\to R'$ is local. The module $M'$ is the localization of $N$ corresponding to $A\to S'$. Before this localization,

$$N/I'N\cong(M/IM)\otimes_BB'$$

is flat over $B'$ by base change. Localization in the acting algebra preserves this flatness: tensor an injection of $B'$-modules with $N/I'N$ and then apply the exact localization functor. Thus $M'/I'M'$ is flat over $B'$. The [local flatness criterion for a proper ideal](#native-algebra-lemma-variant-local-criterion-flatness) reduces the problem to vanishing of $\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',B')$.

We prove the two surjections needed for that vanishing. Choose a free $R$-module $F$ mapping onto $M$, with kernel $K$, and put

$$T=\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B),\qquad
L=\operatorname{im}(K/IK\longrightarrow F/IF).$$

The sequence $0\to L\to F/IF\to M/IM\to0$ stays exact after tensoring with any $B$-module, since its last term is flat. Tensoring $T\to K/IK\to L\to0$ with $B'$ is right exact. It follows that the kernel of $K\otimes_RB'\to F\otimes_RB'$ is the image of $T\otimes_BB'$. The kernel is $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B')$, so we obtain

$$T\otimes_RR'=T\otimes_BB'
\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B').$$

For the second map, let $K'$ be the kernel of $F\otimes_RR'\to N$. There is a surjection $K\otimes_RR'\to K'$. After tensoring over $R'$ with $B'$, every element of

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(N,B')
=\ker(K'\otimes_{R'}B'\longrightarrow F\otimes_RB')$$

therefore has a lift in $K\otimes_RB'$. That lift has zero image in $F\otimes_RB'$, so belongs to $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B')$. Hence

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,B')
\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(N,B').$$

These maps are the natural comparison maps, as is apparent from the free presentation. Neither argument assumes flatness of $R\to R'$.

Tor in the last display commutes with localization of its $A$-module argument. Indeed, compute it by a free $R'$-resolution of $B'$; tensoring that resolution with $N$ gives a complex of $A$-modules, and exact localization commutes with its homology. Consequently,

$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(N,B')\otimes_AS'
\cong\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',B').$$

The two surjections show that the localized target is generated, over $S'$, by the natural images of elements of $T$. Those images are all zero by hypothesis. Thus the target vanishes, and the ideal criterion gives the required flatness. This is also the transport argument used in the [eventual-flatness lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-colimit-eventually-flat). ∎

#### Lemma. Detecting faithful flatness on fibres

For a flat $R$-module $M$, the following conditions are equivalent:

1. Tensoring with $M$ is faithfully flat: it preserves and reflects exactness of complexes of $R$-modules.
2. If $N$ is a nonzero $R$-module, then $M\otimes_RN\ne0$.
3. For each prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R$, one has $M\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\ne0$.
4. For each maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $R$, one has $M/\mathfrak mM\ne0$.

**Proof.** Under (1), the identity of a nonzero module cannot become zero after tensoring. Equivalently, reflection of exactness applied to the complex $0\to N\to0$ prevents its middle term from becoming zero. This proves (2). Residue fields are nonzero modules, so (2) implies (3), and restricting to maximal primes proves (3)$\Rightarrow$(4).

Suppose (4) holds. Let $N_1\to N_2\to N_3$ be a complex that becomes exact at its middle term after tensoring with $M$. Its middle homology $H$ satisfies $H\otimes_RM=0$: flatness identifies the tensor of its kernel and image with the kernel and image of the tensored complex. If $x\in H$ is nonzero, its annihilator $I$ is proper, and the cyclic submodule it generates gives an injection $R/I\hookrightarrow H$. Flatness would then give

$$M/IM\hookrightarrow H\otimes_RM=0.$$

Choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supset I$. The quotient map $M/IM\to M/\mathfrak mM$ would force the latter module to be zero, contradicting (4). Hence $H=0$. Tensoring already preserves exactness by flatness, and now also reflects it, proving (1). No finite-generation condition on any of these modules is used. ∎

#### Remark. Quotient and localization descriptions of a fibre

Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a ring map and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. Write $S_{\mathfrak p}=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}S$ and

$$\begin{aligned}
C&=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\otimes_RS\\
&\cong S_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak p}\\
&\cong(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}(S/\mathfrak pS).
\end{aligned}$$

The canonical diagram has the following two halves, joined along the column $R\to S$:

$$\begin{array}{ccccc}
C&\longleftarrow&S_{\mathfrak p}&\longleftarrow&S\\
\uparrow&&\uparrow&&\uparrow\\
\kappa(\mathfrak p)&\longleftarrow&R_{\mathfrak p}&\longleftarrow&R
\end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{ccccc}
S&\longrightarrow&S/\mathfrak pS&\longrightarrow&C\\
\uparrow&&\uparrow&&\uparrow\\
R&\longrightarrow&R/\mathfrak p&\longrightarrow&\kappa(\mathfrak p).
\end{array}$$

For example, the first horizontal arrow in the upper row is quotient by $\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak p}$, while the last is localization by $R\setminus\mathfrak p$. The displayed identifications of $C$ identify the two outer columns, including their structure maps. Every square commutes.

The [localization description of spectra](#native-algebra-lemma-spec-localization) and the [quotient description](#native-algebra-lemma-spec-closed) show that each horizontal arrow induces a homeomorphism from the spectrum of its target onto a subspace of the spectrum of its source. After applying $\operatorname{Spec}$, all four squares are fibre squares of topological spaces. For localization the relevant subspace consists of primes avoiding the multiplicative set, and its inverse image is the same avoidance condition upstairs. For quotient it consists of primes containing the ideal, and its inverse image is the containment condition for the extended ideal. These descriptions verify both the sets and their subspace topologies.

In particular, primes of $C$ correspond exactly to primes of $S$ whose contraction is $\mathfrak p$. A commutative unital ring has a prime ideal precisely when it is nonzero. Thus

$$\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Spec}(S)\to
\operatorname{Spec}(R))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\ne0.$$

If $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(S)$ contracts to $\mathfrak p$, extend the two halves by placing, respectively, the rows

$$\kappa(\mathfrak q)\ \longleftarrow\ S_{\mathfrak q}\
\longleftarrow\ S$$

$$S\ \longrightarrow\ S/\mathfrak q\
\longrightarrow\ \kappa(\mathfrak q)$$

above the $S$-row. The vertical maps from that row, from left to right across the joined diagram, are

$$\begin{gathered}
C\to\kappa(\mathfrak q),\qquad
S_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q},\qquad 1_S,\\
S/\mathfrak pS\to S/\mathfrak q,\qquad
C\to\kappa(\mathfrak q).
\end{gathered}$$

They exist because $\varphi(R\setminus\mathfrak p)$ avoids $\mathfrak q$, and because $\mathfrak pS\subset\mathfrak q$. The two maps from $C$ agree under its canonical identifications. This gives the extended commutative diagram with identical outer columns. Its new horizontal maps, too, are quotients or localizations and induce homeomorphisms onto their images on spectra.

#### Lemma. Six descriptions of an isolated point

Let $S$ be a finite-type algebra over a field $k$, and let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(S)$. The following conditions are equivalent:
