1. The singleton $\{\mathfrak q\}$ is open in $\operatorname{Spec}(S)$.
2. The $k$-vector space $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is finite dimensional.
3. There is $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $D(g)=\{\mathfrak q\}$.
4. The dimension $\dim_{\mathfrak q}\operatorname{Spec}(S)$ of the space at this point is zero.
5. The point $\mathfrak q$ is closed and $\dim S_{\mathfrak q}=0$.
6. The residue extension $\kappa(\mathfrak q)/k$ is finite and $\dim S_{\mathfrak q}=0$.

When these hold, there is a product decomposition

$$S\cong S_{\mathfrak q}\times S'$$

with $S'$ a finite-type $k$-algebra, whose first projection is localization at $\mathfrak q$. Moreover, every $g$ as in (3) gives the canonical isomorphism $S_g\cong S_{\mathfrak q}$.

**Proof.** First assume (1). Choose a principal neighborhood $D(g)=\{\mathfrak q\}$. Its only prime is maximal in $S_g$. Since $S_g$ is finite type over $k$, the [Nullstellensatz](#native-algebra-theorem-nullstellensatz) makes its residue field $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ finite over $k$. The subalgebra $S/\mathfrak q\subset\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is then a finite-dimensional domain over $k$. Multiplication by any nonzero element is injective on that finite-dimensional space and hence surjective, so the subalgebra is a field. Thus $\mathfrak q$ is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}(S)$ as well as open.

The [clopen product decomposition](#native-algebra-lemma-disjoint-implies-product) gives $S=S_1\times S'$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(S_1)$ the single point $\mathfrak q$. The factor $S_1$ is local and equals $S_{\mathfrak q}$ canonically. It is a finite-type, zero-dimensional $k$-algebra. [Noether normalization](#native-algebra-lemma-noether-normalization) makes it finite over a polynomial subalgebra with zero variables, hence finite over $k$. This proves (1)$\Rightarrow$(2) and the asserted product decomposition. Both factors are quotients of $S$, so are finite type.

Assume (2). The ring $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is Artinian and local, hence has only one prime. For the localization map, write

$$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow S\longrightarrow
S_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0.$$

The ring $S$ is Noetherian, so $K$ is finite over $S$. The module $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is finite over $S$ because any finite $k$-basis also generates it as an $S$-module; thus $Q$ is finite as well. Both $K$ and $Q$ vanish after localization at $\mathfrak q$. Choose a common $g\notin\mathfrak q$ killing finite generating sets of both modules after localization. Then $S_g\to S_{\mathfrak q}$ is an isomorphism, so $D(g)=\{\mathfrak q\}$. This proves (2)$\Rightarrow$(3), while (3)$\Rightarrow$(1) follows from the definition of a principal open.

An open singleton has dimension zero, giving (1)$\Rightarrow$(4). Conversely, (4) supplies a principal neighborhood $D(g)$ of dimension zero. Its ring $S_g$ is Noetherian, so the [zero-dimensional ring theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-dimension-zero-ring) makes its spectrum a finite discrete space. The point $\mathfrak q$ is isolated there, and hence in $\operatorname{Spec}(S)$. This proves (4)$\Rightarrow$(1).

The [dimension formula at a point](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-at-a-point-finite-type-field) reads

$$\dim_{\mathfrak q}\operatorname{Spec}(S)
=\dim S_{\mathfrak q}+\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak q).$$

For a closed point the Nullstellensatz makes the transcendence degree zero, so (5) implies (4). Under (4), both nonnegative terms on the right vanish. The residue field is a finitely generated field extension of $k$, so transcendence degree zero makes it finite; this gives (6). Finally, under (6) the finite-dimensional-domain argument in the first paragraph makes $S/\mathfrak q$ a field, proving (5).

The product assertion was obtained above. For any $g$ satisfying (3), the ring $S_g$ has exactly one prime and is consequently local. Its localization at that prime changes nothing, and equals $S_{\mathfrak q}$. This proves the assertion for every such $g$. ∎

#### Lemma. Finiteness after arbitrary base change

Given $R\to S$, an $S$-module $M$, and $R\to R'$, put

$$S'=S\otimes_RR',\qquad M'=M\otimes_RR'.$$

Then:

1. If $M$ is finite over $S$, then $M'$ is finite over $S'$.
2. If $M$ is finitely presented over $S$, then $M'$ is finitely presented over $S'$.
3. If $S$ is a finite-type $R$-algebra, then $S'$ is a finite-type $R'$-algebra.
4. If $S$ is a finitely presented $R$-algebra, then $S'$ is a finitely presented $R'$-algebra.

**Proof.** The canonical identification

$$M\otimes_SS'\cong M\otimes_RR'$$

sends $m\otimes(s\otimes r')$ to $sm\otimes r'$. Its inverse sends $m\otimes r'$ to $m\otimes(1\otimes r')$; the balancing relations verify that both maps are well-defined. Tensoring a finite generating surjection $S^n\to M$ with $S'$ gives a surjection $(S')^n\to M'$. Tensoring a finite presentation $S^a\to S^b\to M\to0$ gives the right exact sequence $(S')^a\to(S')^b\to M'\to0$. These prove (1) and (2).

For the algebra assertions, take any polynomial presentation

$$S=R[x_i\mid i\in E]/(f_j\mid j\in F).$$

The universal property of polynomial algebras and quotients identifies its base change with

$$S'=R'[x_i\mid i\in E]/(f'_j\mid j\in F),$$

where $f'_j$ is obtained by mapping every coefficient to $R'$. Equivalently, a map from this displayed algebra to an $R'$-algebra is exactly an $R$-algebra map from $S$ compatible with its $R'$-structure, which is the tensor-product universal property. If $E$ is finite, the resulting algebra is finite type. If both $E$ and $F$ are finite, its presentation is finite. This proves (3) and (4), with no flatness assumption on the base change. ∎

#### Lemma. Formal smoothness from a square-zero section

Let $P\to S$ be a surjection of $R$-algebras with kernel $J$, where $P$ is a polynomial algebra on any set of variables. Then $S$ is formally smooth over $R$ if and only if $P/J^2\to S$ admits an $R$-algebra section.

**Proof.** The kernel of $P/J^2\to S$ is $J/J^2$ and has square zero. If $S$ is formally smooth, lift the identity map of $S$ across this surjection. The lift is the required section.

Conversely, fix a section $\sigma\colon S\to P/J^2$. Test formal smoothness against an $R$-algebra $A$, an ideal $I\subset A$ with $I^2=0$, and an $R$-algebra map $u\colon S\to A/I$. Lift the image under $u$ of each polynomial variable independently to $A$. Those choices define an $R$-algebra map $\psi\colon P\to A$ lifting $P\to S\to A/I$, even if the variable set is infinite. For each $j\in J$, one has $\psi(j)\in I$, so $\psi(J^2)=0$. The induced map $\bar\psi\colon P/J^2\to A$, composed with $\sigma$, lifts $u$. This proves the lifting property. ∎

#### Lemma. The split conormal criterion

For a polynomial presentation $P\twoheadrightarrow S$ over $R$ with kernel $J$, formal smoothness of $S$ over $R$ is equivalent to split exactness of

$$0\longrightarrow J/J^2\xrightarrow{\ d\ }
E\longrightarrow\Omega_{S/R}\longrightarrow0,$$

where $E=\Omega_{P/R}\otimes_PS$.

Here $d$ sends $j\bmod J^2$ to $dj\otimes1$, and splitting is as a sequence of $S$-modules. The assertion permits an arbitrary variable set.

**Proof.** Right exactness is the [quotient differential sequence](#native-algebra-lemma-differential-seq). Suppose first that $S$ is formally smooth, and take the section $\sigma\colon S\to C=P/J^2$ supplied by the preceding lemma. If $\pi\colon C\to S$ is the quotient map, then

$$D(c)=c-\sigma(\pi(c))\in J/J^2$$

defines an $R$-derivation from $C$ to the $S$-module $J/J^2$. In fact, write $c=\sigma(s)+n$ and $c'=\sigma(s')+n'$ with $n,n'\in J/J^2$. Their product has nilpotent part $sn'+s'n$, since $nn'=0$. This is exactly the product rule, and $D$ vanishes on the image of $R$. Its restriction to $J/J^2$ is the identity.

For clarity, the canonical map

$$\Omega_{P/R}\otimes_PS
\longrightarrow\Omega_{C/R}\otimes_CS$$

is an isomorphism. Applying the quotient differential sequence to $P\to P/J^2$ shows that its possible kernel is generated by $d(J^2)$. Every such differential is a sum of terms $j\,dj'$ with $j,j'\in J$, which vanish after tensoring with $S$. The derivation $D$ therefore induces an $S$-linear retraction $E\to J/J^2$ of the first arrow. This proves both its injectivity and the splitting of the sequence.

For the reverse implication, choose an $S$-linear section

$$\tau\colon\Omega_{S/R}\longrightarrow E.$$

For each $\lambda\in S$, choose a lift $x_\lambda\in P$. Exactness gives $f_\lambda\in J$ with

$$df_\lambda=dx_\lambda-\tau(d\lambda)\quad\text{in }E.$$

Set $y_\lambda=x_\lambda-f_\lambda$, so $dy_\lambda=\tau(d\lambda)$ in $E$ and $y_\lambda$ maps to $\lambda$. We claim that

$$s\colon S\longrightarrow P/J^2,\qquad
\lambda\longmapsto y_\lambda\bmod J^2$$

is an $R$-algebra section. The injectivity of $J/J^2\to E$ says that whenever $h\in J$ and $dh=0$ in $E$, one has $h\in J^2$. This observation verifies every required identity.

First, another pair of choices for the same $\lambda$ gives a difference $h\in J$ whose differential is zero, since both corrected lifts have differential $\tau(d\lambda)$. Thus the value of $s$ is independent of the choices. Next,

$$y_\lambda+y_\mu-y_{\lambda+\mu}\in J,\qquad
d(y_\lambda+y_\mu-y_{\lambda+\mu})
=\tau(d\lambda+d\mu-d(\lambda+\mu))=0.$$

The difference belongs to $J^2$, so $s$ is additive. For multiplication, the coefficients of $y_\lambda$ and $y_\mu$ in $E$ are their images $\lambda$ and $\mu$ in $S$. Hence

$$\begin{aligned}
d(y_\lambda y_\mu-y_{\lambda\mu})
&=\lambda\tau(d\mu)+\mu\tau(d\lambda)-\tau(d(\lambda\mu))\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}$$

The element being differentiated lies in $J$, and hence in $J^2$. This proves $s(\lambda)s(\mu)=s(\lambda\mu)$. Written in the original lifts, the same calculation uses

$$y_\lambda y_\mu-y_{\lambda\mu}
\equiv x_\lambda x_\mu-x_{\lambda\mu}
-x_\mu f_\lambda-x_\lambda f_\mu+f_{\lambda\mu}
\pmod{J^2},$$

because $f_\lambda f_\mu\in J^2$.

Finally, if $\lambda$ is the image of $r\in R$, then $y_\lambda-r\in J$ and $d(y_\lambda-r)=\tau(d\lambda)=0$. Thus $s(\lambda)$ is the image of $r$ in $P/J^2$. This proves compatibility with the base ring and, taking $r=1$, preservation of the unit. The composite $S\xrightarrow{s}P/J^2\to S$ is the identity by construction. The preceding square-zero-section criterion now proves formal smoothness. ∎

#### Lemma. The naive cotangent complex of a quotient

For a surjection $A\twoheadrightarrow B$ with kernel $I$, there is a homotopy equivalence

$$\mathrm{NL}_{B/A}\simeq[I/I^2\longrightarrow0],$$

where the conormal module occupies homological degree one. In particular,

$$H_1(L_{B/A})=I/I^2.$$

**Proof.** The algebra $A$, viewed over itself, is a polynomial algebra on the empty set. Thus $A\twoheadrightarrow B$ is an allowed polynomial presentation. Its conormal complex has terms $I/I^2$ and $\Omega_{A/A}\otimes_AB=0$. The complete comparison-of-presentations theorem, AG-CA 16, Theorem 7.1 identifies this complex with the canonical presentation complex up to homotopy. Its proof constructs polynomial lifts in both directions and a derivation homotopy between each composite and the identity; it applies equally to an empty or infinite variable set.

Taking degree-one homology gives the asserted module. Here $H_1(L_{B/A})$ is the notation for $H_1(\mathrm{NL}_{B/A})$ used in these algebraic criteria. The assertion about the two-term complex makes no claim that the full cotangent complex has no higher homology. ∎

#### Lemma. Finite modules over a Noetherian ring

If $R$ is Noetherian and $M$ is a finite $R$-module, then every submodule of $M$ is finite, the module $M$ is finitely presented, and each increasing sequence of submodules of $M$ stabilizes.

**Proof.** We prove the submodule assertion by induction on the size of a generating list for $M$. The zero module is immediate. A cyclic module has the form $R/I$; its submodules are $J/I$ with $I\subset J$, and each such $J$ has a finite generating list.

For a list of length $n>1$, let $M_0$ be the submodule generated by its first $n-1$ members. The quotient $M/M_0$ is cyclic. Given $N\subset M$, the sequence

$$0\longrightarrow N\cap M_0\longrightarrow N
\longrightarrow\operatorname{im}(N\to M/M_0)\longrightarrow0$$

has finitely generated end terms by induction. A finite generating list of the first term, together with lifts of a generating list of the last, generates $N$. This proves the assertion.

Now choose a finite free surjection $R^n\to M$. Its kernel is a submodule of a finite module and is therefore finite. A generating list of that kernel gives a finite presentation of $M$.

Finally, if $N_1\subset N_2\subset\cdots\subset M$, their union $N$ is a submodule, hence has finitely many generators. All these generators occur in one $N_j$, so $N_i=N_j$ for every $i\geq j$. More generally, this explains the equivalence between the ascending chain condition and finite generation of every submodule: if a submodule were not finite, repeatedly choosing an element outside the submodule generated by the previous choices would give a strictly increasing chain. ∎

#### Lemma. Spectrum embeddings from unit multiples

*Historical source:* EGA I, Corollary 1.2.4.

Suppose $\varphi\colon R\to S$ has the property that every $g\in S$ can be expressed as $u\varphi(f)$, where $f\in R$ and $u$ is a unit of $S$. Then contraction gives a homeomorphism

$$\operatorname{Spec}(S)\longrightarrow
\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Spec}(S)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)).$$

**Proof.** Write $j$ for the contraction map. It is continuous, since $j^{-1}(D(f))=D(\varphi(f))$. If primes $\mathfrak q_1,\mathfrak q_2$ have the same contraction, membership of $g=u\varphi(f)$ in either prime is equivalent to membership of $f$ in that common contraction. The primes therefore have exactly the same elements, proving injectivity.

For the same expression of $g$, the unit $u$ does not affect its principal open, so

$$D(g)=j^{-1}(D(f)),\qquad
j(D(g))=j(\operatorname{Spec}S)\cap D(f).$$

Principal opens form a basis. Thus the continuous bijection onto the image sends each basic open to an open of that image, and its inverse is continuous. ∎

#### Lemma. A product ring gives a disjoint spectrum

The projections from $R=R_1\times R_2$ induce a homeomorphism

$$\operatorname{Spec}(R_1)\amalg\operatorname{Spec}(R_2)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}(R).$$

**Proof.** Let $e_1=(1,0)$ and $e_2=(0,1)$. Their sum is one, their product is zero, and each is idempotent. Inverting $e_1$ makes it equal to one and makes $e_2$ zero. The first projection consequently induces

$$R_{e_1}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }R_1,\qquad
(a,b)/e_1^n\longmapsto a.$$

Its inverse is $a\mapsto(a,0)/1$; the identity $(1,0)/1=1$ verifies that this is a unital homomorphism. The same construction identifies $R_{e_2}$ with $R_2$.

Every prime of $R$ contains one of $e_1,e_2$, because their product is zero, and cannot contain both, because their sum is one. Hence $D(e_1)$ and $D(e_2)$ form a disjoint open cover. Each is also closed, being the complement of the other. The spectrum-localization homeomorphisms identify these two pieces with the two displayed spectra, and agree with the original projections. Their union is the required homeomorphism. This also covers a zero factor. ∎

#### Lemma. The equalizer for a finite principal cover

If $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ generate the unit ideal of $R$, then

$$0\longrightarrow R\xrightarrow{\alpha}\bigoplus_iR_{f_i}
\xrightarrow{\beta}\bigoplus_{i,j}R_{f_if_j}$$

is exact. The first map sends $r$ to its local images. The $(i,j)$ component of the second is the difference between the images of the $i$th and $j$th entries on their common localization.

**Proof.** We prove the same assertion with an arbitrary $R$-module $M$ in place of $R$:

$$0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow\bigoplus_iM_{f_i}
\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{i,j}M_{f_if_j}.$$

The maps are $m\mapsto(m/1)_i$ and $(s_i)_i\mapsto(s_i-s_j)_{i,j}$ after passing to the indicated localizations. Their composite is zero.

Exactness can be checked at maximal ideals. To recall why, localization is exact and so commutes with the homology modules of this complex. A nonzero element $h$ of a module has a proper annihilator; in a maximal ideal containing that annihilator, $h/1$ remains nonzero, since no element outside that ideal can kill $h$. Thus vanishing of every maximal localization forces a module to be zero.

At a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, at least one $f_a$ is a unit in $R_{\mathfrak m}$. Localization twice identifies the $a$th term with $M_{\mathfrak m}$ and the $(a,i)$ overlap with $(M_{\mathfrak m})_{f_i}$. The first map is injective because its $a$th component is the identity. If a tuple belongs to the kernel of the difference map, its $a$th entry is an element $s$ of $M_{\mathfrak m}$, and the $(a,i)$ equality says that its $i$th entry is exactly the image of $s$. The tuple therefore comes from the first map. This proves exactness at each maximal localization, hence globally. Taking $M=R$ proves the stated ring sequence. If the cover is empty, its unit-ideal hypothesis forces $R=0$, and the sequence is again exact. ∎

#### Definition. Formally étale algebras

An $R$-algebra $S$ is **formally étale** if, for every $R$-algebra $A$ and every ideal $I\subset A$ satisfying $I^2=0$, reduction gives a bijection

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-alg}}(S,A)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-alg}}(S,A/I).$$

Thus each $R$-algebra map from $S$ to a square-zero quotient lifts to $A$ in exactly one way.

#### Lemma. Right exactness of tensor products

For an exact sequence of $R$-modules

$$M_1\xrightarrow{f}M_2\xrightarrow{g}M_3\longrightarrow0$$

and any $R$-module $N$, the sequence

$$M_1\otimes_RN\xrightarrow{f\otimes1}M_2\otimes_RN
\xrightarrow{g\otimes1}M_3\otimes_RN\longrightarrow0$$

is exact.

**Proof.** We give the tensor–Hom argument, including the adjunction it uses. For arbitrary $R$-modules $U,N,P$, an $R$-linear map $a\colon U\otimes_RN\to P$ determines

$$U\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P),\qquad
u\longmapsto(n\longmapsto a(u\otimes n)).$$

Additivity and the scalar relation in a tensor product make this map $R$-linear. Conversely, an $R$-linear map $b\colon U\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P)$ gives the bilinear function $(u,n)\mapsto b(u)(n)$, and hence a unique map $U\otimes_RN\to P$. The two constructions are inverse, are linear on the Hom modules, and commute with maps in each argument. They prove the natural adjunction.

A map $M_2\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P)$ that vanishes on $f(M_1)$ factors uniquely through $M_3$, because $M_3$ is the cokernel of $f$. Under this adjunction, it follows that a map $M_2\otimes_RN\to P$ vanishing on the image of $f\otimes1$ factors uniquely through $M_3\otimes_RN$. This proves that $M_3\otimes_RN$ is the cokernel of $f\otimes1$. Explicitly, if $Q$ is that cokernel, the factorization property constructs maps $Q\to M_3\otimes_RN$ and back; uniqueness makes their composites the identities. The first map is the one induced by $g\otimes1$. It is also visibly surjective, since each generator $m_3\otimes n$ lifts by choosing a preimage of $m_3$ under $g$. These facts prove the displayed exact sequence. ∎

#### Lemma. When an element vanishes in a directed colimit

Let $(M_i,\mu_{ij})$ be a system of modules over a directed preordered set, and let $\mu_i\colon M_i\to M=\operatorname{colim}_iM_i$ be its structure maps. Then

$$\mu_i(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mu_{ij}(x)=0\text{ for some }j\geq i.$$

**Proof.** Here is the explicit colimit construction. Start with the disjoint union of the sets $M_i$ and declare $x\in M_i$ equivalent to $y\in M_j$ when their images agree in some $M_k$ with $k\geq i,j$. Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate. For transitivity, move the two witnessing equalities to a common upper index; the middle representatives then agree there, giving equality of the first and last representatives.

Add two classes by moving their representatives to any common upper index and adding there. Define scalar multiplication using any representative. To check independence of representatives or of the upper index, move the finitely many equality witnesses to one further upper index. The proposed results agree at that index. The same procedure reduces all module axioms to the corresponding axioms in one $M_k$. The maps $M_i\to M$ are linear and compatible. Every compatible family of maps $M_i\to Q$ has a unique induced linear map on these classes, because equivalent representatives have the same image. This proves the universal property of the colimit.

All stage zeros represent the same class. Applying the equivalence relation to $x\in M_i$ and $0\in M_i$ gives exactly the criterion stated above. Neither the preorder nor the module transition maps are required to be injective. ∎

#### Lemma. Integral algebras over a field

Let $S$ be an algebra over a field $k$.

1. A finite-dimensional $k$-algebra that is a domain is a field.
2. An integral $k$-algebra that is a domain is a field.
3. In any integral $k$-algebra, every prime ideal is maximal.

**Proof.** For (1), take $0\ne s\in S$. Multiplication by $s$ is injective since $S$ is a domain. It is therefore surjective on the finite-dimensional $k$-space $S$, so some $t$ satisfies $st=1$.

For (2), any $s\in S$ belongs to the finite-dimensional subalgebra $k[s]$: a monic equation for $s$ expresses every sufficiently high power in terms of lower powers. This subalgebra is a domain, so (1) makes it a field. Each nonzero $s$ thus has an inverse already in $k[s]$, and hence in $S$.

For (3), take a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$. The domain $S/\mathfrak q$ is integral over $k$, because monic equations descend to quotients. Part (2) makes it a field, so $\mathfrak q$ is maximal. If $S$ has no primes the assertion is vacuous. ∎

#### Lemma. A flat local map is faithfully flat

Every flat local homomorphism $R\to S$ of local rings is faithfully flat.

**Proof.** If $\mathfrak m$ and $\mathfrak n$ are their maximal ideals, locality gives $\mathfrak mS\subset\mathfrak n$, so $S/\mathfrak mS\ne0$. This is the only maximal fibre of the base. The [maximal-fibre test for a flat module](#native-algebra-lemma-ff), applied to the $R$-module $S$, proves faithfulness. No finiteness or Noetherian hypothesis is needed. ∎

#### Lemma. Faithful flatness and surjectivity on spectra

For a flat ring map $R\to S$, the following are equivalent:

1. The map is faithfully flat.
2. Every prime of $R$ is the contraction of a prime of $S$.
3. Every maximal ideal of $R$ is the contraction of a prime of $S$.

**Proof.** The [fibre diagram](#native-algebra-remark-fundamental-diagram) identifies primes above $\mathfrak p$ with primes of $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. Thus $\mathfrak p$ has a preimage exactly when that fibre ring is nonzero. The all-prime and maximal-prime fibre conditions are precisely the two equivalent tests in the [faithfully flat module lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-ff). This proves all three equivalences, including the empty-spectrum case. ∎

#### Lemma. Isolating one finite branch by an étale neighborhood

Let $R\to S$ be finite type, let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(S)$ contract to $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$, and suppose the map is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$. There exist an étale $R$-algebra $R'$, a prime $\mathfrak p'$ above $\mathfrak p$, and a product decomposition

$$S\otimes_RR'=A\times B$$

such that:

1. The canonical residue map $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak p')$ is an isomorphism.
2. The algebra $A$ is finite over $R'$.
3. There is exactly one prime $\mathfrak r$ of $A$ above $\mathfrak p'$.
4. This prime contracts to $\mathfrak q$ in $S$.
5. No prime of $B$ contracts both to $\mathfrak q$ in $S$ and to $\mathfrak p'$ in $R'$.

**Proof.** Let $C\subset S$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $S$, and set $\mathfrak q_C=\mathfrak q\cap C$. The complete arbitrary-base algebraic Zariski Main theorem is AG-MO 06, Theorem 2A.1. It supplies $g\in C\setminus\mathfrak q_C$ with $C_g=S_g$. This is a pointwise theorem and requires only finite type.

Put $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and consider $F=S\otimes_Rk$ and $F_C=C\otimes_Rk$. The chosen point $\bar{\mathfrak q}\in\operatorname{Spec}(F)$ is isolated by the quasi-finite fibre criterion. Its image $\bar{\mathfrak q}_C$ lies in the open on which $(F_C)_g=F_g$, so it too is isolated. It is closed because $F_C$ is integral over $k$, and every prime in an integral algebra over a field is maximal. Moreover, $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ is the only point of $\operatorname{Spec}(F)$ above $\bar{\mathfrak q}_C$: any point above it avoids $g$ and must correspond under that localization isomorphism.

The clopen singleton gives

$$F_C=F_1\times F_2,\qquad
\operatorname{Spec}(F_1)=\{\bar{\mathfrak q}_C\}.$$

Let $e=(1,0)$. Since $F_C=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}(C/\mathfrak pC)$, write $e$ as $c/r$ with $c\in C$ and $r\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$. Thus the image of $c$ is $(\bar r,0)$. In particular, $c$ avoids $\bar{\mathfrak q}_C$ and belongs to every other prime of $F_C$.

Choose a monic equation $f(c)=0$ over $R$. In $k[T]$ write

$$\bar f=T^a\bar h,\qquad \bar h(0)\ne0.$$

Both factors are monic. Multiplying $f$ by $T$ if necessary ensures $a\geq1$ while keeping $f(c)=0$.

We spell out the étale factor-lifting construction. For any monic $f\in R[T]$ and coprime monic factors $\bar h,\bar i$ over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, the case $f=1$ has the immediate lifts $h=i=1$ over $R$. Otherwise introduce coefficient variables for monic polynomials $H,I$ of their respective degrees. The coefficient equations $HI=f$ define an $R$-algebra $U$ with equally many variables and equations. Evaluating at $\bar h,\bar i$ gives $U\to\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The coefficient Jacobian represents

$$k[T]_{<\deg\bar h}\oplus k[T]_{<\deg\bar i}
\longrightarrow k[T]_{<\deg f},$$

$$ (v,w)\longmapsto\bar i\,v+\bar h\,w.$$

It is invertible: reduce modulo $\bar h$ to determine $v$ uniquely using the inverse of $\bar i$, then divide the remainder by the monic $\bar h$ to determine $w$. Consequently its determinant $\Delta$ has nonzero value at the chosen evaluation. The [coefficient-Jacobian construction](#native-algebra-example-factor-polynomials-etale) makes $R'=U_\Delta$ étale over $R$. The kernel $\mathfrak p'$ of its evaluation in $k$ contracts to $\mathfrak p$. The fraction field of the image contains $\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p)=k$ and is contained in $k$, so its residue field is canonically $k$, even when $\mathfrak p$ is not maximal.

The same coefficient matrix over $U_\Delta$ is invertible. Solving it with target polynomial $1$ gives a Bézout identity for $H,I$. Their images $h,i\in R'[T]$ therefore satisfy

$$f=hi,\qquad \alpha h+\beta i=1$$

for suitable polynomials $\alpha,\beta$, and have the prescribed reductions. This construction also permits prescribed factors which are not monic. If their leading coefficients are $\lambda$ and $\lambda^{-1}$, first invert a base element outside $\mathfrak p$ so that $\lambda$ lifts to a unit $u$. Apply the monic construction to $\lambda^{-1}\bar h$ and $\lambda\bar i$, and then multiply the lifts by $u$ and $u^{-1}$. The product, Bézout property and specified reductions are preserved. This preliminary principal localization is étale and keeps the same residue field.

Apply the construction with $\bar i=T^a$ and the above $\bar h$. In $C\otimes_RR'$, the elements $h(c),i(c)$ have product zero and generate the unit ideal. Their principal opens are disjoint and cover the spectrum, giving

$$C\otimes_RR'=C_1\times C_2,$$

$$C_1=(C\otimes_RR')_{i(c)},\qquad
C_2=(C\otimes_RR')_{h(c)}.$$

The corresponding decomposition of the target is

$$S\otimes_RR'=S_1\times S_2,$$

$$S_1=(S\otimes_RR')_{i(c)},\qquad
S_2=(S\otimes_RR')_{h(c)}.$$

The marked fibres are still $F_C$ and $F$. On the first factor of $F_C$, the element $i(c)$ becomes $\bar r^a$, a unit; on the second it is zero. The factor $C_1$ therefore has precisely $\bar{\mathfrak q}_C$ in its marked fibre. The unique-preimage property proved above shows that $S_1$ has precisely $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ in its marked fibre, while $S_2$ has no point over it. As a direct factor, $C_1$ is a quotient of the integral $R'$-algebra $C\otimes_RR'$, hence is integral over $R'$. Similarly, $S_1$ is finite type over $R'$. Base change and localization of $C_g=S_g$ give

$$(C_1)_g\cong(S_1)_g.$$

It remains to make $S_1$ finite by shrinking the base. We give the general argument. Suppose $T\to D\to E$ are ring maps, $D$ is integral over $T$, $E$ is finite type over $T$, and $D_g\to E_g$ is an isomorphism. If $g$ is a unit in $D\otimes_T\kappa(\mathfrak t)$, then the image of $V(g)\subset\operatorname{Spec}(D)$ under the integral map is a closed set missing $\mathfrak t$. Choose $b\in T\setminus\mathfrak t$ whose principal open avoids that image. No prime of $D_b$ contains $g$, so $g$ is a unit there, and also in $E_b$. The localization isomorphism then gives $D_b\cong E_b$. Thus $E_b$ is integral and finite type over $T_b$, hence finite: monic equations for a finite algebra generating list bound the powers needed to generate it as a module.

For $D=C_1$, the image of $g$ avoids the unique prime of its marked fibre, so is a unit in that fibre. Apply this argument at $\mathfrak p'$, using the [closed-image property of integral maps](#native-algebra-lemma-going-up-closed). Replace $R'$ by the resulting principal localization, and localize both product factors. The first factor is now finite. Étaleness and the canonical residue-field isomorphism persist, and the marked fibres have not changed. Taking $A=(S_1)_b$ and $B=(S_2)_b$ proves all five assertions. ∎

#### Lemma. Fibrewise injectivity over an arbitrary local base

Let $R\to S$ be local, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset R$, and let $u\colon M\to N$ be $S$-linear. Assume that $S$ is essentially of finite presentation over $R$, that $M,N$ are finitely presented over $S$, that $N$ is flat over $R$, and that

$$M/\mathfrak mM\longrightarrow N/\mathfrak mN$$

is injective. Then $u$ is injective and $\operatorname{coker}u$ is flat over $R$.

**Proof.** The [finite local-model construction](#native-algebra-lemma-limit-module-essentially-finite-presentation) gives a directed system

$$R_\lambda\longrightarrow S_\lambda,\qquad
u_\lambda\colon M_\lambda\longrightarrow N_\lambda$$

with colimit the given data. To include the map, descend finite presentations of both modules, images of the finitely many source generators, and the finitely many relations which these images satisfy. At one common stage this defines $u_\lambda$, and later maps are its base changes. Each $R_\lambda$ is essentially finite type over $\mathbb Z$, each $S_\lambda$ is a local localization of a finite-type $R_\lambda$-algebra, and both modules are finite over $S_\lambda$. In particular these rings are Noetherian. For $\mu\geq\lambda$, the ring $S_\mu$ is a localization of $S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu$, and the modules change by the same base change and localization.

By [eventual flatness](#native-algebra-lemma-colimit-eventually-flat), choose a stage at which $N_\lambda$ is $R_\lambda$-flat. It remains flat at every later stage: first make the arbitrary base change on $R_\lambda$, then localize in the acting algebra. We restrict to this cofinal tail.

Write $\mathfrak m_\lambda$ for the maximal ideal of $R_\lambda$, $\kappa_\lambda=R_\lambda/\mathfrak m_\lambda$, and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. The local transition maps give embeddings of these residue fields, with colimit $\kappa$. Put $\bar M_\lambda=M_\lambda/\mathfrak m_\lambda M_\lambda$ and $\bar M=M/\mathfrak mM$. We must make the residue map $u_\lambda$ injective at a finite stage.

Fix one index $\lambda$ and consider

$$E_\lambda=\bar M_\lambda\otimes_{\kappa_\lambda}\kappa,
\qquad \Psi_\lambda\colon E_\lambda\longrightarrow\bar M.$$

The ring

$$T_\lambda=(S_\lambda/\mathfrak m_\lambda S_\lambda)
\otimes_{\kappa_\lambda}\kappa$$

is a localization of a finite-type $\kappa$-algebra, hence Noetherian. The module $E_\lambda$ is finite over it, so $\ker\Psi_\lambda$ has a finite generating list $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r$.

Each $\xi_i$ uses only finitely many coefficients in $\kappa$. Represent these at a residue-field stage $\kappa_\mu$, with $\mu\geq\lambda$. Its image in $\bar M_\mu$ becomes zero in $\bar M=\operatorname{colim}_\nu\bar M_\nu$. The directed-colimit zero criterion makes that image zero at some later index. After taking one common upper index for the finite list, all the $\xi_i$ map to zero in $E_\mu$. This includes the case of an empty generating list.

For any $\nu\geq\mu$, the model base-change property gives

$$E_\nu=W_\nu^{-1}E_\lambda$$

for the image of a multiplicative set from $S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\nu$ in $T_\lambda$. Every element of $W_\nu$ maps to a unit in $S/\mathfrak mS$, because it was inverted in the ring $S_\nu$ mapping to $S$. If $x=y/w\in E_\nu$ maps to zero in $\bar M$, then $\Psi_\lambda(y)=0$. Express $y$ as a $T_\lambda$-linear combination of the $\xi_i$. These generators already vanish in $E_\mu$, and thus in $E_\nu$, so $x=0$. We have proved that $\Psi_\nu$ is injective for all $\nu\geq\mu$.

Since $\kappa_\nu\to\kappa$ is a field extension, $\bar M_\nu\to E_\nu$ is injective as well. Hence $\bar M_\nu\to\bar M$ is injective. Its composite with the assumed injection $\bar u\colon\bar M\to\bar N$ factors through the residue map $\bar u_\nu$. If an element is killed by $\bar u_\nu$, this composite kills it, so it is zero. Therefore $\bar u_\nu$ is injective.

At such a stage, the complete Noetherian fibre-injectivity theorem is AG-CA 08, Lemma 5.1, with its local flatness proof in Section 4. It applies to the finite $S_\nu$-modules $M_\nu,N_\nu$ and the $R_\nu$-flat target. It proves that $u_\nu$ is injective and its cokernel $Q_\nu$ is flat over $R_\nu$. Its proof first obtains injection modulo every power of the maximal ideal, uses Krull intersection over $S_\nu$, and then applies the Tor form of the local criterion to the cokernel.

Directed colimits preserve these injections: an element mapping to zero in the target colimit does so at a finite later stage, where the corresponding map is injective. Cokernels commute with the colimit, so $\operatorname{coker}u=\operatorname{colim}_\nu Q_\nu$. The [flatness theorem for varying-ring colimits](#native-algebra-lemma-colimit-rings-flat) makes this an $R$-flat module. Thus both conclusions hold without a Noetherian assumption on the original rings. ∎

#### Remark. A cyclic flat module that is not projective

Finite generation does not suffice for the implication from flatness to projectivity. Let $R=C^\infty(\mathbb R)$, let $\mathfrak m$ be the kernel of evaluation at $0$, and put
$$I=\{f\in R:f\text{ vanishes on some open interval containing }0\}.$$
Then the localization $R_{\mathfrak m}$ is the cyclic module $R/I$, and it is flat but not projective.

To identify this localization, use smooth cutoff functions: for any neighborhood $U$ of $0$, there is a smooth function $\chi$ supported in $U$ and equal to $1$ on a smaller neighborhood. Such functions follow, for example, from $\rho(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$ and $\rho(t)=0$ for $t\leq0$. For $0<a<b$ with $[-b,b]\subset U$, one may take
$$\chi(x)=
\frac{\rho(b^2-x^2)}
{\rho(b^2-x^2)+\rho(x^2-a^2)}.$$
The denominator is positive everywhere, so this formula has the stated properties.

If $f$ becomes zero in $R_{\mathfrak m}$, some $s$ with $s(0)\ne0$ satisfies $sf=0$. On a neighborhood where $s$ is nonzero, $f$ vanishes. Conversely, if $f\in I$, choose a cutoff supported where $f$ vanishes. Then $\chi f=0$ and $\chi(0)=1$, which kills $f$ in the localization. Thus the kernel of $R\to R_{\mathfrak m}$ is exactly $I$. This map is surjective: for $f/h$ with $h(0)\ne0$, multiply the smooth function $f/h$ on a neighborhood of $0$ by a cutoff supported there, and extend by zero. The resulting global function represents the given fraction. This proves $R_{\mathfrak m}\cong R/I$.

Localization is flat. The ideal $I$ is nonzero, since it contains a nonzero smooth function supported away from $0$, and is proper, since it does not contain $1$. If $R/I$ were projective, the quotient map would split as an $R$-module map. The associated projection $R\to I$ is multiplication by an idempotent $e$, so $I=eR$. A smooth idempotent takes values only in $\{0,1\}$ and is constant on the connected space $\mathbb R$. It generates either zero or all of $R$, contradicting the two properties of $I$. This proves nonprojectivity.

#### Lemma. Exact finite-module completion and flatness of the completed ring

Fix an ideal $I$ in a Noetherian ring $R$, and use a hat for $I$-adic completion. The map $R\to\widehat R$ is flat, and completion preserves exact sequences of finite $R$-modules.

**Proof.** The complete filtration and inverse-limit argument is *Completion*, §§1–3, Theorems 3.1–3.2. In an exact sequence $0\to N\to M\to L\to0$ of finite modules, Artin–Rees makes the filtrations $I^nN$ and $N\cap I^nM$ cofinal. The quotient sequences have surjective transitions on their left terms, so their inverse limits are exact. Comparing the two filtrations identifies the left limit with $\widehat N$. This proves exactness of completion on these modules.

The same proof, applied to a finite presentation, identifies $M\otimes_R\widehat R$ with $\widehat M$: both are the cokernel of the original presentation matrix acting on finite free $\widehat R$-modules. In particular, for every ideal $J\subset R$, the map
$$J\otimes_R\widehat R\longrightarrow\widehat R$$
identifies with the injective map $\widehat J\to\widehat R$. Here $J$ is finite because $R$ is Noetherian. The [ideal criterion for flatness](#native-algebra-lemma-flat) therefore proves that $\widehat R$ is flat over $R$. ∎

#### Lemma. Composition of flatness and faithful flatness

Suppose $R\to R'$ is flat and $M'$ is flat as an $R'$-module. Then $M'$ is flat over $R$. If both given flatness assertions are faithful, the resulting one is faithful too. Taking $M'$ to be an $R'$-algebra gives the corresponding assertions for compositions of ring maps.

**Proof.** For every $R$-module $N$ there is a natural isomorphism
$$M'\otimes_{R'}(R'\otimes_RN)\ \longrightarrow\ M'\otimes_RN.$$
It sends $m'\otimes(r'\otimes n)$ to $r'm'\otimes n$. Its inverse sends $m'\otimes n$ to $m'\otimes(1\otimes n)$. The balancing relations make both maps well-defined; those same relations show that the two composites fix every elementary tensor. Naturality follows by applying a homomorphism to $n$.

An injection of $R$-modules stays injective after tensoring first with $R'$ and then with $M'$. Under this natural identification, their composite is tensoring over $R$ with $M'$. Hence $M'$ is $R$-flat. If the first two functors also detect nonzero modules, their composite does: a nonzero $N$ gives a nonzero $R'\otimes_RN$, then a nonzero $M'\otimes_{R'}(R'\otimes_RN)$. The [faithful-flatness criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-ff) gives the last assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Completeness after completing an arbitrary module

For a Noetherian ring $R$, an ideal $I$, and any $R$-module $M$, its completion is $I$-adically complete. For every $n\geq0$, the canonical maps identify
$$I^n\widehat M=\widehat{I^nM},
\qquad
\widehat M/I^n\widehat M=M/I^nM.$$
The completion on $I^nM$ uses its own $I$-adic filtration.

**Proof.** Noetherianity makes $I$ finitely generated. Apply the [completion-kernel theorem for a finitely generated ideal](#native-algebra-lemma-hathat-finitely-generated), which proves these identities and completeness without requiring $M$ to be finite. Its filtration comparison uses $I^a(I^nM)=I^{a+n}M$. Thus its canonical injection of $\widehat{I^nM}$ into $\widehat M$ has image exactly $I^n\widehat M$, as asserted. ∎

#### Lemma. Flat terms of a universally exact sequence

Let $0\to M_1\to M_2\to M_3\to0$ remain exact after tensoring with every $R$-module. If $M_2$ is flat, then $M_1$ and $M_3$ are flat.

**Proof.** Fix an injection $N\to N'$ and write $N''=N'/N$. Tensor the given sequence with each of $N,N',N''$. This gives three short exact rows, and the maps between them commute with every row map.

First, $M_1\otimes_RN\to M_1\otimes_RN'$ is injective: its composite into $M_2\otimes_RN'$ factors as the injective row map into $M_2\otimes_RN$ followed by the injection supplied by flatness of $M_2$. This proves flatness of $M_1$.

For the other end, suppose $z\in M_3\otimes_RN$ dies in $M_3\otimes_RN'$. Lift $z$ to $x\in M_2\otimes_RN$. In the middle row the image of $x$ comes from some $y\in M_1\otimes_RN'$. Its image in $M_2\otimes_RN''$ is zero, so injectivity of the bottom row forces the image of $y$ in $M_1\otimes_RN''$ to be zero. Right exactness of tensor products now lifts $y$ from an element $y_0\in M_1\otimes_RN$. Subtract the row image of $y_0$ from $x$. The difference dies in $M_2\otimes_RN'$, hence is zero by flatness of $M_2$. Its image in $M_3\otimes_RN$ was $z$, so $z=0$. Thus tensoring with $M_3$ preserves every injection, proving its flatness. ∎

#### Proposition. Coherence detected by products of flat modules

*Historical source:* Chase, Theorem 2.1.

For a commutative ring $R$, the following are equivalent:

1. Every finitely generated ideal of $R$ is finitely presented; that is, $R$ is coherent.
2. The product of every family of flat $R$-modules is flat.
3. The module $R^A=\prod_{\alpha\in A}R$ is flat for every set $A$.

**Proof.** We first establish the two tensor-product criteria used in both directions. For an $R$-module $M$ and a family $(Q_\alpha)$, the projections define
$$\theta_{M,(Q_\alpha)}\colon
M\otimes_R\prod_\alpha Q_\alpha
\longrightarrow
\prod_\alpha(M\otimes_RQ_\alpha).$$
The following four properties are equivalent: $M$ is finitely generated; this map is surjective for every family; it is surjective for every constant family $Q_\alpha=Q$ and every index set; and it is surjective for the families $Q_\alpha=R$ alone. Replacing “finitely generated” by “finitely presented” and “surjective” by “bijective” gives another four equivalent properties.

For finite generation, take generators $m_1,\ldots,m_s$. Any tuple on the right has coordinates expressible as $\sum_{j=1}^s m_j\otimes q_{\alpha j}$. It is the image of $\sum_jm_j\otimes(q_{\alpha j})_\alpha$. Thus finite generation gives surjectivity for every family. Restricting families gives the next two implications. Conversely take the index set to be the underlying set of $M$, and consider the tuple whose coordinate indexed by $m$ is $m$. If $\theta_{M,(R)}$ is surjective, this tuple comes from a finite sum
$$\sum_{j=1}^s m_j\otimes(r_{j,m})_{m\in M}.$$
Coordinate comparison gives $m=\sum_jr_{j,m}m_j$ for every $m\in M$. Hence the displayed finite list generates $M$.

For finite presentation, choose $R^u\to R^v\to M\to0$ with $u,v$ finite. Tensoring with $\prod Q_\alpha$ gives a cokernel presentation. Tensoring with each $Q_\alpha$ and then taking the product gives a second cokernel presentation: products of module surjections are surjective, and kernels and images are computed coordinatewise. Finite free modules commute with products, by rearranging the finitely many coordinates. Thus the first two terms and their maps in these presentations agree, and their cokernels agree. This proves bijectivity of $\theta$ for every family.

For the converse it suffices to assume bijectivity for the families $Q_\alpha=R$. The finite-generation result supplies a surjection $F=R^v\to M$ with $v$ finite; let $K$ be its kernel. Fix a set $A$ and a tuple in $K^A$. View it in $F^A$, and lift it through the isomorphism $F\otimes_RR^A\cong F^A$. Its image in $M\otimes_RR^A$ is zero, because its image in $M^A$ is zero and $\theta_{M,(R)}$ is injective. The right-exact tensor sequence therefore lifts it from $K\otimes_RR^A$. This proves that
$$K\otimes_RR^A\longrightarrow K^A$$
is surjective for every $A$. The criterion just proved makes $K$ finitely generated. A finite generating list for $K$ completes a finite presentation of $M$. The intervening constant-family conditions follow by restriction, so all four finite-presentation criteria are established.

Now assume (1), and write $Q=\prod_\alpha Q_\alpha$ with each $Q_\alpha$ flat. For a finitely generated ideal $J$, coherence and the product criterion identify
$$J\otimes_RQ\ \cong\ \prod_\alpha(J\otimes_RQ_\alpha).$$
Each map $J\otimes_RQ_\alpha\to Q_\alpha$ is injective. Their product is injective, so the canonical map $J\otimes_RQ\to Q$ is injective. The [ideal flatness test](#native-algebra-lemma-flat) proves (2). Taking every factor equal to $R$ gives (3).

Finally assume (3). For a finitely generated ideal $J$, flatness of $R^A$ makes $J\otimes_RR^A\to R^A$ injective. The finite-generation criterion says its image is $J^A$, so $\theta_{J,(R)}$ is bijective for every $A$. The finite-presentation criterion makes $J$ finitely presented. This gives (1) and completes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma. Noetherian rings are coherent

Every Noetherian ring is coherent.

**Proof.** Each ideal is a finite module, and every finite module over a Noetherian ring is finitely presented, by the [finite-module theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-noetherian-basic). In particular each finitely generated ideal has the presentation required in the definition of coherence. ∎

#### Remark. Strict henselization as a union of finite étale local extensions

Let $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ be local, fix $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$, and identify the residue field of $R^h$ with $\kappa$. For each finite intermediate extension $\kappa\subset L\subset\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$, the [finite étale equivalence](#native-algebra-lemma-henselian-cat-finite-etale) gives a finite étale local $R^h$-algebra $A_L$ with its specified residue identification $\kappa(A_L)=L$. This marked algebra is unique up to unique marked isomorphism. The marking is necessary: the unmarked extension may have automorphisms.

Every inclusion $L\subset L'$ lifts uniquely to $A_L\to A_{L'}$, by full faithfulness of that equivalence. Uniqueness makes these arrows compose compatibly. They are local, since their residue maps are the prescribed field inclusions, and they are étale by [the theorem on maps between étale algebras](#native-algebra-lemma-map-between-etale). In particular they are flat local maps, hence faithfully flat and injective. We may therefore write their colimit as a union:
$$H=\bigcup_{\kappa\subset L\subset\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}},\ [L:\kappa]<\infty}A_L.$$

Each $A_L$ is henselian, by the finite-local-algebra result in *Henselian local rings and henselization*, Proposition 3.1. The residue maps give $H\to\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. Its kernel consists of the union of the stage maximal ideals, and every element outside this kernel is already a unit at a stage. Thus $H$ is local with residue field $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. To check henselianity, take a monic polynomial over $H$ with a specified simple root in that residue field. Its coefficients and that root lie at a common finite stage. The root equation and nonzero derivative hold in that stage's residue field, which embeds in $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. Henselianity there lifts the root. Hence $H$ is strictly henselian.

Here is the identification with the strict henselization, including the required compatibility. Given a local map $R\to T$ to a henselian local ring and a compatible embedding $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}\to\kappa(T)$, the ordinary henselization property extends it uniquely to $R^h\to T$. For each $L$, [henselian evaluation](#native-algebra-lemma-map-into-henselian) then gives a unique map $A_L\to T$ inducing the chosen embedding of $L$. These maps are compatible by uniqueness. They yield a local map $H\to T$ with the prescribed residue embedding, and every such map has those same restrictions, so is unique.

This is precisely the marked universal property of the strict henselization in Theorem 5.1. Apply the two universal properties to $H$ and $R^{sh}$ to obtain inverse marked local maps. Thus $H\cong R^{sh}$. The same theorem constructs $R^{sh}$ as a filtered colimit of étale $R$-algebras; this identification proves that property for the displayed union as well.

#### Lemma. Evaluating an ind-étale algebra in a henselian local ring

Let $R\to S$ be any homomorphism with $S$ henselian local, and put $\mathfrak p=R\cap\mathfrak m_S$. Suppose $A$ is a filtered colimit of étale $R$-algebras. Choose a prime $\mathfrak q\subset A$ over $\mathfrak p$ and a $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-embedding
$$\tau\colon\kappa(\mathfrak q)\longrightarrow\kappa(S).$$
There is exactly one $R$-algebra map $f\colon A\to S$ whose inverse image of $\mathfrak m_S$ is $\mathfrak q$ and whose residue map is $\tau$.

**Proof.** Write $A=\operatorname{colim}_iA_i$ and let $\mathfrak q_i$ be the contraction of $\mathfrak q$. The local map $(A_i)_{\mathfrak q_i}\to A_{\mathfrak q}$ induces an embedding $\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. Compose with $\tau$. The [étale evaluation theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-map-into-henselian) supplies a unique map $f_i\colon A_i\to S$ with precisely that prime and residue embedding. For every transition arrow, the two possible evaluations of its source have the same residues and therefore agree. The maps $f_i$ consequently define $f\colon A\to S$.

For an element represented in $A_i$, membership in $\mathfrak q$ is equivalent to membership in $\mathfrak q_i$, and hence to its image under $f_i$ lying in $\mathfrak m_S$. Thus $f^{-1}(\mathfrak m_S)=\mathfrak q$. Every element of $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is represented by a quotient of two elements of $A$, with denominator outside $\mathfrak q$; these elements occur at a common stage. The residue formula there shows that $f$ induces $\tau$ on this quotient. Finally, any other map with the prescribed data restricts to each $f_i$ by uniqueness of étale evaluation. It equals $f$ on the colimit. ∎

#### Proposition. Two successive localizations

For multiplicative subsets $S,T$ of a ring $A$, let $\overline S$ be the image of $S$ in $T^{-1}A$. There is a canonical isomorphism
$$\overline S^{-1}(T^{-1}A)\ \cong\ (ST)^{-1}A.$$

**Proof.** The localization at $ST$ inverts both $S$ and $T$, since each multiplicative subset contains $1$. Its structure map therefore factors through the two successive localizations. Conversely, the successive localization inverts every product $st$, so its structure map factors through $(ST)^{-1}A$. The resulting maps have the formulas
$$\frac{a/t}{s/1}\longmapsto\frac{a}{st},
\qquad
\frac{a}{st}\longmapsto\frac{a/t}{s/1}.$$
The universal properties prove they are well-defined. Their composites are the unique endomorphisms extending the original structure map from $A$, hence are identities. The argument includes multiplicative subsets containing zero, when the corresponding rings are zero. ∎

#### Proposition. Localization preserves exact sequences

*Historical source:* FAC, Chapter II, §4, no. 48, Lemma 1, p. 241. The fraction construction there assumes $0\notin S$; the zero localization is included below.

For any multiplicative subset $S\subset A$, localization is an exact functor on $A$-modules.

**Proof.** Recall that $m/s=m'/s'$ precisely when some $t\in S$ kills $s'm-sm'$. Addition and scalar multiplication use common denominators. These relations identify localization with extension of scalars by the inverse maps
$$
\begin{aligned}
S^{-1}A\otimes_AM&\longrightarrow S^{-1}M,\\
(a/s)\otimes m&\longmapsto am/s,\\
S^{-1}M&\longrightarrow S^{-1}A\otimes_AM,\\
m/s&\longmapsto (1/s)\otimes m.
\end{aligned}
$$
The fraction relation makes the first formula independent of representatives and balanced over $A$. For the second, the relation $t(s'm-sm')=0$ becomes $s'm-sm'=0$ after extending scalars, since $t$ is invertible; division by $ss'$ then proves independence. The elementary tensor identities prove that these maps are inverse.

Take an exact sequence $L\xrightarrow{u}M\xrightarrow{v}N$. Its localization is a complex. If $m/s$ is in the localized kernel, there is $t\in S$ with $tv(m)=0$. Choose $\ell\in L$ with $u(\ell)=tm$. Then
$$m/s=u(\ell)/(ts),$$
which lies in the localized image. The reverse inclusion follows from $vu=0$. Applying this to sequences with a zero end also preserves injections and surjections, proving exactness. If $0\in S$, every localized module is zero and the conclusion holds directly. ∎

#### Lemma. Descent of finite projectivity along a flat local map

Let $R\to S$ be flat and local, with both rings local. For a finite $R$-module $M$,
$$M\text{ is finite projective over }R
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
M\otimes_RS\text{ is finite projective over }S.$$
No finite-presentation assumption on $M$ is needed.

**Proof.** Finite projectivity is preserved by base change, since a splitting from a finite free module remains a splitting after tensoring. Conversely, suppose $M_S=M\otimes_RS$ is finite projective. It is finite free, by the [finite-projective criteria](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-projective). Choose lifts $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ of a basis of $M/\mathfrak m_RM$. They generate $M$ by Nakayama. The identification
$$M_S/\mathfrak m_SM_S
\cong(M/\mathfrak m_RM)\otimes_{\kappa(R)}\kappa(S)$$
shows that $M_S$ has rank $r$ and that the images of these lifts are a basis modulo $\mathfrak m_S$. Relative to any free basis of $M_S$, the square matrix of the lifts has determinant nonzero in $\kappa(S)$ and thus a unit in $S$. They are therefore an $S$-basis.

The surjection $R^r\to M$ defined by the lifts becomes an isomorphism over $S$. The map $R\to S$ is [faithfully flat because it is flat and local](#native-algebra-lemma-local-flat-ff). Flatness identifies the base change of the kernel with zero; faithful flatness forces the kernel to be zero. Thus $M\cong R^r$. This also covers $r=0$: Nakayama gives $M=0$. ∎

#### Lemma. Openness of the Cohen–Macaulay fibre locus of fixed dimension

Suppose $R\to S$ is flat and finitely presented. For $d\geq0$, consider the primes $\mathfrak q$ of $S$ such that, on putting $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$,
$$\begin{gathered}
S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}
\text{ is Cohen–Macaulay},\\
\dim_{\mathfrak q}(S/R)=d.
\end{gathered}$$
This subset of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ is open. Here $\dim_{\mathfrak q}(S/R)$ is dimension at the point of the fibre scheme, rather than the dimension of its local ring alone.

**Proof.** We first prove the field calculation used twice below. Let $k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\to T$ be quasi-finite, with $T$ a finite-type $k$-algebra. At a prime $\mathfrak r\subset T$, write $\mathfrak a$ for its contraction and set
$$A=k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]_{\mathfrak a},
\qquad B=T_{\mathfrak r},
\qquad e=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak r).$$
The residue extension $\kappa(\mathfrak a)\subset\kappa(\mathfrak r)$ is finite, and the local closed fibre of $A\to B$ has dimension zero, by quasi-finiteness. In particular $\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak a)=e$. The polynomial local ring $A$ is regular; a full proof over arbitrary fields is *Regular local rings*, Proposition 3.3. The [field dimension formula at a point](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-at-a-point-finite-type-field) gives
$$\dim A=d-e,
\qquad
\dim_{\mathfrak r}\operatorname{Spec}T=\dim B+e.$$

If $B$ is Cohen–Macaulay and $\dim_{\mathfrak r}\operatorname{Spec}T=d$, these identities give $\dim B=\dim A$. Since the local closed fibre has dimension zero, the [Cohen–Macaulay flatness criterion over a regular base](#native-algebra-lemma-cm-over-regular-flat) makes $B$ flat over $A$.

Conversely, suppose $B$ is flat over $A$. The [flat local dimension formula](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-base-fibre-equals-total) gives $\dim B=\dim A$. A regular system of parameters $a_1,\ldots,a_h$ of $A$ is regular, where $h=\dim A$, by the [regular-local parameter theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-regular-ring-cm). It stays regular in $B$: after the first $j$ parameters, the quotient of $B$ is flat over the corresponding quotient of $A$, and tensoring the injection defined by $a_{j+1}$ preserves injectivity. All successive quotients of $B$ are nonzero since these parameters lie in its maximal ideal. Thus $B$ has depth at least $h=\dim B$, and hence is Cohen–Macaulay. The second dimension identity gives $\dim_{\mathfrak r}\operatorname{Spec}T=d$. This proves the equivalence in full, including nonclosed points and $d=0$.

Now fix a point $\mathfrak q$ in the asserted locus. By the [quasi-finite polynomial model](#native-algebra-lemma-quasi-finite-over-polynomial-algebra), after a principal localization of $S$ away from $\mathfrak q$ there is a quasi-finite map
$$P=R[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\longrightarrow S.$$
Keep this localization in the notation. If $\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak q\cap P$ and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$, the induced local map in the fibre is
$$P_{\mathfrak q'}/\mathfrak pP_{\mathfrak q'}
\longrightarrow S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}.$$
These are precisely the relevant localizations of the polynomial and source algebras over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The field equivalence proves that this map is flat.

Apply the [general fibrewise flatness criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-criterion-flatness-fibre) to
$$R_{\mathfrak p}\longrightarrow P_{\mathfrak q'}
\longrightarrow S_{\mathfrak q},\qquad M=S_{\mathfrak q}.$$
The last algebra is essentially finitely presented over $R_{\mathfrak p}$, the middle is essentially of finite type, $M$ is a nonzero finitely presented module over itself, and it is $R_{\mathfrak p}$-flat by the assumed flatness of $S$. The fibre condition has just been proved. Thus $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $P_{\mathfrak q'}$.

The algebra $S$ is finitely presented over $P$: take its finite presentation over $R$ and add the $d$ relations identifying the variables of $P$ with their chosen images. Therefore general openness of flatness, Theorem 6.4, gives $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$ such that $S_g$ is flat over $P$. The proof of that theorem includes the finite-model flatness argument and the Noetherian flat-locus theorem; the latter uses the full generic-freeness proof in *Flat morphisms*, §5. Thus no Noetherian hypothesis on $R$ has been introduced.

For any $\mathfrak r\in\operatorname{Spec}S_g$, base change this flat, quasi-finite map from $P$ to the residue field at $\mathfrak r\cap R$. The resulting map is again flat and quasi-finite over a polynomial ring in $d$ variables. The converse half of the field equivalence shows that its local source ring is Cohen–Macaulay and its dimension at $\mathfrak r$ is $d$. Hence every point of $D(g)$ is in the specified locus. Together with the initial localization, this gives an open neighborhood of the original $\mathfrak q$ inside the locus. ∎

#### Lemma. Coefficients of a monic divisor

Let $K$ be a field and suppose the monic polynomial
$$f=x^n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_ix^i$$
divides
$$g=x^m+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b_jx^j$$
in $K[x]$. Then:

1. Every $a_i$ is integral over any subring $R_0\subset K$ containing all the $b_j$.
2. For any subring $R\subset K$ containing both lists of coefficients, every $a_i$ belongs to $\sqrt{(b_0,\ldots,b_{m-1})R}$.

**Proof.** Pass to a [splitting field](#context-fields-section-splitting-fieds) for $g$ and list its roots with multiplicity. Each root satisfies the monic equation $g=0$ over $R_0$, hence is integral over $R_0$. The roots of $f$ form a sublist, and its coefficients are signed elementary symmetric polynomials in that sublist. The [closure of integral elements under addition and multiplication](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-closure-is-ring) makes these coefficients integral, proving (1).

For (2), the monic quotient $h=g/f$ has degree $m-n$. Comparing coefficients from the highest degree downward expresses each coefficient of $h$ as a coefficient of $g$ minus a sum of products of coefficients of $f$ and coefficients of $h$ already found. Induction puts all of them in $R$. This also covers $m=n$, when $h=1$.

Set $J=\sqrt{(b_0,\ldots,b_{m-1})R}$ and $\overline R=R/J$. It is reduced, and reduction of $fh=g$ gives a product of monic polynomials equal to $x^m$. At a minimal prime $\mathfrak l$ of $\overline R$, its localization is a field, by the [minimal-prime localization lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-minimal-prime-reduced-ring). In that field a monic divisor of $x^m$ of degree $n$ is $x^n$. Hence every image $\overline a_i$ is zero in $\overline R_{\mathfrak l}$. The zero criterion for localization supplies $s_i\notin\mathfrak l$ with $s_i\overline a_i=0$, so primality implies $\overline a_i\in\mathfrak l$.

The intersection of the minimal primes equals the nilradical: every prime contains a minimal prime, and the nilradical is the intersection of all primes. Since $\overline R$ is reduced, this intersection is zero. Thus each $\overline a_i=0$, or $a_i\in J$, as claimed. If $\overline R=0$ the conclusion is immediate; if $n=0$ there are no coefficients $a_i$ to check. ∎

#### Lemma. A finite algebra containing prescribed integral elements

Let $R\to S$ be a homomorphism and let $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in S$. These elements are all integral over $R$ if and only if some $R$-subalgebra of $S$ is finite as an $R$-module and contains every $s_i$.

**Proof.** Suppose $s_i$ satisfies a monic equation of degree $d_i\geq1$. In $R[s_1,\ldots,s_n]$, that equation expresses every power $s_i^{d_i}$ as a combination of lower powers. Repeated reduction in each variable shows that the finitely many monomials
$$s_1^{e_1}\cdots s_n^{e_n},
\qquad 0\leq e_i<d_i,$$
span this algebra as an $R$-module. This is the required finite subalgebra. For an empty list, the image of $R$ itself is cyclic and suffices.

Conversely, every element of an algebra finite over $R$ is integral over $R$, by the [finite-algebra integrality theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-is-integral). Apply this to the proposed subalgebra and its elements $s_i$. The argument uses the image of $R$ in $S$ and does not require injectivity. ∎

#### Lemma. The clopen partition defined by an idempotent

An idempotent $e\in R$ gives the disjoint decomposition
$$\operatorname{Spec}R=D(e)\amalg D(1-e).$$
Both parts are open and closed.

**Proof.** In each residue field the equation $e^2=e$ forces the image of $e$ to be either $0$ or $1$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
D(e)&=\{\mathfrak p:e=1\text{ in }\kappa(\mathfrak p)\}
=V(1-e),\\
D(1-e)&=\{\mathfrak p:e=0\text{ in }\kappa(\mathfrak p)\}
=V(e).
\end{aligned}
$$
Exactly one of these alternatives holds at every prime. The displayed equalities also identify each open set as the closed complement of the other. They include $e=0$, $e=1$, and the empty spectrum of the zero ring. ∎

#### Lemma. A principal open is the spectrum of a localization

For $f\in R$, contraction identifies $\operatorname{Spec}R_f$ homeomorphically with $D(f)\subset\operatorname{Spec}R$. The inverse sends $\mathfrak p\in D(f)$ to $\mathfrak pR_f$.

**Proof.** In the [spectrum-localization theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-spec-localization), take the multiplicative set of powers of $f$. Its disjointness from a prime is exactly $f\notin\mathfrak p$. That theorem proves the contraction-extension bijection and identifies principal-open bases on both sides, so it proves the asserted homeomorphism and inverse. ∎

#### Theorem. Chevalley’s theorem on constructible images

Let $R\to S$ be finitely presented. The image of every constructible subset of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ is constructible in $\operatorname{Spec}R$.

**Proof by polynomial elimination.** We supply the affine-set reductions and both terminal cases of the degree induction.

On an affine spectrum, a retrocompact open is the same as a quasi-compact open. Indeed the whole spectrum is quasi-compact, so retrocompactness implies quasi-compactness. Conversely a quasi-compact open is a finite union of principal opens; its intersection with another such union is again a finite union of principal opens, using $D(a)\cap D(b)=D(ab)$. Consequently the definition of constructibility as finite unions of differences of retrocompact opens gives the following description:
$$E=\bigcup_{\nu=1}^r
\bigl(D(f_\nu)\cap V(g_{\nu1},\ldots,g_{\nu m_\nu})\bigr).$$
These sets form the Boolean algebra generated by principal opens. The converse is immediate from the same finite-union description. The [Zariski-topology construction](#native-algebra-lemma-zariski-topology) gives the principal-open basis, and the [affine quasi-compactness lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-quasi-compact) supplies the required finiteness of principal covers.

This description also proves two image rules. Under $\operatorname{Spec}R_c\cong D(c)$, clear powers of $c$ from each element defining a basic constructible piece. Its image has the form
$$D(ca)\cap V(b_1,\ldots,b_m),$$
where $a,b_j\in R$. Under $\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)\cong V(I)$, with $I=(h_1,\ldots,h_\ell)$ finitely generated, lift all defining elements to $R$. The corresponding image is
$$D(a)\cap V(h_1,\ldots,h_\ell,b_1,\ldots,b_m).$$
Finite unions prove both rules for every constructible subset of the localized or quotient spectrum.

We now treat $R[x]$. First, if $f=\sum_{i=0}^n a_ix^i$, a prime $\mathfrak p$ belongs to the image of $D(f)$ exactly when
$$\kappa(\mathfrak p)[x]_{\overline f}\ne0.$$
This polynomial ring is a domain, so its localization is nonzero exactly when $\overline f\ne0$, or equivalently some $a_i\notin\mathfrak p$. Therefore
$$\operatorname{image}(D(f))=\bigcup_{i=0}^nD(a_i).$$
This is quasi-compact open. Since arbitrary opens are unions of principal opens, the projection $\operatorname{Spec}R[x]\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is open as well.

The second terminal case is $D(f)\cap V(g)$ when the leading coefficient of $g$ is invertible. Divide by that unit, making $g$ monic of degree $d$. If $d=0$, the set is empty. Otherwise $A=R[x]/(g)$ is free over $R$ on $1,x,\ldots,x^{d-1}$: monic division gives both spanning and uniqueness. Let the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by $f$ on $A$ be
$$P(T)=T^d+r_{d-1}T^{d-1}+\cdots+r_0.$$
Its formation commutes with passage to $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, since the multiplication matrix and its determinant reduce coefficientwise. Over this field, multiplication by $\overline f$ is nilpotent if and only if the reduced characteristic polynomial is $T^d$. In one direction a basis adapted to the kernels of successive powers gives a triangular matrix with zero diagonal. In the other direction [Cayley–Hamilton](#native-algebra-lemma-charpoly) makes its $d$th power zero. Multiplication is nilpotent precisely when the element $\overline f$ is nilpotent, by evaluating a power of the operator on $1$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{image}(D(f)\cap V(g))
&\Longleftrightarrow (A\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p))_{\overline f}\ne0\\
&\Longleftrightarrow \mathfrak p\in\bigcup_{i=0}^{d-1}D(r_i).
\end{aligned}
$$
Here a localization at one element is zero exactly when some power of that element is zero. A nonzero fibre algebra has a prime, which supplies the point upstairs. This proves the second terminal case with an explicit finite list of coefficients.

For a general basic piece
$$D(f)\cap V(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\subset\operatorname{Spec}R[x],$$
discard zero equations and order the remaining ones by degree. Induct, for all coefficient rings at once, on the integer
$$N=\sum_{g_i\ne0}(\deg g_i+1).$$
If there are no equations, the first terminal case applies. Otherwise write $c$ for the nonzero leading coefficient of a least-degree equation $g_1$. Split the base into $V(c)$ and $D(c)$. On the closed part, pass to $R/(c)$: the degree of $g_1$ drops, or it becomes zero, so $N$ decreases. The closed-image rule returns the resulting constructible image to $\operatorname{Spec}R$.

On $D(c)$, the leading coefficient of $g_1$ is a unit. If this ring is zero, the part is empty; if $g_1$ is constant, its vanishing set is empty. If localization lowers the degree of any equation or makes one zero, $N$ has already decreased and induction applies. Otherwise the degree order is unchanged. If $g_1$ is the sole equation, the second terminal case applies. If another equation $g_j$ remains, its degree is at least that of $g_1$; subtract a suitable multiple $a x^{\deg g_j-\deg g_1}g_1$ to cancel its leading term. This leaves the defining ideal unchanged and strictly lowers $\deg g_j$, or removes a zero equation. Thus each nonterminal branch reduces $N$. The localization image rule brings its constructible image back to the original base. Combining the two parts completes the induction.

Finally write $S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J$ with $J$ finitely generated. The closed-image rule first regards the chosen constructible set as one in polynomial affine space. Project away one variable at a time, applying the one-variable theorem over each intervening coefficient ring. After all $n$ projections its image in $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is constructible. This includes $n=0$, when only the closed-image rule is needed. ∎

There is also a complete proof by finite models in *Quasi-finite morphisms and Chevalley’s theorem*, §§3–5, Theorem 5.1. It descends the finite algebra presentation and the finitely many Boolean conditions to a finite-type $\mathbb Z$-subalgebra. Sections 3–4 prove Noetherian Chevalley using the irreducible-closed constructibility criterion and a normalization argument for the generic image. The general proof checks equality of images after base change through the nonzero tensor product of the two residue fields over their common field. This proves the same arbitrary-ring statement.

#### Lemma. Specialization and generization of constructible subsets

Let $E$ be a constructible subset of $\operatorname{Spec}R$. If $E$ is stable under specialization, it is closed. If it is stable under generization, it is open.

**First proof, by realizing an affine image.** Each basic piece
$$D(f)\cap V(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$$
is the image of the spectrum of the finitely presented algebra
$$B=(R/(g_1,\ldots,g_m))_f
\cong R[z]/(g_1,\ldots,g_m,fz-1).$$
A finite union of such images is the image of $\operatorname{Spec}(\prod_\nu B_\nu)$, by the [product-spectrum theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-spec-product).

This product is again finitely presented. One explicit presentation adjoins finitely many orthogonal idempotents $e_\nu$ summing to $1$, and variables $z_\nu$ with
$$
\begin{gathered}
e_\nu z_\nu=z_\nu,\qquad
e_\nu g_{\nu j}=0,\qquad
f_\nu z_\nu=e_\nu.
\end{gathered}
$$
Together with $e_\nu^2=e_\nu$, $e_\nu e_\mu=0$ for $\nu\ne\mu$, and $\sum e_\nu=1$, these relations split the presented algebra into the factors $B_\nu$. On the $\nu$th factor only $z_\nu$ survives, and its remaining equations are exactly those for $B_\nu$. Thus the displayed finite presentation has the required product. The empty union is the spectrum of the zero algebra, which has the presentation $R/(1)$.

We have realized $E$ as an affine-spectrum image. If it is specialization-stable, the [closed-image lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-image-stable-specialization-closed) makes it closed. If it is generization-stable, its constructible complement is specialization-stable, hence closed by what was just proved. Then $E$ is open.

**Second proof, using the spectral topology.** The affine spectrum is spectral: it is quasi-compact and has the quasi-compact basis $D(f)$ closed under finite intersections; distinct primes are distinguished by such opens; and every nonempty irreducible closed subset has a unique generic point, by the [irreducibility theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-irreducible). Indeed an irreducible $V(I)$ has prime radical, and is the closure of that prime.

For completeness, its constructible topology, generated by the opens $D(f)$ and their complements $V(f)$, is compact. Given an ultrafilter $\mathscr U$ of subsets of the spectrum, put
$$\mathfrak p_{\mathscr U}=\{f\in R:V(f)\in\mathscr U\}.$$
The identities $V(0)=\operatorname{Spec}R$, $V(1)=\varnothing$, $V(-f)=V(f)$, and $V(f)\cap V(g)\subset V(f+g)$ show that this is a proper additive subgroup. The inclusion $V(f)\subset V(af)$ gives ideal stability. Finally $V(fg)=V(f)\cup V(g)$ and the ultrafilter alternative give primality. Every basic constructible neighborhood of $\mathfrak p_{\mathscr U}$ belongs to $\mathscr U$: for a condition $D(f)$ use $f\notin\mathfrak p_{\mathscr U}$, and for $V(g)$ use $g\in\mathfrak p_{\mathscr U}$. Finite intersections preserve membership. Thus every ultrafilter converges, proving compactness. The empty spectrum is compact directly.

A constructible set is open and closed in this topology, hence compact. If $\mathfrak p$ is in the Zariski closure of $E$, then
$$\{E\cap D(f):f\notin\mathfrak p\}$$
has the finite intersection property: a finite intersection is $E\cap D(\prod f)$, and this Zariski neighborhood of $\mathfrak p$ meets $E$. These are closed subsets in the constructible topology on $E$, so compactness gives a prime $\mathfrak q\in E$ lying in all of them. This means $\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p$. If $E$ is specialization-stable, it follows that $\mathfrak p\in E$. Hence $E$ is closed. The complement argument again proves the generization assertion. This is the spectral-space argument in affine form; the complete compactness route also appears in *Flat morphisms*, §3, Lemma 3.1. ∎

#### Lemma. Integral elements form a subalgebra

For any ring map $R\to S$, the elements of $S$ integral over $R$ form an $R$-subalgebra.

**Proof.** Given two integral elements $a,b$, the [finite-subalgebra criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-integral) places them in the finite algebra $R[a,b]\subset S$. This algebra contains $a+b$, $ab$, and $-a$, all integral by the converse direction of that criterion. It also contains the image of every element of $R$, which is integral since it satisfies a monic linear equation. Thus the integral elements contain the structural image and are closed under the algebra operations. ∎

#### Lemma. Integrality over an ideal and its graded algebra

Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a homomorphism, let $I\subset R$ be any ideal, and form
$$\mathcal R(I)=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^nt^n\subset R[t].$$
An element $s\in S$ is integral over $I$ if and only if $st\in S[t]$ is integral over $\mathcal R(I)$.

**Proof.** If
$$s^d+\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\varphi(a_j)s^j=0,
\qquad a_j\in I^{d-j},$$
then multiplication by $t^d$ gives a monic equation for $st$, with coefficient of $(st)^j$ equal to $\varphi(a_j)t^{d-j}$. That coefficient comes from $\mathcal R(I)$.

Conversely, suppose $(st)^d+\sum_{j<d}b_j(st)^j=0$ with $b_j\in\mathcal R(I)$, interpreted through its map to $S[t]$. Take the homogeneous component of degree $d$ in this equality. Only the degree-$d-j$ component of $b_j$ contributes to the term indexed by $j$; it has the form $a_jt^{d-j}$ for some $a_j\in I^{d-j}$. Comparing the coefficient of $t^d$ gives the displayed equation for $s$. This comparison takes place in $S[t]$ and remains valid when $\varphi$ is not injective. ∎

#### Lemma. Five tests for a point to lie in the image

Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ and $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$. The following are equivalent:

1. Some prime of $S$ contracts to $\mathfrak p$.
2. $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is nonzero.
3. $S_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak p}$ is nonzero.
4. $(S/\mathfrak pS)_{\mathfrak p}$ is nonzero.
5. $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak pS)=\mathfrak p$.

In these expressions the subscript $\mathfrak p$ means localization using $R\setminus\mathfrak p$.

**Proof.** The [fibre-ring identifications](#native-algebra-remark-fundamental-diagram) identify the three rings in (2)–(4), and identify their spectra with the primes of $S$ lying over $\mathfrak p$. A ring has a prime exactly when it is nonzero. This proves equivalence of (1)–(4).

For the last condition, a localization of $S/\mathfrak pS$ is zero exactly when some element of the multiplicative set becomes zero there: equivalently, some $a\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ has $\varphi(a)\in\mathfrak pS$. Thus (4) says that no such $a$ exists. The contraction of $\mathfrak pS$ always contains $\mathfrak p$, so the absence of such an $a$ is precisely (5). ∎

#### Lemma. Localizing the integral closure

Let $A\to B$ be any ring map, let $T\subset A$ be multiplicative, and let $B'\subset B$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $B$. Then the integral closure of $T^{-1}A$ in $T^{-1}B$ is $T^{-1}B'$.

**Proof.** Exactness of localization embeds $T^{-1}B'$ into $T^{-1}B$. If $b\in B'$ satisfies a monic equation of degree $n$, division by $t^n$ shows that $b/t$ satisfies a monic equation over $T^{-1}A$. This gives one inclusion.

For the converse take $z=b/t\in T^{-1}B$ integral over $T^{-1}A$. Choose an equation
$$\begin{gathered}
z^n+\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i/t_i)z^{n-i}=0,\\
a_i\in A,\qquad t_i\in T.
\end{gathered}$$
Put $u=t\prod_i t_i\in T$. Then $y=uz$ is represented by the actual element $(\prod_i t_i)b$ of $B$, and $c_i=u^ia_i/t_i$ is an element of $A$. Multiplying the equation by $u^n$ gives
$$P(y)=y^n+\sum_{i=1}^nc_i y^{n-i}=0
\quad\text{in }T^{-1}B.$$
The element $P(y)\in B$ need not yet be zero. The localization zero criterion gives $v\in T$ with $vP(y)=0$ in $B$. Set $w=vy$. Then in $B$,
$$w^n+\sum_{i=1}^nv^ic_iw^{n-i}=v^nP(y)=0.$$
This is monic, so $w\in B'$. Finally $z=w/(vu)$ belongs to $T^{-1}B'$. The proof clears both the coefficient denominators and the possible localization zero witness, without a torsion-free assumption. ∎

#### Lemma. Base change preserves integral and finite maps

Given $R\to S$ and $R\to R'$, set $S'=R'\otimes_RS$. If $S$ is integral over $R$, then $S'$ is integral over $R'$. If $S$ is finite over $R$, then $S'$ is finite over $R'$.

**Proof.** Choose any algebra generating family $(s_\lambda)$ for $S$. In the integral case each generator satisfies a monic equation over $R$. The images $1\otimes s_\lambda$ satisfy the same equations after applying $R\to R'$ to the coefficients. They generate $S'$ as an $R'$-algebra. Since integral elements form a subalgebra, all of $S'$ is integral over $R'$.

In the finite case choose module generators $s_1,\ldots,s_n$. If $s=\sum_i a_is_i$, then
$$r'\otimes s=\sum_i r'\varphi'(a_i)(1\otimes s_i).$$
Every tensor is a finite sum of such elementary tensors, so the $1\otimes s_i$ span $S'$ over $R'$. This proves finiteness. Neither assertion needs flatness of the base change. ∎

#### Lemma. Prime lifting is specialization lifting

A ring map $R\to S$ has going down exactly when the induced spectrum map lifts generizations. It has going up exactly when that map lifts specializations.

**Proof.** The closure of a prime $\mathfrak p$ as a point of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is $V(\mathfrak p)$. Thus $\mathfrak p_1$ specializes $\mathfrak p_0$ exactly when $\mathfrak p_0\subset\mathfrak p_1$, and it is a generization exactly when the inclusion is reversed.

For going down, begin with $\mathfrak q_1\subset S$ over $\mathfrak p_1$ and a generization $\mathfrak p_0\subset\mathfrak p_1$. Lifting that generization means finding $\mathfrak q_0\subset\mathfrak q_1$ over $\mathfrak p_0$, which is precisely the going-down requirement. Conversely a going-down lift supplies that point for every such pair. For going up, start with $\mathfrak q_0$ over $\mathfrak p_0$ and $\mathfrak p_1\supset\mathfrak p_0$; the required specialization is a prime $\mathfrak q_1\supset\mathfrak q_0$ over $\mathfrak p_1$. These are exactly the going-up data in both directions. ∎

#### Lemma. An injective ring map reaches every minimal prime

If $R\to S$ is injective, each minimal prime of $R$ is the contraction of a prime of $S$.

**Proof.** Fix a minimal prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$. Exact localization gives an injection $R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak p}$. The source is nonzero, so the target is nonzero and has a prime.
