Its contraction to $R_{\mathfrak p}$ must be the unique prime of that ring: primes there correspond to primes of $R$ contained in the minimal prime $\mathfrak p$. Pulling the chosen prime back to $S$ therefore gives a prime contracting to $\mathfrak p$, as required. ∎

#### Lemma. Modules over a localization

For a multiplicative set $T\subset R$, restriction of scalars identifies the category of $T^{-1}R$-modules with the full subcategory of $R$-modules on which every $t\in T$ acts invertibly.

**Proof.** Restriction has this property since $t/1$ is a unit of the localized ring. Conversely suppose $N$ has the stated invertible operators. Write $r_N$ for multiplication by $r$, and define the action of a fraction by
$$\frac r t\ \longmapsto\ r_Nt_N^{-1}.$$
All multiplication operators commute, and their inverses commute with them as well. If $r/t=r'/t'$, some $u\in T$ kills $t'r-tr'$. Its action is invertible, so
$$t'_Nr_N=t_Nr'_N.$$
Multiplying by the two inverse denominator operators proves that the proposed action is independent of the fraction representative.

The usual common-denominator formulas for addition and multiplication now give addition and multiplication of these operators. The fraction $1/1$ acts as the identity, so they define a $T^{-1}R$-module structure. It is the only extension: $1/t$ must act by $t_N^{-1}$. Every $R$-linear map between two such modules commutes with each $t$ and therefore with its inverse, so it is automatically linear for this extended action. The extension and restriction functors leave underlying groups and maps unchanged, and uniqueness of the extended action makes them inverse. If $0\in T$, its invertibility forces $N=0$, agreeing with the category of modules over the zero ring. ∎

#### Lemma. Exact sequences detected by Hom

For maps $M_1\xrightarrow{u}M_2\xrightarrow{v}M_3$ of $R$-modules:

**(1)** The sequence $M_1\to M_2\to M_3\to0$ is exact if and only if, for every $N$, the sequence
$$0\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_3,N)
\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_2,N)
\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_1,N)$$
is exact.

**(2)** The sequence $0\to M_1\to M_2\to M_3$ is exact if and only if, for every $N$, the sequence
$$0\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,M_1)
\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,M_2)
\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,M_3)$$
is exact.

All Hom maps are induced by $u$ and $v$; no projectivity hypothesis is imposed.

**Proof of (1).** If the original sequence is exact, a map from $M_3$ is determined by its composite with the surjection $v$. A map $M_2\to N$ kills $u$ precisely when it descends uniquely through $M_2/\operatorname{im}u\cong M_3$. These two observations prove the stated Hom exactness.

Conversely assume the Hom sequences are exact. With $N=M_3$, the image of $\operatorname{id}_{M_3}$ is $v$, and the complex condition forces $vu=0$. Let $q\colon M_2\to C=\operatorname{coker}u$. The relation $vu=0$ factors $v$ as $bq$ for a map $b\colon C\to M_3$. Apply exactness with $N=C$ to $q$, which kills $u$: it gives $a\colon M_3\to C$ with $av=q$. Hence $abq=q$, and surjectivity of $q$ gives $ab=\operatorname{id}_C$. Also $bav=bq=v$. Injectivity of $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_3,M_3)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(M_2,M_3)$ gives $ba=\operatorname{id}_{M_3}$. Thus $b$ is an isomorphism and $v$ is the cokernel of $u$, proving the required exactness.

**Proof of (2).** If the original sequence is exact, the injection $u$ gives an injection on Hom sets. A map $N\to M_2$ killed by $v$ has image in $\ker v=\operatorname{im}u$ and factors uniquely through $M_1$. This gives exactness.

Conversely, the complex condition for $N=M_1$, applied to the identity, yields $vu=0$. Let $K=\ker u$. Its inclusion into $M_1$ maps to zero in $M_2$, so injectivity of the Hom map with $N=K$ forces this inclusion to be zero; therefore $u$ is injective. Let $L=\ker v$, with its inclusion $j\colon L\to M_2$. Exactness with $N=L$ supplies $h\colon L\to M_1$ with $uh=j$. Hence every element of $\ker v$ is in $\operatorname{im}u$. The opposite containment follows from $vu=0$, completing the proof. ∎

#### Lemma. Module maps and finite witnesses in a directed algebra colimit

Let $(R_i)$ be a directed system of $A$-algebras with colimit $R$, and let $M,N$ be $A$-modules.

1. If $M$ is finite and two maps $u,u'\colon M\to N$ become equal after tensoring with $R$, they become equal after tensoring with some $R_i$.
2. If $N$ is finite and $u\colon M\to N$ becomes surjective over $R$, it is surjective after tensoring with some $R_i$.
3. If $N$ is finitely presented, every $R$-linear map $v\colon N\otimes_AR\to M\otimes_AR$ is the base change of an $R_i$-linear map $v_i\colon N\otimes_AR_i\to M\otimes_AR_i$ for some $i$.
4. If $M$ is finite, $N$ is finitely presented, and $u\colon M\to N$ becomes an isomorphism over $R$, it becomes an isomorphism over some $R_i$.

No transition map is assumed injective or flat.

**Proof.** For every $A$-module $L$, there is a natural identification
$$L\otimes_AR\cong\operatorname{colim}_i(L\otimes_AR_i).$$
One can obtain it from the tensor universal property: compatible balanced maps at all stages are exactly a balanced map with the colimit algebra. The [element criterion for a directed colimit](#native-algebra-lemma-zero-directed-limit) therefore applies. Finitely many representatives occur at a common stage, and finitely many elements zero in the colimit become zero together at some later stage.

For (1), choose generators $m_1,\ldots,m_s$ of $M$. The finitely many differences $(u-u')(m_j)\otimes1$ vanish in $N\otimes_AR$, hence vanish in $N\otimes_AR_i$ at one stage. The tensors $m_j\otimes1$ generate the base-changed source, so the two maps agree there.

For (2), choose generators $n_1,\ldots,n_t$ of $N$ and preimages of $n_j\otimes1$ in $M\otimes_AR$. Represent these preimages at one stage. Their images under $u$ need not yet equal $n_j\otimes1$ at that stage, but the finitely many differences vanish in the colimit. Enlarge the stage once more to kill all these differences. The images now contain a generating list of $N\otimes_AR_i$, proving surjectivity.

For (3), choose a finite presentation $A^s\to A^t\to N\to0$, with images $n_1,\ldots,n_t$ of the standard generators and relation vectors $(a_{\ell1},\ldots,a_{\ell t})$ for $1\leq\ell\leq s$. At a common stage choose $z_j\in M\otimes_AR_i$ representing $v(n_j\otimes1)$. Each relation image
$$\sum_{j=1}^t a_{\ell j}z_j$$
is zero in the colimit. Enlarge $i$ until all are zero. Right exactness of tensoring the chosen presentation shows that the assignment $n_j\otimes1\mapsto z_j$ now defines $v_i$, whose base change is $v$.

For (4), apply (3) to the inverse of $u\otimes_AR$, obtaining $v_i$. The composites of $v_i$ with the base-changed $u$ agree with the identity after passing to $R$. Both source modules at this stage are finite: $M$ is finite, and finite presentation makes $N$ finite. On the directed tail above $i$, the finite-generator argument of (1), now over $R_i$, kills both lists of differences at one common later stage. The resulting maps are inverse there. This argument allows the descended $v_i$ to be defined only over $R_i$; it need not arise from an $A$-linear map. ∎

#### Lemma. Removing initial terms of a quasi-regular sequence

Let $M$ be a module over any ring $R$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_c$ be $M$-quasi-regular. For $0\leq i\leq c$, put
$$\begin{gathered}
\overline R=R/(f_1,\ldots,f_i),\\
\overline M=M/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)M.
\end{gathered}$$
Then the remaining images $\overline f_{i+1},\ldots,\overline f_c$ are $\overline M$-quasi-regular over $\overline R$.

**Proof.** It is enough to remove $f_1$ and repeat. Put $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ and write $\overline J$ for the ideal generated by the remaining elements in $R/(f_1)$. The quasi-regularity isomorphism identifies the associated graded module with
$$\operatorname{gr}_J(M)\cong(M/JM)[X_1,\ldots,X_c],$$
where the initial form of multiplication by $f_1$ is multiplication by $X_1$.

For every $n\geq1$ we claim
$$J^nM\cap f_1M=f_1J^{n-1}M.$$
One inclusion follows from $f_1\in J$. For the other suppose $f_1m\in J^nM$. If $n=1$, the conclusion $m\in J^0M$ needs no argument. If $n\geq2$ and $m\notin J^{n-1}M$, choose the largest $j$ in the finite range $0\leq j\leq n-2$ for which $m\in J^jM$. Then $m$ has nonzero class in $J^jM/J^{j+1}M$. Multiplication by $X_1$ is injective on a polynomial module, so $f_1m$ has nonzero class in $J^{j+1}M/J^{j+2}M$. This contradicts $f_1m\in J^nM\subseteq J^{j+2}M$. Hence $m\in J^{n-1}M$, proving the claim. The argument chooses a degree in a finite range and does not require separation of the $J$-adic filtration.

Now for $n\geq1$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\overline J^n\overline M/\overline J^{n+1}\overline M
&\cong J^nM\big/\bigl(J^{n+1}M+(J^nM\cap f_1M)\bigr)\\
&=J^nM\big/\bigl(J^{n+1}M+f_1J^{n-1}M\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$
In degree zero the quotient is $M/JM$. The resulting graded module is therefore obtained by setting $X_1=0$ in the polynomial module above:
$$\operatorname{gr}_{\overline J}(\overline M)
\cong(M/JM)[X_2,\ldots,X_c].$$
The isomorphism has the prescribed generator images, so it is the quasi-regularity map for the remaining sequence. Its final quotient is still $M/JM$. Iterating proves the statement, including the original and empty remaining sequences. ∎

#### Lemma. The dimension formula in a Cohen–Macaulay local ring

If $R$ is Noetherian local and Cohen–Macaulay, then for every prime $\mathfrak p$,
$$\dim R=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim(R/\mathfrak p).$$

**Proof.** Choose a prime chain of maximum length below $\mathfrak p$ and one of maximum length from $\mathfrak p$ to the maximal ideal. Their lengths are $\dim R_{\mathfrak p}$ and $\dim(R/\mathfrak p)$, respectively. Each is saturated in its interval. The first begins at a minimal prime, since otherwise it could be extended, and the second ends at the maximal ideal. Concatenation is consequently a maximal chain in $\operatorname{Spec}R$. The [Cohen–Macaulay maximal-chain theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-maximal-chain-cm) says its length is $\dim R$, proving the equality. The same conclusion follows from the [full-support Cohen–Macaulay module version](#native-algebra-lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-cm), taking the module to be $R$. ∎

#### Lemma. One nonzero relation eliminates one polynomial variable

Let $k$ be a field and let $0\ne I\subsetneq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. There are polynomials $y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}$ such that
$$k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I$$
is finite over the subalgebra generated by their images. Moreover the $y_i$ may lie in the image of $\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.

**Proof.** Choose a nonzero $F\in I$. A nonzero constant cannot belong to the proper ideal, so $F$ has positive degree and $n\geq1$. It suffices to prove the assertion for the quotient by $(F)$.

Choose an integer $B$ larger than every exponent appearing in a monomial of $F$. For $1\leq i<n$ put
$$e_i=B^i,\qquad y_i=x_i-x_n^{e_i}.$$
For the exponent vector $\alpha$ of any monomial occurring in $F$, the integer
$$w(\alpha)=\alpha_n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}B^i\alpha_i$$
is its base-$B$ encoding, so these weights are distinct. In
$$F(y_1+T^{e_1},\ldots,y_{n-1}+T^{e_{n-1}},T),$$
the highest power of $T$ comes uniquely from the highest-weight original monomial, taking its highest $T$-term in every factor. Its coefficient is the nonzero coefficient of that original monomial, an element of $k^\times$. Divide by this coefficient. The resulting polynomial is monic in $T$ with coefficients in $k[y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}]$, and it vanishes at the class of $x_n$.

Thus $x_n$ is integral over the subalgebra generated by the $y_i$. Every other $x_i$ equals $y_i+x_n^{e_i}$, so the quotient by $(F)$ is generated over that subalgebra by this single integral element and is finite. Passing to the quotient by $I$ preserves finiteness. The formulas for $y_i$ have integer coefficients. For $n=1$ the list is empty and the argument is simply monic normalization of the one-variable polynomial $F$. ∎

#### Lemma. An integral overring has the same dimension

If $R\subset S$ is an integral extension, then $\dim R=\dim S$, with no Noetherian assumption.

**Proof.** Every prime of $R$ has a prime above it by [lying over for integral overrings](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-overring-surjective). Starting above the first prime of a finite chain in $R$, repeated [going up](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-going-up) lifts the whole chain to $S$. Distinct contractions ensure that all its inclusions remain strict. This proves $\dim R\leq\dim S$.

Conversely, contract any finite strict chain in $S$ to $R$. Two comparable primes over the same base prime must coincide, by [integral incomparability](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-no-inclusion). Hence every contracted inclusion is strict, giving $\dim S\leq\dim R$. Taking suprema over all finite chains covers infinite dimensions as well. If $R=0$, its unital overring is also zero and the two spectra are empty. ∎

#### Lemma. Five tests for dimension one

For a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$, the following conditions are equivalent.

1. The dimension of $R$ is one.
2. Its Hilbert–Samuel degree $d(R)$ is one.
3. Some nonnilpotent $x\in\mathfrak m$ satisfies $V(x)=\{\mathfrak m\}$.
4. Some nonnilpotent $x\in\mathfrak m$ satisfies $\sqrt{xR}=\mathfrak m$.
5. A principal ideal is an ideal of definition, whereas the zero ideal is not.

Here an ideal of definition means an ideal with radical $\mathfrak m$.

**Proof.** Suppose (1). The [finiteness of minimal primes](#native-algebra-lemma-noetherian-irreducible-components) and [prime avoidance](#native-algebra-lemma-silly) give an element of $\mathfrak m$ outside every minimal prime: each minimal prime is strictly smaller than $\mathfrak m$. Any other prime must be $\mathfrak m$, since a nonminimal prime strictly below $\mathfrak m$ would give a chain of length two. The chosen element therefore belongs to exactly one prime, namely $\mathfrak m$. It is not nilpotent, since nilpotents belong to every prime. This proves (3).

The [radical description of closed subsets](#native-algebra-lemma-zariski-topology) identifies (3) with (4). If $\sqrt{xR}=\mathfrak m$ and $x$ is nilpotent, then $\sqrt0=\mathfrak m$. Conversely, if $\sqrt0=\mathfrak m$, every element of $\mathfrak m$ is nilpotent. Thus (4) and (5) are equivalent.

Assume (5), and write $I=xR$ for the principal ideal of definition. Multiplication by $x^j$ maps $R/I$ onto $I^j/I^{j+1}$. Consequently
$$\ell_R(R/I^{n+1})\leq(n+1)\ell_R(R/I).$$
The eventual polynomial has degree at most one. The [dimension-zero criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-0-d-0), proved just below, says that degree zero would make the zero ideal an ideal of definition. Hence the degree is one, proving (2).

For the remaining implication, suppose $d(R)=1$. If a chain of length two exists, extend its upper endpoint to $\mathfrak m$ and retain a chain
$$\mathfrak p\subsetneq\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak m.$$
Put $B=R/\mathfrak p$. The [Hilbert-function exact-sequence lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-hilbert-ses-chi) gives $d(B)\leq1$. Since $B$ has a nonzero prime strictly below its maximal ideal, the dimension-zero criterion excludes $d(B)=0$. Choose $x\in\mathfrak q\setminus\mathfrak p$. Multiplication by its image in the domain $B$ gives
$$0\longrightarrow B\xrightarrow{x}B\longrightarrow B/xB\longrightarrow0.$$
The same exact-sequence lemma says that $\chi_{I,B/xB}$ has degree strictly less than one: the two copies of $\chi_{I,B}$ cancel. Thus $B/xB$ is zero-dimensional. But the images of $\mathfrak q$ and $\mathfrak m$ are two distinct primes of that quotient, a contradiction. Therefore $\dim R\leq1$; degree one excludes dimension zero, so (1) holds.

The [general dimension, growth and parameter theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-dimension) also yields (1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2)$\Leftrightarrow$(5). The argument above retains the direct prime-avoidance and Hilbert-growth proof in dimension one. ∎

#### Lemma. Dimension zero and constant Hilbert growth

A Noetherian local ring $R$ has dimension zero precisely when $d(R)=0$.

**Proof.** If the lengths $\ell_R(R/\mathfrak m^{n+1})$ are eventually constant, then $\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}=0$ for large $n$. Nakayama applied to the finite module $\mathfrak m^n$ gives $\mathfrak m^n=0$. The filtration by powers of $\mathfrak m$ now proves that $R$ has finite length, and its only prime is $\mathfrak m$.

Conversely, dimension zero means $\sqrt0=\mathfrak m$. In a Noetherian ring the nilradical is nilpotent: take finitely many generators of it, choose a nilpotence exponent for each, and use the pigeonhole principle on sufficiently long products of generators. Hence some power of $\mathfrak m$ vanishes. The finite filtration again gives finite length, and the Hilbert function $\ell_R(R/\mathfrak m^{n+1})$ is eventually the positive constant $\ell_R(R)$. Its degree is zero. This also proves the finite-length characterization used above. ∎

#### Lemma. Hilbert polynomials in an exact sequence

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $I$ have radical $\mathfrak m$, and consider finite modules in an exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow M'\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow M''\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $\chi_Q(n)=\ell_R(Q/I^{n+1}Q)$, using the same notation for its eventual numerical polynomial. Set $\deg0=-\infty$ and $d(0)=-\infty$. Then:

1. If $M'$ has infinite length, the polynomial $\chi_M-\chi_{M''}-\chi_{M'}$ has degree strictly below $\deg\chi_{M'}$.
2. The degree of $\chi_M$ is $\max\{\deg\chi_{M'},\deg\chi_{M''}\}$.
3. One has $d(M)=\max\{d(M'),d(M'')\}$.

**Proof.** We first supply both finite-colength comparisons needed in the argument. Identify $M'$ with its image in $M$. By [Artin–Rees](#native-algebra-lemma-artin-rees), there is $c\geq0$ such that, for $n\geq c$,
$$M'\cap I^nM=I^{n-c}N,\qquad N=M'\cap I^cM.$$
Since $I^cM'\subset N$, the quotient $M'/N$ has finite length $l$. Taking lengths in the quotient exact sequence gives
$$\chi_M(n)=\chi_{M''}(n)+\chi_N(n-c)+l\qquad(n\geq c).$$
Indeed the kernel of $M/I^{n+1}M\to M''/I^{n+1}M''$ is $M'/I^{n+1-c}N$, whose length is $l+\chi_N(n-c)$. The same identity is valid at $n=c-1$ if $\chi_Q(-1)=0$. Subtracting consecutive identities therefore also proves
$$\varphi_M(n)=\varphi_{M''}(n)+\varphi_N(n-c)\qquad(n\geq c),$$
where $\varphi_Q(n)=\ell_R(I^nQ/I^{n+1}Q)$. These are the full shifted equalities, not just a comparison of leading terms.

Next let $Q'\subset Q$ be any finite-colength inclusion of finite modules, and put $a=\ell_R(Q/Q')$. Choose $b\geq0$ with $I^bQ\subset Q'$. For $n\geq b$, the inclusions
$$I^{n+1}Q'\subset I^{n+1}Q\subset I^{n+1-b}Q'$$
give
$$a+\chi_{Q'}(n-b)\leq\chi_Q(n)\leq a+\chi_{Q'}(n).$$
If $Q$ has infinite length, so does $Q'$. Their eventual polynomials have positive degree: degree zero would imply stabilization of the lengths, then $I^nQ=I^{n+1}Q$, and Nakayama would force $I^nQ=0$ and finite length. The displayed bounds show that the two polynomials have the same degree and leading coefficient. Their difference consequently has smaller degree. This proves the full finite-colength assertion for arbitrary $Q'\subset Q$.

Apply this comparison to $N\subset M'$ when $M'$ has infinite length. The shifted equality expresses the desired error polynomial as the sum
$$\begin{aligned}
\chi_M-\chi_{M''}-\chi_{M'}
={}&l+\bigl(\chi_N(n-c)-\chi_N(n)\bigr)\\
&+\bigl(\chi_N(n)-\chi_{M'}(n)\bigr).
\end{aligned}$$
The second line has smaller degree by the finite-colength comparison. Translating a positive-degree polynomial changes only terms below its leading degree, so the first line does too. This proves (1). Nonzero Hilbert polynomials have positive leading coefficients. Thus adding $\chi_{M'}$ and $\chi_{M''}$ cannot cancel their highest terms, and (1) yields (2) in this case.

If $M'$ has finite length, a power of $I$ annihilates it. Artin–Rees then gives $M'\cap I^nM=0$ for sufficiently large $n$. Hence
$$\chi_M(n)=\chi_{M''}(n)+\ell_R(M')\qquad(n\gg0).$$
If $M'\ne0$ the added constant is positive; if $M'=0$ it is zero. This proves (2), including the case $M''=0$. For a nonzero finite module the degree in (2) is its invariant $d$, independent of the chosen ideal of definition. If $M'=0$ or $M''=0$, exactness identifies $M$ with the other module; if $M=0$, both end modules vanish. The convention $d(0)=-\infty$ therefore proves (3) in every remaining case. ∎

#### Lemma. Reduced algebras after separable scalar extension

Suppose $S$ is a reduced algebra over a field $k$. If $K/k$ is separable, or if it is separably generated, then $K\otimes_kS$ is reduced. Neither $S$ nor $K$ is required to be finitely generated.

**Proof for a separable extension.** A tensor and a proposed nilpotence relation involve finitely many elements of $K$ and $S$. Choose a finitely generated intermediate field $K_0/k$ and a finite type subalgebra $S_0\subset S$ containing them. The map
$$K_0\otimes_kS_0\longrightarrow K\otimes_kS$$
is injective: first tensor the injection $S_0\subset S$ with the vector space $K_0$, then tensor $K_0\subset K$ with $S$. Thus it suffices to prove reducedness for $K_0\otimes_kS_0$. The algebra $S_0$ is reduced, and the definition of separability makes $K_0/k$ separably generated. We may therefore assume these two finiteness conditions.

There are finitely many minimal primes $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_t$ of $S$. The map
$$S\longrightarrow\prod_{\nu=1}^t\operatorname{Frac}(S/\mathfrak p_\nu)$$
is injective: its kernel is the intersection of the minimal primes, which is zero. Equivalently, this is the embedding into the finite product of fields supplied by the [total-fraction-ring description](#native-algebra-lemma-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points). Tensoring preserves the injection, and it commutes with this finite product. The zero algebra causes no difficulty; otherwise it is enough to prove the assertion for a domain $S$.

Choose a separating transcendence basis $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ and a primitive element $\alpha$ as in the [field-generation lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-generating-finitely-generated-separable-field-extensions). Put $F=k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ and let $P\in F[T]$ be the monic separable minimal polynomial of $\alpha$. The ring
$$A=F\otimes_kS$$
is a localization of the domain $S[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$, so it is a domain. Moreover
$$K\otimes_kS\cong A[T]/(P).$$
Monicity makes the right side free over $A$, on the powers of $T$ below $\deg P$. It therefore embeds into $E[T]/(P)$, where $E=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. A Bézout identity between $P$ and $P'$ over $F$ remains valid over $E$. Thus $P$ factors over $E$ into distinct irreducible polynomials, and the Chinese remainder theorem makes $E[T]/(P)$ a finite product of fields. Its subring $A[T]/(P)$ is reduced. This proves the claim.

**Proof for a separably generated extension.** This route does not first assume that every such extension is separable. Choose a separating transcendence basis $\{x_i\}_{i\in J}$, so $K$ is separable algebraic over $k(x_i\mid i\in J)$. Given a finite list $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s\in K$, choose for each $\lambda_j$ a monic separable annihilating polynomial over that rational field. Only finitely many variables occur in its coefficients and in a Bézout identity with its derivative. All these data therefore lie in $F_T=k(x_i\mid i\in T)$ for some finite $T\subset J$. The minimal polynomial of each $\lambda_j$ over $F_T$ divides the chosen separable polynomial; it is consequently separable. Hence
$$F_T(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s)/F_T$$
is finite separable. Such subfields form a directed family: for two of them, include both finite variable sets and both generator lists, and enlarge $T$ to include all the needed coefficients. Their union is $K$.

Each member is finitely generated and separably generated over $k$, so the domain-and-separable-polynomial argument above applies to it and every finite type reduced subalgebra of $S$. The tensor injections and finite nilpotence witnesses from the first paragraph then prove reducedness for the entire tensor product. ∎

#### Lemma. Exchanging one element to obtain a separating basis

Let $k$ have characteristic $p>0$, and suppose
$$K=k(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1})$$
with $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ a transcendence basis. Assume that taking $p$-th powers carries every finite $k$-linearly independent family in $K$ to a $k$-linearly independent family. Some index $j\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\}$ then has the following property: the $n$ elements obtained by omitting $x_j$ form a separating transcendence basis.

**Proof.** A nonzero polynomial relation among the $n+1$ generators exists. Choose one, $F\in k[X_1,\ldots,X_{n+1}]$, with smallest total degree. Its degree is positive. If $F$ factored into two nonconstant polynomials, one factor would vanish at the generators, contradicting minimality. Thus $F$ is irreducible.

Suppose every exponent in every monomial of $F$ were divisible by $p$. Write
$$F=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha X^{p\alpha}.$$
The corresponding elements $x^\alpha$ are pairwise distinct: equality between two would already give a nonzero polynomial relation of total degree at most $\deg(F)/p<\deg(F)$. The relation
$$\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(x^\alpha)^p=0$$
and the hypothesis therefore force the family $(x^\alpha)_\alpha$ to be linearly dependent. A nontrivial dependence gives a polynomial relation of total degree at most $\deg(F)/p$, again impossible. Hence $\partial F/\partial X_j\ne0$ for some $j$.

Regard $F$ as a polynomial in $X_j$. Choose a nonzero coefficient of a positive power of $X_j$. Its total degree is smaller than $\deg F$, so it cannot vanish upon evaluation at the other generators. The evaluated polynomial is therefore nonconstant, and $x_j$ is algebraic over
$$L=k(x_1,\ldots,\widehat{x_j},\ldots,x_{n+1}).$$
Since $K/L$ is algebraic, $L$ has transcendence degree $n$. It is generated by the displayed $n$ elements, so they are algebraically independent. Evaluation therefore identifies their polynomial ring with $k[X_i\mid i\ne j]$.

Gauss' lemma now transfers the irreducibility of $F$ to $L[T]$. Its derivative in $T$ is nonzero, since $\partial F/\partial X_j\ne0$ and the other variables remain algebraically independent. An irreducible polynomial with nonzero derivative is separable. It follows that $K=L(x_j)$ is finite separable over $L$, proving the assertion. For $n=0$ the remaining list is empty and $L=k$, so the same argument includes that case. ∎

#### Lemma. Split transitivity for a formally smooth map

For ring maps $A\to B\to C$ with $C$ formally smooth over $B$, the canonical sequence
$$0\longrightarrow\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_BC
\longrightarrow\Omega_{C/A}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{C/B}\longrightarrow0$$
is split exact as a sequence of $C$-modules.

**Proof.** Right exactness is the differential transitivity sequence. Put $V=\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_BC$, and give the square-zero extension $C\oplus V$ its $B$-algebra structure
$$b\longmapsto\bigl(b,db\otimes1\bigr).$$
Formal smoothness lifts the identity $C\to C$ across the $B$-algebra surjection $C\oplus V\to C$. Write this lift as $c\mapsto(c,Dc)$. Its second component is an $A$-derivation with $D(b)=db\otimes1$. Universality gives a $C$-linear map $\Omega_{C/A}\to V$ whose composite with $V\to\Omega_{C/A}$ is the identity. The first arrow is consequently a split injection; right exactness identifies its complement with $\Omega_{C/B}$.

One can also use the original cotangent-complex argument. The [formal-smoothness criterion](#native-algebra-proposition-characterize-formally-smooth) makes $H_1(\mathrm{NL}_{C/B})$ zero and $\Omega_{C/B}$ projective. The [cotangent transitivity sequence](#native-algebra-lemma-exact-sequence-nl) then gives injectivity on the left, and projectivity splits the resulting short exact sequence. ∎

#### Lemma. Differentials commute with directed colimits

Let $(R_i\to S_i)_{i\in I}$ be a compatible system indexed by a directed set, with colimit $R\to S$. There is a canonical isomorphism
$$\Omega_{S/R}\cong\operatorname*{colim}_{i\in I}\Omega_{S_i/R_i}.$$
The colimit on the right carries its natural $S$-module structure; the transition maps of differential modules are linear over the corresponding ring maps.

**Proof.** Denote that colimit by $V$. For $s\in S$, choose a representative $s_i\in S_i$ and let $\delta(s)$ be the image of $ds_i$ in $V$. Two representatives become equal at a later index, and functoriality of differentials then makes their images equal. Thus $\delta$ is well-defined. Move finitely many representatives to a common index to check additivity and the Leibniz rule. An element of $R$ comes from some $R_i$, where its image has zero differential; hence $\delta$ is an $R$-derivation.

If $N$ is an $S$-module and $D\colon S\to N$ is an $R$-derivation, its restriction to each $S_i$ annihilates $R_i$. The resulting maps $\Omega_{S_i/R_i}\to N$ are compatible and induce a unique $S$-linear map $V\to N$ carrying $\delta(s)$ to $D(s)$. Conversely every such linear map produces a derivation. Uniqueness follows because the elements $ds_i$ generate every differential module. Thus $(V,\delta)$ represents precisely the universal derivation of $S$ over $R$.

In terms of the defining presentation, the same argument says that every generator $ds$ and every relation expressing additivity, the product rule, or vanishing on a base element is represented at some index; a finite collection of such relations is represented at a common later index. This is the presentation proof of the same canonical isomorphism. ∎

#### Lemma. A separating basis and one additional generator

Suppose $K/k$ is both finitely generated and separably generated, and put $r=\operatorname{trdeg}_kK$. There are $x_1,\ldots,x_{r+1}\in K$ such that $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ form a transcendence basis,
$$K=k(x_1,\ldots,x_{r+1}),$$
and $x_{r+1}$ is separable over $k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$.

**Proof.** Choose a separating transcendence basis $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ and put $F=k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$. The extension $K/F$ is algebraic and separable. It is finite, since a finite list of generators of $K/k$ also generates it over $F$, and each such generator is algebraic.

Here is the needed primitive-element argument. If $F$ is infinite, choose generators $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_s$ of a nontrivial finite separable extension $E/F$. There are $[E:F]$ distinct embeddings of $E$ into an algebraic closure fixing $F$. This count follows along a tower of simple extensions: each embedding extends once for each distinct root of the next separable minimal polynomial, so the counts multiply by the successive degrees.

For each pair of distinct embeddings $\sigma,\tau$, the polynomial
$$\sum_{i=1}^s T^{i-1}\bigl(\sigma(\alpha_i)-\tau(\alpha_i)\bigr)$$
is nonzero, because the embeddings differ on a generator. There are only finitely many pairs and finitely many roots to avoid. Choose $c\in F$ avoiding all of them, and set $\theta=\sum_i c^{i-1}\alpha_i$. Its images under all $[E:F]$ embeddings are distinct. Hence its minimal polynomial has at least $[E:F]$ roots, and therefore degree exactly $[E:F]$. This forces $E=F(\theta)$.

If $F$ is finite, $E$ is a finite field. Its multiplicative group is cyclic, as follows. In a finite abelian group the least common multiple $e$ of all element orders is itself the order of an element: for each prime dividing $e$, choose an element whose order contains the largest required power of that prime, take its component of that prime-power order, and multiply these commuting components. In $E^\times$ every element is a root of $T^e-1$, so $|E^\times|\leq e$. The reverse inequality follows from the existence of the element of order $e$. Thus this element generates $E^\times$, and in particular generates $E$ as a field over $F$.

Apply these arguments to $E=K$. A primitive generator is separable over $F$ because $K/F$ is separable. If $K=F$, take the additional generator to be zero. This proves all three assertions, including $r=0$. ∎

#### Lemma. Localizing the base or the target of differentials

For a ring map $A\to B$, the following canonical identifications hold.

1. If a multiplicative subset $U\subset A$ maps to units of $B$, then $\Omega_{B/A}\cong\Omega_{B/U^{-1}A}$.
2. For a multiplicative subset $U\subset B$, one has $U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}\cong\Omega_{U^{-1}B/A}$.

**Proof.** For (1), an $A$-derivation into a $B$-module vanishes on the image of $a\in A$. If $u\in U$, differentiating $u\,u^{-1}=1$ shows that it vanishes on $u^{-1}$ as well, since $u$ acts invertibly. It therefore vanishes on the entire image of $U^{-1}A$. The two types of derivations coincide for every target module, which proves the canonical identification.

For (2), put $N=U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}$ and define
$$\delta(b/u)=u^{-1}db-bu^{-2}du.$$
We check the fraction relation explicitly. If $b/u=b'/u'$, there is $v\in U$ with $v(bu'-b'u)=0$. Differentiating this equality in $N$, and using the fact that $bu'-b'u$ is zero after localization, gives
$$u'\,db+b\,du'-u\,db'-b'\,du=0.$$
Divide by $uu'$, and write $q=b/u=b'/u'$. The resulting equation is
$$\frac{db}{u}-\frac{db'}{u'}
=q\left(\frac{du}{u}-\frac{du'}{u'}\right),$$
which is exactly the equality of the two proposed values of $\delta$. In this argument $v$ is invertible in $U^{-1}B$, so cancellation of its action on $N$ is justified.

For addition, expand the formula at $(bu'+b'u)/(uu')$ and use
$$d(uu')=u\,du'+u'\,du.$$
The cross terms cancel, leaving $\delta(b/u)+\delta(b'/u')$. For multiplication the same expansion gives
$$\delta\left(\frac{bb'}{uu'}\right)
=\frac{b}{u}\delta\left(\frac{b'}{u'}\right)
+\frac{b'}{u'}\delta\left(\frac{b}{u}\right).$$
The formula vanishes on the image of $A$ and sends $1$ to zero. Thus it is an $A$-derivation, inducing a map $\Omega_{U^{-1}B/A}\to N$.

In the other direction the derivation $B\to\Omega_{U^{-1}B/A}$ induces the canonical map from $N$. The two composites fix every $db$, and in the target localization the product rule forces
$$d(b/u)=u^{-1}db-bu^{-2}du.$$
Since these differentials generate the respective modules, both composites are identities. The proof also covers a multiplicative set containing zero, when the localized ring and both modules are zero. ∎

#### Definition. Perfect fields

A field $k$ is called **perfect** when every extension field of $k$ is separable over $k$.

#### Lemma. Finite purely inseparable enlargement

Given a finitely generated field extension $K/k$, there are finite purely inseparable extensions $k'/k$ and $K'/K$ fitting into a commutative square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
k&\longrightarrow&K\\
\big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow\\
k'&\longrightarrow&K'
\end{array}$$
such that $K'/k'$ is separably generated.

**Proof.** In characteristic zero the identity extensions work. Suppose the characteristic is $p>0$. Choose a transcendence basis $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ of $K/k$, and put $F=k(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$. The extension $K/F$ is finite.

We use its separable-then-purely-inseparable decomposition, with the following justification. The elements of $K$ separable over $F$ form a subfield $E$: any finite list of separable elements generates a finite separable extension, and hence its sums, products and inverses are separable. For any algebraic element $a$, write its irreducible polynomial in the form $g(T^{p^e})$, with $g'\ne0$, by repeatedly dividing all exponents by $p$ while the derivative is zero. The polynomial $g$ is irreducible, so $a^{p^e}$ is separable over $F$. Thus $K/E$ is purely inseparable. This also proves uniqueness: an element separable over a field and purely inseparable over it must belong to that field, since its minimal polynomial cannot have both distinct roots and only one distinct root. Consequently any separable intermediate field over which $K$ is purely inseparable contains every element separable over $F$ and equals $E$.

Induct on $d=[K:E]$, simultaneously for all finitely generated extensions with a chosen transcendence basis. If $d=1$, the basis already separates and no enlargement is needed. Otherwise choose $\beta\in K\setminus E$ with $\beta^p=\alpha\in E$. Such a choice follows by taking the penultimate member of a shortest chain of successive $p$-th powers taking an element of $K\setminus E$ into $E$. Let
$$P(T)=T^n+a_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n\in F[T]$$
be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$. It is separable.

Write each $a_i$ as a quotient of two polynomials in $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ with coefficients in $k$. Only finitely many coefficients occur. In an algebraic closure containing $K$, adjoin their $p$-th roots to $k$ to obtain a finite purely inseparable extension $k_1/k$. Also put $y_i=x_i^{1/p}$ and
$$F_1=k_1(y_1,\ldots,y_r),\qquad L=KF_1.$$
Each $a_i$ is a $p$-th power in $F_1$: replace each coefficient of its numerator and denominator by its chosen root and replace each monomial $x^\gamma$ by $y^\gamma$. Frobenius recovers the original rational function. Its denominator is nonzero because its $p$-th power is the original nonzero denominator.

The extension $F_1/F$ is finite purely inseparable, as is $L/K$. The elements $y_1,\ldots,y_r$ are algebraically independent over $k_1$. Indeed a hypothetical relation can be raised to a sufficiently large $p$-power to put its coefficients in $k$; its monomials then become distinct monomials in the algebraically independent $x_i$. This would give a nonzero relation over $k$. Thus $F_1$ is a rational function field over $k_1$.

Let $E_1=EF_1$. The extension $E_1/F_1$ is separable, because the separable equations for generators of $E/F$ remain separable after extending scalars. The extension $L/E_1$ is purely inseparable. By the uniqueness argument above, $E_1$ is exactly the maximal separable subfield of $L/F_1$.

Choose $b_i\in F_1$ with $b_i^p=a_i$, and form
$$Q(T)=T^n+b_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+b_n.$$
Then $Q(T)^p=P(T^p)$, and $Q(\beta)^p=P(\alpha)=0$, so $Q(\beta)=0$. Moreover $Q$ is separable. In an algebraic closure Frobenius is bijective, and its bijection from the roots of $Q$ to the roots of $P$ preserves their multiplicities, as the displayed polynomial identity shows. Since $P$ has distinct roots, so does $Q$. Therefore $\beta$ is separable over $F_1$, and hence $\beta\in E_1$.

This proves the strict decrease:
$$[L:E_1]\leq[K:E(\beta)]
<[K:E]=d.$$
For the first inequality, a basis of $K$ over $E(\beta)$ spans the compositum $KE_1=L$ over $E_1$. The second inequality holds because $\beta\notin E$. The inclusions and identifications used here are summarized by
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
K&\longrightarrow&L\\
\big\uparrow&&\big\uparrow\\
E(\beta)&\longrightarrow&E_1\\
\big\uparrow&&\big\Vert\\
E&\longrightarrow&E_1\\
\big\uparrow&&\big\uparrow\\
F&\longrightarrow&F_1\\
\big\uparrow&&\big\uparrow\\
k&\longrightarrow&k_1.
\end{array}$$
Every square commutes inside the chosen algebraic closure. In particular the repeated right-hand entry records the newly obtained inclusion of $\beta$ in the separable subfield.

Apply induction to the finitely generated extension $L/k_1$, with transcendence basis $y_1,\ldots,y_r$ and smaller inseparable degree. It supplies finite purely inseparable extensions $k_2/k_1$ and $L'/L$ with $L'/k_2$ separably generated. Their composites $k_2/k$ and $L'/K$ are finite purely inseparable. Taking $k'=k_2$ and $K'=L'$ gives the required square. ∎

#### Lemma. Separating transcendence bases imply separability

Every separably generated extension $K/k$ is separable.

**Proof.** In characteristic zero every finitely generated intermediate field has a transcendence basis over which its finite algebraic extension is separable, since irreducible polynomials have nonzero derivative. Hence the assertion follows from the definition of separability.

In characteristic $p>0$, apply the [separably generated scalar-extension proof](#native-algebra-lemma-separable-extension-preserves-reducedness) to the reduced $k$-algebra $k^{1/p}$. It shows that $K\otimes_k k^{1/p}$ is reduced. The [separability criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-separable-field-extensions) then gives separability of $K/k$. That proof of reducedness uses a separating basis directly, so this implication does not assume the conclusion it is proving. ∎

#### Lemma. Separability passes to intermediate fields

If $K/k$ is separable and $k\subset K'\subset K$, then $K'/k$ is separable.

**Proof.** Any intermediate field finitely generated over $k$ inside $K'$ is also such an intermediate field inside $K$. By separability of $K/k$, it is separably generated over $k$. This is precisely the definition of separability for $K'/k$.

Equivalently, for every field extension $L/k$, the vector-space injection $K'\subset K$ remains injective after tensoring with $L$. Thus $K'\otimes_kL$ embeds into the reduced ring $K\otimes_kL$ and is reduced. The geometric reducedness criterion gives the same conclusion. ∎

#### Lemma. Flatness through Tor

For an arbitrary $R$-module $M$, the following five tests are equivalent.

1. Tensoring with $M$ is exact.
2. $\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M,N)=0$ for every $R$-module $N$ and every $i>0$.
3. $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,N)=0$ for every $R$-module $N$.
4. $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)=0$ for every ideal $I$ of $R$.
5. The equality in (4) holds for every finitely generated ideal $I$.

**Proof.** If $M$ is flat, tensoring a free resolution of $N$ with $M$ preserves exactness in positive degrees. Computing Tor from this resolution proves (2). The implications (2)$\Rightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(4)$\Rightarrow$(5) simply restrict the indices or modules being tested.

Suppose (5). For a finitely generated ideal $I$, the sequence $0\to I\to R\to R/I\to0$ gives
$$0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)
\longrightarrow M\otimes_RI\longrightarrow M.$$
This is the relevant portion of the [long exact Tor sequence](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-long-exact-sequence-tor); the preceding term is $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R)=0$. One obtains that sequence by tensoring the short exact sequence with a free resolution of $M$. Each free term preserves its exactness, and the resulting short exact sequence of complexes has the usual connecting maps on homology. Thus the vanishing in (5) makes $I\otimes_RM\to M$ injective for every finitely generated ideal. The [full ideal criterion for flatness](#native-algebra-lemma-flat) implies (1). No finiteness assumption on $M$ or Noetherian assumption on $R$ enters this argument. ∎

#### Lemma. Generators remain generators after enlarging scalars

Let $R\to S$ be a ring map and let $M$ be an $S$-module. If $M$ is finite over $R$, it is finite over $S$.

**Proof.** Choose $R$-module generators $m_1,\ldots,m_t$. Every expression $\sum r_im_i$ is also an $S$-linear expression, using the images of the coefficients $r_i$ in $S$. The same list therefore generates over $S$. This includes the empty list when $M=0$. ∎

#### Lemma. Simple modules and length one

For an $R$-module $M$, these assertions are equivalent: $M$ is simple; $\ell_R(M)=1$; and $M\cong R/\mathfrak m$ for a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.

**Proof.** A simple module is nonzero and has no submodules besides zero and itself. This says exactly that its only strict chain from zero to the whole module has length one. If $\mathfrak m$ is maximal, the submodules of $R/\mathfrak m$ correspond to ideals containing $\mathfrak m$, so this quotient is simple.

Conversely, take $0\ne x\in M$ when $M$ is simple. The nonzero submodule $Rx$ is all of $M$, so the map $R\to M$, $r\mapsto rx$, identifies $M$ with $R/I$, where $I=\operatorname{Ann}_R(x)$. The ideal is proper because $x\ne0$. An ideal $I\subsetneq J\subsetneq R$ would give a nonzero proper submodule $J/I$ of $R/I$. No such $J$ exists, so $I$ is maximal. ∎

#### Lemma. Comparing length under restriction of scalars

For an $S$-module $M$ and a ring map $R\to S$,
$$\ell_R(M)\geq\ell_S(M).$$
Equality holds when the ring map is surjective. Length is allowed to be infinite.

**Proof.** Every strict chain of $S$-submodules is a strict chain of $R$-submodules. Taking suprema of the possible chain lengths proves the inequality, also when these lengths are unbounded. If $R\to S$ is onto, an $R$-submodule is closed under every scalar of $S$, since that scalar has a lift in $R$. The two collections of submodules coincide, giving equality. ∎

#### Lemma. Localization and polynomials preserve geometric reducedness

If a $k$-algebra $R$ is geometrically reduced, then so are every localization $U^{-1}R$ and the polynomial algebra $R[x]$.

**Proof.** A localization of a reduced ring is reduced. Indeed, if $(a/u)^n=0$, some $v\in U$ satisfies $va^n=0$. Then $(va)^n=0$, so $va=0$ and $a/u=0$. A polynomial ring over a reduced ring is also reduced: the injections into the product of the domains $R/\mathfrak p$, over all prime ideals $\mathfrak p$, induce an injection on polynomial rings. Each target polynomial ring is a domain, and a subring of their product has no nonzero nilpotents.

For any extension field $K/k$, the canonical tensor identifications give
$$\begin{aligned}
K\otimes_k U^{-1}R&\cong U^{-1}(K\otimes_kR),\\
K\otimes_k R[x]&\cong(K\otimes_kR)[x].
\end{aligned}$$
The ring $K\otimes_kR$ is reduced by hypothesis. Apply the two preceding observations to conclude. In the first line $U$ denotes its image in the tensor algebra; even if that image contains zero, the conclusion still holds. ∎

#### Lemma. Generic finite presentation for an inclusion of domains

Let $R\subset S$ be domains with $S$ finite type over $R$. There are nonzero elements $f\in R$ and $g\in S$ such that $S_{fg}$ is finitely presented over $R_f$.

**Proof.** Induct on the number of chosen algebra generators. With no generators $S=R$, and $f=g=1$ works.

For one generator, write $S=R[t]\cong R[T]/Q$. If $Q=0$, this is already a polynomial presentation. Otherwise choose $0\ne h\in Q$ of smallest degree $d$ and let $f\ne0$ be its leading coefficient. The inclusion $R\subset S$ implies $d\geq1$. Inverting $f$ makes $f^{-1}h$ monic. Division by it shows that
$$R_f[T]/(f^{-1}h)\longrightarrow S_f$$
is an isomorphism. To justify injectivity, any element of its kernel has a representative of degree below $d$. Clear the finitely many powers of $f$ in its coefficients. Since $S$ is a domain and $f\ne0$, vanishing in $S_f$ implies vanishing of the resulting polynomial in $S$. A nonzero such polynomial would contradict the minimal choice of $d$. Thus the remainder is zero. This gives a finite presentation, with $g=1$.

Now take $n>1$ generators $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ and set $S_0=R[t_1,\ldots,t_{n-1}]\subset S$. By induction, choose $0\ne f\in R$ and $0\ne g_0\in S_0$ with
$$R_f\longrightarrow B=(S_0)_{fg_0}$$
finitely presented. The algebra $S_{fg_0}$ is generated over the domain $B$ by the single element $t_n$. The one-generator argument supplies $0\ne a\in B$ such that
$$B_a\longrightarrow(S_{fg_0})_a$$
is finitely presented. Write $a=b/(fg_0)^N$ with $0\ne b\in S_0$. Localizing $B$ at $a$ is the same as localizing it at $b$.

A principal localization is finitely presented, using one variable and the relation $aZ-1$; finite presentation is preserved under composition. Hence the composite from $R_f$ to $(S_{fg_0})_a=S_{fg_0b}$ is finitely presented. Taking $g=g_0b\ne0$ proves the assertion. This explicitly returns the intermediate denominator to an element of the original algebra $S$. ∎

#### Lemma. Smoothness and regularity with separable residue field

Let $S$ be a finite type algebra over a field $k$, and let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ have residue field separable over $k$. Then $S$ is smooth over $k$ at $\mathfrak q$ if and only if $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is regular.

**Proof.** Write $R=S_{\mathfrak q}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak qR$ and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. We first give the conormal calculation in its full useful scope: for any Noetherian local $k$-algebra $R$ with finitely generated separable residue field, the natural map
$$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa$$
is injective.

Put $A=R/\mathfrak m^2$ and $N=\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. Choose a separating transcendence basis $\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_r$ of $\kappa/k$ and a separable primitive element $\bar y$ over $F=k(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_r)$, using the [field-generation lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-generating-finitely-generated-separable-field-extensions). Lifts $x_i\in A$ define a map $F\to A$: every nonzero polynomial in the $\bar x_i$ is nonzero in the residue field, so its value at the lifts is a unit of the local ring $A$.

Let $P\in F[T]$ be the monic minimal polynomial of $\bar y$, and choose any lift $y\in A$. Evaluating coefficients through $F\to A$, one has $P(y)\in N$ and $P'(y)\in A^\times$. Since $N^2=0$, the correction
$$y'=y-\frac{P(y)}{P'(y)}$$
satisfies $P(y')=0$. It therefore extends $F\to A$ to a $k$-algebra section $\sigma\colon\kappa=F[T]/(P)\to A$ of the residue map. In the trivial primitive extension take $\bar y=0$ and $P=T$.

The map $D\colon A\to N$ defined by $D(a)=a-\sigma(\bar a)$ is a $k$-derivation when $N$ is viewed as an $A$-module through $\kappa$. Indeed the product of two elements of $N$ vanishes, giving the Leibniz rule, and $D$ vanishes on $k$. It restricts to the identity on $N$. Thus the conormal map into $\Omega_{A/k}\otimes_A\kappa$ has a retraction and is injective. The quotient $R\to A$ does not change this differential fibre: every differential of a product of two elements of $\mathfrak m$ vanishes after tensoring with $\kappa$. This proves the claimed injection and the split exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2
\longrightarrow\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa
\longrightarrow\Omega_{\kappa/k}\longrightarrow0.$$
Alternatively, formal smoothness of $\kappa/k$ supplies the section $\kappa\to R/\mathfrak m^2$ directly; the same derivation then proves the injection. This is the full subargument in *Smooth algebras over a field and the Jacobian criterion*, §3, Theorem 3.2.

Now set $t=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa$. The differentials of a separating basis form a basis of $\Omega_{\kappa/k}$. To see the effect of the additional primitive generator, its defining separable equation has invertible derivative in that generator; differentiating it solves uniquely for that generator's differential and imposes no relation on the basis differentials. Thus $\dim_\kappa\Omega_{\kappa/k}=t$. By [differential localization](#native-algebra-lemma-differentials-localize), the middle term of the exact sequence is $\Omega_{S/k}\otimes_S\kappa$. Consequently
$$\begin{aligned}
\dim_\kappa(\Omega_{S/k}\otimes_S\kappa)
&=\dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)+t\\
&\geq\dim R+t\\
&=\dim_{\mathfrak q}\operatorname{Spec}S.
\end{aligned}$$
The last equality is the [pointwise dimension formula](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-at-a-point-finite-type-field). Equality in the middle inequality holds exactly when the Noetherian local ring $R$ is regular. The differential criterion, proved in full in §§1–2 of the same Jacobian-criterion lesson, identifies equality between differential dimension and point dimension with smoothness. This proves both implications. ∎

#### Theorem. Zariski's Main Theorem in affine algebra

Let $S$ be finite type over an arbitrary ring $R$, let $C\subset S$ be the subring of elements integral over $R$, and suppose $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$. Then some $g\in C\setminus\mathfrak q$ makes the canonical map
$$C_g\longrightarrow S_g$$
an isomorphism.

**Proof.** We retain the monogenic calculation, the conductor step and the induction through a finite intermediate algebra. The complete argument also appears in *Quasi-finite morphisms and Chevalley's theorem*, §2A, Theorem 2A.1. Its two conductor inputs have complete proofs in *The theorem on formal functions*, Appendix Z, at the exact locators used below.

We first record the pointwise operations used in the proof. The [isolated-fibre criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-isolated-point-fibre) characterizes quasi-finiteness for finite type maps by isolation of the selected point in its fibre. For $A\to B\to D$ with $D$ finite type over $A$, the same algebra generators generate $D$ over $B$. A principal open isolating a prime of $D$ in its fibre over $A$ still isolates it in the smaller fibre over $B$. Thus enlarging the intermediate base preserves quasi-finiteness at that prime, without any finiteness assumption on $B/A$. Localizing the base and source away from their selected primes also preserves and reflects the property: the local fibre is unchanged, and in the fibre topology the source localization is an open neighborhood of the point.

We also need the full four-ring assertion. In a commutative square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
A&\longrightarrow&B\\
\big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow\\
A'&\longrightarrow&B'
\end{array}$$
suppose $A\to B$ is finite type and $B\otimes_AA'\to B'$ is surjective. Let $\mathfrak q'$ contract to $\mathfrak q\subset B$ and to $\mathfrak p'\subset A'$, with $\mathfrak p\subset A$ their common contraction. Quasi-finiteness at $\mathfrak q$ implies it at $\mathfrak q'$. Indeed the isolated closed point $\mathfrak q$ in $B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ gives a product decomposition $H_1\times H_2$, where $H_1$ is the finite-dimensional local fibre algebra at that point. After extending to $\kappa(\mathfrak p')$ and taking the quotient defining the new fibre, its idempotent gives a factor $H'_1$, a quotient of $H_1\otimes_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak p')$. This factor is finite-dimensional. The chosen prime lies in it, since the idempotent of $H_1$ maps to one in its residue field. The spectrum of a finite-dimensional algebra over a field is finite and discrete, so $\mathfrak q'$ is isolated in its fibre. The quotient map also ensures finite type over $A'$. This proves the assertion with all four rings arbitrary.

**The monogenic case.** Suppose $S=R[x]=R[X]/I$, and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. Some polynomial in $I$ has a coefficient outside $\mathfrak p$. Otherwise the fibre would be $\kappa(\mathfrak p)[X]$, which has no isolated points: its zero prime has transcendental residue field, and every nonzero prime contains that zero prime as a distinct generization. Thus we have a relation
$$a_mx^m+\cdots+a_0=0$$
with coefficients in $C$, at least one outside $\mathfrak q$. Initially the coefficients come from $R$; allowing $C$ permits the following degree reduction.

For $m\geq1$, the element $a_mx$ is integral over $C$. Multiplying the relation by $a_m^{m-1}$ gives a monic equation in $a_mx$. Transitivity puts $a_mx$ in $C$, since $C$ is the integral closure of $R$ in $S$. If $a_m\notin\mathfrak q$, then $x=(a_mx)/a_m\in C_{a_m}$, and $C_{a_m}=S_{a_m}$. If $a_m\in\mathfrak q$, replace the leading two terms by
$$\bigl(a_mx+a_{m-1}\bigr)x^{m-1}.$$
This reduces the degree while retaining a coefficient outside $\mathfrak q$, because $a_mx\in\mathfrak q$. A degree-zero relation with its coefficient outside $\mathfrak q$ is impossible. The process therefore reaches a leading coefficient outside $\mathfrak q$ and proves the monogenic case. All localized inclusions used here are injective by exactness of localization.

**The conductor step.** Now suppose $R\subset S$, that $R$ is integrally closed in $S$, and that $S$ is finite over $R[x]$ for an element $x\in S$. The map from the polynomial ring $R[X]$ need not be injective. Let
$$J=\{u\in S:uS\subset R[x]\}.$$
It is an ideal of $S$, contained in $R[x]$. The complete coefficient lemma is Appendix Z, Lemma Z.6, including the monic-denominator and leading-coefficient arguments in Z.1–Z.5. It says that
$$\begin{gathered}
u\sum_{i=0}^m a_ix^i\in\sqrt J\\
\Longrightarrow\quad ua_i\in\sqrt J\quad(0\leq i\leq m),
\end{gathered}$$
for $u\in S$ and $a_i\in R$. These hypotheses allow zero divisors and a noninjective map $R[X]\to S$.

Set $\bar S=S/\sqrt J$ and $\bar R=R/(R\cap\sqrt J)$. The canonical maps form the commutative diagram
$$\begin{array}{ccccc}
R&\longrightarrow&R[X]&\longrightarrow&S\\
\big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow\\
\bar R&\longrightarrow&\bar R[X]&\longrightarrow&\bar S.
\end{array}$$
Here $\bar R$ embeds in $\bar S$, the horizontal composites are the structural maps, and $\bar S$ is finite over the image $\bar R[\bar x]$ of $\bar R[X]$. Both $\bar R$ and $\bar S$ are reduced. The coefficient lemma says that $\bar x$ is strongly transcendental over $\bar R$: an equation $\bar u\sum\bar a_i\bar x^i=0$ forces every $\bar u\bar a_i=0$.

The complete strong-transcendence theorem, Appendix Z, Lemma Z.11, with Z.8–Z.10 and the polynomial-normality proof in §0, now says that $\bar R\to\bar S$ has no quasi-finite points. Its proof passes to one minimal component and then to a normal domain by integral extension; it makes no Noetherian or finiteness-of-normalization assumption. If $J\subset\mathfrak q$, the four-ring assertion above would carry quasi-finiteness at $\mathfrak q$ to $\mathfrak q/\sqrt J$, a contradiction. Hence choose $u\in J\setminus\mathfrak q$.

The definition of the conductor gives $R[x]_u=S_u$: for $s\in S$, one has $s=(us)/u$ and $us\in R[x]$. The contracted point of $R[x]$ is quasi-finite over $R$, because the local fibre ring is the same as that of $S$. The integral closure of $R$ inside $R[x]$ is still $R$. The monogenic case therefore supplies $a\in R\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $R_a=R[x]_a$. Write the image of $u$ there as $b/a^N$, with $b\in R$. Since $u$ and $a$ avoid the chosen prime, so does $b$. Inverting $h=ab$ makes both $a$ and $u$ units, and yields
$$R_h=R[x]_h=S_h.$$
This proves the finite-over-one-generator case when the base is integrally closed in the target.

**Induction.** Replace $R$ by its image in $S$ if necessary. This preserves the fibre at the selected point, finite type and the integral closure. Choose $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in S$ such that $S$ is finite over $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, and induct on $n$. Such a list exists because a finite algebra-generating list works.

If $n=0$, then $S$ is integral over $R$, so $C=S$. If $n=1$, replace the base by $C$. Quasi-finiteness persists by the intermediate-base observation. The same finite module generators span $S$ over $C[x_1]$, and transitivity makes $C$ integrally closed in $S$. The conductor step supplies the required element of $C$.

For $n>1$, let $D$ be the integral closure of $R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}]$ in $S$. Again $D\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$, $D$ is integrally closed in $S$, and $S$ is finite over $D[x_n]$. The conductor step gives $v\in D\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $D_v=S_v$.

To use induction, a finite type intermediate algebra is essential. Choose a finite $R$-algebra generating list of $S_v$, and write its members as $y_j/v^{e_j}$ with $y_j\in D$. Let
$$E=R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},v,y_1,\ldots,y_t]\subset D.$$
Then $E_v=S_v$: surjectivity follows from the chosen generators, and injectivity from localization of inclusions. Every added generator is integral over $R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}]$, so $E$ is finite over that ring. At $\mathfrak q_E=E\cap\mathfrak q$, its local ring and local fibre agree with those of $S$, proving quasi-finiteness of $E/R$ at $\mathfrak q_E$.

Let $F$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $E$. Induction gives $w\in F\setminus\mathfrak q_E$ with $F_w=E_w$. Express $v=c/w^N$ in that ring, with $c\in F$. The equality implies $c\notin\mathfrak q_E$, since $v,w$ avoid the prime. Put $g=wc$. Inverting $g$ makes $w$ and $v$ units, so
$$F_g=E_g=S_g.$$
Finally $F\subset C\subset S$, and localization of these inclusions is injective. The outer equality forces $C_g=S_g$. The element $g$ belongs to $C\setminus\mathfrak q$, completing the proof. ∎

#### Lemma. Finite-dimensional algebras are Artinian

An algebra finite-dimensional over a field is an Artinian ring.

**Proof.** Its ideals are vector subspaces. Every strict descent of ideals strictly decreases their nonnegative integer dimensions, so a descending chain must stop. This is the Artinian condition. ∎

#### Lemma. Artinian rings and zero-dimensional Noetherian rings

Every Noetherian ring of dimension zero is Artinian. Conversely, an Artinian ring is Noetherian and has dimension at most zero.

**Proof.** Let $R$ be Noetherian of dimension zero. Its [finitely many minimal primes](#native-algebra-lemma-noetherian-irreducible-components) are also all of its maximal ideals; write them as $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_t$. Thus the spectrum is a finite discrete space. Its nilradical
$$N=\bigcap_{i=1}^t\mathfrak p_i$$
is nilpotent, since it has finitely many generators, each nilpotent. Choose $e\geq1$ with $N^e=0$. Distinct maximal ideals are comaximal, and so are their $e$-th powers: from $a+b=1$ with $a,b$ in the two ideals, expand $(a+b)^{2e-1}$.

For pairwise comaximal ideals intersection equals product. The Chinese remainder theorem therefore gives
$$R\cong\prod_{i=1}^tR/\mathfrak p_i^e,$$
because $\prod_i\mathfrak p_i^e=N^e=0$. Each factor has just one prime, hence is local with nilpotent maximal ideal, and it identifies canonically with $R_{\mathfrak p_i}$. This is also the [local-factor decomposition](#native-algebra-lemma-product-local) obtained from the open-and-closed points of the spectrum.

In each factor the filtration by powers of its maximal ideal has finitely many nonzero terms. Its layers are finite-dimensional over the residue field, since the factor is Noetherian. Consequently each factor, and then their finite product, has finite length as an $R$-module. A descending chain of ideals strictly decreases length whenever it changes, so $R$ is Artinian. This retains the local-factor proof and supplies the finite-length step.

Now suppose $R$ is Artinian. The [finite-length theorem for Artinian rings](#native-algebra-lemma-artinian-finite-length) gives finite length of the module $R$, hence the ascending chain condition and Noetherianity. Every prime is maximal: its quotient is an Artinian domain, and such a domain is a field. Indeed, for $0\ne a$ its descending chain $(a^n)$ stabilizes, giving $a^n=a^{n+1}b$ for some $b$; cancellation yields $ab=1$. Thus no chain of distinct prime ideals has positive length.

The original decomposition route gives the same conclusion: an Artinian ring has [finitely many maximal ideals](#native-algebra-lemma-artinian-finite-nr-max) and [nilpotent Jacobson radical](#native-algebra-lemma-artinian-radical-nilpotent), so its local factors each have only their maximal prime. The zero ring is Artinian and Noetherian with empty spectrum; this explains the phrase “at most zero” in the converse. ∎

#### Proposition. Regular local rings and global dimension

For a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$, the following conditions are equivalent:

1. $\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa$ is finite.
2. The global dimension of $R$, taken over all $R$-modules, is finite.
3. $R$ is regular.

When these conditions hold,
$$\operatorname{gl.dim}R=\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa
=\dim R=\dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2).$$

**Proof.** Put $d=\dim R$ and $e=\dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)$. For a regular local ring the [resolution theorem](#uncovered-algebra-proposition-regular-finite-gl-dim) gives global dimension at most $d$, including arbitrary modules. Thus (3) implies (2), and (2) immediately implies (1).

If $p=\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa$ is finite, the [embedding-dimension bound](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-length-resolution-residue-field) and the [depth bound](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-dim-gl-dim) give
$$e\leq p\leq d.$$
The number of generators of the maximal ideal always bounds dimension, so $d\leq e$. Equality follows, which is precisely regularity. Finally, under these equivalent conditions,
$$e\leq\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa
\leq\operatorname{gl.dim}R\leq d=e.$$
The complete homological argument, including the characteristic-free Koszul comparison for the first inequality, is Regular local rings, Section 2. The unrestricted global-dimension step uses the cyclic-module test and its transfinite proof in Projective dimension, Sections 1–2. ∎

#### Lemma. Projective syzygies do not depend on the chosen resolution

Let $M$ have finite projective dimension $d$ over a ring $R$. Suppose
$$F_e\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_0
\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0$$
is exact, every $F_i$ is projective, and $e\geq0$, $e\geq d-1$. The kernel at $F_e$ is projective; when $e=0$ this means $\ker(F_0\to M)$. No finiteness condition on these modules is required.

**Proof.** Induct on $d$, allowing every eligible $e$. If $d=0$, the surjection onto $M$ splits. Its kernel is a direct summand of $F_0$, hence projective. Repeat this splitting along the given sequence to reach its last kernel.

Suppose $d>0$ and choose a projective resolution of length $d$,
$$0\longrightarrow P_d\longrightarrow\cdots
\longrightarrow P_0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $K=\ker(F_0\to M)$ and $L=\ker(P_0\to M)$. [Schanuel's construction](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-schanuel) gives
$$P_0\oplus K\cong F_0\oplus L.$$
If $e=0$, the inequality forces $d=1$. Then $L\cong P_1$, so $P_0\oplus K$ is projective, and its summand $K$ is projective.

For $e>0$, the module $F_0\oplus L$ has a projective resolution of length at most $d-1$: add $F_0$ to the final surjection $P_1\to L$ and use the identity on that summand. Through the displayed isomorphism, the other sequence provides
$$F_e\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_2
\longrightarrow P_0\oplus F_1
\longrightarrow P_0\oplus K\longrightarrow0.$$
The final map is the identity on $P_0$ together with the map $F_1\to K$; the preceding map has zero $P_0$ component. Apply the induction hypothesis to the actual projective dimension, which is at most $d-1$, and to the index $e-1$. For $e\geq2$ its last kernel is the original kernel. For $e=1$ it is
$$\ker(P_0\oplus F_1\longrightarrow P_0\oplus K)
=0\oplus\ker(F_1\longrightarrow K),$$
and $K\hookrightarrow F_0$ identifies this with the kernel of $F_1\to F_0$. Both cases prove the claim. ∎

#### Lemma. Length after restricting scalars

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ be local, and let $B$ be semilocal with maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_1,\ldots,\mathfrak m_n$. Suppose a map $A\to B$ contracts each $\mathfrak m_i$ to $\mathfrak m$ and gives finite extensions $\kappa_i=\kappa(\mathfrak m_i)$ of $\kappa$. For a $B$-module $M$ of finite length,
$$\ell_A(M)=\sum_{i=1}^n[\kappa_i:\kappa]\,
\ell_{B_{\mathfrak m_i}}(M_{\mathfrak m_i}).$$
In particular, restriction of scalars gives a module of finite length.

**Proof.** Take a composition series of $M$. Each simple quotient is $B/\mathfrak m_i$ for exactly one $i$, by the [description of simple modules](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-length-1). As an $A$-module it is a $\kappa$-vector space of dimension $[\kappa_i:\kappa]$, and this equals its length.

Localizing the series at $\mathfrak m_i$ kills every quotient belonging to another maximal ideal: an element in that other ideal but outside $\mathfrak m_i$ becomes a unit. The quotients belonging to $\mathfrak m_i$ become the simple $B_{\mathfrak m_i}$-module $\kappa_i$. Thus their number is $\ell_{B_{\mathfrak m_i}}(M_{\mathfrak m_i})$. Add the $A$-lengths of all the factors to obtain the formula. An empty composition series covers $M=0$; if $B=0$, the empty sum does as well. ∎

#### Lemma. Finite ring maps are integral

If $S$ is finite as an $R$-module, every element of $S$ is integral over $R$.

**Proof.** Choose module generators $v_1,\ldots,v_t$ of $S$. For $s\in S$, write $sv_i=\sum_j a_{ij}v_j$ with $a_{ij}\in R$. Multiplication by the adjugate of $sI_t-(a_{ij})$ shows that the monic polynomial
$$P(T)=\det(TI_t-(a_{ij}))$$
satisfies $P(s)v_i=0$ for every $i$. The generators span $1$, so $P(s)=0$ in $S$. This determinant argument does not require a basis. If $S=0$, the polynomial $1$, or the degree-one polynomial $T$, gives the assertion directly. This is the faithful finite-module test in the [integrality criterion](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-characterize-integral-element). ∎

#### Lemma. Finite algebras and integral generators

For a ring map $R\to S$, the following are equivalent:

1. $S$ is a finite $R$-module.
2. $S$ is integral over $R$ and finitely generated as an $R$-algebra.
3. Some finite list of algebra generators of $S$ consists of elements integral over $R$.

**Proof.** Module generators also generate as an algebra, and the preceding lemma proves their integrality, giving (1) implies (2). The implication (2) implies (3) follows by choosing algebra generators.

For (3), write $S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_t]$ and choose monic equations for the $x_i$, of positive degrees $d_i$. Replacing a power $x_i^{d_i}$ with a combination of smaller powers repeatedly expresses every polynomial in the $x_i$ as a linear combination of
$$x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_t^{a_t},
\qquad 0\leq a_i<d_i.$$
This is a finite spanning set over $R$, proving (1). With no generators, its sole monomial is $1$. The argument also proves the finite-list assertion of the [integrality criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-integral). ∎

#### Lemma. Surjectivity and exactness for completion

Fix an ideal $I$ of an arbitrary ring $R$, and write
$$\widehat X=\varprojlim_{n\geq1}X/I^nX$$
for an $R$-module $X$. The following statements hold.

1. If $\varphi\colon M\to N$ is surjective modulo $I$, then $\widehat\varphi$ is surjective.
2. Every surjective module map remains surjective on completion.
3. If $0\to K\to M\to N\to0$ is exact and $N$ is flat, its completed sequence is exact, including both zero endpoints.
4. For finite $M$, the canonical map $M\otimes_R\widehat R\to\widehat M$ is surjective.

Neither $I$ nor the modules in the first three statements need be finitely generated.

**Proof.** For (1), the cokernel $C$ of $\varphi$ satisfies $C=IC$, and hence $C=I^nC$ for every $n$. Thus each map $M/I^nM\to N/I^nN$ is onto. Equivalently, this is the nilpotent-ideal form of [Nakayama's lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-nak) over $R/I^n$; it does not use finite generation.

Set $K_n=\varphi^{-1}(I^nN)$. We have compatible exact sequences
$$0\longrightarrow K_n/I^nM
\longrightarrow M/I^nM
\longrightarrow N/I^nN\longrightarrow0.$$
Their left transition maps are also onto. Indeed, take $x\in K_n$ and express
$$\varphi(x)=\sum_j z_jy_j,\qquad z_j\in I^n.$$
Surjectivity modulo $I$ supplies $m_j\in M$ such that $y_j-\varphi(m_j)\in IN$. Then
$$x'=x-\sum_jz_jm_j,\qquad
\varphi(x')=\sum_jz_j\bigl(y_j-\varphi(m_j)\bigr)\in I^{n+1}N.$$
Thus $x'\in K_{n+1}$ and $x'-x\in I^nM$, as required. All sums here are finite, by the definition of an ideal times a module.

The [countable inverse-limit exactness lemma](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-mittag-leffler) now proves (1). In this surjective-transition case its lifting argument is especially direct: lift the first component of a compatible element of $\widehat N$; after lifting its next component, the discrepancy from the previous lift lies in $K_n/I^nM$. Lift that discrepancy to $K_{n+1}/I^{n+1}M$ and subtract it. Induction constructs a compatible lift in $\widehat M$. Statement (2) is an immediate instance.

For (3), tensor the given short exact sequence with $R/I^n$. Flatness of $N$ kills its first Tor and gives
$$0\longrightarrow K/I^nK\longrightarrow M/I^nM
\longrightarrow N/I^nN\longrightarrow0.$$
The left transitions are quotient maps, so the same lifting argument gives surjectivity on inverse limits. Kernel equality and injectivity are checked component by component, proving the whole completed sequence exact.

For (4), choose a surjection $R^t\to M$ with $t$ finite. By (2), completion gives an onto map $\widehat R^{\,t}\to\widehat M$. On a tuple $(a_i)$ this map is $\sum_i a_iv_i$, where the $v_i$ are the chosen generators of $M$. It factors through the canonical map $M\otimes_R\widehat R\to\widehat M$, so that map is onto. ∎

#### Lemma. Separated finite modules over complete rings

Suppose $R\to\widehat R$ is an isomorphism for the $I$-adic topology. If $M$ is finite and $\bigcap_{n\geq1}I^nM=0$, then $M\to\widehat M$ is an isomorphism.

**Proof.** The preceding lemma makes
$$M\cong M\otimes_R\widehat R\longrightarrow\widehat M$$
surjective. An element has zero image exactly when it belongs to every $I^nM$. The assumed intersection is zero, giving injectivity as well. ∎

#### Lemma. Going up and maximal ideals

For a ring map having the going-up property, the contraction of every maximal ideal is maximal.

**Proof.** Let $\mathfrak q$ be maximal in the target and $\mathfrak p$ its contraction. Choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supseteq\mathfrak p$ in the source. Going up gives a prime $\mathfrak q'\supseteq\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak m$. Maximality forces $\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak q$, hence $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak p$. ∎

#### Lemma. Reducedness descends through faithful flatness

If $R\to S$ is faithfully flat and $S$ is reduced, then $R$ is reduced.

**Proof.** A faithfully flat map is [injective](#native-algebra-lemma-faithfully-flat-universally-injective). A nilpotent element of $R$ therefore embeds as a nilpotent element of $S$, which is zero. Injectivity makes the original element zero. ∎

#### Lemma. Smooth algebras over reduced rings are reduced

If $R$ is reduced and $R\to S$ is smooth, then $S$ is reduced.

**Proof.** First assume $R$ is Noetherian. The finite presentation makes $S$ Noetherian. Smoothness gives flatness and regular fibres, hence reduced fibres. The [Noetherian flat-ascent lemma](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-reduced-goes-up-noetherian) then shows that $S$ is reduced.

For arbitrary reduced $R$, use [finite smooth models](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-presentation-fs-noetherian): there is a finitely generated $\mathbf Z$-subalgebra $R_0\subset R$ and a smooth $R_0$-algebra $S_0$ with $S\cong R\otimes_{R_0}S_0$. The larger finitely generated subalgebras of $R$ form a directed system; base-changing $S_0$ along them keeps it smooth.

Let $x\in S$ satisfy $x^2=0$. Its expression uses finitely many coefficients from $R$, so at some larger stage it comes from an element $x_0$ of the corresponding smooth algebra. The equality $x^2=0$ also holds at a sufficiently large stage, by the finite-witness property of a directed colimit. Replace the stage so that $x_0^2=0$ there. Its base ring, being a subring of $R$, is reduced and Noetherian. The first paragraph makes that smooth algebra reduced, so $x_0=0$ and hence $x=0$. Finally, if a nonzero nilpotent had least vanishing exponent $r\geq2$, its nonzero power of exponent $r-1$ would have square zero. Therefore exclusion of nonzero square-zero elements proves reducedness. ∎

#### Lemma. A regular quotient cuts out part of a parameter system

*Source credit:* FAC, Chapter III, §5, no. 75, proof of Theorem 3, pp. 269–270.

In the cited geometric setting, the ideal of a nonsingular subvariety in a local ring of projective space is generated by as many equations as its codimension. The successive colon equalities recorded there express regularity of those equations. The following local argument identifies the generators intrinsically.

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be regular local, and suppose $R/I$ is regular local. There is a minimal generating list $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ for $\mathfrak m$ such that $I=(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ for some $0\leq c\leq d$.

**Proof.** Put $d=\dim R$, $\dim(R/I)=d-c$, and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. Since $I$ is proper, $I\subseteq\mathfrak m$. The cotangent-space quotient gives an exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow (I+\mathfrak m^2)/\mathfrak m^2
\longrightarrow\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2
\longrightarrow\mathfrak m/(I+\mathfrak m^2)
\longrightarrow0.$$
Regularity of both rings says that the middle and final dimensions are $d$ and $d-c$. Choose $x_1,\ldots,x_c$ in $I$ representing a basis of the kernel, and extend it to a basis using $x_{c+1},\ldots,x_d\in\mathfrak m$. Nakayama makes this a minimal generating system.

The regular-parameter quotient theorem, equivalently the parameter assertion in [regular rings are Cohen–Macaulay](#native-algebra-lemma-regular-ring-cm), shows that
$$A=R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$$
is a regular local domain of dimension $d-c$. It surjects onto $R/I$. If its kernel were nonzero, choose a nonzero element $g$ in that kernel. It is a nonunit and a nonzerodivisor in the domain $A$. The [one-equation dimension result](#native-algebra-lemma-one-equation) would give
$$\dim(R/I)\leq\dim(A/gA)=\dim A-1,$$
contrary to their equal dimensions. Thus the kernel is zero and $I=(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$.

This argument includes $c=0$, with an empty initial list, and dimension zero, when $A$ is a field and cannot have a nonzero proper kernel. Because a regular parameter system is a regular sequence, the source's colon assertions are exactly
$$(x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1}):x_j=(x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1}),
\qquad 1\leq j\leq c.$$
They say that multiplication by $x_j$ is injective after dividing by its predecessors. ∎

#### Lemma. Fibrewise injectivity over a Noetherian target

Let $R\to S$ be local, with $S$ Noetherian, and let $\mathfrak m$ be the maximal ideal of $R$. Suppose $N$ is finite over $S$, $M$ is flat over $R$, and $u\colon N\to M$ is $R$-linear. If
$$N/\mathfrak mN\longrightarrow M/\mathfrak mM$$
is injective, then $u$ is injective and its cokernel is $R$-flat. The base ring $R$ need not be Noetherian, and no $S$-module structure on $M$ is required.

**Proof.** We first prove that $u_n\colon N/\mathfrak m^nN\to M/\mathfrak m^nM$ is injective for every $n\geq1$. The case $n=1$ is assumed. Set $V_n=\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}$ and $\kappa=R/\mathfrak m$. Tensoring the quotient sequence gives right-exact rows
$$\begin{array}{ccccc}
N\otimes_R V_n&\longrightarrow&N/\mathfrak m^{n+1}N&\longrightarrow&N/\mathfrak m^nN\longrightarrow0\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow u_{n+1}&&\downarrow u_n\\
M\otimes_R V_n&\longrightarrow&M/\mathfrak m^{n+1}M&\longrightarrow&M/\mathfrak m^nM\longrightarrow0 .
\end{array}$$
The lower left horizontal map is injective by flatness of $M$. The left vertical map is the tensor product over $\kappa$ of $u_1$ with $V_n$, since $V_n$ is killed by $\mathfrak m$; it is injective too. No injectivity of the upper left horizontal map is assumed.

If $z\in\ker u_{n+1}$, its image on the top right is zero by the induction hypothesis. Write $z$ as the image of $y\in N\otimes_R V_n$. Its image along the bottom row is zero. Injectivity of the bottom horizontal map, followed by that of the left vertical map, gives $y=0$ and hence $z=0$. This proves the induction.

The ideal $\mathfrak mS$ lies in the maximal ideal of $S$. [Krull intersection](#native-algebra-lemma-intersect-powers-ideal-module-zero), applied to the finite $S$-module $N$, gives $\bigcap_n\mathfrak m^nN=0$. Any element of $\ker u$ belongs to that intersection, so $u$ is injective.

Put $Q=M/u(N)$. The Tor sequence and flatness of $M$ identify
$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(Q,R/J)
\cong\ker(N/JN\longrightarrow M/JM)$$
for every ideal $J\subset R$. If $J$ is proper, it lies in $\mathfrak m$, and $R/J\to S/JS$ is local with Noetherian target. The source module $N/JN$ is finite over $S/JS$, the target $M/JM$ is flat over $R/J$, and the map on residue quotients is the given $u_1$. The injectivity already proved, applied over $R/J$, makes this kernel zero. For $J=R$ it is zero directly. The [Tor criterion for flatness](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-flat) now gives flatness of $Q$. ∎

#### Lemma. The universal derivation represents derivations

For a ring map $R\to S$ and an $S$-module $M$, composition with the universal derivation gives a natural isomorphism
$$\operatorname{Hom}_S(\Omega_{S/R},M)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_R(S,M),
\qquad \alpha\longmapsto\alpha\circ d.$$

**Proof.** Start with the free $S$-module having symbols $[s]$ for all $s\in S$. Its quotient defining $\Omega_{S/R}$ imposes precisely
$$[s+t]-[s]-[t],\qquad
[st]-s[t]-t[s],\qquad [r]\quad(r\in R),$$
where $r$ in the final expression denotes its image in $S$. A function $D\colon S\to M$ extends uniquely to a linear map from the free module.
