It annihilates these relations exactly when $D$ is additive, obeys the Leibniz rule, and vanishes on $R$. Those are the conditions for an $R$-derivation. Thus it factors uniquely through $\Omega_{S/R}$ exactly in that case. Composition with a homomorphism of target modules commutes with this construction, proving naturality. ∎

#### Lemma. Noetherianity of an adic completion

Let $I$ be a finitely generated ideal of a ring $R$. If $R/I$ is Noetherian, then $\widehat R=\varprojlim_nR/I^n$ is Noetherian and complete for the ideal $I\widehat R$.

**Proof.** The [completion-kernel theorem for finite ideals](#native-algebra-lemma-hathat-finitely-generated) gives
$$\widehat R/I^n\widehat R\cong R/I^n$$
and completeness of $\widehat R$ for $I\widehat R$. We may therefore replace $R$ by $\widehat R$ and prove that a complete ring with the two stated finiteness properties is Noetherian.

Choose generators $f_1,\ldots,f_t$ of $I$. Sending $T_i$ to the initial class of $f_i$ gives a surjective graded map
$$(R/I)[T_1,\ldots,T_t]\longrightarrow
\operatorname{gr}_I(R)=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^n/I^{n+1}.$$
The polynomial ring is Noetherian, so the graded ring is too. For an arbitrary ideal $J\subset R$, its initial ideal is
$$\bigoplus_{n\geq0}(J\cap I^n)/(J\cap I^{n+1})
\ \subseteq\ \operatorname{gr}_I(R).$$
Choose finitely many homogeneous generators and lift them to $g_j\in J\cap I^{d_j}$, where $d_j$ is the degree of the corresponding generator.

If $x\in J\cap I^n$, its initial class is a sum of these generators with coefficients of degrees $n-d_j$, using only $d_j\leq n$. Lifting those coefficients gives $a_j\in I^{n-d_j}$ for these indices; use $a_j=0$ for the others. Then
$$x-\sum_j a_jg_j\in J\cap I^{n+1}.$$
Beginning at $n=0$ and applying this to each successive remainder constructs coefficients $a_{j,n}\in I^{\max(0,n-d_j)}$ such that
$$x-\sum_{n=0}^{N}\sum_j a_{j,n}g_j\in I^{N+1}.$$
For fixed $j$, the coefficients tend to zero $I$-adically, so completeness defines $A_j=\sum_{n\geq0}a_{j,n}\in R$. Multiplication by $g_j$ and addition of finitely many terms are continuous. Separatedness therefore gives $x=\sum_jA_jg_j$. Thus the $g_j$ generate $J$.

If the initial ideal is zero, the same argument puts $J$ in every $I^n$, so $J=0$. Hence every ideal is finitely generated, proving Noetherianity. ∎

#### Lemma. Flatness detected by every ideal-power quotient

Let $R\to S$ be a map of Noetherian rings, let $I\subset R$, and let $M$ be finite over $S$. Suppose $M/I^nM$ is flat over $R/I^n$ for all $n\geq1$. Then $M_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $R$ whenever $\mathfrak q\supseteq IS$. In particular $M$ is flat over $R$ if $S$ is local and $IS$ lies in its maximal ideal.

**Proof.** Let
$$K=\ker(I\otimes_RM\longrightarrow M).$$
For every $n$, the inclusion $I/I^n\hookrightarrow R/I^n$ remains injective on tensoring with the assumed flat module $M/I^nM$. Thus the image of $K$ in
$$\begin{aligned}
(I/I^n)\otimes_{R/I^n}(M/I^nM)
&\cong(I/I^n)\otimes_RM\\
&\cong(I\otimes_RM)/I^{n-1}(I\otimes_RM)
\end{aligned}$$
is zero. The last identification follows by tensoring $I^n\to I\to I/I^n\to0$: the image of $I^n\otimes_RM$ is $I^{n-1}(I\otimes_RM)$. Consequently
$$K\subseteq I^{n-1}(I\otimes_RM)\quad(n\geq1).$$

The module $I\otimes_RM$ is finite over $S$, because $I$ is finite over the Noetherian ring $R$. At a chosen $\mathfrak q\supseteq IS$, localizing these inclusions and applying [Krull intersection](#native-algebra-lemma-intersect-powers-ideal-module-zero) over $S_{\mathfrak q}$ gives $K_{\mathfrak q}=0$. This is the intersection consequence of Artin–Rees used in the original argument.

Put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$. The localized module $M_{\mathfrak q}/IM_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $R_{\mathfrak p}/IR_{\mathfrak p}$, by the case $n=1$ and localization of flat modules. Also $K_{\mathfrak q}=0$ is the vanishing of
$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R_{\mathfrak p}}
(M_{\mathfrak q},R_{\mathfrak p}/IR_{\mathfrak p}).$$
The [ideal variant of the local flatness criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-variant-local-criterion-flatness) for $R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}$ now makes $M_{\mathfrak q}$ flat over $R_{\mathfrak p}$. Since $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is flat over $R$, it is flat over $R$ as well. Taking $\mathfrak q$ to be the maximal ideal proves the final assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. A countable Mittag–Leffler system has an element in its limit

Let $(X_i)$ be an inverse system of nonempty sets over a countable directed index set. If the images in each fixed $X_i$ stabilize for sufficiently large indices, then $\varprojlim_iX_i$ is nonempty.

**Proof.** Enumerate the indices and recursively choose an increasing sequence $j_n$ dominating the first $n$ indices and the previously chosen $j_{n-1}$. It is cofinal. Restriction to this sequence does not change the limit: a compatible sequence supplies a value at any original index by mapping down from a $j_n$ above it, independently of which such $n$ is used.

We can thus work with a system indexed by the positive integers. Replace $X_n$ by the eventual image $Y_n$ of its later terms. Stabilization and nonemptiness give $Y_n\ne\varnothing$. The transition $Y_{n+1}\to Y_n$ is surjective: for $y\in Y_n$, choose a stage late enough that the images at both $n$ and $n+1$ have stabilized, and lift $y$ from that stage. Its image in $X_{n+1}$ lies in $Y_{n+1}$ and maps to $y$.

Choose an element of $Y_1$ and then a preimage at each successive stage. Countable choice, as supplied by the axiom of choice, produces a compatible sequence. Its images in the $X_n$ give the required element of the inverse limit. ∎

[^1]: A set-sized collection of representatives suffices: restrict the objects $A'\to A$ to algebras $A'$ presented as quotients of $R[x_1,x_2,\ldots]$. This keeps the same finite-presentation constructions.

[^2]: In the notation of the flatness argument, right exactness applied to $K\to N_2\to Q\to0$ identifies the kernel of $N_2\otimes_RM\to Q\otimes_RM$ with the image of $K\otimes_RM$. The surjection $N_1\to K$ identifies this image with that of $N_1\otimes_RM$. Injectivity of $Q\otimes_RM\to N_3\otimes_RM$ then leaves this kernel unchanged on composing into $N_3\otimes_RM$. Hence the original three-term sequence is exact after tensoring. These are precisely the roles of the second and fourth arrows' injectivity in that argument.

[^3]: The injective maps $L\otimes_RM\to M^{\oplus n}$ and $L'\otimes_RM\to M^{\oplus n}$ identify both source modules with submodules of the same module, compatibly with $L\subseteq L'$. Their quotient therefore injects into $(M^{\oplus n})/(L\otimes_RM)$. Right exactness identifies the source quotient with $(L'/L)\otimes_RM=K\otimes_RM$, giving the claimed injection.

[^4]: If $I=0$, generators of $S^{-1}M$ already generate $M_f$ for some $f\in S$. If $I=\mathfrak p$ is prime and $S=R\setminus\mathfrak p$, generators of the residue fibre $M\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ generate $M_f$ for some $f\notin\mathfrak p$. In this second case every element of $S+I$ is still outside $\mathfrak p$.

#### Infinitesimal lifting and completed local rings

#### Definition. Local complete-intersection maps

A finite-type ring map $A\to B$ is a *local complete intersection* when, in a finite polynomial presentation $B=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J$, the kernel $J$ is a Koszul-regular ideal. The condition can be checked in one such presentation and then holds in every one.

#### Lemma. Noetherian henselizations and their completions

*Source credit:* EGA IV, Theorem 18.6.6 and Proposition 18.8.8.

For a local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$, fix a separable closure of $\kappa$ for the strict henselization. The following are equivalent: $R$ is Noetherian; $R^h$ is Noetherian; $R^{sh}$ is Noetherian. Under these conditions:

1. The maximal-ideal completions $\widehat{R^h}$ and $\widehat{R^{sh}}$ are Noetherian complete local rings.
2. The canonical map $\widehat R\to\widehat{R^h}$ is an isomorphism.
3. Both maps $R^h\to\widehat{R^h}$ and $R^{sh}\to\widehat{R^{sh}}$ are flat.
4. The map $\widehat R\to\widehat{R^{sh}}$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of its target.
5. With the compatible residue-field marking,
   $$(\widehat R)^{sh}\cong\widehat R\otimes_{R^h}R^{sh}.$$
6. The canonical comparison gives
   $$\widehat{(\widehat R)^{sh}}\cong\widehat{R^{sh}}.$$

**Proof.** The maps $R\to R^h\to R^{sh}$ are faithfully flat, their maximal ideals are extended from $\mathfrak m$, and their residue fields are $\kappa$ and the chosen $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$. These properties and the marked universal constructions are proved in Henselian local rings, Sections 4–5. Thus [Noetherian descent](#native-algebra-lemma-descent-noetherian) proves the reverse implications.

Assume $R$ is Noetherian. For $B=R^h$ or $R^{sh}$, the ideal $\mathfrak mB$ is finite and $B/\mathfrak mB$ is a field. The [Noetherian completion lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-completion-noetherian) therefore makes $C=\widehat B$ Noetherian and complete. It is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak mC$: this follows from its quotients $C/\mathfrak m^nC=B/\mathfrak m^nB$, whose maximal ideals are nilpotent. Equivalently, an element with nonzero residue is inverted at every quotient level, and the compatible inverses give an inverse in $C$. This proves (1) before assuming Noetherianity of $B$.

For the ordinary henselization, its universal property gives compatible isomorphisms
$$R/\mathfrak m^n\cong R^h/\mathfrak m^nR^h.$$
Indeed, $R/\mathfrak m^n$ is henselian because its maximal ideal is nilpotent. The induced map from $R^h$ gives an inverse to the displayed map. The other composite is the identity by uniqueness for the henselian quotient $R^h/\mathfrak m^nR^h$. Taking limits proves (2), as in Proposition 6.1.

We next prove (3) without assuming that $B$ is Noetherian. The pointed étale construction expresses $B$ as a filtered colimit of local étale neighborhoods $R_i$, each Noetherian, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_i=\mathfrak mR_i$. Their transition maps and maps into $B$ are flat and local. In the ordinary case $R_i^h=R^h$, so (2) applied to $R_i$ identifies $C$ with $\widehat{R_i}$. Noetherian completion flatness makes $C$ flat over every $R_i$.

For the strict case, choose a basis of $B/\mathfrak mB$ over $R_i/\mathfrak m_i$ and lift its elements once to $e_\alpha\in B$. The same lifts give, for all $n$, isomorphisms
$$\bigoplus_\alpha R_i/\mathfrak m_i^n
\ \cong\ B/\mathfrak m_i^nB.$$
Here is why an infinite basis causes no problem. The module on the right is flat over the Artinian local ring on the left's coefficient side. The cokernel of the indicated free-module map vanishes modulo its nilpotent maximal ideal, hence is zero. Flatness of the target makes the kernel inject after residue tensoring; because the residue map is a basis isomorphism, the kernel also equals its maximal-ideal multiple, and nilpotence makes it zero. These isomorphisms are compatible in $n$ because the lifts were fixed. Hence $C$ is the completion of a free $R_i$-module, of possibly infinite rank, and [completed direct sums are flat](#native-more-algebra-lemma-completed-direct-sum-flat).

In both cases $C$ is flat over every stage. A finite relation with coefficients in $B$ has its coefficients at one stage. The equational flatness criterion there trivializes the relation, and the same finite expressions work over $B$. This is also the [flat-colimit criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-colimit-rings-flat), so $B\to C$ is flat. It is local with nonzero residue field, hence faithfully flat. Descent from the already Noetherian $C$ proves that both henselizations are Noetherian. The complete stagewise argument, including the arbitrary-rank basis construction, is Theorem 6.3.

The [formal étaleness of henselization](#native-more-algebra-lemma-henselization-formally-smooth) implies the required adic formal smoothness of $R\to R^{sh}$. The [completion comparison for formal smoothness](#native-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth-completion) then proves (4).

A complete local ring is henselian, so the marked map $R^h\to\widehat R$ exists. Apply the [strict henselization tensor comparison](#native-algebra-lemma-sh-from-h-map), with $(\widehat R)^h=\widehat R$, to obtain (5).

For (6), put $A=\widehat R$, $B=R^{sh}$ and $T=A^{sh}=A\otimes_{R^h}B$. The map $B\to T$ induces $\alpha\colon\widehat B\to\widehat T$. On the other hand, $\widehat B$ is complete local with residue field $\kappa^{\mathrm{sep}}$, hence strictly henselian. Its canonical local map from $A$, with this residue marking, extends uniquely to $T\to\widehat B$. Completion gives $\beta\colon\widehat T\to\widehat B$.

To check these maps are inverse, the tensor presentation and (2) give, compatibly in $n$,
$$\begin{aligned}
T/\mathfrak m^nT
&\cong(A/\mathfrak m^nA)\otimes_{R^h}B\\
&\cong(R^h/\mathfrak m^nR^h)\otimes_{R^h}B\\
&\cong B/\mathfrak m^nB.
\end{aligned}$$
The first map is induced by $B\to T$. The map $T\to\widehat B$ gives its inverse: on the tensor factors it uses the canonical maps from $A$ and $B$, and these become precisely the displayed quotient identifications. The maximal ideals of $T$ and $B$ are both generated by $\mathfrak m$, so these quotients compute their completions. Passing to inverse limits proves $\beta\alpha=1$ and $\alpha\beta=1$, establishing the omitted inverse check. ∎

#### Lemma. Making a lift of a unit invertible

If $\bar u$ is a unit of $A/I$, there is an étale map $A\to A'$ inducing $A/I\cong A'/IA'$ and a unit $u'\in A'$ whose residue is $\bar u$.

**Proof.** Lift $\bar u$ to $f\in A$ and take $A'=A_f$. This principal localization is étale, and the image $u'=f/1$ is invertible. Its reduction is
$$A_f/IA_f\cong(A/I)_{\bar u}=A/I,$$
since $\bar u$ was already a unit. Under this identification $u'$ reduces to the prescribed element. ∎

#### Lemma. An intersection identity from first Koszul homology

Let $I\subset A$, and suppose the images of $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ in $A/I$ have vanishing first Koszul homology. For $J=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$,
$$I\cap J=IJ.$$

**Proof.** The Koszul terms are free, so the quotient $A\to A/I$ gives a short exact sequence of complexes
$$0\to I\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g)
\to K_\bullet(A,g)\to K_\bullet(A/I,\bar g)\to0.$$
The homology sequence, together with the assumed $H_1=0$, makes
$$H_0(I\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g))=I/IJ
\longrightarrow H_0(K_\bullet(A,g))=A/J$$
injective. Its kernel is $(I\cap J)/IJ$, proving the equality. Empty lists give $J=0$ and the same conclusion. ∎

#### Lemma. Complete-intersection maps are local on the target

Suppose $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ generate the unit ideal in $S$. If each map $R\to S_{g_j}$ is a local complete intersection, then so is $R\to S$.

**Proof.** A Koszul-regular ideal is locally finitely generated along its vanishing set, by definition; off that set it is the unit ideal locally. A finite affine cover therefore makes it finitely generated. Consequently a local complete-intersection algebra has a finite presentation. The [finite-cover finiteness criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-cover) now makes $S$ finitely presented over $R$. Choose $S=P/I$ with $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $I$ finite.

Fix $\mathfrak q\supseteq I$ in $P$. Choose a lift $h_j\in P$ of some $g_j$ with $h_j\notin\mathfrak q$, and set
$$Q=P[T],\qquad z=Th_j-1,\qquad
I_j=(I,z),\qquad\mathfrak q_j=(\mathfrak q,z).$$
The quotient $Q/\mathfrak q_j=(P/\mathfrak q)_{h_j}$ is a domain, so $\mathfrak q_j$ is prime. Also $Q/I_j=S_{g_j}$, making $I_j$ Koszul-regular.

Choose $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in I$ whose classes form a basis of the conormal fibre $(I/I^2)\otimes_S\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. The [principal-localization conormal calculation](#native-algebra-lemma-principal-localization-nl) identifies the conormal fibre of $I_j$ with this fibre plus the line generated by $z$. Thus $z,f_1,\ldots,f_r$ give a basis at $\mathfrak q_j$.

Since $I_j$ is finite, Nakayama makes these elements generate it in the local ring $Q_{\mathfrak q_j}$; the finite cokernel vanishes on some principal neighborhood. Shrink that neighborhood further so that $I_j$ also has a Koszul-regular generating list. Such a list is quasi-regular, and its conormal classes form a basis. Its length is therefore $r+1$. By [independence of generators of fixed length](#native-more-algebra-lemma-independence-of-generators), the particular list $z,f_1,\ldots,f_r$ is Koszul-regular on a principal neighborhood $Q_h$ with $h\notin\mathfrak q_j$.

Multiplication by $z=Th_j-1$ is injective on $Q$: if $z\sum a_iT^i=0$, the constant coefficient gives $a_0=0$, then successive coefficients give every $a_i=0$. It remains injective after localization. Thus the one-element sequence $z$ is Koszul-regular. [Koszul truncation](#native-more-algebra-lemma-truncate-koszul-regular) makes the images of $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ a Koszul-regular generating list of the image of $I$ in
$$Q_h/(z)\cong(P_{h_j})_{\bar h}.$$
Write $\bar h=a/h_j^N$. Because $h\notin\mathfrak q_j$, we have $a\notin\mathfrak q$. The displayed ring is $P_{ah_j}$, with $ah_j\notin\mathfrak q$. We have therefore found the required principal neighborhood in the original polynomial ring. Since this works for every $\mathfrak q\supseteq I$, the ideal $I$ is Koszul-regular. ∎

#### Lemma. Global complete intersections give Koszul-regular equations

If $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ is a relative global complete intersection, its displayed equations form a Koszul-regular sequence.

**Proof.** Put $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$. Multiplication by each $f_i$ on the Koszul complex is null-homotopic, so $J$ annihilates its homology. At a prime not containing $J$, a generator becomes a unit and all homology vanishes. At a prime containing $J$, the [global-CI regular-sequence theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal) makes the displayed equations a regular sequence in the localized polynomial ring. [Regular sequences are Koszul-regular](#native-more-algebra-lemma-regular-koszul-regular), so their positive homology vanishes there too. A module vanishing at every prime is zero, proving the claim. ∎

#### Definition. Four regularity conditions on an ideal

For an ideal $I$ of a ring $R$, each condition below is imposed locally along $V(I)$. For every $\mathfrak p\supseteq I$, there must be a $g\notin\mathfrak p$ and a finite generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ of $I_g$ in $R_g$ of the specified kind:

1. A *regular ideal* admits a regular generating sequence.
2. A *Koszul-regular ideal* admits a Koszul-regular generating sequence.
3. An *$H_1$-regular ideal* admits a generating sequence with zero first Koszul homology.
4. A *quasi-regular ideal* admits a quasi-regular generating sequence.

The neighborhood and list may depend on $\mathfrak p$. If $V(I)$ is empty, these conditions are vacuous.

#### Lemma. Relative regularity under arbitrary base change

Let $A\to B$ and $A\to A'$ be ring maps, put $B'=B\otimes_AA'$, and set $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subset B$. Assume $B/J$ is flat over $A$. Then quasi-regularity of the list $f_i$ implies quasi-regularity of its image in $B'$, and $H_1$-regularity implies $H_1$-regularity of its image.

**Proof.** Suppose the list is quasi-regular. Each graded piece $J^n/J^{n+1}$ is the direct sum of copies of $B/J$ indexed by degree-$n$ monomials, and is therefore $A$-flat. The sequences
$$0\to J^n/J^{n+1}\to B/J^{n+1}\to B/J^n\to0$$
prove by induction that every $B/J^n$ is $A$-flat. Tensoring $0\to J^n\to B\to B/J^n\to0$ then identifies $J^n\otimes_AA'$ with its image in $B'$, namely $(J')^n$. Tensoring the sequence between two successive powers identifies
$$ (J')^n/(J')^{n+1}
\cong(J^n/J^{n+1})\otimes_AA'.$$
The monomial descriptions and their multiplication maps thus base-change to the same descriptions over $B'/J'$. This is quasi-regularity of the specified images.

For the second assertion, the [first-homology base-change surjection](#native-more-algebra-lemma-base-change-h1-regular) gives
$$H_1(K_\bullet(B,f))\otimes_AA'
\longrightarrow H_1(K_\bullet(B',f'))\longrightarrow0.$$
Its proof uses flatness only of $B/J$, as assumed here. Vanishing of the source forces vanishing of the target. ∎

#### Lemma. The regularity notions agree for finite local modules

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $M\ne0$ be finite, and take $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in\mathfrak m$. The following are equivalent: the list is $M$-regular; it is $M$-Koszul-regular; it is $M$-$H_1$-regular; it is $M$-quasi-regular. In particular the four notions agree for lists in $\mathfrak m$ acting on $R$.

**Proof.** Successive injectivity gives [positive Koszul exactness](#native-more-algebra-lemma-regular-koszul-regular). Positive exactness includes vanishing in degree one. The [first-homology argument](#native-more-algebra-lemma-h1-regular-quasi-regular) then gives quasi-regularity, including its arbitrary-module formulation. Finally the [Noetherian local quasi-regularity theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-quasi-regular-regular) gives regularity for this finite module. Its nonzero quotient condition is satisfied: an ideal generated inside $\mathfrak m$ cannot kill $M$ by Nakayama. These implications close the cycle. ∎

#### Lemma. Completion preserves and detects regularity

A Noetherian local ring $A$ is regular exactly when its maximal-ideal completion $\widehat A$ is regular.

**Proof.** If $\widehat A$ is regular, the faithfully flat local completion map and [descent of regularity](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-under-regular) imply that $A$ is regular.

Conversely, assume $A$ regular and put $d=\dim A$. A minimal list of $d$ generators of its maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ generates the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\widehat A$ of the completion. The [dimension comparison](#native-more-algebra-lemma-completion-dimension) says $\dim\widehat A=d$. Thus its embedding dimension is at most its dimension; the reverse inequality always holds, so $\widehat A$ is regular.

Alternatively, the completion map is flat and local with closed fibre $A/\mathfrak m$, a field. The [regular-base, regular-fibre ascent theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre) proves the same conclusion. ∎

#### Lemma. A derivation detects a non-pth-power element

Let $B$ be a domain of characteristic $p>0$ that is a finite-type algebra over a Noetherian complete local ring. If $f\in B$ does not belong to $\operatorname{Frac}(B)^p$, there is a derivation $D\colon B\to B$ with $D(f)\ne0$.

**Proof.** Choose a finite-type map $R\to B$ with $R$ Noetherian complete local. Its image is a quotient of $R$, so it is again Noetherian complete local; it is a domain of characteristic $p$ because it embeds in $B$. Replace $R$ by that image. The [complete-domain normalization theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-complete-local-noetherian-domain-finite-over-regular) gives a finite subring extension $k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]\subset R$. Replacing the base by this power-series ring still makes $B$ a finite-type algebra.

[Normalization over a domain](#native-algebra-lemma-noether-normalization-over-a-domain) now provides
$$R\subset A=R[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]\subset B'\subset B,$$
where $B'$ is finite over $A$ and $B'_g=B_g$ for some $0\ne g\in R$. The fraction fields of $B'$ and $B$ agree. Choose $N\geq0$ with $f'=g^{pN}f\in B'$. This element is still not a $p$th power in that field. If a derivation $D'$ of $B'$ detects $f'$, the [extension lemma below](#native-more-algebra-lemma-derivation-extends) extends $g^MD'$ to $B$ for a suitable $M$. In the common fraction field its value on $f$ is
$$g^{M-pN}D'(f')\ne0,$$
because derivations in characteristic $p$ kill $g^{pN}$. It is therefore enough to treat a finite extension of domains $A\subset B$.

Write $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ and $L=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$; then $L/K$ is finite. Use the coefficient rings $A_J$ and their fields $K_J$ from the [power-series subfield lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-power-series-ring-subfields). They satisfy $\bigcap_JK_J=K^p$ and are downward directed. The finite-extension conclusion of the [field-intersection lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-intersection-subfields) gives
$$\bigcap_J L^pK_J=L^p.$$
Since $f\notin L^p$, some $J$ has $f\notin L^pK_J$. By the [p-basis constant-field test](#native-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis), $df$ is then nonzero in $\Omega_{L/K_J}$. A linear functional on this $L$-vector space that does not kill $df$ gives a $K_J$-derivation $\delta\colon L\to L$ with $\delta(f)\ne0$.

The extensions $A_J\subset A\subset B$ are finite, so choose finitely many $A_J$-module generators $b_1,\ldots,b_t$ of $B$. Express each $\delta(b_i)$ as a fraction in $B$ and let $h\ne0$ be the product of their denominators. Since $\delta$ kills $A_J$, the derivation $h\delta$ sends every $A_J$-linear combination of the $b_i$ into $B$. Its restriction is the required derivation, and its value on $f$ is nonzero. ∎

#### Lemma. Extension of derivations

Let $D\colon R\to R$ be a derivation of a ring.

1. For any ideal $I$, there is a canonical extension $\widehat D\colon\widehat R\to\widehat R$ to the $I$-adic completion.
2. For any multiplicative subset $S$, there is a unique extension to $S^{-1}R$.
3. Suppose $R\subset R'$ is a finite-type extension, $g\in R$ is a nonzerodivisor on $R'$, and $R_g=R'_g$. Some $g^ND$ extends to a derivation of $R'$.

**Proof.** The product rule gives $D(I^{n+1})\subset I^n$. Thus applying $D$ to a representative defines compatible additive maps
$$R/I^{n+1}\longrightarrow R/I^n.$$
Passing to their inverse limit, and identifying a sequence with its shifted tail, defines $\widehat D$. At level $n$, compute the product of two inputs using representatives at level $n+1$. The product rule in $R$, reduced modulo $I^n$, gives the product rule for the output. The same computation proves additivity and that $1$ maps to zero. These maps also commute with $R\to\widehat R$. The construction is continuous, lowering the filtration index by at most one, and is unique among continuous extensions because the image of $R$ is dense and $\widehat R$ is separated. No finiteness hypothesis on $I$ or $R$ is used.

For localization the only possible formula is
$$D(r/s)=\frac{D(r)}s-\frac{rD(s)}{s^2}.$$
It is well defined even in the presence of zero divisors. Indeed, equality of two fractions means that $t(s'r-sr')=0$ for some $t\in S$. After differentiating this equality and localizing, the factor $t$ is a unit and $s'r-sr'=0$, so $D(s'r-sr')=0$. These two equalities give equality of the proposed values after bringing them to a common denominator.

For the algebra laws, the map $r\mapsto r+\varepsilon D(r)$ is a ring homomorphism to $(S^{-1}R)[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$. It sends each $s\in S$ to a unit, whose inverse is $s^{-1}-\varepsilon s^{-2}D(s)$. The localization universal property extends this homomorphism, and its $\varepsilon$-coefficient is exactly the displayed formula. Comparing coefficients proves additivity and Leibniz. Finally, differentiating $s\cdot s^{-1}=1$ forces that formula, proving uniqueness.

For the third assertion, choose algebra generators $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ of $R'$ and a common $a\geq0$ with $g^ax_i\in R$. Localize $D$ and set $E=g^{a+1}D$. Then
$$E(x_i)=gD(g^ax_i)-a(g^ax_i)D(g)\in R.$$
Also $E(R)\subset R$. Applying Leibniz to a polynomial in the $x_i$, including its coefficients in $R$, now shows that $E$ maps $R'$ into $R'$. The nonzerodivisor condition identifies $R'$ with its image in $R'_g$, so this restriction is an actual derivation of $R'$ extending $g^{a+1}D$. ∎

#### Lemma. Regularity of polynomial root extensions

Suppose $R$ is regular and a derivation $D\colon R\to R$ sends $f\in R$ to a unit. Then
$$R[Z]/(P(Z)-f)$$
is regular for every $P\in\mathbf Z[Z]$. In particular this holds for $P(Z)=Z^n$ for every $n\geq1$.

**Proof.** The polynomial ring $R[Z]$ is regular by [regular ascent](#native-algebra-lemma-regular-goes-up). Extend $D$ coefficientwise, putting $D(Z)=0$. It annihilates $P(Z)$, including when $P$ is constant, so it sends $P(Z)-f$ to the unit $-D(f)$. Apply the [derivation criterion for a regular hypersurface](#native-more-algebra-lemma-quotient-regular). No monicity condition on $P$ is needed. ∎

#### Lemma. The fibres of henselization

Let $R$ be Noetherian local and $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. There are finitely many primes $\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_t$ of $R^h$ above $\mathfrak p$, and finitely many primes $\mathfrak r_1,\ldots,\mathfrak r_s$ of $R^{sh}$ above it. The canonical maps identify
$$R^h\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong
\prod_{i=1}^t\kappa(\mathfrak q_i),
\qquad
R^{sh}\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong
\prod_{j=1}^s\kappa(\mathfrak r_j).$$
Every displayed residue field is algebraic separable over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$.

**Proof.** Both henselizations are Noetherian by the [henselization comparison theorem](#native-more-algebra-lemma-henselization-noetherian). As they are filtered colimits of étale $R$-algebras, all the assertions follow from the [Noetherian ind-étale fibre lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-filtered-colimit-etale-noetherian-fibres).

Here is also the direct proof through a domain. Henselization commutes with quotient by $\mathfrak p$:
$$R^h/\mathfrak pR^h\cong(R/\mathfrak p)^h,\qquad
R^{sh}/\mathfrak pR^{sh}\cong(R/\mathfrak p)^{sh}.$$
For the first equality the quotient on the left is henselian, and a local map from $R/\mathfrak p$ to a henselian local ring extends uniquely from $R$ to $R^h$; the extension kills $\mathfrak pR^h$. This proves the universal property. The same argument with the chosen separable residue-field marking proves the strict version: the quotient is strictly henselian and has the same marked residue field. The quotient permanence and both universal properties are proved in Henselian local rings and henselization, Sections 3–5; Section 6, Proposition 6.1 gives the associated maximal-ideal-power comparisons.

Replace $R$ by $R/\mathfrak p$, so it is a domain and the fibre in question is the generic fibre. Write $T$ for either henselization. It has finitely many minimal primes, and flat going down shows that every minimal prime contracts to $(0)$: a nonzero contraction would have the smaller prime $(0)$ beneath it, forcing a smaller prime in $T$. Conversely every prime over $(0)$ is minimal. To justify this converse, primes in a fibre of an ind-étale map are incomparable: after base change to the fraction field, a strict inclusion would contract to a strict inclusion at a finite étale stage, a product of fields. A minimal prime contained in a prime over $(0)$ must therefore equal it.

Since $R$ is reduced, so is $T$ by [reducedness of henselizations](#native-more-algebra-lemma-henselization-reduced). Its generic fibre is thus a reduced Noetherian ring whose primes are precisely the finitely many minimal primes just found, all maximal. The [dimension-zero theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-dimension-zero-ring) and the [localization description at reduced minimal primes](#native-algebra-lemma-minimal-prime-reduced-ring) identify it with the product of its residue fields. These are canonically the residue fields of the corresponding primes of $T$. Each field is a filtered union of images of finite separable field factors from the étale stages; consequently it is algebraic separable over the fraction field of $R$. This proves the original assertions after undoing the quotient. ∎

#### Proposition. Formal smoothness and regular maps of complete local rings

Let $A\to B$ be a local homomorphism of Noetherian complete local rings. Write $k=A/\mathfrak m_A$ and $\bar B=B/\mathfrak m_AB$. The following conditions are equivalent:

1. $A\to B$ is a regular map.
2. $B$ is flat over $A$ and $\bar B$ is geometrically regular over $k$.
3. $B$ is flat over $A$ and $k\to\bar B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $\bar B$.
4. $A\to B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $B$.

**Proof.** The [flatness and closed-fibre criterion](#native-more-algebra-proposition-fs-flat-fibre-fs) identifies (2), (3) and (4). A regular map has a geometrically regular closed fibre, so (1) implies (2). Assume the other three conditions and fix a prime $\mathfrak p\subset A$. We must prove geometric regularity of $B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$.

By [formal-smoothness base change](#native-more-algebra-lemma-base-change-fs), replace $A\to B$ by $A/\mathfrak p\to B/\mathfrak pB$. Quotients of these complete Noetherian local rings remain complete, and the induced map is formally smooth for the quotient maximal-ideal topology. We may therefore assume that $A$ is a domain and the chosen prime is zero.

The [complete-domain normalization theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-complete-local-noetherian-domain-finite-over-regular) gives a regular subring $A_0\subset A$, finite in $A$, with the same residue field as $A$. The ring $A_0$ is a power-series ring over a field, or over a Cohen ring. Apply the [closed-fibre equation-lifting construction](#native-more-algebra-remark-what-does-it-mean) to $A_0\to A\to B$. It supplies a Noetherian complete local $A_0$-algebra $C$, formally smooth for its maximal-ideal topology, with
$$B\cong C\widehat\otimes_{A_0}A=C\otimes_{A_0}A.$$
The first equality uses flatness of $B/A$. For the second, $A$ is finite over $A_0$, so the tensor product is finite over $C$ and already complete for the relevant ideal-adic topology. If $K_0=\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)$ and $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, the desired fibre is obtained from $C\otimes_{A_0}K_0$ by the field extension $K_0\subset K$. Geometric regularity is preserved by field extension. It suffices to prove the assertion with regular power-series base $A_0$ and target $C$.

Rename that pair $A\to B$. Flatness, the regular base, and the regular closed fibre imply that $B$ is regular by [regular local ascent](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre). Its localization $B\otimes_A K$, where $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, is therefore regular. If $K$ has characteristic zero, the [field criterion for geometric regularity](#native-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular) finishes the proof.

In the remaining case $A=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$ in characteristic $p>0$. It is enough to test finite purely inseparable extensions $L/K$. Induct on their degrees. The case $L=K$ was just proved. For a nontrivial extension choose $K\subset M\subset L$ with $[L:M]=p$, and write
$$L=M(u),\qquad u^p=f\in M\setminus M^p.$$
There is a finite $A$-subalgebra $A'\subset M$ with fraction field $M$: take finitely many algebraic generators of $M/K$ and multiply each by a nonzero element of $A$ so that its monic equation has coefficients in $A$. If necessary replace $u$ by $bu$ for a nonzero denominator $b\in A'$ of $f$. Then the new $f=b^pf$ belongs to $A'$ and is still outside $M^p$, while the extension $L/M$ is unchanged. Thus
$$A''=A'[Z]/(Z^p-f)$$
is a finite domain extension with fraction field $L$.

The ring $A'$ is Noetherian complete local. Indeed it is finite over the complete henselian local ring $A$, so it decomposes as a finite product of complete local rings; being a domain leaves exactly one factor. The [non-pth-power derivation lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-find-d) gives a derivation $D\colon A'\to A'$ with $D(f)\ne0$.

Set $T=B\otimes_A A'$. It is finite over $B$, hence a product of Noetherian complete local rings $T_\nu$. Each $A'\to T_\nu$ is local: the contraction of its maximal ideal lies over $\mathfrak m_A$, and $A'$ has only one such maximal ideal. Base change gives formal smoothness of $A'\to T$ for $\mathfrak m_BT$. Passage to each local factor preserves the lifting property, since idempotents lift uniquely across square-zero ideals. The induced topology on $T_\nu$ is its maximal-ideal topology: its closed fibre over $B$ is local Artinian, so the two defining ideals have cofinal powers.

Apply [derivation lifting](#native-more-algebra-lemma-lift-derivation-through-fs) to each factor and combine the resulting derivations to extend $D$ to $T$. Localizing gives a derivation of
$$T\otimes_{A'}M=B\otimes_A M$$
whose value on $f$ is a unit, because $D(f)$ is a nonzero element of the field $M$. By induction $B\otimes_A M$ is regular. The [polynomial root-extension criterion](#native-more-algebra-lemma-degree-p-extension-regular) now makes
$$B\otimes_A L\cong
(B\otimes_A M)[Z]/(Z^p-f)$$
regular. This completes the purely inseparable induction, proves geometric regularity of every fibre, and establishes (1). ∎

#### Lemma. Algebraic and adic formal smoothness

Let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a ring map.

1. Suppose $\varphi$ is algebraically formally smooth. Give $R$ a linear topology and $S$ a pre-adic topology, subject only to continuity of $\varphi$. The resulting map has the topological formal-smoothness property.
2. Suppose $\varphi$ is continuous for the $\mathfrak m$-adic and $\mathfrak n$-adic topologies. Formal smoothness for these topologies is equivalent to formal smoothness with $R$ discrete and $S$ still $\mathfrak n$-adic.

Here topological formal smoothness tests continuous maps to discrete rings across square-zero quotients.

**Proof.** For (1), take a square-zero ideal $J$ in a discrete ring $D$ and a lifting diagram
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
S&\longrightarrow&D/J\\
\uparrow&&\uparrow\\
R&\longrightarrow&D .
\end{array}$$
Algebraic formal smoothness supplies an $R$-algebra lift $\psi\colon S\to D$. Since the topology on $S$ is pre-adic, choose a defining ideal $\mathfrak n$. Continuity of its given map to $D/J$ means that $\mathfrak n^k$ has zero image for some $k$. Thus $\psi(\mathfrak n^k)\subseteq J$ and $\psi(\mathfrak n^{2k})\subseteq J^2=0$. The lift is continuous, proving (1).

For (2), formal smoothness with the discrete base immediately supplies lifts for the diagrams with continuous $\mathfrak m$-adic base map. Conversely, consider a diagram with the base viewed as discrete. Continuity of $\varphi$ supplies $r$ with $\varphi(\mathfrak m^r)\subseteq\mathfrak n$, and continuity of the top map supplies $k$ with $\mathfrak n^k$ killed in $D/J$. Commutativity puts the image of $\mathfrak m^{rk}$ under $R\to D$ in $J$, so $\mathfrak m^{2rk}$ is killed in $D$. That base map is therefore already $\mathfrak m$-adically continuous. The assumed adic lifting property applies and gives the desired continuous lift. ∎

#### Lemma. Formal smoothness is unchanged by adic completion

Equip $R,S$ with topologies defined by finitely generated ideals $\mathfrak m,\mathfrak n$, and suppose $R\to S$ is continuous. Write $\widehat R,\widehat S$ for these completions and $\widehat{\mathfrak n}=\mathfrak n\widehat S$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $R\to S$ is formally smooth for the specified adic topologies.
2. $R\to\widehat S$ is formally smooth for the $\widehat{\mathfrak n}$-adic target topology.
3. $\widehat R\to\widehat S$ is formally smooth for the completed adic topologies.

**Proof.** Finite generation of the ideals gives the [canonical quotient identities](#native-algebra-lemma-hathat-finitely-generated)
$$\widehat R/\mathfrak m^n\widehat R\cong R/\mathfrak m^n,
\qquad
\widehat S/\mathfrak n^n\widehat S\cong S/\mathfrak n^n,$$
as well as completeness for the extended ideals. A continuous map from either original ring to a discrete ring factors through one of these quotients. The quotient identities therefore extend it uniquely to a continuous map from its completion; restriction is the inverse operation.

Apply this correspondence to the maps into a discrete ring $D$ and into $D/J$, for any square-zero ideal $J$. It identifies the lifting diagrams for (1), (2) and (3), and also identifies their continuous lifts. Compatibility with the base map follows either on each quotient or by uniqueness of extension from the dense original ring. The completed map $\widehat R\to\widehat S$ is defined by this same continuous-extension construction. Thus existence of a lift in any one of the three forms is equivalent to existence in the others. The preceding lemma allows the base topology to be viewed as discrete whenever that convention is used. ∎

#### Lemma. A derivation criterion for a regular hypersurface

Let $R$ be regular and $f\in R$. If there is a derivation $D\colon R\to R$ whose value $D(f)$ becomes a unit in $R/(f)$, then $R/(f)$ is regular.

**Proof.** Check the claim at any prime $\mathfrak q$ of $R$ containing $f$. The [localization rule for derivations](#native-more-algebra-lemma-derivation-extends) extends $D$ to $R_{\mathfrak q}$. The hypothesis implies $D(f)\notin\mathfrak qR_{\mathfrak q}$. But Leibniz sends the square of the maximal ideal into that ideal. Hence
$$f\notin(\mathfrak qR_{\mathfrak q})^2.$$
In the regular local ring $R_{\mathfrak q}$, the element $f$ is therefore part of a minimal generating system for the maximal ideal. Such a system is a regular sequence, by [regular local Cohen–Macaulayness](#native-algebra-lemma-regular-ring-cm). Quotienting by its first element gives dimension and embedding dimension both one less, so $R_{\mathfrak q}/(f)$ is regular local. This proves regularity at every prime of $R/(f)$; if the quotient is zero, there are no primes to check. ∎

#### Lemma. Completion of an arbitrary direct sum is flat

Let $R$ be Noetherian, let $I\subset R$ be any ideal, and let $\Lambda$ be any set. Then
$$\widehat{\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}R}$$
is flat over $R$.

**Proof.** Put $A=\widehat R$. The quotient identities for Noetherian completion identify
$$\widehat{\bigoplus_\lambda R}
\cong\widehat{\bigoplus_\lambda A},$$
where the right completion is for $IA$. The ring $A$ is Noetherian, complete and flat over $R$. Flatness over $A$ therefore suffices. Replace $R$ by $A$.

The [completed-sum inclusion](#native-more-algebra-lemma-ui-completion-direct-sum-into-product) is universally injective:
$$\widehat{\bigoplus_\lambda R}
\ \hookrightarrow\ \prod_\lambda R.$$
The product is flat because a Noetherian ring is coherent and the [coherence criterion for products](#native-algebra-proposition-characterize-coherent) makes every product of copies of $R$ flat. A [universally injective submodule of a flat module is flat](#native-algebra-lemma-ui-flat-domain). These two facts prove the assertion, with no restriction on the size of $\Lambda$.

There is also a direct equational proof in Henselian local rings, Lemma 6.2. In the description by coefficient families tending to zero, a finite relation has columns in a finite syzygy module. Artin–Rees writes these columns using its generators with coefficients still tending to zero. Those coefficient families trivialize the relation in the completed sum, proving flatness by the equational criterion. This proof has the same arbitrary-rank scope. ∎

#### Lemma. Formal étaleness and adic smoothness of henselizations

For a local ring $R$, the three maps
$$R\longrightarrow R^h,\qquad
R^h\longrightarrow R^{sh},\qquad
R\longrightarrow R^{sh}$$
are formally étale. Each is also formally smooth when its target is given its maximal-ideal topology.

**Proof.** The ordinary and strict pointed-neighborhood constructions write these maps as filtered colimits of étale algebras. For the middle map, one may use the marked finite étale extensions of the henselian ring $R^h$; their residue fields run through the finite subextensions of the chosen separable closure. The constructions and their universal properties are in Henselian local rings, Sections 4–5.

Étale algebras are formally étale. Given a square-zero lifting problem for such a colimit, lift its map on each stage. Existence comes from formal étaleness of the stages, and uniqueness makes their lifts compatible with every transition. The universal property of the colimit gives the unique lift. This is the [formal-étale colimit lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-colimit-formally-etale).

In particular the three maps are algebraically formally smooth. A continuous map from one of these targets to a square-zero quotient kills some power $\mathfrak n^k$ of its maximal ideal modulo the square-zero ideal. Any algebraic lift then kills $\mathfrak n^{2k}$, hence is continuous. Thus [algebraic-to-adic formal smoothness](#native-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth) gives the second assertion. No Noetherian hypothesis is used. ∎

#### Lemma. Replacing ideal generators without changing regularity

Let $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ in a ring $R$. If $I$ has a quasi-regular, $H_1$-regular, or Koszul-regular generating list of length $r$, respectively, then $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ has the same property.

**Proof.** Start with a quasi-regular generating list $g_1,\ldots,g_r$. It identifies $I/I^2$ with $(R/I)^r$ and makes the canonical maps
$$\operatorname{Sym}_{R/I}^n(I/I^2)\longrightarrow I^n/I^{n+1}$$
isomorphisms. The classes of the $f_i$ give a surjection $(R/I)^r\to I/I^2$. After the first identification this is a surjective square matrix. It has a right inverse because its target is free; taking determinants proves its determinant a unit, so it is invertible. Hence the $f_i$ also give a basis, and the displayed intrinsic graded maps prove their quasi-regularity.

Write $g_j=\sum_i a_{ij}f_i$ and put $\Delta=\det(a_{ij})$. Both sets of classes are bases of $I/I^2$, so $\Delta$ is invertible modulo $I$. On degree-one generators, the map
$$e_j^{\,g}\longmapsto\sum_i a_{ij}e_i^{\,f}$$
extends by exterior powers to a chain map $K_\bullet(g)\to K_\bullet(f)$: applying the differential gives exactly the chosen expression for $g_j$. It becomes an isomorphism after inverting $\Delta$.

Koszul homology is killed by $I$, since exterior multiplication by $e_i$ is a homotopy for multiplication by the corresponding generator. Thus $\Delta$, being invertible modulo $I$, already acts invertibly on this homology. The map on homology is consequently an isomorphism before localization as well.

An $H_1$-regular list is [quasi-regular](#native-more-algebra-lemma-h1-regular-quasi-regular), and a Koszul-regular list is $H_1$-regular. Applying the preceding comparison to either kind of list $g$ transfers the required homology vanishing to $f$. This proves all three assertions. ∎

#### Lemma. Removing a Koszul-regular initial segment

Suppose both $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ and $f_1,\ldots,f_n,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ are Koszul-regular in $A$. Then the images of the $g_j$ are Koszul-regular in $A/(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$.

**Proof.** Put $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$. The augmented complex $K_\bullet(A,f)\to A/I$ is a finite free resolution. The exterior decomposition for a direct sum identifies
$$K_\bullet(A,f,g)
=\operatorname{Tot}\bigl(K_\bullet(A,f)\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g)\bigr).$$
On a pure tensor in degrees $p,q$, the differential is $d\otimes1+(-1)^p1\otimes d$, which is the Koszul differential for the concatenated list.

Tensor the augmentation $K_\bullet(A,f)\to A/I$ with this bounded free complex $K_\bullet(A,g)$. The resulting total-complex map is a quasi-isomorphism. To see this directly, its cone is the total complex of a bounded double complex whose columns are exact: each column is the acyclic augmentation cone tensored with a finite free module. Filter the total complex by the degree in $K_\bullet(A,g)$. The successive quotients are shifts of these exact columns; induction through the finite filtration proves the total cone acyclic. Hence
$$K_\bullet(A,f,g)\ \simeq\
(A/I)\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g)
=K_\bullet(A/I,\bar g).$$
The left complex has no positive homology by hypothesis, and the right complex therefore has none either. Empty initial or final lists are covered by the same argument. ∎

#### Lemma. Successive injectivity gives Koszul exactness

*Source credit:* FAC, Chapter III, §3, no. 62, Proposition 1, pp. 254–255; §4, no. 69, Lemma 1, p. 262; §5, no. 75, proof of Theorem 3, pp. 269–270.

Let $M$ be any module over a ring $R$. If multiplication by $f_i$ is injective on $M/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})M$ for each $i$, then $K_\bullet(R,f_1,\ldots,f_r)\otimes_RM$ has zero homology in every positive degree. No nonvanishing condition on the final quotient is needed. In particular every module-regular sequence, and every ring-regular sequence, is Koszul-regular.

**Proof.** For an empty list there are no positive terms. For one element the assertion is precisely injectivity of its multiplication map. For a longer list, multiplication by $f_1$ gives a termwise injective map on $K_\bullet(R,f_2,\ldots,f_r)\otimes_RM$. Its cokernel is
$$K_\bullet(R/(f_1),\bar f_2,\ldots,\bar f_r)
\otimes_{R/(f_1)}(M/f_1M).$$
The mapping cone of that injective map is quasi-isomorphic to its cokernel: the kernel of the natural cone-to-cokernel map is the contractible cone of the identity on the source. The cone itself is the Koszul complex of the whole list, after the usual exterior decomposition and degree signs. The hypotheses descend to the shorter list acting on $M/f_1M$, so induction makes the cokernel complex acyclic in positive degrees. The same holds for the original complex. ∎

In no. 62 the required hypothesis is exactly successive injectivity, applied there to $t_0^k,\ldots,t_r^k$. The positive cochain Koszul exactness used in that text follows from this argument with the corresponding degree convention; it identifies the degree-zero cocycles and removes the intermediate cohomology.

No. 69 specializes to powers of polynomial variables. For $k\geq1$ those powers form a regular sequence; for $k=0$ they are units, so a one-variable contraction makes the Koszul complex contractible. Removing its final ring term gives the indicated graded resolution of the ideal generated by the powers.

No. 75 uses the exterior basis indexed by increasing tuples for the equations of a nonsingular subvariety. Its augmented complex resolves the local quotient. The printed general differential has sign $(-1)^j$, while its degree-one formula sends $e\langle i\rangle$ to $f_i$. To agree with that formula, the general differential is
$$d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_q})
=\sum_{j=1}^q(-1)^{j+1}f_{i_j}
\,e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_j}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_q}.$$
If every positive differential instead receives the opposite sign, multiplication by $(-1)^q$ in homological degree $q$ gives a chain isomorphism. Thus the printed inconsistency is corrected without changing the exactness conclusion.

#### Lemma. The first Koszul homology has a base-change surjection

Let $A\to B$, let $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subset B$, and suppose $B/J$ is $A$-flat. For any map $A\to A'$, put $B'=B\otimes_AA'$ and let $f'_i$ be the images. The canonical map
$$H_1(K_\bullet(B,f))\otimes_AA'
\longrightarrow H_1(K_\bullet(B',f'))$$
is surjective.

**Proof.** Let $Z=\ker(B^r\xrightarrow{(f_i)}B)$ and $H=H_1(K_\bullet(B,f))$. Split the low-degree Koszul complex into
$$\begin{gathered}
0\to J\to B\to B/J\to0,\\
0\to Z\to B^r\to J\to0,\\
\bigwedge^2 B^r\to Z\to H\to0.
\end{gathered}$$
After tensoring over $A$, the first sequence remains short exact because its quotient is flat. Thus $J\otimes_AA'$ injects into $B'$ with image $J'$. Right exactness of the second sequence makes
$$Z\otimes_AA'\longrightarrow
\ker((B')^r\longrightarrow B')$$
surjective. The third sequence identifies $H\otimes_AA'$ with the cokernel of the map from $(\bigwedge^2B^r)\otimes_AA'$. Exterior powers of this finite free $B$-module commute with the indicated base change; its image is exactly the Koszul boundary image in the target kernel. Passing to cokernels yields the claimed surjection. Neither flatness of $B$ over $A$ nor flatness of $A'$ over $A$ was used. ∎

#### Lemma. Positive Koszul exactness includes degree one

An $M$-Koszul-regular list is $M$-$H_1$-regular. Taking $M=R$ gives the ring version.

**Proof.** The first property asks for zero homology in every positive degree; the second asks only for degree one. ∎

#### Lemma. Vanishing of first Koszul homology implies quasi-regularity

For an arbitrary $R$-module $M$, an $M$-$H_1$-regular list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ is $M$-quasi-regular.

**Proof.** Write $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$. The assertion is that, for every $n\geq0$, the monomial map
$$\bigoplus_{\substack{\nu\in\mathbf N^r\\|\nu|=n}}M/JM
\longrightarrow J^nM/J^{n+1}M,\qquad
(\bar m_\nu)\longmapsto\sum_\nu m_\nu f^\nu$$
is an isomorphism. It is always surjective. The cases $r=0$ and $n=0$ are immediate.

The hypothesis gives exactness of
$$\bigwedge^2R^r\otimes_RM
\longrightarrow R^r\otimes_RM
\longrightarrow JM\longrightarrow0,$$
where $(e_i\wedge e_j)\otimes m$ maps to $(f_ie_j-f_je_i)\otimes m$. Tensor with $R/J$. The first map becomes zero, giving
$$JM/J^2M\cong(M/JM)^r.$$
This proves the degree-one assertion. The right side is a direct sum of copies of $M/JM$; no freeness of $M/JM$ is asserted.

For $n\geq2$, suppose $\xi=\sum_{|\nu|=n}m_\nu f^\nu$ belongs to $J^{n+1}M$. First consider the coefficient $m_*=m_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}$. Collect all other monomials according to one of the factors $f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1}$, obtaining
$$\xi=\sum_{i<r}b_if_i+m_*f_r^n.$$
Because $\xi\in J^{n+1}M$, it also admits a decomposition
$$\xi=\sum_{i\leq j<r}c_{ij}f_if_j
+\sum_{i<r}c'_if_if_r^n+c''f_r^{n+1}.$$
Indeed, a degree-$(n+1)$ monomial either has at least two factors from the first $r-1$ entries, has exactly one, or has none; the remaining factors are absorbed into the module coefficients. Subtracting the two expressions gives a relation among
$$f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},f_r^n$$
whose last coefficient is $m_*-c''f_r$. This list is $M$-$H_1$-regular by the [multiplication lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-mult-koszul-regular), applied repeatedly to the last entry. Every relation is therefore a Koszul boundary. Its last coordinate lies in $\sum_{i<r}f_iM$, so $m_*\in JM$. This also covers $r=1$, when the indicated sum is zero.

To obtain every coefficient, pass to the faithfully flat Laurent polynomial ring
$$T=R[X_1,\ldots,X_r,X_r^{-1}].$$
Flat base change preserves the exact sequence defining first-homology vanishing. The invertible change of generators
$$g_i=f_i-\frac{X_i}{X_r}f_r\quad(i<r),
\qquad g_r=\frac{f_r}{X_r}$$
therefore gives another $M\otimes_RT$-$H_1$-regular list generating $JT$. Express $\xi$ through $f_i=g_i+X_ig_r$ for $i<r$ and $f_r=X_rg_r$. Its coefficient of $g_r^n$ is
$$\sum_{|\nu|=n}m_\nu X^\nu.$$
The case just proved puts this element in $J(M\otimes_RT)$. The Laurent monomials form an $R$-basis of $T$, and the displayed monomials are distinct. After passage to $(M/JM)\otimes_RT$, coefficient uniqueness makes every $\bar m_\nu$ zero. Thus every $m_\nu\in JM$, proving injectivity of the monomial map in degree $n$. ∎

#### Lemma. Completion does not change local dimension

For a Noetherian local ring $(A,\mathfrak m)$,
$$\dim A=\dim\widehat A.$$

**Proof.** The completion has maximal ideal $\widehat{\mathfrak m}=\mathfrak m\widehat A$, the same residue field as $A$, and compatible quotient isomorphisms
$$A/\mathfrak m^n\cong\widehat A/\widehat{\mathfrak m}^{\,n}
\qquad(n\geq1).$$
The [restriction-of-scalars length formula](#native-algebra-lemma-pushdown-module), with its residue degree equal to one, gives equality of their lengths over $A$ and $\widehat A$, respectively. Their local Hilbert functions thus coincide. The [dimension-growth theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-dimension) identifies the degree of each eventual length polynomial with the dimension of the corresponding ring, proving the equality.

Alternatively, $A\to\widehat A$ is flat and local, and its closed fibre is the common residue field. The [local flat dimension formula](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-base-fibre-equals-total) gives the dimension of the target as $\dim A$ plus the fibre dimension zero. ∎

#### Lemma. Coefficient subfields of power-series fraction fields

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, with $p$-basis $(b_i)_{i\in I}$. For $n,m\geq0$, set
$$A=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]][Y_1,\ldots,Y_m],
\qquad K=\operatorname{Frac}(A).$$
For each finite subset $J\subset I$, define
$$k_J=k^p(b_i:i\notin J),\qquad
A_J=k_J[[X_1^p,\ldots,X_n^p]][Y_1^p,\ldots,Y_m^p],
\qquad K_J=\operatorname{Frac}(A_J).$$
Then $A$ is finite over $A_J$, and these fields satisfy
$$K^p\subset K_J,\qquad
\bigcap_JK_J=K^p,\qquad
K_{J\cup J'}\subset K_J\cap K_{J'}.$$
Thus they have all the properties required in the [field-intersection lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-intersection-subfields).

**Proof.** The bounded-exponent monomials in the $b_j$, $j\in J$, form a basis of $k$ over $k_J$, of size $p^{|J|}$. One can check this directly in the full $p$-basis expansion: the span of the monomials supported outside $J$ is already the field $k_J$, and grouping exponents in and outside $J$ proves both spanning and independence.

An explicit $A_J$-basis of $A$ is
$$\left\{
\prod_{j\in J}b_j^{e_j}\prod_{\nu=1}^nX_\nu^{a_\nu}
\prod_{\mu=1}^mY_\mu^{c_\mu}:
0\leq e_j,a_\nu,c_\mu<p
\right\}.$$
Expand each coefficient in the finite $k_J$-basis and group all variable exponents modulo $p$. This gives the asserted expansion even for formal series, and uniqueness follows coefficient by coefficient. Equivalently, finiteness of the coefficient extension and the [finite-completion theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-after-completion) first give finiteness for the formal-series rings; adjoining the polynomial variables and their $p$th powers gives the displayed finite extension.

Frobenius sends every element of $A$ into $A_J$, so it sends every fraction into $K_J$. This remains true for formal series because each coefficient of a sum or product involves only finitely many terms. The refinement inclusion follows directly from $k_{J\cup J'}\subset k_J\cap k_{J'}$.

It remains to compute the intersection. Write any $z\in K$ as $f/g^p$, with $f,g\in A$ and $g\ne0$; for an initial fraction $a/b$, use $f=ab^{p-1}$ and $g=b$. Suppose $z$ belongs to every $K_J$, and fix $J$. Choose $a,c\in A_J$, $c\ne0$, with $z=a/c=ac^{p-1}/c^p$. Then
$$c^pf=ac^{p-1}g^p\in A_J.$$
Every $A_J$-derivation of $A$ kills $c^p$ and the right side, so it kills $f$, since $A$ is a domain. The formal partial derivatives in the $X_\nu$ and the ordinary partial derivatives in the $Y_\mu$ are such derivations. Their vanishing on $f$ means that all its exponents are multiples of $p$.

For each $j\in J$, the coordinate derivation on $k$ over $k_J$ extends coefficientwise to $A$, fixing the variables. It is a derivation on formal series by the finite coefficient formula for products, and it is zero on $A_J$. The [constant-field test for a p-basis](#native-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis) says that their common kernel in $k$ is $k_J$. Hence every coefficient of $f$ belongs to $k_J$, and $f\in A_J$.

Finally $\bigcap_Jk_J=k^p$. Indeed an element of $k$ has a unique finite expansion in the full $p$-basis monomials; membership in $k_{\{j\}}$ removes every monomial with positive $j$th exponent. Doing this for all $j$ leaves only the constant coefficient in $k^p$. It follows that
$$\bigcap_J A_J=A^p.$$
Here an element with all coefficients in $k^p$ and all exponents divisible by $p$ has a $p$th root obtained coefficientwise, with divided exponents; the polynomial variables still have finite support. We conclude that $f=h^p$ for some $h\in A$, and $z=(h/g)^p$. This proves the remaining inclusion. ∎

#### Lemma. Noetherian fibres of ind-étale algebras

Suppose $B$ is a filtered colimit of étale algebras over a ring $A$, and $B$ is Noetherian. For every $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ there are finitely many primes $\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_r$ of $B$ above $\mathfrak p$, and the canonical residue maps give
$$B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong
\prod_{i=1}^r\kappa(\mathfrak q_i).$$
Each factor is an algebraic separable extension of $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. An empty fibre is allowed, with the empty product interpreted as the zero ring.

**Proof.** Put $F=B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. This is a localization of $B/\mathfrak pB$, hence Noetherian. Writing $B=\operatorname{colim}_\lambda B_\lambda$ expresses $F$ as the filtered colimit of the étale $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-algebras $F_\lambda=B_\lambda\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. Each $F_\lambda$ is a finite product of finite separable field extensions, by Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Section 7, Theorem 7.2, whose complete proof includes the local field calculation and finite product decomposition.

Reducedness passes to this colimit without any injectivity assumption on its transitions. A nilpotent element is represented at one stage, and its vanishing power becomes zero at a later stage. That later ring is reduced, so the element itself becomes zero there.

There are also no strict inclusions between primes of $F$. If $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak q'$ existed, an element of their difference would be represented at a stage. Contracting both primes to that stage would give distinct comparable primes of a product of fields, which is impossible. Thus $F$ is reduced and has dimension zero. The [Noetherian dimension-zero theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-dimension-zero-ring) makes it Artinian, and its finite local decomposition is a product of fields. The factors are its residue fields, equivalently the $\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)$ for primes of $B$ over $\mathfrak p$.

For any such factor, an element is represented by an element of some $F_\lambda$: the factor is $F/\mathfrak q$ because $\mathfrak q$ is maximal. The map from $F_\lambda$ to this field factors through one of its finite separable field factors. Thus every element is algebraic and separable over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, proving the final assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Reducedness and henselization

For any local ring $R$, the following three conditions are equivalent:
$R$ is reduced; its henselization $R^h$ is reduced; its strict henselization $R^{sh}$ is reduced.

**Proof.** The maps $R\to R^h\to R^{sh}$ are faithfully flat. In particular they are injective, so reducedness of either target implies reducedness of the preceding rings; this is also the [faithfully flat descent argument](#native-algebra-lemma-descent-reduced).

If $R$ is reduced, every étale $R$-algebra is reduced by [ascent of reducedness under smooth maps](#native-algebra-lemma-reduced-goes-up). Both henselizations are filtered colimits of such algebras. The finite-witness argument from the preceding proof applies: a power vanishing in the colimit vanishes at some stage, where reducedness forces the original element to vanish. Both colimits are therefore reduced. ∎

#### Proposition. Flatness and a formally smooth closed fibre

Let $A\to B$ be a local map of Noetherian local rings, let $k=A/\mathfrak m_A$, and put $\bar B=B/\mathfrak m_AB$. The following are equivalent:

1. $B$ is flat over $A$ and $\bar B$ is geometrically regular over $k$.
2. $B$ is flat over $A$ and $k\to\bar B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $\bar B$.
3. $A\to B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $B$.

**Proof.** The [field theorem](#native-more-algebra-theorem-regular-fs) identifies (1) with (2). Condition (3) implies flatness by the [adic flatness lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth-flat), and base change to $k$ gives the other assertion of (2).

Assume (2). We may complete both local rings. Indeed, the formal-smoothness comparison with completions applies to the closed fibre and to the desired conclusion. Flatness also passes to $\widehat A\to\widehat B$: first $\widehat B$ is flat over $A$, and then every quotient $\widehat B/\mathfrak m_A^n\widehat B$ is flat over $A/\mathfrak m_A^n=\widehat A/\mathfrak m_A^n\widehat A$. The [all-powers flatness criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-module-powers) gives the assertion over $\widehat A$. The closed fibre of the completed map is the completion of $\bar B$. Hence assume $A$ and $B$ complete.

Choose [compatible regular coefficient presentations](#native-more-algebra-lemma-embed-map-noetherian-complete-local-rings)
$$\begin{array}{ccc}R&\longrightarrow&S\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\ A&\longrightarrow&B.\end{array}$$
The vertical maps are surjective. Choose parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ of $R$, with $t_1=p$ in positive residue characteristic. They form part of a parameter system in $S$, and $\bar S=S/\mathfrak m_RS$ is regular. The ring $\bar B$ is also regular. By the [regular quotient theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-regular-quotient-regular), the kernel of $\bar S\to\bar B$ is generated by a parameter subsequence $\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_r$.

Lift the $\bar x_i$ into $\ker(S\to B)$ and quotient $S$ by these lifts. The list $t_1,\ldots,t_d,x_1,\ldots,x_r$ is part of a regular system, so the [parameter-substitution lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-quotient-power-series-ring-over-cohen) shows that the new $S$ is still a power-series ring over a field or Cohen ring. The $t_i$ remain part of its parameters, $R\to S$ stays flat, and now $\bar S=\bar B$.

Set $I=\ker(R\to A)$. The surjection $S/IS\to B$ is a closed-fibre isomorphism and both rings are flat over $A$. It is injective by the [fibrewise injectivity criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-mod-injective). Equivalently, if $H$ is its kernel, tensor the exact sequence with $k$: flatness of $B$ gives $H/\mathfrak m_AH=0$. The ideal $H$ is finite over the Noetherian local ring $S/IS$, so Nakayama gives $H=0$. We have proved
$$B=S\otimes_R A.$$
It is enough to prove formal smoothness of $R\to S$.

Write $K=S/\mathfrak m_S$. Extend the $t_i$ to parameters by $y_1,\ldots,y_m$. Parameter substitution presents $S$ as
$$K[[t_1,\ldots,t_d,y_1,\ldots,y_m]]$$
in residue characteristic zero, or as
$$\Lambda[[t_2,\ldots,t_d,y_1,\ldots,y_m]]$$
over a Cohen ring with residue field $K$ in positive residue characteristic, where $t_1=p$.

Take a discrete square-zero test $T\to T/J$, a map $\varphi\colon R\to T$, and a compatible continuous $\bar\psi\colon S\to T/J$. A power of $\mathfrak m_S$ kills $J$. Filtering $J$ by its powers under this action, exactly as in the field theorem, reduces the lifting problem to $\mathfrak m_SJ=0$. Thus $J$ is a $K$-vector space.

[Formal smoothness over the prime ring](#native-more-algebra-lemma-power-series-ring-over-cohen-fs) first gives a continuous lift $\psi\colon S\to T$ over $\mathbf Q$ or $\mathbf Z$, as appropriate. Keep its coefficient map and the images of the $y_i$, but replace the images of the power-series variables $t_i$ by $\varphi(t_i)$. Their reductions agree with the old ones. Their generated ideal is still nilpotent in $T$, so power-series evaluation defines a continuous lift after this replacement. In the Cohen case the equality on $t_1=p$ is automatic.

The difference $D=\psi|_R-\varphi$ is a derivation into $J$, zero on every $t_i$. Since $\mathfrak m_RJ=0$, it vanishes on all of $\mathfrak m_R$ and factors through a derivation of $k$. It therefore corresponds to a $K$-linear map
$$\Omega_{k/\mathbf Z}\otimes_k K\longrightarrow J.$$
The map
$$\Omega_{k/\mathbf Z}\otimes_k K
\longrightarrow\Omega_{\bar S/\mathbf Z}\otimes_{\bar S}K$$
is injective. In characteristic $p$ this is condition (5) of the field theorem, since $\bar S/k$ is formally smooth. In characteristic zero its composite to $\Omega_{K/\mathbf Z}$ is injective by separability of $K/k$, so the displayed map itself is injective.

Extend the linear functional to the larger vector space and compose with $S\to\bar S$ and the universal differential. This gives a derivation $D'\colon S\to J$ restricting to $D$ on $R$. The map $\psi-D'$ is multiplicative because $J^2=0$ and $D'$ satisfies Leibniz; it preserves $1$, has the correct reduction, and is an $R$-map. Also $D'(\mathfrak m_S^2)=0$, proving continuity of the correction. This solves each filtered lifting step and proves formal smoothness of $R\to S$. Base change gives (3). ∎

#### Lemma. Base change of adic formal smoothness

Suppose $R\to S$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak n$-adic topology of $S$. For any ring map $R\to R'$, the map
$$R'\longrightarrow S'=S\otimes_R R'$$
is formally smooth for the topology defined by $\mathfrak n'=\mathfrak nS'$.

**Proof.** Restrict a continuous square-zero test for $S'/R'$ along $S\to S'$. Formal smoothness gives an $R$-algebra lift $S\to T$. Together with the specified $R'\to T$, tensor universality gives the required $R'$-algebra lift $S'\to T$. If the first lift kills $\mathfrak n^a$, the tensor lift kills $(\mathfrak nS')^a$. Thus the constructed lift is continuous. ∎

#### Remark. Lifting the equations from the closed fibre

Suppose $A\to A'\to B$ are local maps of Noetherian complete local rings, and $A\to A'$ identifies their residue fields with $k$. Assume $B/\mathfrak m_{A'}B$ is formally smooth over $k$ for its maximal-ideal topology. There is a commutative square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}C&\longrightarrow&B\\
\uparrow&&\uparrow\\ A&\longrightarrow&A'\end{array}$$
in which $C$ is Noetherian complete local, $A\to C$ is formally smooth for its maximal-ideal topology, and the induced map
$$C/\mathfrak m_AC\longrightarrow B/\mathfrak m_{A'}B$$
is an isomorphism.

Let $D=C\otimes_A A'$ and let $E=C\widehat\otimes_A A'$ be its completion along $I=\mathfrak m_{A'}D$. Then $E$ is Noetherian complete local and flat over $A'$. The square has the following additional properties:

1. The induced map $E\to B$ is surjective.
2. If $A\to A'$ is surjective, then $C\to B$ is surjective.
3. If $A'$ is finite over $A$, then $B$ is finite over $C$.
4. If $B$ is flat over $A'$, then $E\to B$ is an isomorphism.

**Proof.** The [closed-fibre lifting lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-lift-fs) constructs $A\to C$. Its prescribed fibre map lifts to $C\to B$ by [continuous lifting](#native-more-algebra-lemma-lift-continuous), applied to the closed ideal $\mathfrak m_{A'}B\subset\mathfrak m_B$. The lift is local because its residue map is the specified isomorphism.

The ideal $I$ is finitely generated, and $D/I=C/\mathfrak m_AC$ is Noetherian. The [Noetherian completion theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-completion-noetherian) and the [ideal-power completion identities](#native-algebra-lemma-completion-complete) give
$$E/I^nE=C\otimes_A(A'/\mathfrak m_{A'}^n)=:E_n.$$
Each $A'/\mathfrak m_{A'}^n$ has finite length with factors $k$, and is therefore finite over $A$. Thus $E_n$ is finite over $C$. It is a complete local ring: modulo $\mathfrak m_C$ it is a local Artinian algebra with residue field $C/\mathfrak m_C$, since the finite filtration of $A'/\mathfrak m_{A'}^n$ has residue field $k$. Completeness of finite modules over $C$ and cofinality of the corresponding maximal-ideal powers give the assertion.

The ideal $IE$ lies in the Jacobson radical of the $I$-adically complete ring $E$, so locality of $E/IE$ makes $E$ local. It is also complete for its maximal ideal. To check this explicitly, a compatible sequence modulo its maximal-ideal powers determines an element of every $E_n$, because each $E_n$ is already complete in that topology. These elements are compatible in $n$, hence come from $E=\varprojlim E_n$. They represent the original sequence: for a fixed maximal-ideal power, choose $n$ at least that large and use $I^nE$ contained in that power. Injectivity follows from Krull intersection in the Noetherian local ring $E$.

The ring $C$ is flat over $A$ by adic formal smoothness. Hence $E_n$ is flat over $A'/\mathfrak m_{A'}^n$ for every $n$. The [all-powers criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-module-powers) applied to the Noetherian local target $E$ proves flatness over $A'$.

The map $D\to B$ extends to $E\to B$, since a Noetherian complete local ring is complete along every ideal contained in its maximal ideal. Modulo $\mathfrak m_{A'}^n$, the map to $B/\mathfrak m_{A'}^nB$ is surjective: its cokernel has zero reduction modulo the nilpotent ideal generated by $\mathfrak m_{A'}$, and nilpotent Nakayama applies without a finiteness assumption. In particular, $E/IE\to B/\mathfrak m_{A'}B$ is the chosen isomorphism. It follows that the residue fields of $E$ and $B$ agree and that $\mathfrak m_EB=\mathfrak m_B$. Successively lift a residue and then each homogeneous maximal-ideal error, using finitely many generators of $\mathfrak m_E$. The corrections in $\mathfrak m_E^n$ converge in $E$ and map to the prescribed element of $B$. This proves (1), without assuming that inverse limits preserve arbitrary surjections.

If $A\to A'$ is surjective, $D$ is a quotient of $C$, hence complete along $I$; thus $C\to E\to B$ is surjective. If $A'$ is finite over $A$, $D$ is a finite $C$-module and already complete along the image of $\mathfrak m_A$. The $\mathfrak m_A$- and $\mathfrak m_{A'}$-adic topologies on $A'$ are cofinal, since $A'$ is finite local over $A$. Consequently $D=E$, and the surjection in (1) proves (3).

Finally let $H=\ker(E\to B)$ and assume $B$ flat over $A'$. Tensoring $0\to H\to E\to B\to0$ with $k$ gives $H/\mathfrak m_{A'}H=0$, because the fibre map is an isomorphism. The ideal $H$ is finite over $E$, and $\mathfrak m_{A'}E\subset\mathfrak m_E$, so Nakayama gives $H=0$. This is also the [fibrewise injectivity criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-mod-injective), and proves (4). ∎

#### Lemma. Descent along a split module extension

Let $R\to R'$ identify $R$ with an $R$-module direct summand of $R'$. For an $R$-algebra $S$ and an ideal $\mathfrak n\subset S$, put
$$S'=S\otimes_R R',\qquad\mathfrak n'=\mathfrak nS'.$$
Continuous square-zero lifting for $S'/R'$ with its $\mathfrak n'$-adic topology implies the corresponding formal smoothness of $S/R$ with its $\mathfrak n$-adic topology.

**Proof.** Take a discrete square-zero test $S\to T/J$ over $R$. Put $T'=T\otimes_R R'$ and let $J'$ be the image of $J\otimes_R R'$ in $T'$. This ideal has square zero, and $T'/J'=(T/J)\otimes_R R'$. The base-changed test has a continuous lift $S'\to T'$.

Choose an $R$-module decomposition $R'=R\oplus M$. It gives
$$T'=T\oplus(T\otimes_R M),\qquad
J'=J\oplus J'',\qquad
J''=\operatorname{im}(J\otimes_R M\to T\otimes_R M).$$
The composite $S\to S'\to T'$ reduces to the original map into the embedded copy of $T/J$. Its image therefore lies in
$$T+J'=T\oplus J''.$$
Although $M$ need not be an ideal of $R'$, the submodule $J''$ is an ideal of this last subring: it is stable under $T$, and its products with $J'$ vanish because $(J')^2=0$. Quotienting by $J''$ gives a ring map $S\to T$ that solves the original test. It is continuous, since the lift from $S'$ kills a power of $\mathfrak n'$ and restriction followed by quotient kills the corresponding power of $\mathfrak n$. ∎

#### Lemma. Extending a derivation across a formally smooth map

Let $A\to B$ be a local map of Noetherian local rings, with $B$ complete. If $A\to B$ is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $B$, every derivation $D\colon A\to A$ extends to a derivation $D'\colon B\to B$.

**Proof.** Give $T=B[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$ its complete local topology and define its $A$-algebra structure by
$$a\longmapsto a+\varepsilon D(a),$$
where both terms are read in $B$. This is a ring map by Leibniz. It is local and continuous for the maximal-ideal topologies: the maximal ideal of $T$ is $\mathfrak m_B+\varepsilon B$, and the image of $\mathfrak m_A$ lies there.

The quotient $T/(\varepsilon)$ is $B$. Its identity map is continuous, the ideal $(\varepsilon)$ is closed and square-zero, and $T$ is complete because it is finite over $B$. The [continuous lifting theorem](#native-more-algebra-lemma-lift-continuous) provides an $A$-algebra map $\phi\colon B\to T$ reducing to the identity. Write $\phi(b)=b+\varepsilon D'(b)$. Comparing constant and $\varepsilon$ coefficients proves additivity, Leibniz and $D'|_A=D$, as required. ∎

#### Definition. Formal smoothness for linearly topologized rings

Let $R\to S$ be a continuous homomorphism of linearly topologized rings. It is **formally smooth** if every commutative square of continuous ring maps
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
R&\longrightarrow&T\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
S&\longrightarrow&T/J
\end{array}$$
with $T$ discrete and $J^2=0$ admits a continuous diagonal lift $S\to T$, compatible with both given maps. Base rings in an ideal-adic lifting assertion are given the discrete topology unless a different base topology is specified.

#### Lemma. Continuity for ideal-adic topologies

Give $R$ the $I$-adic topology and $S$ the $J$-adic topology. A ring map $\phi\colon R\to S$ is continuous exactly when
$$\phi(I^a)\subset J$$
for some integer $a\geq1$.

**Proof.** Continuity at zero gives this condition by taking the neighborhood $J$. Conversely, the condition implies $\phi(I^{ab})\subset J^b$ for every $b\geq1$. These are neighborhood bases at zero; translation gives continuity at all points. ∎

#### Lemma. The completed sum embeds universally into the product

Let $R$ be Noetherian and complete for an ideal $I$, and let $\Lambda$ be any set. The natural map
$$C=\widehat{\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}R}
\longrightarrow P=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}R$$
stays injective after tensoring with any $R$-module.

**Proof.** A compatible element of the quotients $\bigoplus_\lambda R/I^n$ specifies a unique family $(c_\lambda)\in P$, by completeness in each coordinate. At each fixed $n$, only finitely many coordinates are nonzero modulo $I^n$. Conversely, every family with this property gives such a compatible element. Thus
$$C=\{(c_\lambda)\in P:
\text{ for each }n,\ c_\lambda\in I^n
\text{ outside a finite set}\},$$
and the natural map is an inclusion.

First tensor with a finite module $Q$. Choose a finite presentation
$$R^s\xrightarrow{A}R^t\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0,$$
which exists because $R$ is Noetherian. Put $L=\operatorname{im}A\subset R^t$. Artin–Rees gives $c\geq0$ such that
$$L\cap I^{n+c}R^t\subseteq I^nL
=A(I^nR^s)\qquad(n\geq0).$$
Consider the canonical diagram with right-exact rows:
$$\begin{array}{ccccc}
C^s&\xrightarrow{A}&C^t&\longrightarrow&Q\otimes_RC\longrightarrow0\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
P^s&\xrightarrow{A}&P^t&\longrightarrow&Q\otimes_RP\longrightarrow0 .
\end{array}$$
All vertical maps are induced by $C\subseteq P$, and the two matrices have the same entries.

Take an element in the kernel of the right vertical map and lift it to $v\in C^t$. Write its coordinate columns as $v_\lambda\in R^t$. Applying the coordinate evaluations of $Q\otimes_RP$ shows that every $v_\lambda$ lies in $L$. These columns tend to zero in the finite-exception sense above.

We can lift the columns through $A$ while retaining that property. For a nonzero $v_\lambda$, choose the largest $n\geq0$ for which $v_\lambda\in I^{n+c}R^t$, if such $n$ exists. It is finite because $\bigcap_n I^nR^t=0$. The displayed inclusion supplies a lift $w_\lambda\in I^nR^s$. If no such $n$ exists, take any lift; if $v_\lambda=0$, choose the zero lift. For each fixed $n$, all but finitely many columns belong to $I^{n+c}R^t$, so these choices put all but finitely many $w_\lambda$ in $I^nR^s$. Consequently $(w_\lambda)$ defines $w\in C^s$ and $Aw=v$.

Right exactness of the upper row now makes the chosen element of $Q\otimes_RC$ zero. Thus the right vertical map is injective for every finite $Q$. Finally, any module is the directed union of its finite submodules. Tensor products commute with these colimits, and filtered colimits of module sequences are exact. Passing to the colimit preserves the proved injections and gives injectivity for every module. ∎

#### Lemma. Functoriality of the Koszul construction

Suppose $\varphi\colon E\to R$ and $\varphi'\colon E'\to R$ are module maps and $\psi\colon E\to E'$ satisfies $\varphi'\psi=\varphi$. The exterior powers of $\psi$ define a morphism of differential graded algebras
$$K_\bullet(\varphi)\longrightarrow K_\bullet(\varphi').$$

**Proof.** In degree $q$ the map sends $e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_q$ to $\psi(e_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge\psi(e_q)$. It preserves exterior products and the unit. In the differential of this image, the coefficient obtained by removing its $i$th factor is $\varphi'(\psi(e_i))=\varphi(e_i)$, with sign $(-1)^{i-1}$.
