Thus applying the differential before or after the map gives the same sum. No freeness assumption on either module is needed. ∎

#### Lemma. Koszul homology is killed by the defining ideal

For a finite list $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in R$, multiplication by each $f_j$ on $K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ is chain-homotopic to zero. Consequently every homology module of this complex is annihilated by $(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$.

**Proof.** If $e_j$ denotes the $j$th degree-one generator, define $h_j(a)=e_j\wedge a$. The product rule gives
$$d h_j(a)+h_jd(a)=f_ja.$$
Thus $h_j$ is the required degree-one homotopy. An element homotopic to zero acts as zero on homology; linear combinations show that the whole ideal acts as zero. This is the [abstract Koszul homotopy](#native-more-algebra-lemma-homotopy-koszul-abstract). ∎

#### Lemma. Joining two Koszul lists

For lists $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ and $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$ there is a natural isomorphism
$$K_\bullet(f,g)\cong
\operatorname{Tot}\bigl(K_\bullet(f)\otimes_RK_\bullet(g)\bigr).$$

**Proof.** Send the generators for the first list to $e_i\otimes1$ and those for the second to $1\otimes u_j$. The exterior direct-sum identity identifies their ordered wedge monomials with a basis on each side. In the tensor product the multiplication rule on homogeneous elements is
$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')
=(-1)^{\deg(b)\deg(a')}(a\wedge a')\otimes(b\wedge b'),$$
so this map respects all exterior relations, including squares of degree-one elements in characteristic two. The total differential is
$$d(a\otimes b)=da\otimes b+(-1)^{\deg(a)}a\otimes db.$$
It takes the first generators to $f_i$ and the second to $g_j$. Its product rule therefore agrees with the Koszul differential on every wedge monomial, proving the isomorphism. Empty lists give the degree-zero factor $R$ and cause no exception. ∎

#### Definition. The Koszul differential

For an $R$-linear map $\varphi\colon E\to R$, the Koszul complex has degree-$q$ term $\bigwedge^q_RE$, with $\bigwedge^0_RE=R$. Its multiplication is exterior multiplication, and its degree-minus-one differential is
$$d(e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_q)
=\sum_{i=1}^q(-1)^{i-1}\varphi(e_i)
e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat e_i\wedge\cdots\wedge e_q.$$
In degree zero the differential is zero. This is the unique graded derivation with $d(e)=\varphi(e)$ in degree one.

The formula is alternating and multilinear, so it is defined on the exterior power even when $E$ is not free. Applying it twice removes each pair of distinct factors in two orders with opposite signs; hence $d^2=0$. It satisfies
$$d(a\wedge b)=da\wedge b+(-1)^{\deg(a)}a\wedge db.$$
Thus the exterior algebra is a graded-commutative differential algebra. The notation $K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ means $E=R^r$ with its standard basis sent to the indicated elements.

#### Lemma. Appending a Koszul entry gives a cone

For $r\geq1$, set $C=K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})$. There is an isomorphism
$$K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\cong
\operatorname{Cone}(f_r\colon C\to C).$$

**Proof.** Use the homological cone convention
$$\operatorname{Cone}(u)_n=B_n\oplus A_{n-1},\qquad
d(b,a)=(d_Bb+u(a),-d_Aa)$$
for a chain map $u\colon A_\bullet\to B_\bullet$. If $e_r$ is the newly adjoined generator, send $(a,b)\in C_n\oplus C_{n-1}$ to $a+e_r\wedge b$. The exterior direct-sum decomposition makes this a degreewise isomorphism, and
$$d(a+e_r\wedge b)=da+f_rb-e_r\wedge db$$
proves compatibility with differentials. This also proves the case $r=1$, and is the free-module specialization of the [abstract cone identification](#native-more-algebra-lemma-cone-koszul-abstract). ∎

#### Lemma. Multiplying the last entry of a Koszul sequence

Fix a list $f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1}$ in $R$, two elements $f,g\in R$, and an $R$-module $M$.

1. If appending $f$ and appending $g$ each give an $M$-$H_1$-regular list, then appending $fg$ does too.
2. The same assertion holds for $M$-Koszul-regular lists.

**Proof.** Put $C=K_\bullet(R,f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})\otimes_RM$. Appending an element $a$ gives its multiplication cone. The short exact sequence from that cone to the shifted complex gives
$$H_i(C)\xrightarrow{a}H_i(C)
\longrightarrow H_i(K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},a)\otimes_RM)
\longrightarrow H_{i-1}(C)\xrightarrow{a}H_{i-1}(C).$$
Thus vanishing of the middle homology says exactly that multiplication by $a$ is surjective on $H_i(C)$ and injective on $H_{i-1}(C)$. If both $a=f$ and $a=g$ have these properties, their composite $fg$ has them as well. Use $i=1$ for (1), and all $i>0$ for (2).

Equivalently, the [multiplication comparison of Koszul complexes](#native-more-algebra-lemma-koszul-mult) gives the original exact segment from the homology for the list ending in $f$, through that ending in $fg$, to that ending in $g$. Vanishing of both outer terms gives the same conclusion. Repeated application permits replacing any last entry by a positive power. ∎

#### Lemma. Flat scalar extension preserves Koszul regularity

Let $\rho\colon R\to S$ be flat, let $M$ be any $R$-module, and set $N=M\otimes_RS$. For every finite list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$:

1. $M$-$H_1$-regularity of the list implies $N$-$H_1$-regularity of $\rho(f_1),\ldots,\rho(f_r)$.
2. $M$-Koszul-regularity implies $N$-Koszul-regularity of the image list.

**Proof.** Base extension identifies the exterior generators and their differentials, giving
$$\bigl(K_\bullet(R,f)\otimes_RM\bigr)\otimes_RS
\cong K_\bullet(S,\rho(f))\otimes_SN.$$
Tensoring with a flat module preserves the kernels, images and quotients defining homology. Consequently the $i$th homology on the right is $H_i(K_\bullet(R,f)\otimes_RM)\otimes_RS$. Vanishing for $i=1$ gives the first assertion, and vanishing for every $i>0$ gives the second. There is no finiteness assumption on $M$. ∎

#### Lemma. An invertible change of generators

Let $X=(x_{ij})\in\operatorname{GL}_r(R)$ and set $g_i=\sum_jx_{ij}f_j$. Then $K_\bullet(g_1,\ldots,g_r)$ and $K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ are isomorphic as differential graded algebras.

**Proof.** Let $e'_i$ denote the generators for $g$ and $e_j$ those for $f$. The map
$$e'_i\longmapsto\sum_jx_{ij}e_j$$
has column matrix $X^{\mathsf T}$ and intertwines the two maps to $R$. Its exterior extension is therefore a chain map by [Koszul functoriality](#native-more-algebra-lemma-functorial). The inverse matrix gives its inverse in every degree. This specifies both the direction of the map and the transpose required by the row-indexed formula for the $g_i$. ∎

#### Lemma. Differential and Frobenius consequences of field intersections

Let $K$ have characteristic $p>0$. Suppose that intermediate fields $K^p\subset K_\alpha\subset K$ satisfy
$$\bigcap_\alpha K_\alpha=K^p,$$
and that any two contain a third member of the family. Then
$$\bigcap_\alpha
\ker\bigl(\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/K_\alpha}\bigr)=0.$$
For every finite extension $L/K$ one also has
$$\bigcap_\alpha L^pK_\alpha=L^p.$$

**Proof.** First assume the family is nonempty. Choose a $p$-basis of $K$ over $\mathbf F_p$ using the [differential basis theorem](#native-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis). A nonzero differential has an expression
$$\eta=\sum_{i=1}^r c_i\,du_i$$
using finitely many distinct elements of that basis, with not all $c_i$ zero. If $\eta$ vanishes after passing to $\Omega_{K/K_\alpha}$, those $du_i$ are dependent there. The same theorem says that the $p^r$ monomials $u^E$, with $0\leq e_i<p$, have a nontrivial relation over $K_\alpha$, since $K_\alpha K^p=K_\alpha$.

Let $V\subset K^{p^r}$ be the kernel of the linear map $(a_E)\mapsto\sum_E a_Eu^E$. If $\eta$ lies in every displayed kernel, each $V\cap K_\alpha^{p^r}$ is nonzero. [Subspace descent](#native-more-algebra-lemma-intersection-subfields-subspace), with ground field $K^p$, supplies a nonzero vector in $V\cap(K^p)^{p^r}$. This contradicts the original $p$-independence of the $u_i$, proving the differential assertion.

For the finite-extension assertion, the result passes up a tower $K\subset M\subset L$. Once it holds for $M/K$, the fields $M_\alpha=M^pK_\alpha$ have intersection $M^p$ and are again downward directed. Moreover
$$L^pM_\alpha=L^pK_\alpha.$$
One may therefore prove the assertion successively along a tower of finite extensions with no proper intermediate fields. Such a tower exists by induction on the degree, choosing a proper intermediate field whenever one exists.

Each nontrivial step without intermediate fields is either separable or purely inseparable of degree $p$. To see this, choose a generator $u$; its minimal polynomial has the form $Q(T^{p^e})$ with $Q$ separable. The intermediate field generated by $u^{p^e}$ is separable over the base. If the step is inseparable, that intermediate field must be the base, so the step is purely inseparable. The absence of intermediate fields then forces its degree to be $p$.

Consider first a finite separable extension $L/K$. Choose a primitive element $u$ and put $\theta=u^p$. The extension $L/K(\theta)$ is both separable and purely inseparable, so $L=K(\theta)$. If $d=[L:K]$, then $1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{d-1}$ is a $K$-basis of $L$ and a $K^p$-basis of $L^p$: the latter assertion follows by applying Frobenius to the basis $1,u,\ldots,u^{d-1}$. Since $K^p\subset K_\alpha\subset K$, the same powers form a $K_\alpha$-basis of $L^pK_\alpha$. In fact their span is the algebra generated by $\theta$ over $K_\alpha$, reduced using its degree-$d$ equation over $K^p$; being a finite-dimensional domain, it is a field. A vector lying in every $L^pK_\alpha$ has unique coordinates in this common $K$-basis. Those coordinates lie in every $K_\alpha$, hence in $K^p$, proving the assertion.

For a purely inseparable step of degree $p$, write $L=K(u)$ with $u^p=t\in K\setminus K^p$. Then
$$L^p=K^p(t),\qquad L^pK_\alpha=K_\alpha(t).$$
The powers $1,t,\ldots,t^{p-1}$ are independent over $K^p$ and span $K_\alpha(t)$ over $K_\alpha$. They need not be independent over $K_\alpha$; for example, $t$ may already belong to that field. Take $z\in\bigcap_\alpha K_\alpha(t)\subset K$, and form the $K$-linear relation space
$$V=\left\{(a_0,\ldots,a_{p-1},b)\in K^{p+1}:
\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}a_it^i-bz=0\right\}.$$
Every $V\cap K_\alpha^{p+1}$ contains a vector with last coordinate $1$. Subspace descent gives a nonzero vector in $V\cap(K^p)^{p+1}$. Its last coordinate cannot vanish, because the powers of $t$ are independent over $K^p$. Dividing by that coordinate expresses $z$ in $K^p(t)=L^p$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. This completes the tower argument.

If the family is empty, interpret intersections inside $K$, $\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}$ and $L$, respectively. The hypothesis then gives $K=K^p$. Such a field is perfect, so its absolute differentials vanish and every finite extension $L$ is perfect. Both conclusions follow in this case as well. ∎

#### Theorem. Formal smoothness over a field

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a Noetherian local algebra over a field $k$. In characteristic zero, $A$ is regular if and only if $k\to A$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak m$-adic topology.

If $k$ has characteristic $p>0$, the following five conditions are equivalent:

1. $A$ is geometrically regular over $k$.
2. $k\to A$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak m$-adic topology.
3. $A\otimes_k k'$ is regular for every finite intermediate extension $k\subset k'\subset k^{1/p}$.
4. $A$ is regular and the boundary map $H_1(L_{K/k})\to\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ is injective.
5. $A$ is regular and the natural map
$$\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\otimes_k K
\longrightarrow\Omega_{A/\mathbf F_p}\otimes_A K$$
is injective.

**Proof.** The characteristic-zero assertion follows from [formal smoothness implying regularity](#native-more-algebra-lemma-fs-implies-regular) and the [converse with separable residue extension](#native-more-algebra-lemma-regular-implies-fs): all extensions of a characteristic-zero field are separable.

In characteristic $p$, the complete [geometric-regularity comparison](#native-more-algebra-proposition-characterization-geometrically-regular) proves the equivalence of (1), (3), (4) and (5). If (2) holds, base change to a finite purely inseparable $k'/k$ gives formal smoothness of $A'=A\otimes_k k'$ for the extended ideal $\mathfrak mA'$. This finite extension has one prime above $\mathfrak m$, and $\mathfrak mA'$ has maximal-ideal radical, so its powers define the maximal-ideal topology of $A'$. The formal-smoothness-to-regularity lemma makes $A'$ regular. The [purely inseparable criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular) then gives (1).

It remains to derive (2) from (5). Consider a square-zero extension $T\to T/J$, a $k$-algebra structure $\varphi\colon k\to T$, and a continuous compatible map $\bar\psi\colon A\to T/J$, with $T$ discrete. Via $\bar\psi$, the ideal $J$ is an $A$-module annihilated by some $\mathfrak m^n$. Filter it by
$$0=\mathfrak m^nJ\subset\mathfrak m^{n-1}J
\subset\cdots\subset J.$$
These are ideals of $T$, and each successive quotient is annihilated by $\mathfrak m$. Lifting through the corresponding successive square-zero quotients reduces the problem to the case $\mathfrak mJ=0$. The action on every layer is independent of the intervening lifts because $J^2=0$. Thus this reduction applies without a finite-generation assumption on $J$.

In the reduced case $J$ is a $K$-vector space. Since $A$ is regular and $K/\mathbf F_p$ is separable, the converse lemma supplies a continuous $\mathbf F_p$-algebra lift $\psi\colon A\to T$. Its failure to respect $k$ is the derivation
$$D=\psi|_k-\varphi\colon k\longrightarrow J.$$
The universal property of differentials gives a $k$-linear map $\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\to J$, hence a $K$-linear map from $\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\otimes_k K$. Condition (5) lets us extend it to a $K$-linear map
$$\xi\colon\Omega_{A/\mathbf F_p}\otimes_A K\longrightarrow J.$$
Compose $\xi$ with the universal differential to obtain a derivation $D'\colon A\to J$ restricting to $D$ on $k$. Then $\psi-D'$ is a ring map: expanding a product gives the required identity by Leibniz, and the product of two values of $D'$ vanishes in $J^2$. It fixes the unit, reduces to $\bar\psi$, and restricts to $\varphi$. It is continuous as well: $D'(\mathfrak m^2)=0$ because $\mathfrak mJ=0$, and $\psi$ already kills some power of $\mathfrak m$. This constructs the desired lift at each layer and proves (2). ∎

#### Lemma. Adic formal smoothness implies flatness

A local map $A\to B$ of Noetherian local rings is flat if it is formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology of $B$.

**Proof.** The [completion comparison](#native-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth-completion) preserves the formal lifting property. It is enough to show flatness of $\widehat A\to\widehat B$: the composite $A\to\widehat B$ is then flat, and faithful flatness of $B\to\widehat B$ descends flatness to $A\to B$. Thus assume both rings complete.

Take the regular coefficient presentations $R\to A$ and $S\to B$ of the next lemma, with $R\to S$ flat. If $I=\ker(R\to A)$, then $S/IS$ is flat over $A$. It is a complete Noetherian local ring, and the surjection $S/IS\to B$ has a closed kernel contained in its maximal ideal. The [continuous lifting theorem](#native-more-algebra-lemma-lift-continuous), applied to the identity map of $B$, gives an $A$-algebra section $B\to S/IS$. Consequently $B$ is an $A$-module direct summand of a flat module, and is flat. ∎

#### Lemma. Compatible regular coefficient presentations

For a local map $A\to B$ between Noetherian complete local rings there is a commutative square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
R&\longrightarrow&S\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
A&\longrightarrow&B
\end{array}$$
whose vertical maps are surjective and with these properties. In residue characteristic zero, $R$ and $S$ are finite-variable power-series rings over fields. In positive residue characteristic $p$, they are such rings over Cohen rings. The images in $S$ of a parameter system for $R$ extend to a regular system of parameters there. Consequently $R\to S$ is flat, with regular closed fibre $S/\mathfrak m_RS$.

**Proof.** The Cohen structure theorem, with its coefficient-ring construction in Sections 4–5, supplies surjections
$$R=\Lambda[[X_1,\ldots,X_a]]\longrightarrow A,
\qquad S_0\longrightarrow B.$$
Choose fields as coefficient rings in residue characteristic zero, and Cohen rings in positive residue characteristic, including when $A$ or $B$ itself has characteristic $p$.

The prime-ring formal smoothness proved below and continuous lifting through the closed kernel of $S_0\to B$ lift $R\to A\to B$ to $\phi\colon R\to S_0$. This lift is local: an element of $\mathfrak m_R$ has image in $\mathfrak m_B$, and the preimage of $\mathfrak m_B$ under the local surjection is $\mathfrak m_{S_0}$.

Set $S=S_0[[Y_1,\ldots,Y_a]]$. Keep $\phi$ on $\Lambda$ and send $X_i$ to $\phi(X_i)+Y_i$; send each $Y_i$ to zero in $B$. These substitutions converge in the maximal-ideal topology and preserve the square. The classes of $\phi(X_i)+Y_i$ are independent in the cotangent space because their $Y_i$ coordinates form the identity matrix. In positive residue characteristic, include $p$ as the first parameter: its class is nonzero in the cotangent space of the Cohen power-series ring $S_0$ and independent of the new $Y_i$ coordinates. Thus the images of the parameters of $R$ extend to a cotangent basis of $S$, hence to a regular system of parameters.

The [flatness criterion over a regular local base](#native-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular) now gives flatness, and quotient by this parameter subsequence is regular by [regular local Cohen–Macaulayness](#native-algebra-lemma-regular-ring-cm). ∎

#### Lemma. Changing parameters in complete power-series rings

Let $F$ be a field and $\Lambda$ a Cohen ring with uniformizer $p$.

1. A regular system of parameters $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ in $F[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$ gives an isomorphism $F[[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]]\to F[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$ by $Y_i\mapsto y_i$.
2. If $z_1,\ldots,z_r$ is part of a regular system of parameters in that ring, then $r\leq n$ and its quotient by these elements is a power-series ring in $n-r$ variables over $F$.
3. If $p,y_1,\ldots,y_n$ is a regular system of parameters in $\Lambda[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$, substitution gives an isomorphism $\Lambda[[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]]\to\Lambda[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$.
4. If $p,z_1,\ldots,z_r$ is part of a regular system of parameters there, then $r\leq n$ and the quotient by the $z_i$ is a power-series ring in $n-r$ variables over $\Lambda$.

**Proof.** For (1), substitution is continuous and induces an isomorphism on residue fields and on degree-one cotangent spaces. The associated graded rings of the source and target power-series rings are polynomial rings on their standard parameters: group series terms by variable degree, and in the Cohen case include the $p$-adic orders of their coefficients. Thus the induced graded map is the invertible linear substitution specified in degree one, and is an isomorphism in every degree. Induction in the short exact sequences between successive maximal-ideal quotients gives an isomorphism on every such quotient. Completeness and separatedness give the asserted ring isomorphism.

The same proof gives (3), using $p$ together with the variables in degree one; the coefficient map fixes $p$. For (2), extend the $z_i$ to a regular system of parameters and apply (1). Quotienting its source by the first $r$ variables leaves the claimed power-series ring. For (4), extend $p,z_1,\ldots,z_r$ to a regular system and use (3), again killing only the $r$ indicated variables and retaining $p$. ∎

#### Lemma. Formal smoothness over the prime ring

The maps
$$\mathbf Q\to F[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]],\qquad
\mathbf F_p\to L[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]],\qquad
\mathbf Z\to\Lambda[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$$
are formally smooth for the maximal-ideal topology, where $F$ has characteristic zero, $L$ has characteristic $p$, and $\Lambda$ is any Cohen ring of residue characteristic $p$.

**Proof.** The coefficient fields are formally smooth over their prime fields by the [separability criterion](#native-algebra-proposition-characterize-separable-field-extensions). For a Cohen ring, Coefficient rings and the Cohen structure theorem, Section 4, Theorem 4.1 proves that
$$\mathbf Z/p^N\mathbf Z\longrightarrow\Lambda/p^N\Lambda$$
is formally smooth for every $N\geq1$. Its proof uses only the Cohen DVR properties and works for every residue field.

In a square-zero test with discrete target $T$ and ideal $J$, continuity of the given map modulo $J$ makes the image of some maximal-ideal power zero. In the Cohen case this puts $p^q$ in $J$ for some $q$, so $p^{2q}=0$ in $T$. Apply the quoted result with $N=2q$ to lift the coefficient map. In the field cases, lift the coefficient field map by its formal smoothness.

Choose arbitrary lifts of the images of the variables. The ideal generated by these lifts, and by $p$ in the Cohen case, has a power contained in $J$, and hence a further power zero. Evaluation of formal series is consequently a finite sum in $T$ once their variable degree is large enough; the lifted coefficient map and variable images define a ring map lifting the given one. The same nilpotence proves its continuity for the full maximal-ideal topology. ∎

#### Lemma. Lifting a formally smooth complete closed fibre

Let $(A,\mathfrak m_A,k)$ be Noetherian complete local. If a Noetherian complete local $k$-algebra $B$ is formally smooth over $k$ for its maximal-ideal topology, then there is a Noetherian complete local $A$-algebra $C$, formally smooth for its maximal-ideal topology, with
$$C\otimes_A k\cong B.$$

**Proof.** Use compatible regular coefficient presentations for the local map $A\to B$ through $k$, obtaining $R\to S$ over $A\to B$. Let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be parameters of $R$, with $t_1=p$ in positive residue characteristic. The ring $\bar S=S/\mathfrak m_RS$ is regular, as is $B$ by formal smoothness over a field. The [regular quotient parameter theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-regular-quotient-regular) makes the kernel of $\bar S\to B$ generated by part of a regular system of parameters $\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_r$.

Lift these elements to the kernel of $S\to B$. The list $t_1,\ldots,t_d,x_1,\ldots,x_r$ extends to a parameter system of $S$. The preceding parameter-substitution lemma shows that $S/(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ is still a power-series ring over its field or Cohen coefficient ring and still contains the images of the $t_i$ as part of a parameter system. Replace $S$ by this quotient. Now $S/\mathfrak m_RS=B$ and $R\to S$ is flat.

The [flatness and closed-fibre formal smoothness criterion](#native-more-algebra-proposition-fs-flat-fibre-fs) makes $R\to S$ formally smooth. Put $C=S\otimes_R A$. Since $R\to A$ is a surjection, $C$ is a quotient of the Noetherian complete local ring $S$, and is therefore Noetherian complete local. Formal smoothness passes to $A\to C$ by base change, with the maximal-ideal topology inherited from $S$, and its closed fibre is $B$. ∎

#### Lemma. Continuous lifting to a complete adic ring

Suppose $R\to S$ is formally smooth for an ideal-adic topology defined by $\mathfrak n\subset S$. Let $T$ be a complete separated adic $R$-algebra, let $J\subset T$ be a closed ideal, and suppose $J^t$ lies in an ideal of definition for some $t\geq1$. Every continuous $R$-algebra map $\psi\colon S\to T/J$ lifts to a continuous $R$-algebra map $S\to T$.

**Proof.** Choose an ideal of definition $I$ with $J^t\subset I$, and put
$$T_{a,b}=T/(J^a+I^b)\qquad(a,b\geq1).$$
The maps $\psi$ give a compatible first row $S\to T_{1,b}$. Lift successively along the first column to obtain maps $S\to T_{a,1}$. Each column step has square-zero kernel because $J^{2a}\subset J^{a+1}$ for $a\geq1$.

For the rest of the grid use the surjection
$$T_{a+1,b+1}\longrightarrow
T_{a+1,b}\times_{T_{a,b}}T_{a,b+1}.$$
Surjectivity follows from the elementary two-ideal fibre-product identity: the two ideals in the numerator quotient have sum $J^a+I^b$. Its kernel is square-zero. Indeed, after quotient by $J^{a+1}+I^{b+1}$ it is contained in the image of $I^b$, whose square is zero since $2b\geq b+1$.

Induction on $a+b$ lifts each compatible pair to the next grid entry by formal smoothness. All maps to these discrete rings are continuous; a pair is continuous because a common sufficiently high power of $\mathfrak n$ is killed by both components. This gives compatible maps at every grid point. Since $J^{bt}\subset I^b$, the diagonal entries $T_{bt,b}$ equal $T/I^b$. Their inverse limit produces an $R$-algebra map $\phi\colon S\to T$.

For every $b$, its reduction modulo $J+I^b$ is that of $\psi$. Closedness gives $\bigcap_b(J+I^b)=J$, so $\phi$ reduces to $\psi$ in $T/J$. Finally, continuity of $\psi$ gives $\phi(\mathfrak n^r)\subset J+I$ for some $r$. Taking the $t$th power yields
$$\phi(\mathfrak n^{rt})\subset(J+I)^t\subset I.$$
Further powers give continuity at every $I^b$. This proves the claim and the compatibility of the lift with the specified topologies. ∎

#### Lemma. Exterior multiplication is a Koszul homotopy

Let $\varphi\colon E\to R$ be an $R$-linear map, let $e\in E$, and put $f=\varphi(e)$. Exterior multiplication $h(a)=e\wedge a$ satisfies
$$dh+hd=f\,1_{K_\bullet(\varphi)}.$$

**Proof.** Since $e$ has degree one, the graded product rule gives $d(e\wedge a)=fa-e\wedge da$. Rearranging proves the identity in every degree. It holds for arbitrary modules $E$ over arbitrary commutative rings. ∎

#### Lemma. A rank-one enlargement of a Koszul complex

For $\varphi\colon E\to R$ and $f\in R$, define $\varphi'\colon E\oplus R\to R$ by $\varphi'(e,a)=\varphi(e)+fa$. Then
$$K_\bullet(\varphi')\cong
\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(f\colon K_\bullet(\varphi)\to K_\bullet(\varphi)\bigr).$$

**Proof.** Write $C=K_\bullet(\varphi)$ and let $e_0$ generate the added copy of $R$. The exterior direct-sum formula gives the isomorphism
$$C_n\oplus C_{n-1}\longrightarrow\bigwedge^n(E\oplus R),
\qquad(a,b)\longmapsto a+e_0\wedge b.$$
Here $e_0$ is placed on the left, fixing the sign convention. The cone differential is $(a,b)\mapsto(da+fb,-db)$. On the exterior side,
$$d(a+e_0\wedge b)=da+\varphi'(e_0)b-e_0\wedge db
=da+fb-e_0\wedge db.$$
This is exactly the image of the cone differential. On a decomposable $b=e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{n-1}$, it says that the first removed factor contributes $fb$, while every other term is minus $e_0$ wedged with the corresponding term of $db$. Thus the equality includes all wedge signs, without a freeness restriction on $E$. ∎

#### Lemma. Multiplication of the last Koszul entry

Let $f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},f,g\in R$. The complex $K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},fg)$ is homotopy equivalent to a cone of a chain map
$$K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},f)[1]
\longrightarrow K_\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},g).$$
For a homological complex $C$, the shift here is $C[1]_n=C_{n+1}$ with differential $-d_C$.

**Proof.** Apply the [rank-one multiplication comparison](#native-more-algebra-lemma-koszul-mult-abstract) to $E=R^{r-1}$ and the map sending its basis to the fixed prefix. The cone and shift conventions are the ones in the [explicit cone-composition proof](#native-more-algebra-lemma-cone-squared). ∎

#### Lemma. Differential bases and p-bases

Let $k\subset K$ be fields of characteristic $p>0$, and put $C=kK^p$. A family $(u_i)_{i\in I}$ in $K$ is called $p$-independent over $k$ when its monomials
$$u^E=\prod_i u_i^{e_i},\qquad 0\leq e_i<p,$$
with finitely many nonzero exponents, are linearly independent over $C$. It is a $p$-basis when these monomials form a $C$-basis of $K$.

The family is $p$-independent exactly when $(du_i)$ is linearly independent over $K$ in $\Omega_{K/k}$. Every $p$-independent family extends to a $p$-basis, including the empty family. Finally, $(u_i)$ is a $p$-basis exactly when $(du_i)$ is a $K$-basis of $\Omega_{K/k}$.

**Proof.** Suppose first that the differentials are independent. For each index $i$, extend the coordinate functional on their span to a $K$-linear functional on $\Omega_{K/k}$. Its composite with the universal differential is a $k$-derivation $\partial_i$ satisfying $\partial_i(u_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Every such derivation kills $C$.

If a nonzero polynomial $F$ over $C$, of degree less than $p$ in each of finitely many variables, vanishes at the corresponding $u_i$, choose one with smallest total degree. It cannot be a nonzero constant. A variable occurring with positive exponent has a nonzero formal partial derivative: its positive exponents are strictly below $p$. Applying the associated derivation gives a nonzero polynomial relation of smaller total degree. This contradiction proves $p$-independence.

Next enlarge a $p$-independent family to a maximal one by Zorn's lemma. Unions of chains remain independent because a relation uses only finitely many elements. Let $F=C(u_i:i\in I)$ for this maximal family. Its bounded-exponent monomials span $F$: their span is a subalgebra, and every nonzero element $a$ of it has $a^p\in C^\times$, hence inverse $a^{p-1}/a^p$ in that span. If $v\in K\setminus F$, then $v^p\in C$ and $T^p-v^p$ is irreducible over $F$. Indeed, over an algebraic closure it has only the root $v$; a proper monic factor has the form $(T-v)^r$ with $1\leq r<p$, whose next coefficient $-rv$ would put $v$ in $F$. Thus $1,v,\ldots,v^{p-1}$ are independent over $F$. Adjoining $v$ would preserve $p$-independence over $C$, contradicting maximality. Therefore $F=K$, proving existence and extension of $p$-bases.

For a $p$-basis, evaluation gives the presentation
$$K\cong C[T_i:i\in I]/(T_i^p-u_i^p:i\in I).$$
Reduction of exponents proves surjectivity, and independence of the reduced monomials proves that there are no further relations. A $k$-derivation kills $C$, while arbitrary prescribed values on the $u_i$ respect every displayed relation. The universal property of differentials now says that the $du_i$ form a basis. Extending any $p$-independent family to a $p$-basis proves independence of its differentials. Conversely, if the $du_i$ already form a basis, the established independence criterion makes the $u_i$ $p$-independent; a proper extension to a $p$-basis would add an independent differential to a spanning family. Hence no extension is needed.

We will also use the resulting constant-field test
$$\ker(d\colon K\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/k})=kK^p.$$
In a $p$-basis expansion, the coordinate derivations differentiate the bounded-exponent monomials. For a fixed coordinate, distinct monomials involving it give distinct differentiated monomials with nonzero exponent coefficients. Vanishing of every coordinate derivative therefore leaves only the constant monomial. This proves the test for arbitrary, possibly infinite, $p$-bases. ∎

#### Lemma. Descent of a vector through intersecting subfields

Let $k\subset K$ be fields and let $(K_\alpha)$ be a nonempty family of intermediate fields such that
$$\bigcap_\alpha K_\alpha=k.$$
Suppose also that any two members contain a third member of the family. For a $K$-linear subspace $V\subset K^n$, where $n\geq1$,
$$V\cap k^n\ne0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
V\cap K_\alpha^n\ne0\ \text{for every }\alpha.$$
Nonemptiness of the family is necessary here: for an empty family the condition on the right would hold even for $V=0$.

**Proof.** A nonzero vector over $k$ supplies the forward implication. For the converse use induction on $n$. In dimension one a nonzero $K$-subspace is all of $K$, and contains $1$.

Assume that the assertion holds in dimension $n-1$ and that all the intersections over $K_\alpha$ are nonzero. If $V$ contains a nonzero vector of $0\oplus k^{n-1}$, the conclusion follows. Otherwise apply the induction hypothesis to
$$W=V\cap(0\oplus K^{n-1}).$$
There is an index $\alpha_0$ for which $V\cap(0\oplus K_{\alpha_0}^{n-1})=0$. Every nonzero vector of $V\cap K_{\alpha_0}^n$ has nonzero first coordinate. Normalize one to obtain $v=(1,v_2,\ldots,v_n)$. Subtracting a suitable multiple of $v$ from any other vector in that intersection leaves first coordinate zero, and therefore gives the zero vector. In particular, $v$ is its unique vector with first coordinate one.

Whenever $K_\beta\subset K_{\alpha_0}$, the same normalization of a nonzero vector over $K_\beta$ must produce this $v$. Hence all its coordinates belong to every such $K_\beta$. These refinements have intersection $k$: given any $\gamma$, choose a common refinement of $\gamma$ and $\alpha_0$. Membership in all refinements thus implies membership in every $K_\gamma$. Consequently $v\in k^n$, as required. ∎

#### Lemma. Formal smoothness forces local regularity

If a Noetherian local $k$-algebra $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ is formally smooth over the field $k$ for its maximal-ideal topology, then $A$ is regular.

**Proof.** Let $k_0$ be the prime field. The extension $k/k_0$ is separable and thus formally smooth, so composing square-zero lifts shows that $A$ is formally smooth over $k_0$. We can work over $k_0$ instead. The [completion comparison for formal smoothness](#native-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth-completion) allows passage to $\widehat A$. Regularity of the completion implies that of $A$ by [regularity descent under completion](#native-more-algebra-lemma-completion-regular), equivalently by flat local descent. Thus assume $A$ complete.

Choose a coefficient field $K\to A$ by [Cohen structure](#uncovered-algebra-theorem-cohen-structure-theorem). It respects the prime field. If $x_1,\ldots,x_e$ lift a basis of $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$, put $P=K[[X_1,\ldots,X_e]]$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak q$. There is a $K$-algebra isomorphism
$$A/\mathfrak m^2\longrightarrow P/\mathfrak q^2,\qquad
x_i\longmapsto X_i,$$
because both rings are the coefficient field plus their square-zero cotangent spaces. Formal smoothness over $k_0$ lifts this map successively to $P/\mathfrak q^n$, using the square-zero kernels at each step. Its limit is a local $k_0$-algebra map $u\colon A\to P$, inducing the chosen residue and cotangent isomorphisms. The later lifts need not respect the chosen copy of $K$; no such assertion is required.

The map $u$ is surjective. The cotangent surjection and residue isomorphism imply surjectivity on each graded piece of the maximal-ideal filtrations, since those graded rings are generated in degree one. Given an element of $P$, lift its residue and then correct the error in degree $n$ by an element of $\mathfrak m^n$, for $n=1,2,\ldots$. These corrections converge in $A$ and their image is the prescribed element of $P$. Hence
$$e=\dim P\leq\dim A\leq\dim_K(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)=e.$$
The last inequality is the usual parameter bound. Equality proves regularity. The resulting surjection is in fact an isomorphism: its regular local source is a domain of dimension $e$, and quotient by any nonzero kernel element would lower dimension. ∎

#### Lemma. Separable residue fields give formal smoothness

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a regular local $k$-algebra, with $K/k$ separable. Then $k\to A$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak m$-adic topology.

**Proof.** Complete $A$, using preservation of regularity and the equivalence of formal smoothness before and after completion. The [coefficient-field power-series description](#native-more-algebra-lemma-power-series-over-residue-field) gives a $k$-algebra isomorphism
$$\widehat A\cong K[[X_1,\ldots,X_d]].$$
The field extension $K/k$ is formally smooth by the separability criterion. Polynomial extension and composition show that $K[X_1,\ldots,X_d]$ is formally smooth over $k$. Passing first to the variable-adic topology and then to its completion preserves formal smoothness by the [adic comparison lemmas](#native-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth). This proves the assertion. ∎

#### Lemma. Multiplication in a rank-one Koszul enlargement

Fix $\varphi\colon E\to R$ and $f,g\in R$. On $E\oplus R$, let $\varphi'_a$ be $\varphi$ on $E$ and multiplication by $a$ on the last summand, for $a=f,g,fg$. There is a chain map
$$K_\bullet(\varphi'_f)[1]\longrightarrow K_\bullet(\varphi'_g)$$
whose cone is homotopy equivalent to $K_\bullet(\varphi'_{fg})$.

**Proof.** The [rank-one cone identification](#native-more-algebra-lemma-cone-koszul-abstract) identifies these three complexes with multiplication cones on $K_\bullet(\varphi)$. The [cone-composition lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-cone-squared) supplies the map and the explicit homotopy equivalence. Its proof works for every underlying chain complex, so no projectivity or finite-generation assumption on $E$ is introduced. ∎

#### Lemma. A power-series description respecting the ground field

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a complete regular local $k$-algebra. If $K/k$ is separable, then there is a $k$-algebra isomorphism
$$A\cong K[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]],\qquad d=\dim A.$$

**Proof.** The [residue-field lifting lemma](#native-more-algebra-lemma-lift-residue-field) gives a $k$-algebra section $K\to A$ of the residue map. Choose lifts of a cotangent basis. The power-series evaluation map for this specified coefficient field is surjective by successive homogeneous approximations. The complete proof in Coefficient rings and the Cohen structure theorem, Section 6, Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.2 then proves injectivity: a nonzero kernel element in the regular power-series domain would force the quotient dimension below $d$. Thus the isomorphism respects $k$ as claimed. ∎

#### Lemma. Comparing the cones of two multiplications

Let $A_\bullet$ be any homological complex of $R$-modules. For $a\in R$, write $C(a)=\operatorname{Cone}(a\colon A_\bullet\to A_\bullet)$. Then $C(fg)$ is homotopy equivalent to the cone of a map
$$u\colon C(f)[1]\longrightarrow C(g).$$
We use $A[1]_n=A_{n+1}$ with differential $-d_A$, and
$$\operatorname{Cone}(v)_n=B_n\oplus A_{n-1},\qquad
d(b,a)=(d_Bb+v(a),-d_Aa).$$

**Proof.** First take $A_\bullet=R$ in degree zero. The shifted complex $C(f)[1]$ has terms in degrees $0,-1$ and differential $-f$. Multiplying its degree-minus-one coordinate by $-1$ gives an isomorphic model with differential $f$. Map its degree-zero term identically to the degree-zero term of $C(g)$, and its other term to zero. In these signed coordinates the cone is the two-term complex
$$P_1=R^2\xrightarrow{\ M\ }P_0=R^2,\qquad
M=\begin{pmatrix}g&1\\0&-f\end{pmatrix}.$$
Thus the displayed matrix uses a specified signed model of the shift.

Define maps $i\colon C(fg)\to P$ and $p\colon P\to C(fg)$ by
$$i_1=\binom{1}{-g},\quad i_0=\binom01,\qquad
p_1=(1,0),\quad p_0=(f,1).$$
Direct multiplication gives $Mi_1=i_0fg$, $p_0M=fgp_1$, and $pi=1$. The degree-one homotopy $h\colon P_0\to P_1$ is
$$h=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Indeed,
$$hM=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\g&1\end{pmatrix}=1-i_1p_1,
\qquad
Mh=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-f&0\end{pmatrix}=1-i_0p_0.$$
This proves the two-term assertion with its omitted homotopy supplied.

For a general complex, the map can be written without any boundedness assumption. Its degree-$n$ component is
$$u_n\colon A_{n+1}\oplus A_n\longrightarrow A_n\oplus A_{n-1},
\qquad (x,y)\longmapsto(y,0).$$
The source differential is $(x,y)\mapsto(-dx-fy,dy)$, so $u$ is a chain map. In the cone of $u$, change the sign of the first coordinate from the shifted summand. The degree-$n$ term becomes
$$P_n=A_n\oplus A_{n-1}\oplus A_n\oplus A_{n-1},$$
with differential
$$d_P(a,b,c,e)=(da+gb+e,\,-db,\,dc-fe,\,-de).$$
The maps and homotopy generalizing the preceding matrices are
$$\begin{aligned}
i_n(x,y)&=(0,y,x,-gy),\\
p_n(a,b,c,e)&=(fa+c,b),\\
H_n(a,b,c,e)&=(0,0,0,a)\in P_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}$$
The first two commute with the differentials by substitution, and $pi=1$. Substitution also gives
$$(d_PH+Hd_P)(a,b,c,e)=(a,0,-fa,e+gb)
=(1-ip)(a,b,c,e).$$
Therefore they are mutually inverse up to chain homotopy for arbitrary $A_\bullet$.

This also explains the tensor-product proof. Totalizing $A_\bullet\otimes_R(R\xrightarrow{a}R)$ gives $C(a)$ after the usual degree signs. Totalization preserves the displayed chain maps, and sends the two-term homotopy to $(-1)^i1\otimes h$ on the summand of $A$-degree $i$: the mixed differential terms cancel, leaving the original homotopy identity. The standard identification
$$A_i\otimes B[1]_j\longrightarrow(A\otimes B)[1]_{i+j},
\qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto(-1)^i a\otimes b,$$
provides the shift signs, and the corresponding cone identification uses the same sign on its shifted summand. Thus the original reduction to a two-term scalar complex and the direct formulas give the same homotopy equivalence. No flatness is needed, since these are actual chain maps and homotopies. ∎

#### Lemma. A section of a separable residue extension

Let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a complete local $k$-algebra, without a Noetherian assumption. If $K/k$ is separable, there is a $k$-algebra map $K\to A$ whose composite with $A\to K$ is the identity.

**Proof.** The [separability criterion](#native-algebra-proposition-characterize-separable-field-extensions) makes $K/k$ formally smooth. Start with the identity $K\to A/\mathfrak m$. Having lifted it to $A/\mathfrak m^n$, lift further to $A/\mathfrak m^{n+1}$; the kernel $\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}$ is square-zero. Choose these lifts compatibly. Their inverse limit is the required $k$-algebra map because $A$ is complete and separated. This is also the [continuous complete-target lifting theorem](#native-more-algebra-lemma-lift-continuous) for the discrete source field and the closed ideal $\mathfrak m$. ∎

#### Marked formal deformation rings

Fix a Noetherian ring $\Lambda$ and a finite map $\Lambda\to k$ to a field. Write $\mathfrak m_\Lambda=\ker(\Lambda\to k)$ and $k'=\Lambda/\mathfrak m_\Lambda$, so $k/k'$ is finite. The ring $\Lambda$ need not itself be local; every local algebra below factors through $\Lambda_{\mathfrak m_\Lambda}$.

The category $\mathcal C_\Lambda$ consists of Artinian local $\Lambda$-algebras equipped with a specified residue-field identification with $k$. Its morphisms are local $\Lambda$-algebra maps respecting these identifications. In $\widehat{\mathcal C}_\Lambda$, the rings are Noetherian complete local with the same residue marking and morphism convention. Completeness always includes separatedness.

#### Lemma. Cotangent surjectivity for complete marked rings

For a map $f\colon R\to S$ in $\widehat{\mathcal C}_\Lambda$, these conditions are equivalent:

1. $f$ is surjective.
2. $\mathfrak m_R/\mathfrak m_R^2\to\mathfrak m_S/\mathfrak m_S^2$ is surjective.
3. The relative cotangent map is surjective:
$$\mathfrak m_R/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda R+\mathfrak m_R^2)
\longrightarrow
\mathfrak m_S/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda S+\mathfrak m_S^2).$$

**Proof.** A surjection with the prescribed residue isomorphism maps the source maximal ideal onto the target one, proving (1) implies (2); quotienting gives (3).

Assume (3), and put $R_n=R/\mathfrak m_R^n$, $S_n=S/\mathfrak m_S^n$. For $n\geq2$, their absolute and relative cotangent spaces are the ones of $R$ and $S$. The [Artinian criterion below](#native-formal-defos-lemma-surjective) therefore gives surjections $R_n\to S_n$ for every $n$, including the residue map at $n=1$.

Let $H_n$ be their kernels. Each $H_n$ has finite length as an $R$-module, being a submodule of $R_n$. For a fixed $n$, the images of all later $H_m$ form a descending sequence of $R$-submodules of $H_n$ and hence stabilize. Thus $(H_n)$ is Mittag–Leffler. The [exact inverse-limit theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-ml-exact-sequence) applied to
$$0\longrightarrow H_n\longrightarrow R_n\longrightarrow S_n\longrightarrow0$$
gives a surjection $R=\varprojlim R_n\to\varprojlim S_n=S$.

There is also a direct completion argument. Once the absolute cotangent map is surjective, the induced maps $\mathfrak m_R^n/\mathfrak m_R^{n+1}\to\mathfrak m_S^n/\mathfrak m_S^{n+1}$ are surjective for every $n$, because the associated graded algebras are generated in degree one over the common residue field. Lift an element's residue and then correct its successive errors using elements of $\mathfrak m_R^n$. The resulting series of corrections converges in $R$ and maps to the chosen element of $S$. The equivalence of the two cotangent tests follows from the same diagram as in the Artinian proof. ∎

#### Lemma. Cotangent surjectivity for Artinian marked rings

For a map $f\colon A\to B$ in $\mathcal C_\Lambda$, surjectivity is equivalent to surjectivity on absolute cotangent spaces, and also equivalent to surjectivity of
$$\mathfrak m_A/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda A+\mathfrak m_A^2)
\longrightarrow
\mathfrak m_B/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda B+\mathfrak m_B^2).$$

**Proof.** If $f$ is surjective, an element lifting a member of $\mathfrak m_B$ has zero residue because the marked residue map is an isomorphism. Thus $f(\mathfrak m_A)=\mathfrak m_B$, proving absolute cotangent surjectivity. The relative assertion is then its quotient.

For the converse comparison, put
$$V=(\mathfrak m_\Lambda/\mathfrak m_\Lambda^2)\otimes_{k'}k,
\quad U_A=\mathfrak m_A/\mathfrak m_A^2,
\quad W_A=\mathfrak m_A/(\mathfrak m_\Lambda A+\mathfrak m_A^2),$$
and define $U_B,W_B$ in the same way. There is a commutative diagram with right-exact rows
$$\begin{array}{ccccc}
V&\longrightarrow&U_A&\longrightarrow&W_A\longrightarrow0\\
\Vert&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
V&\longrightarrow&U_B&\longrightarrow&W_B\longrightarrow0.
\end{array}$$
The first map sends $\lambda\otimes c$ to the class of $\lambda\widetilde c$, where $\widetilde c$ is any lift of $c$. Different lifts differ by a maximal-ideal element, so their products with $\lambda$ agree modulo its square. The image is precisely the contribution of $\mathfrak m_\Lambda A$, or of $\mathfrak m_\Lambda B$. This proves the asserted exactness and naturality. If $W_A\to W_B$ is onto, lift the relative class of any element of $U_B$ to $U_A$; its remaining difference lies in the image of $V$ and can be lifted through the identical left column. Hence $U_A\to U_B$ is onto.

Assume that absolute cotangent map is onto. Then
$$\mathfrak m_B=f(\mathfrak m_A)B+\mathfrak m_B^2.$$
Nakayama over the Artinian local ring $B$, applied to $\mathfrak m_B/f(\mathfrak m_A)B$, gives $\mathfrak m_B=f(\mathfrak m_A)B$. The residue isomorphism now says that $A/\mathfrak m_A\to B/\mathfrak m_AB$ is surjective. For the $A$-module cokernel $Q$ of $A\to B$, this gives $Q=\mathfrak m_AQ$. Since $\mathfrak m_A$ is nilpotent, iteration gives $Q=0$, even without invoking finiteness of $Q$. Thus $f$ is surjective. ∎

### Supporting proofs and references

The following results supply the lower algebraic and topological inputs used above. Each entry records its precise hypotheses and its proof or complete written source. Any outstanding dependency remains identified at its own entry.

#### Noetherian spaces and their components

Every subspace of a Noetherian topological space is Noetherian. Such a space has finitely many irreducible components, and each component contains a nonempty open subset of the whole space.

**Proof.** For a descending chain $F_n$ of closed subsets of a subspace $Y\subset X$, choose closed $Z_n\subset X$ with $F_n=Y\cap Z_n$. Replace $Z_n$ by $Z_1\cap\cdots\cap Z_n$. These new ambient closed sets form a descending chain and still restrict to $F_n$, so ambient stabilization proves subspace stabilization.

The complete finite-decomposition argument is Spectra of rings, Section 4, Theorem 4.3. It works for arbitrary Noetherian spaces: a minimal closed counterexample to finite irreducible decomposition would split into two smaller closed sets, a contradiction. Remove redundant members to obtain the finitely many components $Z_1,\ldots,Z_r$. For each $i$,
$$U_i=X\setminus\bigcup_{j\ne i}Z_j$$
is open and contained in $Z_i$, since the components cover $X$. It is nonempty because an irreducible $Z_i$ cannot be contained in the union of the other finitely many components without being contained in one of them. The empty space has no components, so the assertion there is vacuous. ∎

#### Finite-type morphisms from a field

For any scheme $S$, field $K$, and morphism $f\colon\operatorname{Spec}(K)\to S$, these conditions are equivalent:

1. $f$ is of finite type.
2. $f$ is locally of finite type.
3. Its image lies in an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}(R)\subset S$ for which the induced map $R\to K$ is finite.
4. There is such an affine open in which the image is a closed point $s$, with $K/\kappa(s)$ finite.

**Proof.** A morphism from a one-point space is quasi-compact: every inverse image of an affine open is empty or a singleton. Thus locally finite type and finite type agree here.

Suppose (2), choose an affine neighborhood $\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ of the image, and write $\mathfrak p=\ker(R\to K)$. Then $K$ is a finite-type algebra over the domain $R_0=R/\mathfrak p$. We show that some nonzero $a\in R_0$ has $R_{0,a}$ a field with $K/R_{0,a}$ finite. Apply [normalization over a domain](#native-algebra-lemma-noether-normalization-over-a-domain) to $R_0\subset K$. After inverting a nonzero $a$, it makes $K$ finite over a polynomial subring
$$R_{0,a}[Y_1,\ldots,Y_d]\subset K.$$
A domain over which a field is integral must itself be a field: the inverse of a nonzero element in the larger field satisfies a monic equation, which expresses that inverse in the smaller domain. Therefore the displayed polynomial subring is a field. A polynomial variable cannot be a unit, so $d=0$, and the assertion follows. This is the field-over-domain step needed for the affine neighborhood.

Lift $a$ to $R$. Its image in $K$ is nonzero, so the morphism factors through the principal open $\operatorname{Spec}(R_a)$, and $K$ is finite as an $R_a$-module. This proves (3). Conversely, a finite ring map is of finite type, so (3) implies (2).

For a finite map $R\to K$, the image $R/\mathfrak p$ is a domain over which $K$ is integral, and the inverse argument above makes it a field. Thus $\mathfrak p$ is maximal and $K/\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is finite, proving (4). The finite field extension in (4), together with $R\to R/\mathfrak p$, immediately gives (3). This proves all four equivalences without a Noetherian hypothesis on $S$ or $R$. ∎

#### Stable images in an inverse system

Let $(A_i)$ be an inverse system of sets indexed by a nonempty directed set. Suppose it is Mittag–Leffler: for each $i$, the images in $A_i$ of sufficiently late $A_j$ are constant. Denote that eventual image by $B_i$. Then $(B_i)$ is an inverse subsystem with surjective transition maps and
$$\varprojlim_iB_i=\varprojlim_iA_i.$$
The same assertion holds for inverse systems of groups or modules.

**Proof.** Fix $i\leq j$. Choose an index $l\geq j$ beyond stabilization indices for the images in both $A_i$ and $A_j$. Every element of $B_j$ is the image of an element of $A_l$, so its image in $A_i$ belongs to $B_i$. This proves that transitions restrict to the $B_i$.

Given $b\in B_i$, the same choice of a sufficiently late $l$ lifts it to an element of $A_l$. The image of that element in $A_j$ belongs to $B_j$, proving surjectivity of $B_j\to B_i$. Finally, every coordinate of a compatible family in the $A_i$ belongs to every later image, hence to $B_i$. Conversely a family in the subsystem is already compatible in the original system. This proves equality of limits. Countability is not needed for this stable-image construction; it is needed for the subsequent general nonempty-limit assertion used in [countable Mittag–Leffler exactness](#native-algebra-lemma-ml-exact-sequence). ∎

#### Intersections of powers in finite modules

Let $R$ be Noetherian, $I\subset R$ an ideal, and $M$ a finite $R$-module. The submodule
$$N=\bigcap_{n\geq0}I^nM$$
vanishes on an open neighborhood of every prime containing $I$. If $I\subset\operatorname{Jac}(R)$, then $N=0$.

**Proof.** Noetherian and Artinian rings, Section 6, Theorem 6.1 proves the stronger statement that one element $1+a$, with $a\in I$, annihilates all of $N$. Its complete proof applies Artin–Rees to obtain $IN=N$ and then uses the determinant form of Nakayama; it also proves the converse description by elementwise annihilators.

For any $\mathfrak p\supset I$, the element $1+a$ avoids $\mathfrak p$. Hence $D(1+a)$ is an open neighborhood on which $N$ vanishes. If $I$ lies in the Jacobson radical, $1+a$ is a unit and annihilates only the zero module. These give the two stated consequences with one uniform annihilator. ∎

#### The natural long exact Tor sequence

For modules over any commutative ring $R$, a short exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow M'\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow M''\longrightarrow0$$
gives, for every $N$, a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(N,M')\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(N,M)\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(N,M'')
\xrightarrow{\partial}
\operatorname{Tor}^R_{n-1}(N,M')\longrightarrow\cdots$$
ending in $N\otimes_RM'\to N\otimes_RM\to N\otimes_RM''\to0$.

**Proof.** Resolve $N$ by free modules $P_\bullet$. Tensoring the short exact sequence with each $P_i$ is exact, giving a short exact sequence of complexes $0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0$. For a cycle $z\in Z_n$, lift it to $y\in Y_n$. Its differential $dy$ is the image of a unique $x\in X_{n-1}$. This $x$ is a cycle because $d^2y=0$ and $X\to Y$ is injective. Define $\partial[z]=[x]$.

A different lift of $z$ changes $x$ by a boundary from $X_n$. Changing $z$ by a boundary can be lifted by adding a differential to $y$, leaving $x$ unchanged. Thus the map is well defined.

Exactness follows by three chases. If a cycle of $X$ becomes a boundary $dy$ in $Y$, the image of $y$ is a cycle of $Z$ mapping to it under $\partial$. If a cycle of $Y$ maps to a boundary $dz$ in $Z$, lift $z$ and subtract its differential; the result is a cycle coming from $X$. Finally, if $\partial[z]=0$, its lifted differential is the image of a boundary $dx$ in $X$; subtracting the image of $x$ from the lift makes it a cycle in $Y$ mapping to $z$. These are the three kernel-image equalities repeated along the sequence. Degree zero is right exactness of tensor product.

The construction commutes with maps of short exact sequences and with chain maps between free resolutions, because both the lift and its differential commute with those maps. Homotopic resolution maps induce the same homology map, so the sequence and its connecting homomorphisms are natural in both variables. ∎

#### Reducedness under a flat map of Noetherian rings

Let $R\to S$ be a flat map of Noetherian rings. If $R$ and all rings $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ are reduced, then $S$ is reduced.

**Proof.** A Noetherian ring has [finitely many minimal primes](#native-algebra-lemma-noetherian-irreducible-components), say $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_t$. Their intersection is its nilradical, so reducedness gives an injective map
$$R\longrightarrow\prod_{i=1}^t\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p_i)
=\prod_{i=1}^t\kappa(\mathfrak p_i).$$
Flat tensoring by $S$ preserves this injection. Tensor product commutes with the finite product because a finite product of modules is their direct sum. Hence
$$S\hookrightarrow
\prod_{i=1}^t\bigl(S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p_i)\bigr).$$
Each factor is reduced by hypothesis. A nilpotent of $S$ maps to zero in every factor, and injectivity makes it zero. If $R=0$, then its unital algebra $S$ is also zero, giving the assertion in the empty-spectrum case. This proves the exact ascent statement used by [smooth reducedness](#native-algebra-lemma-reduced-goes-up). ∎

#### Exactness of Mittag–Leffler inverse limits

For integer-indexed inverse systems of modules, a short exact sequence remains exact after inverse limit when the kernel system is Mittag–Leffler.

The complete [countable directed inverse-limit proof](#native-algebra-lemma-ml-exact-sequence) applies at this scope. It proves exactness at the first two terms directly, regards lifts of a compatible target element as a Mittag–Leffler system of nonempty cosets, and uses surjective stable-image transitions along a countable cofinal sequence to choose a compatible lift. No surjectivity of the original transitions is assumed.

#### The finite-submodule test for an integral element

If an element $y$ of an $R$-algebra $S$ preserves a finite $R$-submodule $M\subset S$ containing $1$, then $y$ is integral over $R$.

The complete determinant proof is Integral extensions: lying over, going up and going down, Section 1, Theorem 1.1. Choose generators of $M$ and express multiplication by $y$ as a coefficient matrix over $R$. Its monic characteristic polynomial annihilates every generator by the adjugate identity, hence annihilates $1$, proving the asserted equation for $y$. The generators need not be a basis. Equivalently, $M$ is faithful for the action of $R[y]$: an element acting as zero kills $1$ and is itself zero.

#### Additivity of module length

For a short exact sequence $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ over an arbitrary ring,
$$\ell(M)=\ell(M')+\ell(M'')$$
with values in $\mathbf N\cup\{\infty\}$.

Noetherian and Artinian rings, Section 3, Theorem 3.3 gives the complete composition-series proof: $M$ has finite length exactly when both ends do, and in that case the lengths add. The same equivalence handles all infinite cases. If either end has infinite length, the middle must also; if the middle has infinite length, the two ends cannot both be finite. Thus the formula retains its full extended-value scope.

#### Residue fields as composition factors

For a finite-length module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$, every simple factor is $R/\mathfrak m$ for a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. The number of occurrences of that residue field is
$$\ell_{R_{\mathfrak m}}(M_{\mathfrak m}).$$

The full proofs are Noetherian and Artinian rings, Section 3, Theorems 3.2–3.3 and Proposition 3.4. A nonzero vector in a simple module gives a cyclic presentation, whose kernel is maximal. Localizing a composition series at $\mathfrak m$ retains precisely its factors $R/\mathfrak m$ and kills all the others: for another maximal ideal choose an element in it but outside $\mathfrak m$. The surviving series has simple factors over $R_{\mathfrak m}$, proving the formula and its independence of the chosen series.

#### Schanuel's lemma and its diagram

Suppose two projective presentations of the same module are given over a ring $R$:
$$0\to K\xrightarrow{c_1}P_1\xrightarrow{p_1}M\to0,
\qquad
0\to L\xrightarrow{c_2}P_2\xrightarrow{p_2}M\to0.$$
Then $K\oplus P_2\cong P_1\oplus L$. Moreover, these presentations become isomorphic after adding the other projective module to their first two terms.

**Proof.** Form
$$E=\{(v,w)\in P_1\oplus P_2:p_1(v)+p_2(w)=0\}.$$
Projection onto $P_1$ is onto with kernel $L$; projection onto $P_2$ is onto with kernel $K$. Both sequences split because their quotients are projective. Consequently
$$K\oplus P_2\cong E\cong P_1\oplus L.$$
This is the fibre-product proof of Projective dimension, Lemma 1.1, with a minus sign in one projection to replace equality by a zero sum.

For the diagram, projectivity supplies $a\colon P_1\to P_2$ and $b\colon P_2\to P_1$ satisfying $p_2a=p_1$ and $p_1b=p_2$. Define automorphisms of $P_1\oplus P_2$ by
$$T=\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\a&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Their inverses replace $a,b$ by $-a,-b$. The equalities
$$(p_1,0)T=(p_1,p_2)=(0,p_2)U$$
show that their restrictions identify $E$ with the respective kernels. Using $c_1,c_2$ to identify these kernels gives the commutative diagram
$$\begin{array}{ccccc}
0\to K\oplus P_2&\xrightarrow{(c_1,\,1)}&P_1\oplus P_2&\xrightarrow{(p_1,\,0)}&M\to0\\
\uparrow\,T|_E&&\uparrow\,T&&\Vert\\
0\to E&\longrightarrow&P_1\oplus P_2&\xrightarrow{(p_1,\,p_2)}&M\to0\\
\downarrow\,U|_E&&\downarrow\,U&&\Vert\\
0\to P_1\oplus L&\xrightarrow{(1,\,c_2)}&P_1\oplus P_2&\xrightarrow{(0,\,p_2)}&M\to0 .
\end{array}$$
Every vertical map is an isomorphism. Composing the lower vertical maps with the inverses of the upper ones gives the claimed two-row comparison. ∎

#### Embedding dimension bounds residue-field projective dimension

For a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$,
$$\dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)\leq\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa,$$
where the right side may be infinite.

The full proof is Regular local rings, Lemma 2.1. A minimal generating list of length $e$ defines a Koszul complex mapping to the minimal free resolution of $\kappa$. Comparison modulo $\mathfrak m^2$ makes its degree-$i$ map injective after reduction modulo $\mathfrak m$. The exterior-coordinate map used in the induction is injective in every characteristic: each basis wedge has a coordinate obtained by deleting one of its indices and recording that index, and these coordinates distinguish the wedges. Thus the $i$-th free rank is at least $\binom ei$. In degree $e$ it cannot vanish, which proves the inequality without a characteristic restriction.

#### Resolutions over a regular local ring

Let $R$ be regular local of dimension $d$. A nonzero finite $R$-module $M$ of depth $e$ has a finite free resolution of length $d-e$. Also $\operatorname{gl.dim}R\leq d$, with the supremum taken over arbitrary modules.

These are proved in Projective dimension, Sections 1–4, specifically Theorems 1.5, 2.2, 2.3, 3.1 and Corollary 4.3. A regular parameter sequence gives a Koszul resolution of $\kappa$ of length $d$. Minimal free resolutions and their Tor detection then bound projective dimensions of finite modules. In particular they bound every cyclic quotient $R/J$, since $R$ is Noetherian. The cyclic-module test extends this bound to all modules by a well-ordered generator filtration and compatible projective resolutions; it does not assume arbitrary modules are finite. Finally the Auslander–Buchsbaum formula gives $\operatorname{pd}_RM=d-e$, and a minimal finite free resolution realizes this length.

#### A finite residue-field resolution is bounded by dimension

If $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ is Noetherian local and $n=\operatorname{pd}_R\kappa<\infty$, then $n\leq\dim R$. Regularity is not assumed.

**Proof.** The Auslander–Buchsbaum formula applies to the nonzero finite module $\kappa$. Its depth is zero, including when $R$ is a field. Therefore
$$n+\operatorname{depth}_R\kappa
=\operatorname{depth}R,\qquad n=\operatorname{depth}R.$$
The depth bound for finite modules, applied to $R$ itself, gives $\operatorname{depth}R\leq\dim R$. Combining these equalities and inequality proves the assertion. ∎

#### Finite length from a finitely generated maximal ideal

Let $\mathfrak m$ be a finitely generated maximal ideal of a ring $R$. If $M$ is a finite $R$-module and $\mathfrak m^nM=0$ for some $n$, then $M$ has finite length. Neither locality nor Noetherianity of $R$ is required.

**Proof.** Choose generators $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ of $\mathfrak m$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_s$ of $M$. Products $a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_j}v_l$ form a finite generating list for $\mathfrak m^jM$. Its quotient by $\mathfrak m^{j+1}M$ is therefore a finite-dimensional vector space over $R/\mathfrak m$, and its dimension is its $R$-module length. The filtration
$$M\supset\mathfrak mM\supset\cdots\supset\mathfrak m^nM=0$$
has finitely many such layers. Length additivity proves the assertion. If $n=0$, then $M=0$ and the length is zero. ∎

#### Powers of ideals contained in a radical

If $R$ is Noetherian and $I,J$ are ideals with $J\subset\sqrt I$, then $J^N\subset I$ for some $N\geq1$. In particular, an ideal all of whose elements are nilpotent is a nilpotent ideal.

**Proof.** More generally, only finite generation of $J$ is needed. Write $J=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ and choose positive integers $d_i$ with $a_i^{d_i}\in I$. For $r>0$, take
$$N=1+\sum_{i=1}^r(d_i-1).$$
A degree-$N$ product of the generators contains at least $d_i$ copies of some $a_i$; otherwise its degree would be at most $N-1$. Every such product belongs to $I$, and these products generate $J^N$. For $J=0$, choose $N=1$. Applying this with $I=0$ gives the last assertion. ∎

#### Quasi-finiteness over an intermediate base

Suppose $A\to B\to C$ are ring maps and $C$ is finite type over $A$. If $A\to C$ is quasi-finite at a prime $\mathfrak r$, then so is $B\to C$. No finiteness condition on $B/A$ is required.

The first pointwise argument in the [affine Zariski Main proof](#native-algebra-theorem-main-theorem) proves this directly: the same generators give finite type over $B$, and a principal open isolating $\mathfrak r$ in its fibre over $A$ isolates it in the smaller fibre over $B$.

#### Integral closure near a monogenic quasi-finite point

Let $S=R[X]/I$, let $C$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $S$, and let $\mathfrak q$ be a quasi-finite point of $S/R$. There is $g\in C\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $C_g=S_g$.

The monogenic part of the [affine Zariski Main proof](#native-algebra-theorem-main-theorem) is a complete proof for arbitrary rings. It starts with a relation having a coefficient outside the base prime, puts the leading-coefficient multiple of the generator in $C$, and reduces the degree until that leading coefficient avoids $\mathfrak q$. It does not use the conductor step or the full theorem inductively.

#### Quasi-finiteness is local at the selected fibre point

Let $R\to S$ be finite type, and let $\mathfrak q$ contract to $\mathfrak p$. For $f\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ and $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$, the map $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ exactly when $R_f\to S_{fg}$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak qS_{fg}$.

The pointwise locality argument in the [affine Zariski Main proof](#native-algebra-theorem-main-theorem) gives both directions. The base localization leaves the fibre unchanged; source localization is an open neighborhood of the selected point. Being isolated in that open fibre is equivalent to being isolated in the original fibre, or one may use equality of the local fibre rings and residue extensions.

#### Quasi-finiteness in a four-ring square

Consider a commutative square $R\to S$, $R'\to S'$, with vertical maps $R\to R'$ and $S\to S'$. Assume $S$ is finite type over $R$ and the induced map $S\otimes_RR'\to S'$ is surjective. If $\mathfrak q'\subset S'$ contracts to a quasi-finite point $\mathfrak q\subset S$ of $S/R$, then $S'/R'$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q'$.

The full four-ring argument in the [affine Zariski Main proof](#native-algebra-theorem-main-theorem) constructs the finite-dimensional isolated factor of the original fibre, extends its residue field, and takes its quotient in the new fibre. Its idempotent still selects $\mathfrak q'$, proving the assertion over arbitrary rings.

#### Strong transcendence rules out quasi-finite points

Suppose $R\subset S$ are reduced rings, $x\in S$, and $S$ is finite as an $R[x]$-module. Assume that every equality
$$u\sum_{i=0}^m a_ix^i=0,\qquad u\in S,\ a_i\in R,$$
forces $ua_i=0$ for each $i$. Then $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at no prime of $S$.

The complete proof is *The theorem on formal functions*, Appendix Z, Lemma Z.11. Lemma Z.9 passes the coefficient property to a minimal component using a localization zero witness. Lemma Z.10 treats the resulting domains, first by going down over a normal polynomial ring and then by integral normalization and lying over. Lemma Z.8 carries quasi-finiteness through the required quotient and base-change squares. Section 0 supplies polynomial normality over an arbitrary normal domain. These arguments allow infinitely many minimal primes and do not assume finite normalization.

#### All conductor coefficients lie in the radical

Let $\varphi\colon R[X]\to S$ be finite, and assume $\varphi(R)$ is integrally closed in $S$. Define
$$J=\{s\in S:sS\subset\operatorname{im}\varphi\}.$$
For $u\in S$ and $a_0,\ldots,a_m\in R$,
$$\begin{gathered}
u\,\varphi\left(\sum_{i=0}^m a_iX^i\right)\in\sqrt J\\
\Longrightarrow\quad u\,\varphi(a_i)\in\sqrt J\quad(0\leq i\leq m).
\end{gathered}$$

The full proof is *The theorem on formal functions*, Appendix Z, Lemma Z.6, with Situation Z.4 and Lemmas Z.1–Z.5. Monic division first removes a denominator up to an integral element. Localization and an explicit zero witness then clear the leading coefficient. Applying this to a finite module generating list puts a power of the leading coefficient in the conductor. Raising the original relation to a power and descending through its coefficients proves the radical assertion. Neither $\varphi$ nor its restriction to $R$ is required to be injective.

#### The cotangent space with separable residue

If a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ contains $k$ and $\kappa/k$ is finitely generated and separable, the canonical map
$$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{R/k}\otimes_R\kappa$$
is injective.

The first part of the [separable-residue smoothness proof](#native-algebra-lemma-separable-smooth) proves exactly this local-ring assertion before using finite type for the smoothness conclusion. It lifts a separating basis and corrects the primitive element by one Newton step in $R/\mathfrak m^2$, producing a residue-field section. The resulting derivation retracts the conormal map. The alternative formal-smoothness lift, and the product-rule identification of the differential fibre before and after quotienting by $\mathfrak m^2$, are also supplied there.

#### Extracting a root from power coefficients

Suppose $L/K$ is algebraic and separable in characteristic $p>0$, and $\alpha\in L$. If every coefficient of its minimal polynomial over $K$ is a $p$th power in $K$, then $\alpha$ is a $p$th power in $L$. The same conclusion holds whenever $\alpha$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial $P\in K[T]$ with distinct roots and with all coefficients in $K^p$.

**Proof.** Write $P(T)=\sum_i b_i^pT^i$ and $Q(T)=\sum_i b_iT^i$. In an algebraic closure containing $L$, let $\beta^p=\alpha$. The identity
$$Q(T)^p=P(T^p)$$
gives $Q(\beta)=0$. Frobenius identifies the roots of $Q$ with the roots of $P$, preserving their multiplicities, so $Q$ has distinct roots.

If $\beta\notin L$, its minimal polynomial over $L$ is $T^p-\alpha$. Indeed a nontrivial purely inseparable extension generated by a $p$th root has degree $p$: the minimal polynomial is a polynomial in $T^p$ unless its derivative is nonzero, in which case it is separable and must be linear since $T^p-\alpha$ has only one distinct root. Thus $T^p-\alpha$ would divide $Q$ in $L[T]$, contrary to the distinct-root property. Hence $\beta\in L$. The minimal polynomial in the first assertion has distinct roots by separability, so it is a special case. ∎

#### The separable part of an algebraic extension

For every algebraic extension $E/F$ there is exactly one intermediate field $E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ for which $E_{\mathrm{sep}}/F$ is separable and $E/E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is purely inseparable.

**Proof.** The elements of $E$ separable over $F$ form a field. To check closure, finitely many such elements generate a finite separable extension: adjoining them successively preserves separability, since their minimal polynomials at each step divide separable polynomials over $F$. The usual count of embeddings in a tower proves separability over $F$; sums, products and inverses then belong to that finite separable extension.

Call this field $E_{\mathrm{sep}}$. In characteristic zero it is all of $E$. In characteristic $p$, the irreducible polynomial of any $\alpha\in E$ has the form $G(T^{p^e})$ with $G$ irreducible and with nonzero derivative: repeatedly remove a common $p$th power from its exponents until this is so. Irreducibility then makes $G$ separable. Therefore $\alpha^{p^e}$ belongs to $E_{\mathrm{sep}}$, proving that $E/E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is purely inseparable. The exponent may depend on $\alpha$, so the argument includes infinite algebraic extensions.

For uniqueness, suppose $F\subset T\subset E$ has the stated properties. Separability gives $T\subset E_{\mathrm{sep}}$. Any $\alpha\in E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is separable over $T$, because its minimal polynomial there divides a separable polynomial over $F$; it is also purely inseparable over $T$. Its minimal polynomial is consequently linear, so $\alpha\in T$. This proves the reverse inclusion. ∎

#### Primitive elements and intermediate fields

A finite field extension $E/F$ is generated by one element if and only if it has only finitely many intermediate fields. Both properties hold for every finite separable extension.

**Proof.** Suppose $E=F(\alpha)$, and let $P$ be the monic minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$. For an intermediate field $K$, let $Q$ be its monic minimal polynomial over $K$. Put $L=F(\text{coefficients of }Q)\subset K$. Since $E=L(\alpha)$ and $Q(\alpha)=0$,
$$[E:L]\leq\deg Q=[E:K].$$
The tower formula gives the opposite inequality and then $L=K$. Thus $Q$ determines $K$. It is a monic divisor of $P$ in $E[T]$, and a fixed polynomial has only finitely many monic divisors by unique factorization. There are therefore finitely many possible $K$.

For the converse first suppose $F$ is infinite. A finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ cannot be the union of finitely many proper linear subspaces. For each proposed subspace choose a nonzero linear functional vanishing on it. Their product is a nonzero polynomial in coordinates. A nonzero polynomial over an infinite field cannot vanish on every coordinate tuple, as induction on the number of variables reduces this assertion to the finite root bound in one variable. A tuple where the product is nonzero avoids all the subspaces.

Apply this to the finitely many proper intermediate fields, each an $F$-linear subspace of $E$. An element outside their union generates $E$. When $E=F$, the element $0$ suffices.

If $F$ is finite, so is $E$. Its multiplicative group is cyclic: let $m$ be its exponent, and for each prime dividing $m$ choose an element whose order contains the largest corresponding prime power. Suitable powers of these elements have those prime-power orders, and their product has order $m$ because the orders are coprime. Every nonzero element of $E$ is a root of $T^m-1$, so $|E^\times|\leq m$. The element just constructed gives the reverse inequality. A generator of $E^\times$ thus generates $E$ as a field, proving this case too.

Finally, if $E/F$ is separable of degree $n$, it has $n$ distinct embeddings $\sigma_i$ into an algebraic closure of $F$. This count follows by adjoining finitely many generators and, at each step, extending an embedding through the distinct roots of the next separable minimal polynomial. For infinite $F$, the kernels of the nonzero linear maps $\sigma_i-\sigma_j$ form finitely many proper subspaces. Choose $\alpha$ outside them. Its $n$ distinct images force $[F(\alpha):F]\geq n$, while $F(\alpha)\subset E$ gives the reverse bound. Thus $E=F(\alpha)$. The finite-field case was already proved, completing all assertions. ∎

#### Transcendence bases with prescribed generators

Let $E/F$ be any field extension. If $A\subset G\subset E$, where $A$ is algebraically independent over $F$ and $F(G)=E$, there is a transcendence basis $B$ with $A\subset B\subset G$. All transcendence bases of $E/F$ have the same cardinality.

**Proof.** Order by inclusion the independent subsets of $G$ containing $A$. It is a nonempty family, and the union of a chain remains independent because every polynomial relation uses finitely many elements. Zorn's lemma supplies a maximal member $B$. Each $g\in G$ must be algebraic over $F(B)$, since otherwise it could be adjoined. Every element of $F(G)$ is then algebraic over $F(B)$, as it uses only finitely many such generators. This proves the prescribed-basis assertion.

The full finite exchange and arbitrary-cardinality proof is Krull dimension and Noether normalization, Section 1, Lemma 1.3. Its exchange step keeps previously inserted independent elements fixed and proves the needed algebraic-extension independence statement by a determinant. The infinite case assigns finite supporting subsets of one basis to elements of the other and applies the finite bound; reversing the comparison gives equality. It includes finite, infinite and empty bases. ∎

#### Detecting tensor-product defects in finite subalgebras

Let $R,S$ be algebras over a field $k$. Each of the following properties of $R\otimes_kS$ already holds for $R'\otimes_kS'$ for suitable finitely generated $k$-subalgebras $R'\subset R$ and $S'\subset S$:

1. it is not reduced;
2. it has a nonzero zero divisor;
3. it has an idempotent other than $0$ and $1$.

**Proof.** For any such subalgebras the canonical map
$$R'\otimes_kS'\longrightarrow R\otimes_kS$$
is injective. It factors through $R\otimes_kS'$, and each of the two maps is injective because every vector space over $k$ is flat.

For (1), express a nonzero nilpotent as a finite sum $\sum_i r_i\otimes s_i$ and generate $R',S'$ by its coefficients. The corresponding element in the smaller tensor product is nonzero, and its required power is zero by injectivity.

For (2), choose nonzero elements $x,y$ in the tensor product with $xy=0$, and include the coefficients of finite tensor expressions for both in the two subalgebras. Their preimages remain nonzero, and injectivity makes their product zero there.

For (3), do the same for the coefficients of the idempotent $e$. Injectivity gives $e^2=e$ in the smaller tensor product and preserves its distinction from $0$ and $1$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis on either original algebra is needed. ∎

#### Shifted Hilbert functions for an exact sequence

For a Noetherian local ring $R$, an ideal of definition $I$, and an exact sequence of finite modules
$$0\longrightarrow M'\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow M''\longrightarrow0,$$
there are $N\subset M'$ of finite colength $l$ and an integer $c\geq0$ such that, for every $n\geq c$,
$$\begin{aligned}
\chi_{I,M}(n)&=\chi_{I,M''}(n)+\chi_{I,N}(n-c)+l,\\
\varphi_{I,M}(n)&=\varphi_{I,M''}(n)+\varphi_{I,N}(n-c).
\end{aligned}$$
Here $\chi_{I,Q}(n)=\ell_R(Q/I^{n+1}Q)$ and $\varphi_{I,Q}(n)=\ell_R(I^nQ/I^{n+1}Q)$.

The [complete Hilbert-function proof](#native-algebra-lemma-hilbert-ses-chi) constructs $N=M'\cap I^cM$ using Artin–Rees, proves finite colength, and derives both identities, including the boundary value $n=c$ by setting $\chi_{I,Q}(-1)=0$.

#### Finite colength changes only lower Hilbert terms

Let $R$ be Noetherian local, let $I$ be an ideal of definition, and suppose $Q'\subset Q$ are finite modules with finite-length quotient. If $Q$ has infinite length, the eventual polynomials $\chi_{I,Q}$ and $\chi_{I,Q'}$ have the same positive degree, and their difference has smaller degree.

The [finite-colength argument in the Hilbert-function proof](#native-algebra-lemma-hilbert-ses-chi) proves this for every such inclusion. It chooses $I^bQ\subset Q'$, sets $a=\ell_R(Q/Q')$, and obtains, for $n\geq b$,
$$a+\chi_{I,Q'}(n-b)\leq\chi_{I,Q}(n)
\leq a+\chi_{I,Q'}(n).$$
The two bounds have identical leading terms. Infinite length excludes constant Hilbert growth by Nakayama, so the difference has degree strictly below either original degree.

#### Dimension under surjective prime-chain lifting

Let $R\to S$ satisfy going up or going down, and suppose $\operatorname{Spec}S\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is surjective. Then $\dim R\leq\dim S$, for arbitrary rings.

**Proof.** For going up, start with a prime of $S$ above the bottom member of any finite strict chain in $R$. Lift its successive steps by going up. Distinct contractions ensure that all lifted inclusions are strict. For going down, choose a prime above the top member and lift the same chain in reverse order. Thus every finite chain length in $R$ occurs in $S$. Taking suprema gives the inequality even when dimension is infinite. The empty spectrum is covered by the convention $\dim0=-\infty$. ∎

#### A triangular substitution with one highest term

Let $g\in R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$ be nonconstant over any ring $R$. There are positive integers $e_1\gg e_2\gg\cdots\gg e_n=1$ for which
