$$g(X_1+X_n^{e_1},\ldots,X_{n-1}+X_n^{e_{n-1}},X_n)
=aX_n^d+\text{terms of smaller degree in }X_n,$$
where $d>0$ and $a$ is one of the nonzero coefficients of $g$.

**Proof.** Write $g=\sum_\nu a_\nu X^\nu$ using only its finitely many nonzero coefficients. Choose an integer $B$ larger than every coordinate of those multi-indices and set $e_i=B^{n-i}$. The weights
$$w(\nu)=\nu_1B^{n-1}+\nu_2B^{n-2}+\cdots+\nu_n$$
are distinct by uniqueness of base-$B$ expansions. In the substituted monomial $X^\nu$, its term of highest $X_n$-degree is exactly $X_n^{w(\nu)}$ with coefficient $1$. Every other term has smaller $X_n$-degree, since at least one positive power of a newly added $X_n^{e_i}$ is replaced by $X_i$.

The unique multi-index of largest weight consequently contributes the unique top term of the whole expression, with its unchanged nonzero coefficient $a_\nu$. Its weight is positive because $g$ has a nonconstant term. No coefficient is divided out, so zero divisors in $R$ cause no problem. For $n=1$ the substitution is empty and this is the usual leading term. ∎

#### Dimension through a prime with a full-support Cohen–Macaulay module

If a Noetherian local ring $R$ admits a finite Cohen–Macaulay module with support $\operatorname{Spec}R$, then every prime $\mathfrak p$ satisfies
$$\dim R=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim(R/\mathfrak p).$$

**Proof.** The complete [maximal-chain theorem for full-support CM modules](#native-algebra-lemma-maximal-chain-maximal-cm) says that every maximal prime chain of $R$ has length $\dim R$. Its proof uses the module itself and does not assume that $R$ is CM.

Choose longest chains in $R_{\mathfrak p}$ and in $R/\mathfrak p$. Their lengths are attained because these Noetherian local rings have finite dimension. In $R$, the first runs from a minimal prime to $\mathfrak p$, and the second from $\mathfrak p$ to the maximal ideal. Concatenate them, counting $\mathfrak p$ only once. No step can be refined, since a refinement on either side would contradict the chosen maximal length; neither endpoint can be extended. The resulting maximal chain has the sum of the two lengths. The cited theorem identifies that sum with $\dim R$. ∎

#### Specializations from a constructibly closed set

Let $X$ be spectral. If $E$ is closed in its constructible topology, then every $x\in\overline E$ is a specialization of some point of $E$. Consequently a constructibly closed, specialization-stable subset is closed in the original topology. Dually, a constructibly open subset stable under generalization is open. These statements apply in particular to constructible subsets.

**Proof.** Recall that a spectral space is quasi-compact and sober and has a basis of quasi-compact opens closed under finite intersections. Its constructible topology is generated by those opens and their complements. We first prove the compactness needed here directly from these axioms.

Let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter on the underlying set of a nonempty $X$, and put
$$Z=X\setminus\bigcup\{V:V\text{ is quasi-compact open and }V\notin\mathcal U\}.$$
This is a closed set. It is nonempty: otherwise quasi-compactness of $X$ would give a finite cover by opens outside $\mathcal U$, whose union cannot belong to the ultrafilter. More generally, every quasi-compact open $W\in\mathcal U$ meets $Z$. If it did not, a finite subcover of $W$ by the excluded opens would give the same contradiction.

If an open set meets $Z$, a basis open contained in it and meeting $Z$ must belong to $\mathcal U$, by the definition of $Z$. For two such opens, intersect their chosen basis opens. Their intersection is quasi-compact and belongs to $\mathcal U$, so it meets $Z$ by the preceding paragraph. Hence $Z$ is irreducible. Sobriety gives its generic point $\eta$. A quasi-compact open $V$ contains $\eta$ exactly when it meets $Z$, which is exactly when $V\in\mathcal U$. Thus every basic neighborhood of $\eta$ in the constructible topology belongs to $\mathcal U$: it is a finite intersection of basis opens and their complements with the corresponding membership choices. The ultrafilter converges to $\eta$ in that topology.

This proves compactness by the ultrafilter criterion. Explicitly, any family of closed sets with the finite-intersection property extends to an ultrafilter; a limit of that ultrafilter lies in every member of the family, since each member is closed. The empty space is compact as well.

Now fix $x\in\overline E$ and take all quasi-compact open neighborhoods $U$ of $x$. Each $E\cap U$ is closed in the compact constructible topology, because $E$ is closed there and $U$ is clopen there. Any finite intersection is nonempty: its neighborhood factor is an open neighborhood of $x$, which meets $E$. Compactness therefore provides
$$y\in E\cap\bigcap_{U\ni x,\ U\text{ quasi-compact open}}U.$$
The basis property says that every open neighborhood of $x$ contains $y$. Equivalently, $x\in\overline{\{y\}}$, giving the first assertion.

If $E$ is stable under specialization, this places every point of $\overline E$ in $E$, so $E$ is closed. For the dual assertion, the complement is constructibly closed and specialization-stable, hence closed. Finally, in a spectral space a retrocompact open is quasi-compact, since $X$ itself is quasi-compact; thus constructible subsets, being finite Boolean combinations of these opens, are clopen in the constructible topology. ∎

#### An affine spectrum is spectral

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `lemma-spec-spectral».

For every ring $R$, its spectrum is quasi-compact and $T_0$, has a basis of quasi-compact opens stable under finite intersections, and every nonempty irreducible closed subset has a unique generic point. Hence it is a spectral space.

The second proof of [the constructible-specialization criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-constructible-stable-specialization-closed) verifies these properties from the affine-spectrum foundations and irreducibility theorem. It also gives the complete ultrafilter proof of compactness of the constructible topology and uses that compactness to recover the specialization criterion.

#### Open and closed sets under specialization

In every topological space, closed sets are stable under specialization and open sets are stable under generalization. A subset is specialization-stable exactly when its complement is generalization-stable.

**Proof.** Write $x\preceq y$ when $x\in\overline{\{y\}}$, so $x$ is a specialization of $y$. If a closed set contains $y$, it contains $\overline{\{y\}}$ and hence $x$. For an arbitrary subset $T$, the implication
$$y\in T,\quad x\preceq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in T$$
is equivalent by contraposition to
$$x\notin T,\quad x\preceq y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y\notin T.$$
This is precisely generalization stability of the complement. Applying it to a closed set proves the open-set assertion. ∎

#### Boolean operations on constructible subsets

Constructible subsets of an arbitrary topological space are closed under finite unions, finite intersections and complements.

Here an open $U\subset X$ is retrocompact if $U\cap W$ is quasi-compact for every quasi-compact open $W\subset X$. A constructible subset is a finite union of differences $U\setminus V$ of retrocompact opens. This is the global notion; no Noetherian or spectral hypothesis is imposed on $X$.

**Proof.** Both $X$ and $\varnothing$ are retrocompact opens. Finite unions of retrocompact opens are retrocompact, since intersecting with $W$ gives a finite union of quasi-compact subsets. For two such opens $U_1,U_2$, first $U_2\cap W$ is quasi-compact open, and then retrocompactness of $U_1$ makes $U_1\cap(U_2\cap W)$ quasi-compact. Thus finite intersections are retrocompact too.

For basic differences,
$$(U_1\setminus V_1)\cap(U_2\setminus V_2)
=(U_1\cap U_2)\setminus(V_1\cup V_2),$$
and
$$X\setminus(U\setminus V)=(X\setminus U)\cup V.$$
The right side of the second identity is the union of the two basic differences $X\setminus U$ and $V\setminus\varnothing$. Finite unions hold by definition; distribution proves finite intersections of arbitrary finite unions, and De Morgan's law then proves complements. ∎

#### Realizing a constructible set as an affine image

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `lemma-constructible-is-image».

Every constructible subset of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is the image of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ for a finitely presented $R$-algebra $B$.

The first proof of [the constructible-specialization criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-constructible-stable-specialization-closed) realizes each basic piece by $(R/(g_1,\ldots,g_m))_f$, then takes a finite product. It supplies a finite presentation for that product using orthogonal idempotents and inverse variables, and handles the empty set by $R/(1)$.

#### Principal-open images under affine-line projection

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `lemma-affineline-open».

The projection $\operatorname{Spec}R[x]\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is open. For $f=\sum_i a_ix^i$, the image of $D(f)$ is the quasi-compact open $\bigcup_iD(a_i)$.

The first terminal case in [Chevalley’s polynomial proof](#native-algebra-theorem-chevalley) proves this formula by identifying the fibre with the localization of $\kappa(\mathfrak p)[x]$ at the reduced polynomial. Taking unions proves openness for arbitrary opens.

#### An affine-line equation with invertible leading coefficient

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `lemma-affineline-special».

If the leading coefficient of $g\in R[x]$ is a unit, the image of $D(f)\cap V(g)$ in $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is a finite union of principal opens.

The second terminal case in [Chevalley’s polynomial proof](#native-algebra-theorem-chevalley) constructs them from the coefficients other than the leading coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by $f$ on $R[x]/(g)$. It proves compatibility with residue fields, the nilpotence test, and both directions of the fibre nonemptiness criterion. A constant unit $g$ gives the empty image.

#### Constructible images of finitely presented closed immersions

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `lemma-closed-fp».

For a finitely generated ideal $I\subset R$, the map $\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ carries every constructible subset to a constructible subset.

The closed-image reduction at the start of [Chevalley’s proof](#native-algebra-theorem-chevalley) lifts the finite list defining a basic constructible piece and adjoins a finite generating list of $I$ to its closed equations. It then takes finite unions. Finite generation of $I$ is retained.

#### Constructible images of principal localizations

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `lemma-open-fp».

For $c\in R$, contraction from $\operatorname{Spec}R_c$ sends constructible subsets to constructible subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}R$.

The localization reduction at the start of [Chevalley’s proof](#native-algebra-theorem-chevalley) clears powers of $c$ from each finite list of defining fractions. It expresses the image as a finite union of sets $D(ca)\cap V(b_1,\ldots,b_m)$, including the case of an empty localization.

#### Finite principal-open descriptions of constructible subsets

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `lemma-constructible».

A subset of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is constructible precisely when it is a finite union of pieces $D(f)\cap V(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$.

The initial reduction in [Chevalley’s proof](#native-algebra-theorem-chevalley) identifies retrocompact opens with quasi-compact opens, writes these as finite principal-open unions, and distributes the differences in the definition of constructibility. The reverse implication follows from the same description. This applies to arbitrary rings.

#### A reduced ring and its minimal-prime fields

For every reduced ring $R$, the canonical map
$$R\longrightarrow\prod_{\mathfrak p\text{ minimal}}R_{\mathfrak p}$$
is injective and all its factors are fields. Moreover, the union of the minimal primes is exactly the set of zero divisors, where a zero divisor means an element annihilating a nonzero element.

**Proof.** Localization of a reduced ring is reduced: if $(a/s)^n=0$, some denominator $t$ kills $a^n$, hence $(ta)^n=0$, so $ta=0$ and $a/s=0$. For a minimal prime $\mathfrak p$, the only prime of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$. It is therefore the nilradical and is zero. This local ring is a field, and the kernel of $R\to R_{\mathfrak p}$ is $\mathfrak p$.

The intersection of the minimal primes is the nilradical: every prime contains a minimal one, and the intersection of all primes is the nilradical. Since $R$ is reduced, this intersection is zero. This proves the asserted injection without any finiteness assumption on the set of minimal primes.

If $xy=0$ with $y\ne0$, some minimal prime avoids $y$, and primality puts $x$ in that prime. Conversely, if $x\in\mathfrak p$ for a minimal prime, its image in $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is zero. Some $s\notin\mathfrak p$ then satisfies $sx=0$, and $s\ne0$. Thus $x$ is a zero divisor. In the zero ring the product is empty and equals the zero ring, and both the union and the set of zero divisors are empty. ∎

#### The field calculation for the Cohen–Macaulay locus

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `lemma-where-CM».

Let $k$ be any field, let $T$ be a finite-type $k$-algebra, and let $k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\to T$ be quasi-finite. At $\mathfrak r\in\operatorname{Spec}T$, with contraction $\mathfrak a$, the local map
$$k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]_{\mathfrak a}\longrightarrow T_{\mathfrak r}$$
is flat if and only if $T_{\mathfrak r}$ is Cohen–Macaulay and $\dim_{\mathfrak r}\operatorname{Spec}T=d$.

The proof at the start of [the fixed-dimension Cohen–Macaulay fibre-locus lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-presentation-flat-cm-locus-open) establishes both directions. Quasi-finiteness supplies the zero-dimensional local fibre and finite residue extension. The dimension formula converts the point-dimension condition into equality of local dimensions, and miracle flatness gives one implication. For the other, flatness transports a regular parameter sequence and gives the local dimension equality. The argument includes nonclosed points and nonreduced algebras.

#### Openness of flatness over an arbitrary base

**Complete written proof.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `theorem-openness-flatness».

For a finitely presented algebra $A\to B$ and a finitely presented $B$-module $M$, the locus of primes $\mathfrak q\subset B$ where $M_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $A$ is open. At every such prime there is $g\notin\mathfrak q$ with $M_g$ flat over $A$.

The full proof is *Flatness criteria, dimension and the flat locus*, Theorem 6.4. Sections 1, 5 and 6 give its ideal criterion, Noetherian openness and eventual-flatness argument for finite models. The proof of generic freeness in *Flat morphisms*, §5 supplies the input in Section 5. Theorem 6.4 then passes an actual flat neighborhood from a Noetherian model to $A$. The base ring here is arbitrary; finite presentations are required of both the algebra and the module.

#### Uniqueness for marked henselian ind-étale algebras

Let $R$ be any ring. Suppose $S$ and $S'$ are henselian local rings, each a filtered colimit of étale $R$-algebras. Suppose also that specified residue maps $S\to K$ and $S'\to K$ to one field induce the same map from $R$. There is exactly one $R$-algebra isomorphism $S\to S'$ respecting those residue maps.

**Proof.** Their maximal ideals contract to the same prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R$, and both residue extensions are identified with the given $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-field $K$. Apply the full [ind-étale evaluation theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-map-into-henselian-colimit), first with source $S$ and target $S'$ and then with these roles reversed, using the identity of $K$ as residue embedding. It gives unique local maps $u\colon S\to S'$ and $v\colon S'\to S$ with the required markings. Each composite has the same marking as the identity; uniqueness in the same theorem makes $vu=1$ and $uv=1$. That theorem's proof evaluates every étale stage and uses uniqueness to make the evaluations compatible. Thus it applies to arbitrary $R$ and arbitrary common residue extension $K$, as required. ∎

#### Composition of filtered étale presentations

For maps $A\to B\to C$, assume that $B$ is a filtered colimit of étale $A$-algebras and that $C$ is a filtered colimit of étale $B$-algebras. Then $C$ is a filtered colimit of étale $A$-algebras.

**Proof.** By the complete [finite-presentation factorization criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-when-colimit), it suffices to factor every $A$-algebra map $P\to C$, with $P$ finitely presented over $A$, through an étale $A$-algebra.

Write $B=\operatorname{colim}_i B_i$ and $C=\operatorname{colim}_j C_j$ with the stated étale stages. Finite presentation first factors $P\to C$ through some $C_j$. The [étale descent theorem, part (9)](#native-algebra-lemma-etale) gives a stage $i$ and an étale $B_i$-algebra $D$ with
$$C_j\cong B\otimes_{B_i}D.$$
This is the filtered colimit of $B_{i'}\otimes_{B_i}D$ over stages receiving a map from $i$. Finite presentation of $P$ factors its map once more, through one such algebra $D'=B_{i'}\otimes_{B_i}D$. Étale base change makes $D'$ étale over $B_{i'}$, and composition with the étale map $A\to B_{i'}$ makes it étale over $A$. The resulting $P\to D'\to C$ is the desired factorization. These arguments hold for filtered categories as well as directed sets: the category of arrows out of $i$ is filtered, and every finite diagram can be placed at a common later stage. ∎

#### Finite algebras and quasi-finite points over a henselian base

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be henselian local.

1. A finite $R$-algebra is a finite product of henselian local rings, each finite over $R$.
2. A finite local $R$-algebra is henselian, and its structure map is local.
3. If a finite-type $R$-algebra $S$ is quasi-finite at a prime $\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak m$, then $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is henselian and finite over $R$.
4. In particular, (3) holds at every prime over $\mathfrak m$ whenever $S/R$ is quasi-finite.

**Proof.** Use the full [henselian equivalences](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-henselian), including finite-algebra decomposition and finite-part decomposition for finite-type algebras. If $S$ is finite and local over $R$, integrality makes its maximal ideal contract to a maximal ideal of $R$, necessarily $\mathfrak m$. The map is local. Every finite $S$-algebra is finite over $R$, so decomposes as a finite product of local rings by the henselian criterion for $R$. The same criterion applied to $S$ proves that $S$ is henselian. Decomposing an arbitrary finite $R$-algebra first and applying this argument to its finite local factors proves (1) and (2).

For (3), the finite-part criterion gives $S=S_1\times S_2$, with $S_1$ finite over $R$ and $S_2$ having no quasi-finite point over $\mathfrak m$. Thus $\mathfrak q$ belongs to $S_1$. Decompose that finite algebra into its henselian local factors as above. The point over $\mathfrak m$ is the maximal ideal of one factor, and localization there is that factor itself. This identifies $S_{\mathfrak q}$ as finite and henselian. Part (4) follows at once. The finite-part criterion uses the complete algebraic Zariski Main proof already given in the linked henselian argument. ∎

#### Filtered local limits of henselian rings

A filtered colimit of henselian local rings along local maps is henselian local. If all stages are strictly henselian, so is the colimit.

**Proof.** Let $R=\operatorname{colim}_iR_i$, with maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_i$. Locality of the maps gives a compatible system of residue fields $\kappa_i$ and embeddings between them. The map
$$R\longrightarrow\kappa=\operatorname{colim}_i\kappa_i$$
is surjective; its kernel consists exactly of classes represented in the stage maximal ideals. A class outside this kernel has a representative that is already a unit at its stage. Hence $R$ is local with that kernel as maximal ideal and with residue field $\kappa$.

Given a monic polynomial over $R$ and a specified simple root in $\kappa$, place its coefficients and that root at one stage. The residue fields embed in $\kappa$, so the root equation and the nonzero derivative already hold there. Henselianity of the stage lifts this simple root, and its image in $R$ supplies the required lift. Thus $R$ is henselian.

If every $\kappa_i$ is separably closed, every monic separable polynomial over $\kappa$ splits there. Indeed its coefficients and a Bézout identity with its derivative are defined at a common stage; the identity makes that stage polynomial separable. It splits into linear factors over the separably closed stage field, and the same factorization holds over $\kappa$. Consequently $\kappa$ is separably closed, proving strict henselianity. The finite-data arguments also cover filtered indexing categories. ∎

#### Finite presentation over a Noetherian ring

For a Noetherian ring $R$, every finite $R$-module is finitely presented, every submodule of a finite $R$-module is finite, and every finite-type $R$-algebra is finitely presented over $R$.

**Proof.** Every submodule of $R^s$ is finite, by induction on $s$: projection to the last coordinate has image an ideal of $R$, hence finitely generated, while its kernel is a submodule of $R^{s-1}$. Lift generators of that image and append generators of the kernel. For a submodule of a finite module $M$, take its inverse image under a finite free surjection onto $M$ and then take the images of a finite generating list. This proves the second assertion.

The kernel of a finite free surjection onto $M$ is therefore finite, giving a finite presentation and the first assertion. Finally present a finite-type algebra as $R[X_1,\ldots,X_s]/I$. The complete Hilbert-basis proof in Noetherian and Artinian rings, Section 2 makes the polynomial ring Noetherian. Hence $I$ has finitely many generators, giving the finite algebra presentation. These arguments include zero modules and zero algebras. ∎

#### Finite presentation detected by tensoring with products

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `proposition-fp-tensor».

An $R$-module $M$ is finitely presented exactly when the canonical map
$$M\otimes_R\prod_{\alpha\in A}Q_\alpha
\longrightarrow\prod_{\alpha\in A}(M\otimes_RQ_\alpha)$$
is bijective for every family of modules. It is equivalent to test every constant family, and also equivalent to test only the families with every $Q_\alpha=R$, allowing every set $A$.

The full proof appears in [the coherence theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-characterize-coherent). It compares two cokernels from a finite presentation in one direction. In the other, it first forces finite generation of $M$, then proves that the kernel of a finite free surjection onto $M$ satisfies the product-surjectivity criterion and is therefore finite.

#### Finite generation detected by tensoring with products

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex» / `proposition-fg-tensor».

An $R$-module $M$ is finitely generated exactly when the preceding comparison map is surjective for every family. Testing all constant families gives the same criterion, as does testing only powers of $R$.

The proof in [the coherence theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-characterize-coherent) constructs preimages using any finite generating list. Conversely, take the index set to be the underlying set of $M$ and use the tuple that lists every element of $M$. Any tensor preimage involves only finitely many elements of $M$, and coordinate comparison shows that they generate it. This establishes the criterion for arbitrary modules over arbitrary rings.

#### Symmetry, sums and the tensor unit

For modules $M,N,P$ over a commutative ring $R$, the following maps are canonical isomorphisms:
$$\begin{aligned}
M\otimes_RN&\longrightarrow N\otimes_RM,
&m\otimes n&\longmapsto n\otimes m,\\
(M\oplus N)\otimes_RP&\longrightarrow
(M\otimes_RP)\oplus(N\otimes_RP),
&(m,n)\otimes p&\longmapsto(m\otimes p,n\otimes p),\\
R\otimes_RM&\longrightarrow M,
&r\otimes m&\longmapsto rm.
\end{aligned}$$

**Proof.** Each indicated formula is additive in both inputs and balanced over $R$, so the tensor universal property gives a unique linear map. For symmetry the same formula in the opposite direction is its inverse. For sums, the inverse sends $(m\otimes p,0)$ to $(m,0)\otimes p$ and $(0,n\otimes p)$ to $(0,n)\otimes p$, extending linearly. The composites are identities because $(m,n)=(m,0)+(0,n)$. For the unit map the inverse is $m\mapsto1\otimes m$; the identity $1\otimes rm=r\otimes m$ checks the other composite. Pure tensors generate each tensor product, so these verifications prove all assertions, including uniqueness and naturality. ∎

#### Associativity with a bimodule

Let $A,B$ be commutative rings, let $M$ be an $A$-module and $P$ a $B$-module, and let $N$ be an $(A,B)$-bimodule with commuting left $A$- and right $B$-actions. There is a canonical bimodule isomorphism
$$\bigl(M\otimes_AN\bigr)\otimes_BP
\longrightarrow M\otimes_A\bigl(N\otimes_BP\bigr),
\qquad (m\otimes n)\otimes p\longmapsto m\otimes(n\otimes p).$$

**Proof.** The right $B$-action on $M\otimes_AN$ is $(m\otimes n)b=m\otimes(nb)$. It respects the $A$-balancing relation because the two actions on $N$ commute. Likewise $N\otimes_BP$ has left action $a(n\otimes p)=(an)\otimes p$. Commutativity of $A$ and $B$ also lets $A$ act through $M$ and $B$ act through $P$ on either iterated tensor product. These actions commute.

Both iterated tensors impose exactly the same additivity relations and the two balancing relations
$$am\otimes n\otimes p=m\otimes an\otimes p,\qquad
m\otimes nb\otimes p=m\otimes n\otimes bp.$$
The displayed associativity formula and its reverse therefore descend to the quotients. They preserve both outer actions and are inverse on elementary tensors, which generate the modules. Thus they are inverse bimodule maps, with no finiteness or flatness hypotheses. ∎

#### Finite algebras

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex` / `lemma-produce-finite`.

Suppose $R\to C\to D$ are ring maps, $C$ is integral over $R$, $D$ is finite type over $R$, and $C_g\to D_g$ is an isomorphism for some $g\in C$. If $g$ is a unit in $C\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, then some $b\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ makes $D_b$ finite over $R_b$. The final general argument in [the one-branch étale construction](#native-algebra-lemma-etale-makes-quasi-finite-finite-one-prime) proves this exact statement using the closed image of $V(g)$ under the integral map. No injectivity of $C\to D$ or finite presentation of $D$ is assumed.

#### Étale lifting of prescribed coprime factors

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex` / `lemma-factor-mod-lift-etale`.

For a monic $f\in R[T]$ and a factorization $\bar f=\bar h\bar i$ into coprime polynomials over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, there is an étale $R\to R'$ with a prime $\mathfrak p'$ above $\mathfrak p$, the same canonical residue field, and a factorization $f=hi$ whose factors have the prescribed reductions and generate the unit ideal in $R'[T]$. The coefficient-Jacobian argument in [the one-branch construction](#native-algebra-lemma-etale-makes-quasi-finite-finite-one-prime) proves this, including the Bézout identity, nonmaximal base primes, factors of degree zero, and normalization and restoration of nonmonic factors.

#### Eight descriptions of a zero-dimensional spectrum

For any ring $R$, put $X=\operatorname{Spec}R$. The following are equivalent:

1. $X$ is profinite, meaning an inverse limit of finite discrete spaces.
2. $X$ is Hausdorff.
3. $X$ is totally disconnected.
4. Every quasi-compact open subset of $X$ is also closed.
5. No two distinct prime ideals of $R$ are comparable by inclusion.
6. Every prime ideal is maximal.
7. Every prime ideal is minimal.
8. Every principal open $D(f)$ is closed.

**First proof.** Conditions (5), (6) and (7) are equivalent: primes lie inside maximal ideals and contain minimal primes, so either endpoint condition excludes strict inclusions. Conditions (4) and (8) are equivalent because principal opens are quasi-compact and form a basis; a quasi-compact open is a finite union of them.

Assume (7). Fix $f\in R$ and a prime $\mathfrak p$ containing $f$. The only prime of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is its maximal ideal, since primes there correspond to primes contained in $\mathfrak p$. Hence $f/1$ belongs to its nilradical. Some power of $f/1$ is zero, so there are $n\geq1$ and $s\notin\mathfrak p$ with $sf^n=0$ in $R$. Every prime avoiding $s$ then contains $f$. Thus $D(s)\subset V(f)$ is an open neighborhood of $\mathfrak p$. Varying $\mathfrak p$ proves that $V(f)$ is open, so $D(f)$ is closed. This proves (7)$\Rightarrow$(8) without reducedness or Noetherianity.

Under (8), distinct primes are separated by a principal open and its complement: choose an element belonging to one prime but not the other, interchanging them if necessary. Both sets are open. Thus $X$ is Hausdorff, and any subset containing those two points is disconnected by this separation. This gives (2) and (3).

A Hausdorff space has closed singletons, so (2) makes every prime maximal, giving (6). If two distinct primes were comparable, their two-point subspace would be connected: every open containing the specialization contains its generalization, preventing a separation into two nonempty opens. Thus (3) implies (5). We have proved the equivalence of (2)–(8).

For completeness, under these conditions $X$ has a basis of clopen subsets and is quasi-compact. Consider all finite partitions of $X$ into nonempty clopen cells, ordered by refinement, and the finite discrete set of cells of each partition. Refinements induce maps between these finite sets. A point of $X$ chooses a compatible cell in every partition. Conversely, a compatible choice of cells has the finite-intersection property: a common refinement of finitely many partitions has its selected cell inside every selected cell in that finite list. Quasi-compactness gives a point in their intersection. It is unique because clopen sets separate distinct points. These inverse maps are continuous, since a condition selecting a cell is a basic inverse-limit cylinder and that cell is clopen in $X$. They give a homeomorphism from $X$ to the inverse limit. Hence (2)–(8) imply (1). An inverse limit of finite discrete spaces is Hausdorff, as a subspace of a product of Hausdorff spaces, so (1) implies (2). For the empty spectrum use the constant inverse system with empty finite space; all the other assertions are vacuous.

**Spectral-space proof.** The complete [affine spectral theorem](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-spec-spectral) supplies the spectral axioms for $X$. Under (5) there are no nontrivial specializations or generalizations. Every constructible subset and its complement are therefore specialization-stable. The [constructible-closure theorem](#uncovered-topology-lemma-constructible-stable-specialization-closed) makes both closed in the original topology. In particular, principal opens are clopen, proving (8) by the spectral route. Conversely, Hausdorffness or total disconnectedness excludes nontrivial specializations, and a clopen principal basis separates points as above. Quasi-compactness and the finite-partition construction then give profiniteness. This retains the second proof through spectral topology. ∎

#### The element construction of a directed colimit

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex` / `lemma-directed-colimit`.

For a module system over any directed preordered set, take the disjoint union of its modules and identify two elements precisely when their images agree at a common later index. Addition is performed at a common index and scalar multiplication on a representative. The proof of [the directed-colimit vanishing criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-zero-directed-limit) checks the equivalence relation, independence of all choices, the module axioms and the universal property. It also proves the exact criterion for a representative to give zero. Neither antisymmetry of the indexing preorder nor injectivity of transition maps is required.

#### The tensor–Hom adjunction

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex` / `lemma-hom-from-tensor-product`.

For arbitrary $R$-modules $M,N,P$, there is a natural $R$-linear isomorphism

$$\operatorname{Hom}_R(M\otimes_RN,P)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P)).$$

The proof of [tensor right exactness](#native-algebra-lemma-tensor-product-exact) constructs both maps, checks bilinearity and linearity, verifies that they are inverse, and identifies their compatibility with maps in all three arguments.

#### The module equalizer on a finite principal cover

**Complete proof in this lesson.** Native locator: `algebra.tex` / `lemma-cover-module`.

For any $R$-module $M$ and any finite family $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ generating the unit ideal, the canonical sequence

$$0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow\bigoplus_iM_{f_i}
\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{i,j}M_{f_if_j}$$

is exact, with the last map given by pairwise differences on overlaps. The proof of [the principal-cover equalizer](#native-algebra-lemma-standard-covering) establishes this full module statement before its ring specialization. It checks exactness after maximal localization, where one cover member becomes the whole module, and proves the required detection of a zero module by its maximal localizations.

#### Functoriality of the prime spectrum

A ring homomorphism $\varphi\colon R\to S$ induces a continuous map
$$\operatorname{Spec}S\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}R,
\qquad\mathfrak q\longmapsto\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q).$$
The inverse image of $D(f)$ is $D(\varphi(f))$.

**Proof.** The inverse image ideal is proper because $1$ maps to $1$, and it is prime because a product belongs to it precisely when the corresponding product belongs to $\mathfrak q$. A prime $\mathfrak q$ avoids $\varphi(f)$ exactly when its contraction avoids $f$, proving the formula for principal opens and hence continuity. Contraction under an identity is the identity, and contraction under a composite is successive contraction in reverse order. Thus this construction is the contravariant spectrum functor. ∎

#### Differentials after quotienting by one more ideal power

For a map $R\to S$, any ideal $I\subset S$ and $n\geq1$, put $S'=S/I^{n+1}$. There is a canonical isomorphism
$$\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SS/I^n
\ \cong\ \Omega_{S'/R}\otimes_{S'}S/I^n.$$

**Proof.** The complete [quotient differential sequence](#native-algebra-lemma-differential-seq) presents $\Omega_{S'/R}$ as the quotient of $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SS'$ by the differentials of elements of $I^{n+1}$. The Leibniz rule gives $d(I^{n+1})\subset I^n\Omega_{S/R}$: differentiate a product of $n+1$ ideal elements and each summand still has $n$ such factors. Each element of the ideal power is a finite sum of such products. Tensoring with $S/I^n$ therefore kills this relation map. Right exactness identifies the two remaining terms by the stated isomorphism. No finiteness condition on $I$ or $S$ is used. ∎

#### Formal smoothness of polynomial algebras

For any ring $R$ and any set $J$, the polynomial algebra $R[X_j\mid j\in J]$ is formally smooth over $R$.

**Proof.** In a lifting diagram against a square-zero quotient $T\to T/K$, choose in $T$ a lift of the specified image of each variable $X_j$. The polynomial universal property extends these choices and the given map from $R$ to a unique $R$-algebra map from the polynomial algebra. Its reduction is the prescribed map because it agrees on $R$ and all variables. Polynomial expressions use only finitely many variables, so the construction works for arbitrary $J$, including the empty set. In fact it gives a lift against every surjective ring map, without needing the square-zero assumption. ∎

#### Algebraic residue extensions over a closed base point

Let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ lie above a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $R$. If $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is algebraic over $\kappa(\mathfrak m)$, then $\mathfrak q$ is maximal in $S$.

**Proof.** There are inclusions
$$R/\mathfrak m\subset S/\mathfrak q\subset\kappa(\mathfrak q).$$
Every nonzero element $a$ of the intermediate domain is algebraic over the first field. Its monic minimal polynomial has nonzero constant coefficient; solving that equation for $a^{-1}$ writes the inverse as a polynomial in $a$ with coefficients in $R/\mathfrak m$. The inverse therefore lies in $S/\mathfrak q$, making that domain a field. Thus $\mathfrak q$ is maximal. This is also the [general intermediate-field argument](#uncovered-fields-lemma-subalgebra-algebraic-extension-field), and requires neither finite type nor finite degree. ∎

#### Local dimension at a closed point over a field

If $S$ is a finite-type algebra over a field $k$ and $x$ corresponds to a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, then
$$\dim_x\operatorname{Spec}S=\dim S_{\mathfrak m}.$$

**Proof.** The full [dimension-at-a-point formula](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-at-a-point-finite-type-field) gives the right side plus $\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(\mathfrak m)$. The [Nullstellensatz](#native-algebra-theorem-nullstellensatz) makes this residue field finite over $k$, so that extra term is zero. The component proof of the dimension formula includes reducible and nonreduced algebras and arbitrary ground fields. ∎

#### The algebraic and topological Jacobson conditions

A ring $R$ is Jacobson if and only if the closed points of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ are dense in every closed subset. Here the algebraic condition means that each prime is the intersection of the maximal ideals containing it.

**Proof.** First this algebraic condition is equivalent to the corresponding condition for every radical ideal. If $I=\sqrt I$ and $f\notin I$, the intersection-of-primes description supplies a prime $\mathfrak p\supset I$ avoiding $f$. Some maximal ideal containing $\mathfrak p$ then avoids $f$, by the assumed intersection equality for $\mathfrak p$. This proves the radical-ideal equality. The converse follows by taking $I$ prime.

For a radical ideal $I$, put $J=\bigcap_{\mathfrak m\supset I,\ \mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}\mathfrak m$. The closed points of $V(I)$ are those maximal ideals, and their closure is $V(J)$: a closed set contains all of them exactly when its defining ideal is contained in their intersection. Hence their density in $V(I)$ is equivalent to $V(J)=V(I)$. Both ideals are radical, so the radical-ideal/closed-set correspondence makes this equivalent to $I=J$. This proves both directions, including the empty closed subset, for which the empty intersection is the whole ring. ∎

#### Finite-type field algebras are Jacobson

Every algebra generated by finitely many elements over a field is a Jacobson ring.

**Proof.** The full [Nullstellensatz proof](#native-algebra-theorem-nullstellensatz) states that the polynomial algebra over an arbitrary field is Jacobson. A quotient of a Jacobson ring is Jacobson: prime and maximal ideals of $R/I$ correspond to the respective ideals of $R$ containing $I$, and quotienting their intersection equality preserves it. Every finite-type field algebra is such a polynomial quotient. Equivalently, the radical-ideal form of the same Nullstellensatz says directly that every radical ideal of this algebra is an intersection of maximal ideals. ∎

#### Faithful flatness detected on homomorphisms

An $R$-module $F$ is faithfully flat exactly when it is flat and, for every homomorphism $\alpha\colon M\to N$,
$$\alpha=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\alpha\otimes_R1_F=0.$$

**Proof.** Flatness identifies the image of $\alpha\otimes1_F$ with $(\operatorname{im}\alpha)\otimes_RF$. If $F$ is faithfully flat, tensoring detects zero modules, so a zero tensored map forces $\operatorname{im}\alpha=0$. The forward implication is automatic.

Conversely, apply the assumed zero-map test to $1_M$. If $M\otimes_RF=0$, its identity tensors to zero, so $1_M=0$ and $M=0$. Flatness therefore preserves homology of every complex and detects whether that homology vanishes. It both preserves and reflects exactness, which is faithful flatness. All modules here may be infinitely generated. ∎

#### A Tor surjection after a flat pulled-back module

Let $R\to R'\to R''$ be ring maps and let $M$ be an $R$-module. If $M\otimes_RR'$ is flat over $R'$, then the natural map
$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R')\otimes_{R'}R''
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R'')$$
is surjective.

**Proof.** Choose an exact presentation $0\to K\to P\to M\to0$ with $P$ free, and put
$$T=\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R'),\qquad
L=\operatorname{im}(K\otimes_RR'\to P\otimes_RR').$$
There are exact sequences
$$T\longrightarrow K\otimes_RR'\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow0,$$
$$0\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow P\otimes_RR'
\longrightarrow M\otimes_RR'\longrightarrow0.$$
Tensor the first over $R'$ with $R''$; it remains right exact. Tensor the second with $R''$; its left injection remains injective because its quotient is flat. Consequently
$$\ker(K\otimes_RR''\to P\otimes_RR'')$$
is exactly the image of $T\otimes_{R'}R''$. The kernel is $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R'')$ by the original free presentation. All identifications commute with the structural maps, so the resulting surjection is the natural comparison map. No flatness of either ring map was assumed. ∎

#### The quotient-base Tor comparison

Let $R\to R'$ be a ring map, let $I\subset R$, and put $I'=IR'$ and $M'=M\otimes_RR'$. For every $R$-module $M$, the canonical map
$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R'/I',M)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(R'/I',M')$$
is surjective.

**Proof.** With a free presentation $0\to K\to P\to M\to0$, set $P'=P\otimes_RR'$ and $K'=\ker(P'\to M')$. Right exactness gives a surjection $K\otimes_RR'\to K'$. Write $Q=R'/I'$. Any element in
$$\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',Q)
=\ker(K'\otimes_{R'}Q\to P'\otimes_{R'}Q)$$
lifts to $K\otimes_RQ$. Its image in $P\otimes_RQ=P'\otimes_{R'}Q$ is zero, so the lift belongs to $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,Q)$. This proves the comparison surjection; symmetry of Tor gives the order of arguments in the statement.

The free-resolution description makes the same map explicit. Tensor a free $R$-resolution of $M$ with $R'$. It remains exact at degree zero. To obtain a resolution of $M'$ through degree one, add a free summand in degree two mapping onto the missing degree-one cycles, and continue freely in higher degrees. After tensoring with $Q$, degree-one cycles are unchanged and the degree-two boundary subgroup can only increase. The quotient map on homology is the stated natural surjection. This also verifies directly that no flatness or finiteness hypothesis enters. ∎

#### Intermediate subrings in an algebraic field extension

If $F\subset A\subset E$, where $F,E$ are fields and $E/F$ is algebraic, then the intermediate ring $A$ is a field.

**Proof.** For $0\ne a\in A$, its minimal polynomial over $F$ has the form
$$a^d+c_{d-1}a^{d-1}+\cdots+c_1a+c_0=0,\qquad c_0\ne0.$$
Solving for the inverse gives
$$a^{-1}=-c_0^{-1}(a^{d-1}+c_{d-1}a^{d-2}+\cdots+c_1)\in A.$$
Thus all nonzero elements of $A$ are invertible. Each calculation uses only one algebraic element, so no finite-degree assumption on $E/F$ is needed. Alternatively, $E$ is integral over $A$ because its monic equations over $F$ are also equations over $A$; the integral-domain field criterion gives the same conclusion. ∎

#### Noetherianity over a field or the integers

Every finite-type algebra over a field, and every finite-type algebra over $\mathbf Z$, is Noetherian.

**Proof.** A field has only two ideals. Every ideal of $\mathbf Z$ is principal, so this ring too is Noetherian. The full [Noetherian permanence theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-noetherian-permanence) proves that polynomial rings over a Noetherian base are Noetherian and that quotients remain Noetherian. Presenting the given algebra as a quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables proves both assertions. ∎

#### Differentials in a square with surjective target map

Consider a commutative square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
R&\longrightarrow&S\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\varphi\\
R'&\xrightarrow{\beta}&S',
\end{array}$$
where $\varphi$ is surjective. Then $\Omega_{S/R}\to\Omega_{S'/R'}$ is surjective. Its kernel is the $S$-submodule generated by
$$da\quad\text{for }a\in S\text{ with }\varphi(a)\in\beta(R').$$
In particular these generators include $di$ for every $i\in I=\ker\varphi$.

**Proof by universal derivations.** Let $N$ be the displayed submodule and put $Q=\Omega_{S/R}/N$. For $i\in I$ and $s\in S$, both $di$ and $d(is)$ belong to $N$. The identity
$$i\,ds=d(is)-s\,di$$
therefore shows $I\Omega_{S/R}\subset N$. Thus $Q$ is an $S'$-module. The derivation $S\to Q$, $s\mapsto ds\bmod N$, kills $I$ and descends to $S'$. It kills $\beta(R')$ because every element of that image has a lift $a\in S$ with $da\in N$. It is consequently an $R'$-derivation and gives a map $\Omega_{S'/R'}\to Q$.

Conversely, composition of the universal $R'$-derivation with $\varphi$ is an $R$-derivation on $S$ killing the displayed generators of $N$, so gives $Q\to\Omega_{S'/R'}$. The composites fix every generator $ds'$ or $ds\bmod N$, respectively. They are identities. This identifies $Q$ with $\Omega_{S'/R'}$ and proves the kernel assertion as well as surjectivity.

**Proof from presentations.** The presentation of differentials has generators $[s]$ and relations for addition, multiplication and the base constants. Surjectivity of $S\to S'$ lifts every target generator and every coefficient. The additive and product relations lift to the corresponding relations upstairs. The additional constant relations are precisely $[a]=0$ when $\varphi(a)$ belongs to the new base image. Two lifts of an element of $S'$ differ by $i\in I$, and $di=0$ is among these same relations. Coefficients differing by $I$ have no further effect, by $I\Omega_{S/R}\subset N$ proved above. Hence quotienting by exactly $N$ gives the target presentation, proving the same result. Both arguments account for the quotient ideal and the change of base. ∎

#### Associated components of a Cohen–Macaulay module

Let $M$ be a finite Cohen–Macaulay module over a Noetherian local ring $R$. Every $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}_R(M)$ is minimal in $\operatorname{Supp}M$, and
$$\dim(R/\mathfrak p)=\dim\operatorname{Supp}M.$$
In particular, there are no embedded associated primes.

**Proof.** For $M\ne0$, the complete depth bound and component proof are Regular sequences, depth and Cohen–Macaulay modules, Sections 3–4, Theorems 3.1 and 4.1. They give
$$\operatorname{depth}M\leq\dim(R/\mathfrak p)
\leq\dim\operatorname{Supp}M.$$
The outer quantities agree because $M$ is CM, so both inequalities are equalities. If $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ were a smaller prime in the support, adjoining it to a chain above $\mathfrak p$ of this maximal length would produce a longer chain in the support, a contradiction. Thus $\mathfrak p$ is minimal. For $M=0$, both the associated-prime and support sets are empty and the statement is vacuous. The historical source for this component statement is EGA, Chapter 0, Proposition 16.5.4. ∎

#### Associated primes surviving a power quotient

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $M$ be finite, and let $x\in\mathfrak m$. If $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Ass}M$ and $\mathfrak q$ is minimal over $\mathfrak p+(x)$, then
$$\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(M/x^nM)$$
for some $n\geq1$.

**Proof.** Choose $L\subset M$ isomorphic to $R/\mathfrak p$. The complete [Artin–Rees lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-artin-rees) supplies $n\geq1$ with $L\cap x^nM\subset xL$: if its stabilization index is $c$, take $n\geq c+1$. The image
$$\overline L=L/(L\cap x^nM)\subset M/x^nM$$
then surjects onto $L/xL=R/(\mathfrak p+(x))$. Hence $\mathfrak q$ is in its support. Both $\mathfrak p$ and $x^n$ annihilate $\overline L$, so every prime of that support contains $\mathfrak p+(x)$. Minimality of $\mathfrak q$ over the latter ideal makes it a minimal support prime of $\overline L$.

Here is the needed minimal-support fact. For a finite module $N$ over a Noetherian ring and a minimal support prime $\mathfrak q$, the localization $N_{\mathfrak q}$ is nonzero and supported only at the maximal ideal of $R_{\mathfrak q}$. The radical of its annihilator is that maximal ideal; finite generation makes a power annihilate the module. A last nonzero power layer therefore contains a nonzero element killed by the maximal ideal. Represent it by $z/1$, rescaling a fraction by a unit if necessary. For a finite list of generators of $\mathfrak q$, clear denominators in the equations saying they kill $z/1$. Multiplying $z$ by the product of those denominators gives $z'\in N$ with $\mathfrak qz'=0$ and $z'_{\mathfrak q}\ne0$. No element outside $\mathfrak q$ can annihilate it. Thus $\operatorname{Ann}(z')=\mathfrak q$, proving that $\mathfrak q$ is associated.

Apply this to $\overline L$. An element with annihilator $\mathfrak q$ retains that annihilator under the displayed inclusion into $M/x^nM$, proving the assertion. The exponent cannot in general be replaced by $1$; the Artin–Rees choice is part of the argument. ∎

#### Support under quotients and exact sequences

For an arbitrary ring $R$ and module $M$:

1. If $M$ is finite, then $\operatorname{Supp}(M/IM)=\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(I)$ for every ideal $I$.
2. A submodule or quotient of $M$ has support contained in $\operatorname{Supp}M$.
3. An exact sequence $0\to N\to M\to Q\to0$ gives $\operatorname{Supp}M=\operatorname{Supp}N\cup\operatorname{Supp}Q$.

**Proof.** Localization is exact, so the last two assertions follow by checking whether each localized module is zero. For (1), if $I$ contains an element outside $\mathfrak p$, then $I_{\mathfrak p}=R_{\mathfrak p}$ and the quotient localization is zero. If $I\subset\mathfrak p$, Nakayama for the finite $R_{\mathfrak p}$-module $M_{\mathfrak p}$ says
$$M_{\mathfrak p}/I_{\mathfrak p}M_{\mathfrak p}=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M_{\mathfrak p}=0.$$
This proves exactly the claimed intersection formula. Finiteness is used only for (1); the other support rules apply to all modules. ∎

#### Cohen–Macaulayness under a quotient of local rings

Let $R\to S$ be a surjection of Noetherian local rings and $N$ a finite $S$-module. Then $N$ is CM over $R$ if and only if it is CM over $S$.

**Proof.** Every sequence in the maximal ideal of $R$ acts on $N$ through its image in the maximal ideal of $S$. Its successive quotient modules and multiplication maps are unchanged. Conversely, any sequence from the latter maximal ideal lifts to the former. Thus the possible regular-sequence lengths, and hence depths, agree.

The support of $N$ over $R$ lies in the closed subset defined by $\ker(R\to S)$. The quotient correspondence identifies this support homeomorphically with its support over $S$, preserving all strict prime chains and therefore its dimension. Equality of depth and support dimension is consequently the same over either ring. The zero module is CM under both conventions as well. ∎

#### Permuting a regular sequence

If $M$ is a finite module over a Noetherian local ring and $x_1,\ldots,x_c$ is $M$-regular, every permutation is $M$-regular. Here regularity includes a nonzero final quotient.

**Proof.** It suffices to interchange adjacent entries. On the quotient by the entries preceding them, write the pair as $x,y$ and the finite module as $L$. Both elements belong to the maximal ideal, since the final regular quotient is nonzero.

Let $K=\ker(y\colon L\to L)$. Injectivity of $y$ modulo $x$ makes every $z\in K$ equal to $xz'$ for some $z'\in L$. Since $x$ is injective on $L$, the equality $0=yz=xyz'$ implies $yz'=0$. Thus $K=xK$. The module $K$ is finite by Noetherianity, so Nakayama gives $K=0$. Hence $y$ is injective on $L$.

If $xz=yw$, reduce modulo $x$. Injectivity of $y$ on $L/xL$ gives $w=xw'$; cancellation of $x$ then yields $z=yw'$. Thus $x$ is injective on $L/yL$. The final quotient by $(x,y)$ has not changed, so it is nonzero, and the subsequent entries act on the same quotient modules. This swaps the adjacent pair. Adjacent transpositions generate all permutations, proving the result. ∎

#### An equation good for a chosen maximal regular sequence

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $M\ne0$ be finite and CM, and put $d=\dim\operatorname{Supp}M>0$. Fix an $M$-regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_d$. Call $g\in\mathfrak m$ good for this data if
$$\dim\bigl(\operatorname{Supp}M\cap V(g,f_1,\ldots,f_i)\bigr)
=d-i-1\qquad(0\leq i<d).$$
Then $g$ is injective on $M$, and $M/gM$ is CM with maximal regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_{d-1}$.

**Proof.** The full good-element induction occurs inside the second proof of the [CM equation lemma](#native-algebra-lemma-cm-one-g). The support quotient formula identifies the definition here with the one used there. For clarity, its induction proceeds as follows.

When $d=1$, the kernel of $g$ is supported at the maximal ideal and has finite length. Multiplication by $f_1$ is injective on it, hence surjective by equality of lengths, and Nakayama kills the kernel. The nonzero quotient $M/gM$ has dimension zero and is CM.

For $d>1$, the good-element identities with $i\geq1$ give the same hypothesis on $M/f_1M$ and the list $f_2,\ldots,f_d$. That quotient is CM of dimension $d-1$ by the regular-element depth and dimension formulas. Induction makes $g$ injective there and makes $f_2,\ldots,f_{d-1}$ regular on $M/(f_1,g)M$. Thus $f_1,g$ is a regular pair on $M$. The preceding permutation argument changes its order, giving injectivity of $g$ on $M$ and of $f_1$ on $M/gM$. The remaining list is then regular as well. The $i=0$ good-element identity and the support quotient formula give dimension $d-1$ to $M/gM$, so this length-$d-1$ list is maximal and the quotient is CM. Nakayama keeps each required final quotient nonzero. ∎

#### Finite global dimension and uniform regular dimension

Let $R\ne0$ be Noetherian and let $n\geq0$ be an integer. The following conditions are equivalent:

1. The global dimension of $R$, over all modules, is $n$.
2. Every prime localization is regular local and $\dim R=n$.
3. Every maximal localization is regular local of dimension at most $n$, and one has dimension $n$.
4. Every prime localization is regular local of dimension at most $n$, and one has dimension $n$.

**Proof.** We first establish the uniform local criterion
$$\operatorname{gl.dim}R\leq n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{gl.dim}R_{\mathfrak m}\leq n
\text{ for every maximal }\mathfrak m.$$
One direction holds because localization preserves projective resolutions. Any $R_{\mathfrak m}$-module can be regarded as an $R$-module, and localizing it returns the same module.

For the converse, begin with a finite $R$-module $M$. If $n>0$, choose $n$ finite free terms of a resolution and write its last kernel as $K_n$:
$$0\longrightarrow K_n\longrightarrow F_{n-1}
\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow F_0
\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0.$$
Noetherianity makes $K_n$ finite and finitely presented. The local bound and [independence of the last syzygy](#native-algebra-lemma-independent-resolution) make every $(K_n)_{\mathfrak m}$ projective. The complete [finite-projectivity criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-finite-projective) makes $K_n$ projective over $R$. Thus $\operatorname{pd}_R M\leq n$. For $n=0$, apply that same projectivity criterion directly to $M$, since each $M_{\mathfrak m}$ is projective.

This bounds in particular every cyclic module $R/I$. The full cyclic-module criterion, including its transfinite proof, then bounds the projective dimension of every module, with no finite-generation assumption. This proves the uniform local criterion.

The complete [local homological characterization](#native-algebra-proposition-finite-gl-dim-regular) says that a Noetherian local ring of finite global dimension is regular, and its global dimension equals its Krull dimension. Applying the uniform criterion for every integer bound gives
$$\operatorname{gl.dim}R
=\sup_{\mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}\operatorname{gl.dim}R_{\mathfrak m}.$$
This equality includes the value infinity. Also
$$\dim R=\sup_{\mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}\dim R_{\mathfrak m}
=\sup_{\mathfrak p\text{ prime}}\dim R_{\mathfrak p},$$
because every finite prime chain lies below a maximal ideal and localization preserves that chain. Finite integer suprema of these nonempty sets are attained.

Now (1) gives regularity at every prime by localization and the local characterization; the two suprema give (2)–(4). Conversely, (3) and the local characterization give global dimension at most $n$, while the indicated maximal localization gives the reverse inequality. Condition (4) gives the same upper bound and its indicated prime localization gives the lower bound. Condition (2) implies (4) by the dimension supremum. All four conditions are therefore equivalent. A regular Noetherian ring of unbounded dimension does not satisfy these finite conditions. ∎

#### Global generators of a polynomial maximal ideal

Let $P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, where $k$ is any field, and let $\mathfrak m$ be maximal. There are $n$ polynomials generating $\mathfrak m$ in $P$ itself. The local ring $P_{\mathfrak m}$ is regular of dimension $n$.

**Proof.** By the complete [Nullstellensatz](#native-algebra-theorem-nullstellensatz), $E=P/\mathfrak m$ is a finite extension of $k$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the image of $x_i$, and set
$$E_i=k(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_i),\qquad E_0=k.$$
The [algebraic intermediate-ring argument](#uncovered-fields-lemma-subalgebra-algebraic-extension-field) gives $E_i=k[\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_i]$. Thus every coefficient of the monic minimal polynomial of $\alpha_i$ over $E_{i-1}$ lifts to a polynomial in the preceding variables. Choose such lifts, keeping the leading coefficient equal to $1$, and call the resulting polynomial in $x_i$ $f_i$.

Inductively, quotienting by $f_1,\ldots,f_i$ gives
$$k[x_1,\ldots,x_i]/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)\cong E_i.$$
Indeed, after the preceding quotient, the new equation is exactly the minimal polynomial of $\alpha_i$ over the field $E_{i-1}$. At $i=n$ the quotient is $E$ with its specified images of all variables, so its kernel is precisely $\mathfrak m$. Hence $\mathfrak m=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ globally.

Moreover,
$$P/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)\cong E_i[x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n].$$
These quotients are domains. Their kernels form a strict prime chain of length $n$ ending at $\mathfrak m$: at each step a nonconstant monic polynomial in the next variable becomes zero. The same chain survives in $P_{\mathfrak m}$, giving dimension at least $n$. The full [local dimension and parameter theorem](#native-algebra-proposition-dimension) bounds dimension by the number of maximal-ideal generators, here at most $n$. Dimension and embedding dimension are therefore both $n$, which is regularity. This argument includes inseparable residue extensions. For $n=0$, $P=k$, the maximal ideal is generated by the empty list and the dimension is zero. ∎

#### Internal graded Ext: shifts, exact sequences and comparison

Let $S$ be a graded ring and let $M,N$ be graded $S$-modules. Write $M(a)_j=M_{j+a}$. A map of internal degree $b$ sends $M_j$ into $N_{j+b}$; write its group as $\operatorname{GrHom}_b(M,N)$ and take the direct sum over $b$ for $\operatorname{GrHom}(M,N)$. Choose a resolution $L_\bullet\to M$ by direct sums of twists of $S$, with differentials of degree zero, and define
$$\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N)
=\bigoplus_{b\in\mathbf Z}
H^q\bigl(\operatorname{GrHom}_b(L_\bullet,N)\bigr).$$
For homogeneous $s\in S_d$, multiplication on the target sends a degree-$b$ map to a degree-$(b+d)$ map. This defines the graded $S$-module structure.

The six properties are as follows.

1. $\operatorname{GrExt}^0_S(M,N)=\operatorname{GrHom}(M,N)$.
2. For every integer $a$ and every $q\geq0$,
   $$\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M(a),N)
   \cong\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N(-a))
   \cong\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N)(-a).$$
3. An exact sequence $0\to N_1\to N_2\to N_3\to0$ gives the graded long exact sequence
   $$\cdots\longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N_1)
   \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N_2)
   \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N_3)
   \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^{q+1}_S(M,N_1)
   \longrightarrow\cdots.$$
4. An exact sequence $0\to M_1\to M_2\to M_3\to0$ gives the sequence with reversed first-variable order,
   $$\cdots\longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M_3,N)
   \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M_2,N)
   \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M_1,N)
   \longrightarrow\operatorname{GrExt}^{q+1}_S(M_3,N)
   \longrightarrow\cdots.$$
5. If $S$ is Noetherian and $M$ is finite, the natural map
   $$\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^q_S(M,N)$$
   is an isomorphism after forgetting the grading. If $N$ is finite as well, these modules are finite.
6. For $S=K[t_0,\ldots,t_r]$ over a field and finite $M$,
   $$\operatorname{GrExt}^q_S(M,N)=0\qquad(q>r+1).$$

**Proof.** First justify the resolution construction. Kernels and cokernels of degree-zero maps are computed in each degree, so graded modules form an abelian category. A degree-zero map from a direct sum of twists lifts through a surjection: lift the image of each homogeneous basis element in its specified degree. Such sums are therefore projective. Taking one basis element for each homogeneous generator gives a graded free surjection onto any module. Repeating on its graded kernel produces a resolution. Over a Noetherian ring, a finite module admits one with finitely many basis elements in each resolution term, since each kernel is finite and its homogeneous components generate it.

A map of modules lifts to their resolutions inductively: the image required at the next degree lies in a kernel, the following differential surjects onto that kernel, and projectivity gives the lift. If two chain maps lift the same map, their difference in degree zero lifts through the first differential. After this first homotopy term is chosen, subtract its contribution; at the next degree the remaining difference again lies in the next kernel. Induction gives a homotopy in every degree. All these choices take place among maps of degree zero. Thus the resulting Ext functors and comparison maps are independent of the chosen resolution and are functorial.

For (1), the degree-zero cohomology kernel consists exactly of maps $L_0\to N$ that kill the image of $L_1$. These are maps from $M$, in each internal degree.

For (2), twist the entire resolution by $a$. Its Hom groups satisfy
$$\operatorname{GrHom}_b(L_i(a),N)
=\operatorname{GrHom}_{b-a}(L_i,N)
=\operatorname{GrHom}_b(L_i,N(-a)).$$
These identifications commute with the cochain differentials. Taking cohomology and assembling the degrees gives precisely the indicated negative shift.

For (3), each $\operatorname{GrHom}_b(L_i,-)$ preserves the short exact sequence, by graded projectivity with the corresponding target twist. The connecting map on cohomology is obtained by lifting a cocycle to the middle complex and taking its differential in the first complex. A change of lift changes it by a boundary. This gives the long exact sequence in each internal degree; direct sums are exact, and multiplication by homogeneous elements commutes with the construction. The resulting sequence is one of graded modules with maps of degree zero.

For (4), construct compatible resolutions of the three modules. Choose graded free surjections $L^1_0\to M_1$ and $L^3_0\to M_3$, and lift the latter map to $M_2$. Their direct sum surjects onto $M_2$. Its kernel fits into an exact sequence between the other two kernels: surjectivity on the right follows by correcting a lift by an element of $L^1_0$. Repeat this construction on the kernels. It produces a short exact sequence of resolutions
$$0\longrightarrow L^1_\bullet\longrightarrow L^2_\bullet
\longrightarrow L^3_\bullet\longrightarrow0$$
that splits in every degree. Applying $\operatorname{GrHom}_b(-,N)$ therefore gives a short exact sequence of cochain complexes in the reverse order. The same cocycle-lifting construction gives (4), with the stated variance. Resolution comparison and homotopy show that these are the natural connecting maps.

For (5), use a resolution finite graded free in every degree. An ungraded homomorphism from one such term is a finite sum of homogeneous maps: the images of finitely many homogeneous basis elements have only finitely many homogeneous components in total. Thus
$$\operatorname{GrHom}(L_i,N)=\operatorname{Hom}_S(L_i,N)$$
as ungraded modules for every $i$. This is an isomorphism of cochain complexes. Cohomology commutes with the direct sum over internal degrees because the differentials preserve those degrees, proving the comparison. When $N$ is finite, each Hom term is finite; its kernels and their quotients are finite by Noetherianity. Finally the complete [polynomial global-dimension proof](#native-algebra-proposition-finite-gl-dim-polynomial-ring) bounds ordinary Ext by $r+1$. Applying (5) proves (6).

*Historical context.* FAC, Chapter III, §4, no. 68, pp. 261–262, uses this internal Hom and Ext convention; agreement with ordinary Hom and Ext requires the stated finiteness boundary. The contravariant sequence and finiteness are inputs to the duality calculations in no. 72, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2, pp. 265–267. The twist by $S(-r-1)$ in §5, no. 77, p. 271, changes internal degree according to (2) and leaves cohomological degree unchanged. These observations preserve the graded meaning of the Hilbert-syzygy bound used there. ∎

#### Component dimension and closed specializations

Let $S$ be a finite-type algebra over a field $k$, let $\mathfrak p$ be prime, and let $x\in X=\operatorname{Spec}S$ be its point. Then
$$\dim_xX
=\max_{\substack{Z\text{ an irreducible component}\\x\in Z}}\dim Z
=\min_{\substack{\mathfrak m\supset\mathfrak p\\\mathfrak m\text{ maximal}}}
\dim S_{\mathfrak m}.$$

**Proof.** The full [dimension-at-a-point proof](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-at-a-point-finite-type-field) establishes the first equality, including that every nonempty open in a finite-type integral component has its full dimension. We prove the closed-specialization equality explicitly.

Write the finitely many irreducible components of $X$ as $Z_1,\ldots,Z_s$. Let $J$ index those containing $x$, and put
$$d=\max_{j\in J}\dim Z_j,\qquad
T=\bigcup_{j\notin J}Z_j,\qquad U=X\setminus T.$$
If a closed point $y$ corresponds to $\mathfrak m\supset\mathfrak p$, every $Z_j$ with $j\in J$ contains $y$: closed sets contain all specializations of their points. The first equality applied at $y$, together with the [closed-point dimension formula](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-dimension-closed-point-finite-type-field), therefore gives $\dim S_{\mathfrak m}\geq d$.

The subset $V(\mathfrak p)\cap U$ is a nonempty open in $V(\mathfrak p)$, since it contains $x$. The complete [Jacobson argument](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-finite-type-field-jacobson) makes the closed points of $X$ dense in this closed subset. Choose one such $y$ in $V(\mathfrak p)\cap U$. It lies in every component indexed by $J$ and in none of the others. Consequently the same two dimension formulas give $\dim S_{\mathfrak m}=d$ at this particular closed specialization. The lower bound is attained, proving the minimum equality. No irreducibility or reducedness of $S$ was imposed. ∎

#### Maximal chains in a finite-type field domain

If $S$ is a finite-type integral domain over a field, every maximal prime chain in $S$ has length $\dim S$. In particular,
$$\dim S_{\mathfrak m}=\dim S$$
for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.

**Proof.** Present $S=P/\mathfrak q$ for $P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $\mathfrak q$ prime. A maximal chain in $S$ starts at its zero ideal, ends at a maximal ideal, and is saturated between its endpoints. The corresponding chain in $P$ starts at $\mathfrak q$ and ends at a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$. The complete [polynomial prime-chain theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-height-polynomial-ring) gives its length as
$$\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak n-\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q
=n-\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q,$$
using the preceding [polynomial maximal-ideal calculation](#uncovered-algebra-lemma-dim-affine-space). This number is independent of the endpoint and the saturated chain. Finite dimension ensures that a finite chain extends to such a maximal chain. Hence it is the dimension of $S$. Chains below a specified maximal ideal give the same number after localization, proving the local equality as well. ∎

#### Regular local presentations of a complete intersection

For surjective homomorphisms of local rings $P\to T\to S$ with $P,T$ regular local, the following four conditions are equivalent:

1. The kernel of $P\to S$ is generated by a regular sequence.
2. That kernel has a generating list of length $\dim P-\dim S$.
3. The kernel of $T\to S$ is generated by a regular sequence.
4. That kernel has a generating list of length $\dim T-\dim S$.

The complete proof is the first comparison in [Five local complete-intersection criteria](#native-algebra-lemma-lci-local). It uses the CM parameter criterion in both regular local rings, then the parameter generators of $\ker(P\to T)$. One direction lifts generators; the reverse induction removes a parameter whose class remains nonzero in the larger kernel modulo the maximal ideal. This argument has no ground-field assumption.

The native source locator for this result is `algebra.tex`, `lemma-ci-well-defined`.

#### Extending a local-ring isomorphism to principal neighborhoods

Let $A,B$ be finitely presented algebras over a ring $Q$, and suppose a $Q$-algebra isomorphism $A_{\mathfrak a}\cong B_{\mathfrak b}$ is given. There are $t\in A\setminus\mathfrak a$ and $s\in B\setminus\mathfrak b$ such that this isomorphism is induced by $A_t\cong B_s$.

The complete proof is the second comparison in [Five local complete-intersection criteria](#native-algebra-lemma-lci-local), beginning with a finitely presented map that induces a local isomorphism. After finite denominator clearing, evaluation gives a retraction. Its finitely generated kernel is generated by an explicitly constructed idempotent, which isolates the required component. The final paragraph spreads the given map from finite generators and relations and applies that splitting; it works over an arbitrary common base $Q$.

The native source locator is `algebra.tex`, `lemma-isomorphic-local-rings`.

#### Local dimension at a quasi-finite point

Let $R\to S$ be finite type, and let $\mathfrak q$ lie over $\mathfrak p$. If the map is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$, then
$$\dim S_{\mathfrak q}\leq\dim R_{\mathfrak p}.$$
The base ring may be non-Noetherian.

**Proof.** We use the complete [algebraic Zariski Main theorem](#native-algebra-theorem-main-theorem). Write $B$ for the integral closure of the image of $R$ in $S$. The theorem gives $g\in B\setminus\mathfrak q$ with $B_g=S_g$. Choose finite algebra generators of $S_g/R$ and express them as fractions with numerators $b_1,\ldots,b_t\in B$ and denominators powers of $g$. Then
$$C=R[g,b_1,\ldots,b_t]\subset S$$
means the subalgebra generated by the image of $R$ and the listed elements. It is finite over $R$, by the complete [integral finite-type criterion](#native-algebra-lemma-characterize-finite-in-terms-of-integral). Localization of the inclusion is injective, and the chosen generators make it surjective onto $S_g$. Thus $C_g=S_g$.

For $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak q\cap C$ this gives $C_{\mathfrak r}=S_{\mathfrak q}$. Any finite strict prime chain in $C$ below $\mathfrak r$ contracts to a strict chain in $R$ below $\mathfrak p$, by the full [incomparability argument for integral maps](#native-algebra-lemma-integral-dim-up). The corresponding localized chain has no greater length than $\dim R_{\mathfrak p}$. Taking the supremum proves the inequality, including infinite dimensions.

The original local-base route gives the same conclusion: after replacing $R$ by $R_{\mathfrak p}$, Zariski Main identifies $S_{\mathfrak q}$ with a localization of its integral closure over that base; incomparability bounds the dimension of the integral closure itself by $\dim R_{\mathfrak p}$. If $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is Noetherian, the [local dimension formula](#native-algebra-lemma-dimension-base-fibre-total) instead gives the inequality immediately, because the local fibre at a quasi-finite point has dimension zero. Both routes apply at their stated scopes. ∎

#### Openness of the quasi-finite locus

For a finite-type ring map $R\to S$, the primes where the map is quasi-finite form an open subset of $\operatorname{Spec}S$.

**Proof.** At any such prime $\mathfrak q$, the finite-algebra construction in the preceding proof gives $g\notin\mathfrak q$ and a finite $R$-algebra $C\subset S$ with $C_g=S_g$. For any base prime $\mathfrak p'$, the fibre
$$C\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p')$$
is a finite-dimensional algebra over the residue field. Its localization at $g$ is again finite dimensional: every element of a finite-dimensional algebra is algebraic, and the inverse of an invertible algebraic element is a polynomial in it. Equivalently, the localization is a quotient of this Artinian algebra by the factors where $g$ is nilpotent.

Every local ring in that fibre therefore has dimension zero, with residue field finite over $\kappa(\mathfrak p')$. These are the quasi-finiteness conditions at its points. Since $S_g=C_g$, they hold at every point of $D(g)\subset\operatorname{Spec}S$. This supplies an open quasi-finite neighborhood of each originally chosen point, proving the claim. No Noetherian hypothesis on $R$ is needed. ∎

#### Lifting a nonzerodivisor from the closed fibre

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)$ be a flat local map of Noetherian local rings. If the image of $f\in S$ is a nonzerodivisor on $S/\mathfrak mS$, then multiplication by $f$ on $S$ is injective and $S/fS$ is flat over $R$.

**Proof.** Apply the complete [fibrewise injectivity theorem](#native-algebra-lemma-mod-injective) to
$$u\colon S\longrightarrow S,\qquad s\longmapsto fs.$$
Its source is finite over the Noetherian local target ring $S$, its target module is $R$-flat, and its residue map is injective by hypothesis. The theorem proves both injectivity of $u$ and flatness of its cokernel. Its full proof lifts injectivity through all powers, uses Krull intersection, and repeats the argument after every ideal quotient to obtain the Tor flatness test. Thus both conclusions follow at exactly the required scope. If $f$ is a unit, the map is an isomorphism and its zero cokernel is flat directly. ∎

#### Finitely many algebraic field generators

If $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n$ in an extension field are algebraic over $k$, then $k(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ has finite degree over $k$.

**Proof by adjoining the generators.** Put $E_0=k$ and $E_i=E_{i-1}(\alpha_i)$. The element $\alpha_i$ remains algebraic over $E_{i-1}$, and its monic minimal polynomial of degree $d_i$ gives the basis
$$1,\alpha_i,\ldots,\alpha_i^{d_i-1}$$
over $E_{i-1}$. Spanning is polynomial division, together with the fact that the polynomial quotient by the minimal polynomial is a field; independence is the minimality of its degree. Products of successive basis elements give a basis for the tower: expand coefficients in the earlier basis to prove spanning, and group by the last basis to prove independence. Hence
$$[E_n:k]=\prod_{i=1}^n d_i<\infty.$$
For the empty list the degree is $1$.

**Integral-algebra proof.** Choose a monic equation of degree $e_i$ over $k$ for each $\alpha_i$. Reducing powers in each variable shows that the finitely many monomials
$$\alpha_1^{a_1}\cdots\alpha_n^{a_n},
\qquad 0\leq a_i<e_i,$$
span $A=k[\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n]$ over $k$. For any $0\ne a\in A$, multiplication by $a$ is injective on this finite-dimensional vector space, since it lies in a field. It is therefore surjective and sends some element to $1$. Thus $A$ is a field, equals $E_n$, and is finite over $k$. This also supplies the finite-integral-algebra deduction used in the prerequisite statement. ∎

#### Composing specialization-lifting maps

For continuous maps $X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z$, if specializations lift along both maps, they lift along $gf$. The same assertion holds for generalizations. Here $u\leadsto v$ means $v\in\overline{\{u\}}$.

**Proof.** Given $x\in X$ and a specialization $gf(x)\leadsto z$, first lift along $g$ to obtain $f(x)\leadsto y$ with $g(y)=z$. Then lift along $f$ to obtain $x\leadsto x'$ with $f(x')=y$. The composite image of $x'$ is $z$, as required.

For generalizations, start instead with $z'\leadsto gf(x)$. Lift this along $g$ to $y'\leadsto f(x)$ with $g(y')=z'$, and then along $f$ to $x'\leadsto x$ with $f(x')=y'$. Again $gf(x')=z'$. Thus the assertion holds in both directions of the specialization relation. ∎

#### Images of sets stable under specialization

If specializations lift along a continuous map $f\colon X\to Y$, the image of any specialization-stable subset of $X$ is specialization-stable in $Y$. If generalizations lift, the corresponding assertion holds for generalization-stable subsets.

**Proof.** Let $T$ be specialization-stable, choose $x\in T$, and suppose $f(x)\leadsto y$. A lift gives $x\leadsto x'$ with $f(x')=y$. Stability puts $x'$ in $T$, hence $y$ in $f(T)$.

For the other assertion, let $T$ be generalization-stable and take $y'\leadsto f(x)$ with $x\in T$. Lift to $x'\leadsto x$ with $f(x')=y'$. This time stability under generalization gives $x'\in T$, again proving that the required point belongs to the image. ∎

#### Replacing a filtered category by a directed set

Let $\mathcal I$ be a filtered index category, with a set of objects and arrows. There is a directed partially ordered set $D$ and a functor $u\colon D\to\mathcal I$ such that:

1. For every diagram $M\colon\mathcal I\to\mathcal C$, if $\varinjlim_{d\in D}M(u(d))$ exists, then $\varinjlim_{\mathcal I}M$ exists and the canonical map between them is an isomorphism.
2. For every diagram $N\colon\mathcal I^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal C$, if the restricted inverse limit over $D^{\mathrm{op}}$ exists, then the inverse limit over $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{op}}$ exists and restriction is an isomorphism.

**Proof.** We retain an explicit construction of $D$. Put $\mathcal J=\mathcal I\times\mathbf N$, with a unique arrow $a\to b$ in the second factor whenever $a\leq b$. The category $\mathcal J$ is filtered: choose a common target in $\mathcal I$ and a sufficiently large integer for two objects, and equalize parallel arrows in $\mathcal I$, increasing the integer if needed.

The projection $\pi\colon\mathcal J\to\mathcal I$ is cofinal in the sense of the [cofinality theorem](#uncovered-categories-lemma-cofinal). Indeed, for any $i\in\mathcal I$, the category of arrows $i\to\pi(j)$ has the initial object given by the identity into $(i,0)$. It is therefore nonempty and connected.

Call a subcategory finitely generated if finitely many arrows, including identities for its objects as needed, generate all its arrows by composition.
